title: Neutral Baselines and Neighbor Guarantees for Data Centers
one_liner: A neutral third party installs pre-construction sensors around proposed data centers and administers a developer-funded, automatic payout guarantee to neighbors, so permit fights run on evidence.
customer: Independent and mid-size data center developers seeking 50-500 MW campus approvals in contested counties. County commissions and state regulators are a second buyer because they can make the service a permit condition. Hyperscalers with in-house community teams are not the target.
problem: Permit fights are evidence-poor. Nobody has a pre-construction baseline of well levels, night-time noise, air quality or voltage at homes, so every later complaint about dry wells or a hum can be neither proven nor disproven. Both sides fight on feelings and lawyers. Politics has turned: New York paused environmental permits for data centers of 50 MW or more in July 2026, Texas ordered its environmental regulator to stop issuing new data center permits in September 2026, and local pauses now exist in at least 14 states. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found only 14% of Americans would welcome one nearby.
solution: Baseline-in-a-Box. Over 60-90 days before the application, deploy 30-60 low-cost sensors: property-line night noise, depth and conductivity in volunteer neighbors' wells, PM2.5, night-sky brightness, and voltage sag at homes. Publish a read-only public dashboard. Have a university extension hydrogeologist and an acoustician review the methods. Escrow the data with hash-anchored timestamps so neither side can edit it. Keep monitoring for 10 years. Then add a Neighbor Guarantee: a developer-funded escrow that pays affected households automatically, like parametric crop insurance, when verified well drawdown or noise exceedances occur. No lawsuit is needed.
why_now: In 2026 the moratorium movement jumped from town boards to governors' offices (New York's executive order of July 14, Texas's TCEQ permit halt of September 21). Developers now need social license as much as megawatts, and regulators are actively drafting the frameworks that will say what evidence counts.
revenue_model: The developer pays $75-150k per site for setup, $4-10k per month for monitoring, and an 8-10% administration fee on the guarantee escrow. Counties that write the service into permit conditions create repeat demand. Later, anonymized data licensing to regulators and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The baseline protects the developer more than the opponents. It is the only defense against future exaggerated or mistaken claims, and it turns 'trust us' into 'audit us'. Parametric payouts replace adversarial claims, which is why a rational developer buys it from a neutral party rather than opposing it.
first_30_days: Pick one county with a pending rezoning hearing (Georgia, Virginia, Indiana, Pennsylvania or Texas). Offer the developer's land agent a free 30-day pilot on 10 neighbor wells with an agricultural-extension partner. Build nodes from off-the-shelf parts at about $1.5-3k each. Present the live dashboard at the public hearing and convert that developer to a paid contract. Use the result as the case study for the next 5 developers.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: KETOS (SHIELD / KELP data-center water monitoring), Aethair (Aethair PRO, Environet, Thiamis), Envirosuite (ASX:EVS), Kunak. White space: Nobody found sells the bundle, so the status is 'gap' and not 'open'. The sensor and baseline layer is not open: KETOS (about $45M raised) pitches an independent baseline for data centers, Aethair pitches pre-construction baselines, Envirosuite has community dashboards, and consultancies bundle baselines into permitting. The unserved wedge is what sits on top of the sensors. (1) A neutral administrator holding escrowed, tamper-evident data whose governance the county and community accept, unlike developer-hired consultants and unlike opposition-side groups such as CEDS. (2) The Neighbor Guarantee: an automatic, no-litigation payout to households from a developer-funded escrow when a pre-agreed trigger is hit. No vendor, insurer, county ordinance or developer program found does this. The nearest things are Franklin County, Indiana's draft rule (escrow for 24-hour emergency potable water to impacted neighbors, plus developer-funded monitoring wells), one-off buyouts and lump-sum checks. (3) A 10-year, multi-parameter (wells, noise, PM2.5, voltage) record packaged as a permit-condition template that regulators can adopt. Weak points: the sensor baseline will commoditize; attribution is hard, because well drawdown from drought or other pumping is indistinguishable from data-center drawdown unless the design uses upgradient control wells and pumping records; automatic payouts may look like insurance under state law; and developer counsel may resist a pre-committed payout as an admission of liability. Note: the web-search budget ran out before I could check Crunchbase/YC directly for a startup doing exactly the escrow-plus-parametric bundle, so 'nobody found' means no evidence in about 25 searches, not proof of absence.

title: Interim Smoke-Damage Protocol Before the State Standard
one_liner: Publish and run the defensible smoke, ash and soot assessment protocol that California insurers, adjusters and lawyers will need on January 1, 2027, because the official technical standard will not exist until 2028-2029.
customer: California carriers, the FAIR Plan and their TPAs (for AB 1795's 30-day inspection and testing obligations), plus public adjusters, policyholder attorneys, and escrow, lender and buyer parties in standing-home sales. Homeowners pay via their insurer, PA or directly.
problem: California signed AB 1795 and AB 1642 on Sept 15, 2026. From Jan 1, 2027, insurers must inspect within 30 days, pay for necessary testing, keep paying ALE until restoration, and face a presumption that ash, soot and char in a standing home are fire-caused. But the state toxics department will not finish lead and asbestos standards until end of 2028 and other contaminant standards until 2029. Meanwhile tens of thousands of claims will need a protocol that survives litigation; existing vendor assessments are already accused of being substandard, and capacity of qualified industrial hygienists is scarce and expensive.
solution: An independent, openly published interim assessment protocol built on existing standards (IICRC S700, established sampling and lab methods, EPA/HUD dust-wipe criteria), developed with certified industrial hygienists and a toxicologist. Delivered as a product: a sampling-plan generator (which rooms, surfaces and ducts, how many samples), a trained technician network with kits and a chain-of-custody app, remote IH sign-off, a lab partner, a compliance-clock dashboard for carriers, and a 'smoke clearance certificate' for resale and escrow. Priced at a fraction of full CIH scopes.
why_now: The laws were signed two weeks ago with an effective date of Jan 1, 2027, LA County is investigating Farmers over Eaton/Palisades claim denials, a proposed class action targets vendor assessments, and carriers oppose but must comply. The gap between the compliance date and the state standard is a 2-3 year window in which the best-documented protocol becomes the de facto reference, and other fire states (Colorado, Oregon, Hawaii) are watching.
revenue_model: Per-home assessment of $1,800-$4,500 (paid by insurer under AB 1795 or the policyholder), $500 clearance-certificate add-on, lab pass-through margin, SaaS compliance dashboard for carriers at $2-$5 per claim per month, and training and certification fees for restoration technicians.
non_obvious_insight: In smoke disputes the lab is rarely the fight; the fight is the sampling design and the pass/fail threshold. Carriers whose vendors sample five spots and compare against urban background dust get 'clean' results by construction. Whoever publishes a transparent, replicable sampling grid with chain of custody writes the eventual standard, because regulators borrow the protocol with the most field data.
first_30_days: Recruit two CIHs and one toxicologist as an advisory board and draft 'Interim Smoke Assessment Protocol v0.1' for public comment. Train 6-10 IICRC-certified restoration technicians and buy sampling kits. Sell 20 pilot assessments in Altadena and Palisades at a subsidized $950 through public adjusters and attorneys, gathering data and case studies. Pitch 3 carriers and 2 TPAs on 30-day compliance capacity before January 1, offering a pilot at cost in exchange for using the protocol.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hygiene Technologies International (HygieneTech), Rimkus, Safeguard EnviroGroup (Brad Kovar), EHS Analytical Solutions. White space: Mostly assessment supply and free guidance are crowded, so the raw 'do smoke testing' and 'publish a protocol' layers are not white space. Dozens of CIH-led firms sell $2k-$4k+ assessments and clearance certificates. AIHA, IICRC/RIA/CIRI, Purdue and EFRU already publish free or cheap protocols. Safeguard EnviroGroup is already pitching a 'defensible framework' to carriers. State agencies (AB 1795 drafts) planned to certify IHs, contractors and labs, which undercuts the training-fee line.

Still unserved: (1) Carrier and TPA operations under AB 1795. Nobody offers a claim-level compliance layer with the 30-day inspection clock, an audit-ready sampling plan mapped to zones, chain-of-custody records and an evidence file, sold as software. Carriers are 'technically opposed' but must comply from 1/1/2027, and CAT surge capacity is the pain. (2) Sampling-design defensibility. The fight is over how many samples, where, and against what background, and no independent tool scores a sampling plan or existing IH report for adequacy, though this is what class actions and the Purdue review turn on. (3) A neutral, versioned crosswalk from AIHA/IICRC/40 CFR 745.227 lead-dust levels and 8 CCR 1529 asbestos to a per-home plan, which updates when DTSC issues standards in 2028-29. (4) Pooled, structured sampling data across claims, which is what regulators reuse. EFRU holds only a few dozen homes.

Two facts weaken the 'vacuum' framing. Interim lead and asbestos thresholds already exist in AB 1642 (40 CFR 745.227(e)(8)(viii) and 8 CCR 1529). The vacuum is mainly sampling design and non-lead contaminants such as cyanide, other metals and dioxins.

Structural risks: the buyer conflict, because carriers may not adopt a protocol seen as policyholder-friendly and policyholder-side buyers want a testifying CIH rather than software. Remote IH sign-off and technician-collected samples may run into CIH and certification expectations. Any advantage is capped at the moment DTSC publishes standards.

Research limits: my web-search budget ran out before I could run Crunchbase, YC and TechCrunch-specific queries. The general startup searches (wildfire smoke assessment startup, chain-of-custody kits, technician network) found only wildfire-detection companies (Pano AI, FireScan, FireSafe AI), none in post-fire smoke-damage assessment. Treat 'no funded startup' as probable, not proven.

title: Phantom Load Vetting Desk for Rural Utilities
one_liner: A fee-based 'is this data center developer real?' diligence service for electric co-ops and municipal utilities drowning in 100-1,000 MW inquiries from shell LLCs.
customer: G&T and distribution electric cooperatives, municipal utilities and PUDs (5-person engineering staffs, no data center experience). Secondary: state economic development offices and county governments granting abatements. The utility or its G&T pays per inquiry or on retainer.
problem: Every small utility with transmission access is now getting inquiries for 200-1,000 MW campuses from LLCs formed 90 days ago. Each one eats study money, planning time and political capital, and a wrong bet strands ratepayer-funded infrastructure. Texas's proposed SB 6 rule (16 TAC 25.194, final rule due by end of 2026) would require $50,000/MW of financial security before a study and disclosure of duplicate requests. That pushes speculators into neighboring states and co-ops with softer tariffs. Small utilities have no way to tell a real project from a PowerPoint.
solution: A standardized 12-point 'physical reality' test built from paper trails that real projects leave and phantom ones cannot. (1) Air permit applications for generators, where the genset count implies the MW. (2) An OEM order acknowledgment or slot reservation for MV transformers and switchgear, plus a delivery date that fits the claimed energization date. (3) Recorded site control (deed or option). (4) Water and stormwater filings. (5) A named tenant LOI or offtaker. (6) A GC or EPC that has actually built a campus. (7) A financing letter. (8) Tax-abatement filings. (9) LLC principals cross-checked against other states' filings, to catch the same MW shopped to five utilities. (10) A power-density and cooling design consistent with the load ask. (11) Local land-use posture. (12) Team track record. The deliverable is a red/amber/green memo, a recommended security amount, and a milestone-gated study structure the utility can put in its ESA. Add-ons are a large-load tariff and ESA term-sheet template and a duplicate-request registry that co-ops in a region can pool.
why_now: Large-load tariffs and collateral rules are landing right now: Texas SB 6 (signed June 2025, PUCT rule proposed March 2026, final expected by 12/31/2026), plus AEP Ohio-style minimum-demand tariffs. Each new collateral regime displaces phantom load to the next-weakest utility. Transformer lead times of 3-5 years and switchgear sold out into 2028 mean that a real project without an equipment slot is not real, which gives a very cheap and reliable test. About half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or canceled, so utilities are burned and skeptical.
revenue_model: $7.5K-25K per inquiry vetting memo; $60K-150K/yr retainers for G&T co-ops that field 10+ inquiries a year; $25K-50K one-time tariff/ESA template packages; later a subscription to a multi-utility duplicate-request registry. Utilities can often pass the cost to the applicant as a study-deposit line item.
non_obvious_insight: Outsiders think the hard part of large-load planning is forecasting demand. Insiders know real projects are betrayed by equipment, not slides. A serious 300 MW developer has a transformer slot, a generator count on an air permit and a GC on payroll before the utility ever hears the name. A phantom has none of those. The tell is the logistics trail, and nobody at a 5-person co-op knows where to look. Texas's high collateral will also export the phantom problem to everyone else.
first_30_days: Build scrapers for state air-permit databases in 6-8 states and county deed/LLC records for 3 co-op service territories. Ask 3 co-op contacts (via state electric cooperative associations or a G&T's planning group) for their last 10 inquiries and run free back-tests on how they turned out. Publish a one-page '12 signs your data center inquiry is real' on LinkedIn and co-op association channels. Convert the first 2-3 into paid $7.5K memos on live inquiries and ask for a G&T retainer.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: GridUnity, Clean Power Research (PowerClerk), Enverus, LandGate. White space: I found no direct competitor. No startup, consultancy or association was selling a utility-side, per-inquiry 'is this developer physically real' memo with a recommended collateral amount and milestone-gated study structure. The gap is real but narrow.

What is unserved: (1) External physical-trail verification for small utilities, meaning air-permit generator counts vs claimed MW, recorded deeds and options, LLC principal cross-checks, and OEM or EPC evidence. GridUnity and PowerClerk track applicant-supplied data but do not verify it. Enverus, LandGate and GridCARE serve the developer side. (2) A cross-utility duplicate-request registry. Texas SB 6 mandates duplicate-request disclosure only inside ERCOT. Outside ERCOT there is no pooled registry. Developers do file the same project with several utilities (Latitude Media, Utility Dive). (3) Packaging for 5-person co-op engineering staffs: I found no NRECA vetting checklist or tool, and no small-utility-specific vendor.

Serious weaknesses the founder must address:
- Regulation and tariffs are substituting for vetting. Collateral, study fees and site-control mandates make the applicant self-prove. Exelon cut its estimates about 40% after stricter collateral. AEP Ohio's pipeline fell by more than half after study fees of up to $100K (https://techstartups.com/2026/09/01/ai-data-centers-request-700-gw-of-u-s-power-but-much-of-the-demand-may-be-an-illusion/). Once a co-op requires a deposit, site control and a signed LOI, much of the 12-point test becomes documents the applicant hands over.
- Texas SB 6 / 16 TAC 25.194 applies only in ERCOT (https://www.dlapiper.com/en-us/insights/publications/2026/03/texas-proposes-new-interconnection-standards-for-large-electric-loads). The 'small utilities in neighboring states get the displaced phantoms' claim is plausible but I found no evidence for it.
- Several tests may not be observable by an outsider. OEM order acknowledgments and financing letters are confidential, and real developers often approach the utility before ordering equipment.
- Regulators are absorbing the LLC-transparency piece. Texas ordered an audit requiring true-ownership disclosure, and Pennsylvania issued an August 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW.
- Big engineering consultancies could add this as a service line. I could not verify whether they already do. My web-search budget ran out before I could check.

title: Ground-Truth Diligence for GPU-Backed Lenders
one_liner: Independent-engineer-style diligence and monthly monitoring on the part of a data center build that satellites cannot see: the last 90 days before ready-for-service.
customer: Private credit funds, banks and ABS investors lending against GPUs and neocloud contracts; insurers underwriting delay risk; AI labs and enterprises signing take-or-pay capacity who need to know if the promised RFS date is credible.
problem: GPU-backed loans and offtake contracts are priced on a ready-for-service date. Satellite vendors (SynMax and Industrial Info Resources now cover 2,600+ projects weekly) can show steel, cooling towers and generator yards, but they cannot see the failure zone: utility permission to energize, MV switchgear energization, Level 4/5 commissioning and IST results, liquid-cooling flush and pressure tests, fiber-plant acceptance, OEM startup-tech availability. Percent complete on pay applications is front-loaded and misleading. Meanwhile GPUs costing millions per rack sit idle and depreciate while interest accrues, and lenders are capping neocloud exposure. Traditional IEs are power-plant-oriented, slow and expensive.
solution: A 'Readiness Ladder' of about 40 binary, evidence-backed milestones (utility energization letter, gear serials and bills of lading, Cx level sign-offs, IST pass/fail counts, CDU flush logs, open-punch burn-down rate, OEM startup-tech calendar). Score each project and re-score monthly. Output a probability of RFS by date and covenant or draw-release triggers. Staff it with a bench of ex-data-center PMs and Cx leads who do desk review plus quick site visits. Sell as a 2-week second-opinion product first, then monthly monitoring, integrating vendor satellite feeds as an input rather than competing with them.
why_now: Neocloud credit risk is now the topic. Lenders are capping exposure, deals are stalling on credit risk, and GPU-debt structures (including vendor backstops) are proliferating. Analyses show roughly 40% of AI data center sites with possible delays and about half of 2026 capacity slipping, while operators publicly deny it. Satellite monitoring has commoditized the exterior, which makes the interior truth the scarce and valuable part.
revenue_model: $25K fixed-fee 2-week second opinions; $40K-120K full pre-close diligence; $8K-20K/month per facility monitoring; optional success-based fee for delay-risk insurance placement. Adjacent product: retained RFS-credibility scoring for AI labs choosing between capacity offers.
non_obvious_insight: Percent complete is the wrong metric. The last 5% of a data center can consume 25% of the calendar, and it is dominated by unbounded tasks: the commissioning punch-list burn-down rate and whether the OEM has a startup technician free that month predict RFS far better than construction progress. You can only read those signals if you have run an IST. Also, the RFS date on a marketing sheet is a sales number, not a schedule.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 retired or between-jobs Cx leads and PMs on 1099 contracts. Publish a free 'RFS credibility checklist' and a teardown of one publicly delayed project. Approach 5-10 private credit and infrastructure funds with data center or GPU-lending desks. Offer a fixed-fee $25K second opinion on one live deal, delivered in two weeks, and ask permission to reference the engagement anonymously.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SynMax Vulcan (with Industrial Info Resources data partnership), Currence (formerly Sightline Climate), Epoch AI Frontier Data Centers Hub, SemiAnalysis (consulting, AI Datacenter Model, ClusterMAX). White space: The unserved wedge is narrow but real. (1) No product found in this session combines a binary, evidence-backed 'Readiness Ladder' for the last 90 days before RFS (utility energization letter, MV gear energization, Cx Level 4/5 and IST pass/fail counts, CDU flush and pressure tests, fiber acceptance, punch-list burn-down, OEM startup-tech availability) with a probabilistic RFS-by-date output and draw or covenant triggers. (2) Satellite and database vendors (SynMax, IIR, Currence, Epoch) cover the exterior and the announced schedule, and their materials do not claim commissioning or energization evidence. (3) GPU-deal technical advisors, as described by Peony, focus on fleet, telemetry and power documents rather than data hall commissioning. (4) Traditional IEs are slow, tied to a single lender or borrower, and priced for large project-finance deals. A fixed-fee, two-week, desk-plus-site 'second opinion' for a private credit desk, insurer or offtaker appears unserved. (5) The offtaker and backstop side (AI labs signing take-or-pay capacity, Google or Nvidia-style backstop providers) is structurally underserved because IEs work for lenders. Risks: incumbent IEs and Cx firms can add this as a service line, SemiAnalysis could bolt it on, and the business is people-bound (bench of ex-Cx leads) with limited software moat. Access to sites, contractors and Cx records depends on borrower cooperation, which means lender-imposed information covenants or offtaker leverage.

title: Independent Auditor for AI-Scribed Billing
one_liner: A continuous, coder-signed check on whether ambient AI scribe notes actually support the E/M levels being billed, before the payers or the government find out.
customer: Compliance officers, CFOs and revenue-integrity leaders at health systems and physician groups (20-500 providers), MSOs and PE-backed groups that rolled out ambient AI scribes. Secondary buyer: acquirers doing diligence on scribe-enabled practices.
problem: After ambient scribe rollouts, E/M distributions shift toward 99204-5 and 99214-5. Studies of six health systems show high-acuity visit share up roughly 12-20 points for new visits. Payers respond with AI downcoding and record requests, and the False Claims Act exposure is real if notes carry exam elements or time statements that did not happen. The scribe vendor cannot credibly audit itself, and annual compliance audits of 5-10 charts per provider cannot see systemic drift.
solution: Step 1 is a claims-only drift diagnostic (no EHR integration): compare each provider's E/M and modifier distribution before and after go-live with specialty benchmarks and peers, and rank the provider outliers. Step 2 is a targeted sample review by certified coders of the flagged encounters, checking that MDM or total-time really support the level. Copied-forward text, unsupported time attestations and orders without documented reasoning are the failure patterns. Step 3 is a continuing dashboard plus quarterly audit memos designed to be shown to a payer, auditor or the OIG. It includes a payer downcoding forecast.
why_now: Ambient scribes went mainstream across health systems in 2025-26. Research is documenting the coding-intensity increase and describing a payer-provider 'coding arms race', and payers are turning to their own AI for downcoding. The OIG's compliance program guidance expects organizations to audit new technology used in billing. Nobody independent has a standard offering yet.
revenue_model: $8-15 per audited encounter, or $15-30 per provider per month for the drift monitor plus sampled audits. Enterprise annual contracts of $50-200k. Diligence engagements at $10-25k each.
non_obvious_insight: The risk is not template bloat that scribes create in the HPI and exam. Under the 2021 E/M rules those elements do not count toward the level. The risk is that the scribe's fluent narration makes medical decision making and time statements sound stronger than what the physician did, and audits succeed or fail on MDM and time. Only coders who have survived payer audits know this. That is why a coder-signed audit is worth more than a model score, and why a compliance officer needs a third party, not the scribe vendor's coding module.
first_30_days: Find 3 mid-size groups, ideally with 30-100 providers, that adopted a scribe in the last 12 months, through LinkedIn outreach to compliance and revenue-integrity leads. Offer a free claims-only drift diagnostic, since 12 months of CPT data from their billing system is enough. Show them the outlier providers. Convert to a paid sample-audit engagement ($10-25k) and a monthly monitor. Recruit two certified auditors (CPC, CPMA) as contractors.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: VMG Health (Compliance Risk Analyzer + AI Governance and Targeted Coding Audits), MDaudit, Healthicity (Audit Manager, Compliance Manager, E/M Analyzer/Utilization Benchmarking tool), Ambience Healthcare (scribe vendor with coding). White space: Nobody I found sells a scribe-specific, independent, coder-signed audit product. The gaps are: (1) An explicit before/after go-live drift baseline per provider, benchmarked against specialty peers and other scribe adopters. VMG's Compliance Risk Analyzer and Healthicity's E/M benchmarking do peer outlier analysis but are not framed around scribe go-live cohorts. (2) A review protocol built around what fails audits under the 2021 E/M rules: MDM and time attestations, not HPI/exam bloat. None of the vendor pages I read describe this. (3) An audit memo designed to be handed to a payer, auditor or OIG, plus a payer-downcoding forecast. (4) Independence from the scribe vendor, since Ambience, Abridge and DeepScribe all self-attest coding quality. (5) Scribe-agnostic coverage across a mixed-vendor group. Several legal write-ups recommend exactly the 'post-implementation baseline audit comparing AI-generated coding patterns against prior practice' (https://www.subjecttoinquiry.com/2026/06/ai-assisted-billing-could-create-fca-pitfalls-how-healthcare-companies-can-get-ahead-of-risk/), and none of the articles I read named a vendor that sells it. Caveat: this is a wedge in framing and packaging, not a technology moat. The existing audit firms and platforms (VMG, MDaudit, Healthicity) can run this same claims analysis and coder review, and could rebrand it 'AI scribe audit' within a quarter or two. My search was also incomplete, and startups from 2026 may exist that I did not surface.

title: Sold-Out-of-Trust Radar for Floorplan Lenders
one_liner: Catch dealers that sell floored cars and pocket the payoff by watching the one signal an F&I insider knows can't be hidden: the VIN disappears from public listings but the floorplan payoff never arrives.
customer: Floorplan lenders and their auditors: independent floorplan companies, captive finance arms, regional banks and credit unions with dealer lines, and warehouse lenders that fund subprime and buy-here-pay-here dealers. Pay $15 to $30 per monitored dealer per month plus enterprise data fees.
problem: A dealer sells out of trust when it sells a floored car and does not pay the lender's payoff on time. It is how small cash squeezes become fraud. Ford and Stellantis are in court against Sky Auto Mall over exactly this, and floorplan use is heavier with inventory at roughly 88 days' supply and rates at SOFR plus 200 to 400 bps. Lenders police it with periodic on-site audits (monthly, quarterly or random), so a dealer can sell for weeks before anyone looks. The dealer's own delay makes it worse, since contracts in transit stretch to a week or more before the lender funds, so honest and dishonest dealers look identical in the books.
solution: Daily VIN-level monitoring of each lender's floored inventory against public and licensed listing feeds from the dealer's site and the major marketplaces. When a floored VIN disappears from listings, the tool starts a clock. It cross-checks against lender-provided payoff events and, where available, title and registration transactions and electronic lien releases. If no payoff shows within the expected window (about 7 to 10 days for a clean deal, longer for slow lenders), it flags the dealer and VIN and ranks risk by dealer history and how many VINs are in the queue. Flags trigger a spot audit or a curtailment call. A dealer-facing version shows honest dealers exactly which VINs look 'unpaid' so they can fix processing before the lender calls, and it doubles as an early-warning feed for warehouse lenders.
why_now: Sept 2025's Tricolor and PrimaLend collapses put double-pledged collateral and verification failures in front of every subprime lender and their investors. In March 2026 Ford and Stellantis were still litigating floorplan fraud against Sky Auto Mall. Rising inventory and higher rates increase floorplan reliance. Public listing feeds and cheap LLM data extraction make VIN-level monitoring practical for a team of three.
revenue_model: Per-dealer monthly monitoring fee, a per-alert fee on confirmed cases, and enterprise data licensing to captives and ABS or warehouse investors. Upsell: a contracts-in-transit tracker that gives dealers a lender-verified funding timeline and later powers same-day advances against verified contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The only place SOT cannot hide is the retail listing. A dealer will lie about payoffs, backdate titles and pay one lender with another's money, but it still has to take a car off its website when it sells it, because customers and marketplaces punish stale listings. Auditors check what is on the lot; nobody checks what left the internet. An F&I person knows this from watching sold cars vanish from the site the same day the deal is signed, and from knowing how long a funded payoff should really take.
first_30_days: Build a scraper for a pilot set of 50 dealer inventory pages and a listing-history log. Backtest on cases visible in public court filings (the Sky Auto Mall filings and a handful of others) to show the signal would have fired weeks earlier. Approach three small independent floorplan lenders and two credit unions with dealer floorplan lines, offer a free 60-day pilot on their books, and charge $20 per dealer per month after proving at least one real catch.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: In-house 'website VIN vs floorplan VIN' comparison (SAS Global Forum paper, 'PROC HTTP: Using the Web to Combat Fraud in Auto Finance During a Global Pandemic'), Vero Technologies (VeroOS), SBS Digital Audit (SBS Software), LotCount. White space: Among the products I could find, none sells the specific signal in this idea: an external-behavior signal (a floored VIN vanishing from the dealer site or marketplaces) checked against the lender's own payoff ledger on a running clock, with a ranked daily queue. Existing offerings cover other things. Physical or photo audits (CSI, LotCount, SBS Digital Audit, Netresult) are periodic and dealer-cooperative. Platforms (Vero, Solifi, Alfa, SBS servicing) analyze the lender's own payment and title data. Bank-data tools (Plaid-style) watch dealer cash. DRN covers location. The unserved wedge is mid-size and small lenders that lack data-science teams: independent floorplan companies, credit unions and community banks with dealer lines, and third-party audit firms that need risk-based audit targeting. It is strongest for used-car and buy-here-pay-here dealers, where captives' retail-delivery reports do not exist. Caveats that shrink the white space: (1) captives see retail deliveries within days and can build the signal in-house, and the SAS paper suggests at least one lender did; (2) Vero, SBS and Cox/NextGear could bolt on the signal; (3) a listing that disappears is a noisy signal (wholesaled, transferred, in recon, or the dealer never lists), so precision must be proven; (4) marketplace scraping has terms-of-service risk, so a licensed feed such as MarketCheck is likely needed.

title: Unbundling Edits for Pet Insurance Claims
one_liner: Give pet insurers the claim-edit engine human health has had for 30 years: canonical procedure codes, bundling rules, and price benchmarks for messy vet invoices.
customer: Pet insurance MGAs, carriers and TPAs adjudicating roughly 100k to 2M claims a year, the mid-size players without in-house claims data science. Later, corporate veterinary groups and pet-owner pre-treatment estimate checks.
problem: Veterinary invoices are free-text line items exported from practice-management systems, with no universal procedure code set and no NCCI-style edits. Adjusters hand-review them. Insurers cannot tell that the vet billed anesthesia monitoring, an IV catheter, fluids and the e-collar as separate lines on top of a surgery fee, or what a routine dental cleaning costs in a given ZIP code. Claim severity is inflating with vet consolidation, and insurers answer with blanket premium hikes instead of line-level accuracy.
solution: An API that ingests invoice PDFs or line items. An LLM plus a hand-built taxonomy of the top ~300 vet procedures (about 80% of spend) normalizes each line to a canonical code. A rules layer, built the way NCCI and medically-unlikely edits work, flags unbundling, duplicates and implausible units. A benchmark layer returns usual-and-customary ranges by ZIP and practice type. The adjuster sees pay, reduce or review, with reason codes.
why_now: There are roughly 7 million insured US pets, and the segment is growing at double-digit rates with loss-ratio and price-hike pressure. Corporate vet consolidation is raising invoice complexity. LLMs make invoice line-item normalization, the hard part that took human-health edit vendors years, cheap enough for a two-person team.
revenue_model: Per-claim fee of $0.25-$0.75, or 10-15% of validated savings. A 500k-claim MGA is worth $150-350k a year. Add a benchmark-data license for vet chains and an owner-facing estimate checker later.
non_obvious_insight: Every automation wave in healthcare billing started with standardized codes and claim edits, not with AI. Cotiviti and Optum are basically edit libraries with sales teams. Pet insurance is at the pre-CPT stage. Someone who has spent years living inside code sets, bundling logic and 'this is included in the global fee' arguments can build the missing layer in weeks. Insurers will not fund a fight with vets. They will fund a neutral, consistent, explainable edit that does not vary by adjuster.
first_30_days: Recruit one ex-coder (CPC) and a vet tech consultant. Build the 300-line taxonomy from public estimate sheets and a few hundred sample invoices. Approach 10 pet-insurance MGAs and TPAs with a free retrospective: run 5,000 of their anonymized past invoices and report the dollar share found in bundled, duplicate or out-of-range lines. Convert the best result into a paid pilot on per-claim pricing.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: VetControl (Illingen, Germany), Five Sigma (Clive AI claims adjuster), Sirma (custom ML for PetsBest, now under Synchrony), FairVet. White space: Nobody I found sells a US, insurer-facing, explainable edit library (canonical line-item codes, bundling and duplicate rules, unit plausibility, reason codes) with cross-carrier benchmarks, to mid-size MGAs and TPAs.

- VetControl is the only true direct analog, and it is German, GOT-based, a services-plus-software hybrid, and shows no US customers.
- Five Sigma and Sirma classify line items for coverage, not for pricing or bundling.
- FairVet and Vet Receipt hold consumer-sourced benchmark data with no insurer-grade normalization.
- Trupanion and Lassie built in-house and are not customers.
- Verisk has standardized the policy side only.

The unserved gap is an invoice-derived, ZIP-level, procedure-level price index built from insurer claims, which no owner-upload app can match in volume. It would be joined to explainable pay/reduce/review decisions for mid-size carriers with no data science team.

Structural risk to flag. Human-health edits work because of provider contracts and CMS rules. Pet insurers have no contracts with vets and no 'global fee' concept, and they pay owners by reimbursement. Line-level reductions therefore land on policyholders as balance bills, which invites complaints and regulatory attention. I found no US insurer RFP or public spend for this. The demand evidence is indirect: cost inflation, plus vendors like VetControl selling a similar product in Germany.

title: Medicaid Hours Wallet for Gig Workers
one_liner: A phone-based monthly proof-of-work ledger that turns gig, cash and self-employment activity into state-accepted documentation and 30-day cure packets, paid for by the Medicaid plans and health centers that lose revenue when members drop.
customer: Medicaid managed care organizations with expansion-adult lines, and FQHC and community health center networks. Medicaid is 43-50% of health center revenue, and an MCO is paid capitation per member-month. End users are expansion adults aged 19-64 with irregular income. The MCO or health center pays per retained member; the enrollee pays nothing.
problem: CMS's interim final rule (June 3, 2026) requires states to implement 80 hours a month of work or activity, or $580 a month in income, by Jan 1, 2027. Compliance is checked at application and at renewal, and a noncompliance notice gives 30 calendar days to cure. CBO projects about 4.8M coverage losses from work requirements, largely from reporting complexity. About 9 in 10 affected patients are expected to qualify for an exemption or already comply, yet many will still lose coverage on documentation. Nebraska went live May 1, 2026 with self-attestation, but about 28,000 people there must document twice a year and the state plans to move to verification.
solution: An enrollee-side SMS and app tool. It ingests bank and payment-app statements, gig platform earnings exports (Uber, DoorDash, Cash App, Venmo), pay stub photos and logged volunteer or class hours. It computes whether each month clears $580 or 80 hours and generates the state-specific verification packet. It sends look-back-month reminders and prepares the 30-day cure response. It flags likely exemption candidates, such as medically frail members, from plan claims data. The plan or clinic dashboard shows at-risk members and cure success. The tool only assists and never determines compliance, which is what federal rules allow plans to do.
why_now: The interim final rule was published June 3, 2026, and the national start date is Jan 1, 2027. Nebraska's live rollout is the preview of what other states will face when verification replaces self-attestation. CMS is encouraging automation, but states are spending on caseworker portals, notices and screening tools, not on income documentation for gig workers.
revenue_model: $3-8 per at-risk member per month billed to the MCO, or a success fee of $50-150 per member retained through renewal. FQHC SaaS at $2-5k per month per site with an outcomes dashboard. Later, state contracts for a self-employed and gig documentation module.
non_obvious_insight: Vendors such as Salesforce are building state-facing portals for applicants and caseworkers. The parties with a P&L at stake, the MCOs and health centers, are not yet being sold a member-side tool. KFF's roundup of state outreach plans covers notices, websites and screening tools but does not describe how self-employed or irregular income will be documented (https://www.kff.org/medicaid/medicaid-work-requirements-federal-outreach-requirements-and-state-plans/). State wage-data matching misses 1099, cash and gig work by design. Georgetown's CCF warns that 'verification in this context means burdensome documentation requirements for enrollees' (https://ccf.georgetown.edu/2026/05/11/the-new-medicaid-work-reporting-requirements-are-here-dont-let-the-nebraska-soft-start-fool-you/). The retention math is lopsided: a plan or clinic can pay a few dollars a month per member to protect several hundred dollars of monthly revenue. Sources: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/03/2026-11094/medicaid-program-community-engagement-requirement-for-certain-individuals and https://www.pointcare.com/blog/how-to-prevent-medicaid-coverage-gaps-in-2026
first_30_days: Build the Nebraska flow first, since it is already live. Recruit 50 gig and self-employed Medicaid enrollees through one FQHC partner. Measure how many can produce a compliant $580 or 80-hour packet within 30 days. Take those results to two MCO member-engagement and quality leads for a paid pilot. Sign an LOI with one health center network before Jan 1, 2027.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CMS Emmy (Eligibility Made Easy) app and Emmy API, SteadyIQ (Income Passport / Verification Hub), Digital Public Works, Maximus, Optum, Acentra, Deloitte, Gainwell, Conduent, Curam/Merative (state-side community engagement modules). White space: Nobody I found sells an enrollee-side monthly ledger to MCOs or FQHCs that ingests bank, gig and pay-stub data, computes $580 or 80 hours against a state's look-back rules, and produces a state-specific 30-day cure packet. Nothing turned up in searches, CMS vendor pledges or CBPP/KFF/Georgetown landscape coverage. Vendors sit on either side of that gap. State-side vendors (SteadyIQ, Emmy, Maximus, Optum, Deloitte) sell to state agencies. Provider and plan-side vendors (Pointcare, Findhelp, mPulse) sell eligibility monitoring and outreach without gig-income packet building. The clearest unserved segment is workers with no digital trail: cash, informal and 1099-below-threshold workers such as day labor, cleaning and landscaping. Consent-based verification (CBV) via payroll, bank or gig platforms cannot reach them. The 30-day cure step, meaning a compiled packet after a noncompliance notice, is also not addressed by any product I found. The wedge is narrow and could close quickly. States with CBV (SteadyIQ, Emmy) let the enrollee connect accounts directly, which makes a separate packet redundant there. MCOs may be poor buyers because the IFR bars plans from determining compliance and gives them only a supporting role. Pointcare and Findhelp already own the FQHC and MCO relationships and could add a module. Research limits: my web search budget ran out after four searches, so I relied on page fetches. I could not load the CBPP vendor landscape, the Health Affairs piece or the Federal Register text (all blocked), and I could not confirm what Propel for Plans does or any vendor's funding.

title: Pay Home Inspectors to Find Lead Pipes
one_liner: A micro-bounty network that pays home inspectors, plumbers and water-heater installers to photograph where the service line enters the basement, with AI classification, so utilities can clear 'unknown material' lines for about $40 each instead of $500-3,000 each.
customer: Mid-size municipal and district water utilities (20k-300k connections) with a large 'unknown material' share in their published lead service line inventory. The buyer is the utility director or the lead program manager. A secondary payer is the home buyer, who pays about $29 for a 'Lead Line Certificate' add-on at inspection.
problem: Since the lead and copper inventory requirement, every system has had to classify each service line as lead, galvanized-requiring-replacement, non-lead or unknown. Unknowns are a legal and financial liability, and they are hard to shrink. The only sure verification is potholing or excavation, which costs hundreds to thousands of dollars per line. Customer self-ID by mailer gets a response rate of roughly 10-25%. Absentee landlords and LLCs almost never answer. Utility crews can't look inside private basements, so tens of thousands of unknowns sit in the spreadsheet for years.
solution: A mobile app with a fixed 3-photo protocol: the pipe where it enters the building, a scratch or magnet test close-up, and the meter serial number with the address. A vision model classifies the pipe as copper, galvanized, lead, PEX, PVC or HDPE, or flags it as unresolved. Humans QA the low-confidence cases. Each submission is geo-verified and tamper-evident, and exports in the format the state inventory portal expects. Inspectors and plumbers earn $15-25 per verified line, and the platform earns the spread. The utility gets a reconciled inventory feed and a dashboard showing unknowns falling by ZIP code. The consumer add-on (inspector-branded certificate, sold to the buyer) pays the inspector while giving the utility free data.
why_now: The first inventories were filed in late 2024, and public analyses showed millions of lines still classified 'unknown'. The Lead and Copper Rule Improvements set a 10-year replacement clock that starts around 2027, though federal details keep being revisited and litigated. Several states have their own replacement statutes that don't depend on the federal rule. The $15B in dedicated infrastructure-law lead line money is moving through state revolving funds under spend-down pressure. Vision models are only now accurate enough to classify pipe photos. (Regulatory details are from memory. Verify state acceptance rules before pitching.)
revenue_model: Utilities pay $30-60 per verified line, sold as a per-line contract that fits under small-purchase thresholds. A $10-25k pilot is typical, followed by annual contracts. The consumer-paid certificate ($29) is split with the inspector. Later products are inventory-reconciliation SaaS and an access-agreement workflow for replacement crews.
non_obvious_insight: Utilities think they have a data problem, but they have an eyeballs-in-basements problem. Every home sale (an inspector visits) and every water heater swap (a plumber stands three feet from the service entry) already puts a paid expert next to the exact pipe that matters. Nobody has paid them for a photo yet. Excavation is the wrong tool for a question that visual inspection answers for almost nothing.
first_30_days: Pick one state that accepts documented visual or contractor verification. Pick two utilities in it whose public inventories are more than 40% unknown. Recruit 30 inspectors through local InterNACHI and ASHI chapter meetups and Facebook groups, and pay a launch bonus per photo set. Run a 200-line pilot. Have the utility pothole 30 of those lines as ground truth, then publish the accuracy numbers. Close a $15-25k pilot purchase order with the first utility, using the small-purchase limit that many cities set at $25-50k so no council vote is needed.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: BlueConduit, VODA.ai (Lead Finder / Lead Zero / Lead Management Dashboard), Trinnex leadCAST (used by Durham, NC), Esri ArcGIS Lead Service Line Inventory solution. White space: Nobody I found runs the specific thing proposed: a paid supply-side network of trade professionals (inspectors, plumbers, water-heater installers) who photograph the service entry under a fixed protocol, with vision-AI classification, tamper-evident geo-verification, human QA, and export to state inventory formats, sold to utilities per verified line. Players fall into four groups. (1) Predictive modelers (BlueConduit, VODA.ai) reduce digs statistically but still need ground-truth field samples, and Texas does not accept predictive modeling for official inventories. (2) Customer self-ID portals (Trinnex leadCAST, Esri Survey123, Cognito Forms) collect photos and reach only the 10-25% of owners who respond, and absentee landlords and LLCs almost never do. (3) Hardware probes (Electro Scan, Echologics) need a utility crew at each line. (4) Door-to-door inspection programs (RCAP, engineering firms) are staffed centrally and slowly. The unserved wedge is professional-grade evidence for the non-responding, owner-absent lines at about $30-60 per line, collected by people already inside the building. Two sub-gaps stand out: states that reject modeling but accept documented visual verification, and small or mid-size utilities with no field crews. Caveats: (a) my WebSearch budget ran out after 4 searches, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and GitHub sweeps were not done and a stealth or very early startup in this niche could exist; (b) the search snippet says physical identification methods 'must be conducted or overseen by water system personnel' (state-dependent), so third-party photos may only count as self-ID-grade evidence unless the utility or state accepts contractor verification; (c) the idea's own note that regulatory details are from memory still applies; (d) per-utility supply is limited to home sales and water-heater swaps, so density per utility could be slow; (e) inspectors may resist liability for calling a pipe lead (my recollection, unverified); (f) Trinnex or Esri could add a 'contractor submission' role cheaply.

title: Supplier Divorce Protection: Tool Census and Overrun Forensics
one_liner: When a US manufacturer leaves a Chinese contract manufacturer, we find out which molds and dies it really owns, and prove whether the ex-supplier is still running them off the books.
customer: US OEMs and PE-owned manufacturers ($50M-$500M revenue) that moved or are moving injection-molded, die-cast, stamped or extruded product out of China within the last 24 months, and hold $200k-$5M of tooling there. The buyer is the COO or VP Supply Chain, with General Counsel as co-signer. General counsel and brand-protection managers are the second buyer.
problem: Most small and mid-size OEMs cannot say which tools they own, where they physically sit, or what condition they are in. The paper trail is a PO line item from 2016 and a WeChat thread. When the relationship ends, the supplier slow-walks tool release, demands storage or release fees, and sometimes runs overruns on your tooling on a third shift and sells them to distributors and marketplaces at a discount. You then compete against your own product, and lawyers cannot help because nobody can prove which tool made which part.
solution: Three stacked products. (1) Tool Census: a local partner audits each supplier on video and in person, laser-tags every tool with a serial, records its condition and appraised value, and captures a macro-photo 'fingerprint' library of each cavity (gate vestige, ejector-pin witness marks, texture flaws, parting-line signature). (2) Overrun Watch: monitor Amazon, Alibaba, 1688, Temu, eBay and Walmart Marketplace for look-alike parts, buy samples, and match them to cavity fingerprints, date wheels and lot codes with computer-vision-assisted forensics. That yields evidence packs for marketplace takedowns, CBP IPR recordation, or counsel. (3) Tool Extraction: negotiate release, handle Chinese export paperwork and freight, and re-qualify the tool in Ohio.
why_now: The Reshoring Initiative's 2026 survey shows 36% of OEMs reshored this year, up from 29%. The 2025 tariff whiplash ended a lot of Chinese supplier relationships, and the Feb 2026 Supreme Court IEEPA ruling is now churning sourcing decisions again, so the number of messy breakups is at a peak. Cheap macro-imaging and vision models make tool-mark matching, previously an expensive forensic-lab exercise, feasible at SMB prices.
revenue_model: Tool Census at $6k-$15k per supplier site. Overrun Watch at $2k-$5k per month per product family. Forensic evidence pack at $3k-$8k per case. Extraction at 8-12% of appraised tool value plus pass-through freight. Expected first-year ACV per client is $40k-$120k.
non_obvious_insight: Outsiders think IP loss in China means someone copies your design. Insiders know the far bigger leak is your own paid-for tool running unrecorded shifts, and that every cavity is a physical fingerprint the supplier cannot deny. Ownership of the tooling is the real leverage in any break-up, and almost nobody documents it until the day they need it.
first_30_days: Skip China operations at first. Sell a remote $2,500 'Marketplace Overrun Audit': buy 10 units of the client's product from 1688, Alibaba and Temu, compare them to the golden sample and lot codes, and deliver a one-page verdict. Sign 3 design partners through Ohio plant-manager and Reshoring Initiative networks, and line up a Dongguan or Ningbo audit contractor by referral. Book a one-hour consult with an IP litigator who will white-label the evidence-pack format.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Harris Sliwoski (China Law Blog), Alitheon (FeaturePrint), Red Points, Corsearch (Zeal 2.0, Investigations 360, Distribution Control). White space: Coverage caveat: the WebSearch quota (200 per session) was already used up when I started, so I could not run the planned 6-12 searches. I also could not check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or open-source repos. The findings below come from about 25 direct page fetches, so treat 'nobody does this' as unproven. The vendors most likely missed are the many small China-based QC and sourcing agents that sell 'mold audits' and 'mold relocation', plus PI and investigation firms (Kroll-type). Do a manual pass on those before committing.

What I found: I found no productized, US-facing service that bundles (a) a serialized tool census, (b) cavity-level physical fingerprints, and (c) marketplace test-buy attribution of overruns to a specific tool. The problem is documented and treated as an unproductized legal-advice problem: Harris Sliwoski tells clients to keep an inventory form and audit quarterly, and never mentions a third-party vendor for it. Marketplace monitoring and takedown (Red Points, Corsearch, Alibaba's free IP platform) is commoditized and crowded. Object fingerprinting exists (Alitheon) but is aimed at electronics, aerospace and gray-market diversion, not tool-mark attribution.

Genuinely unserved: (1) cavity-level 'which tool made this part' attribution that holds up as evidence; (2) a tooling census standard for mid-market OEMs, timed to the exit window; (3) an evidence pack designed for counsel that a brand-protection vendor's screenshot-and-takedown workflow does not produce.

Weak points: Extraction (tool 3) is freight, customs and re-qualification work that sourcing agents and forwarders already do at low margin. Monitoring (tool 2, first half) is a commodity. Attribution is legally useful only when the overrun carries the client's IP (trademark, design patent, trade dress) and the client can enforce it. If the part is generic or unbranded, a match proves little. Chinese-court enforceability is unproven here.

title: Contingency Recovery of Unpaid Implant Carve-Outs
one_liner: Find and collect the implant and device carve-out payments that hospitals and surgery centers are owed but never bill, because the invoice lives in accounts payable and not in the billing office.
customer: Physician-owned spine and orthopedic ASCs, plus small and mid-size hospital ortho/spine/cardiac service lines, with commercial payer contracts that carve out implants. Paid 20-30% of recovered dollars.
problem: Many commercial contracts pay implants and high-cost devices separately, at invoice cost plus a markup, but only if the vendor invoice is submitted with the claim. The implant log is in the OR record, the invoice is in supply chain or AP, and the claim is built by billing. Nobody connects them. The claim goes out with L8699 or revenue code 027x lines at billed charges, and the payer pays $0 for the device or folds it into the case rate. The payment posts as 'paid', so nobody notices the loss. This is $5k-$50k per case for spine and joint work.
solution: Ingest the implant log (manufacturer, catalog and lot numbers), AP invoice PDFs (parsed with an LLM), contract carve-out terms extracted from the PDFs, and the 837/835 files. Compute expected carve-out payment versus actual, auto-assemble invoice attachments per payer rules, and file corrected claims and appeals inside timely-filing windows. Run it as a service for the first clients (manual, coder-led), then automate the matching.
why_now: CMS's CY2026 outpatient rule began phasing out the inpatient-only list and added many procedures, mostly musculoskeletal, to the ASC-covered list. More device-heavy spine and ortho cases are moving to ASCs whose small billing staffs have never dealt with carve-outs. Payers are also using AI-driven payment integrity that makes missing attachments an automatic zero.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered carve-out payments. After the first recovery, convert to $1.5-4k/month prospective monitoring per facility.
non_obvious_insight: The loss is invisible in every standard revenue-cycle KPI. Denial rate looks fine and AR looks fine because the line paid 'as billed under the case rate'. The only way to see it is to lay the supply chain invoice next to the contract term next to the 835. Billers know it happens. Supply chain does not know payers pay for it. Finance never audits it. That gap between three departments is the earned secret.
first_30_days: Pick 10 physician-owned spine and ortho ASCs through ASCA chapters and surgeon-owner LinkedIn outreach. Offer a free 90-day lookback audit, since contingency means zero risk to them. Each needs to share 835s, implant logs, invoices and the top three commercial contracts. Do the first three audits by hand with a coder and a spreadsheet, and use the dollars found as the sales collateral. Then automate the invoice parsing.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Aspirion (ContractIQ, payment variance recovery), FinThrive (Contract Manager, A/R Optimizer, Revenue Integrity), Sift Healthcare (RevProtect), Waystar (Claim Attachments, Denial Recovery, Recoupment Manager). White space: Caveat on confidence: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before any of my searches ran, so the competitor check is thinner than requested. It rests on direct fetches of about 15 vendor and trade-publication pages plus Becker's ASC on-site search result pages. The Becker's article bodies returned 403. Crunchbase, Reddit and Product Hunt were not reachable. I also could not confirm Cloudmed/R1 or Experian Contract Manager features (the R1 URL 404'd). Both are plausible incumbents with contract modeling.

What looks unserved, and is specific: (1) a contingency service focused only on the implant/device carve-out. It would join the OR implant log (manufacturer, catalog and lot numbers) to the AP vendor invoice, then to the payer contract carve-out clause, then to the 835 line. None of the general underpayment vendors above advertise this. (2) The buyer is the physician-owned spine/ortho ASC. Enterprise tools like Sift, FinThrive and Aspirion are aimed at health systems. (3) The claim-side fix is assembling the invoice attachment per payer rules and filing a corrected claim inside timely-filing limits. General contract-modeling tools mostly stop at flagging a variance.

Risks to the premise:
- 'Nobody connects them' is overstated. Becker's ran 'ASC Implant Carve-Outs: Opportunities, Challenges & 4 Best Practices' in 2014, so ASC operators know carve-outs exist (https://www.beckersasc.com/asc-coding-billing-and-collections/asc-implant-carve-outs-opportunities-challenges-4-best-practices/). ASC-specialist billers such as SIS/Surgical Notes, National Medical Billing Services and Nimble probably submit implant invoices as routine, so the addressable leakage may sit mostly in ASCs with weak or outsourced generalist billing.
- Any player with a contingency model and payer-contract modeling could add this quickly. Aspirion's ContractIQ is the most obvious.
- Medicare does not carve out implants in the ASC setting, so this is a commercial-contract play only. Each payer contract must be read individually, which limits how far it scales.
- I could not verify the CY2026 IPO-list phase-out and ASC list additions cited in the idea's why-now. CMS's page confirms only that a CY2026 ASC final rule (CMS-1834-FC) exists.

title: Payoff-Triggered Refund Recovery for Credit Unions
one_liner: A payoff-desk plug-in that finds the unearned GAP and service-contract refunds the moment a member pays off, and applies unearned add-on credits in repossession deficiencies. It goes through lenders, not SEO, so it reaches the borrowers the consumer refund sites can't.
customer: Credit unions and regional auto lenders (payoff and collections departments). The lender pays a small SaaS fee or takes a share of recovered money. Second wedge: consumer bankruptcy and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid, at $99 per deficiency audit.
problem: When a borrower pays off early, trades in, or has the car totaled or repossessed, they are owed the unearned pro-rata part of GAP, service contracts and other financed add-ons. Refunds are not automatic. Not the dealer, not the lender and not the administrator processes them, and consumer-refund sites exist because so few people claim. The incentives point the wrong way. The dealer suffers a commission chargeback, so it stalls. The administrator profits from non-cancellation. The lender never owned the product. The borrower doesn't know. In repossession, unearned add-on credits should reduce the deficiency the borrower is sued for, and they rarely appear on deficiency notices. Roughly 3M repossessions a year and subprime 60+ day delinquency at a 32-year record of 6.9% in January 2026 make this a very large pool of missed money.
solution: Ingest the closed-loan document image or loan tape, read the itemized products and financed amounts from the retail installment contract, and match each to its administrator. Compute the pro-rata or earned-basis refund by state rule (New Jersey, for example, requires an automatic refund within 60 days). Auto-generate the cancellation packet with the lender's payoff letter, odometer statement, signature or letter of authority, and the state statute citation, then track it to payment. Stalled cases escalate to the state insurance department with a complaint file. The moat is a database of roughly 60 administrators' actual cancellation requirements and response behavior, plus the 50-state rule set. The repossession product reconciles deficiency notices against the same data and outputs an attorney-ready exhibit.
why_now: Record delinquencies and about 3M repossessions a year, roughly 84-month loans with about 30% of trade-ins underwater, and long terms mean most loans die early and carry stacked add-ons. Credit unions are under member-experience and fee-optics pressure, and California's SB 766 now requires dealers to keep refund and cancellation records. LLMs can finally read messy contract images and cancellation forms cheaply enough to run at scale.
revenue_model: Credit union pays $3 to $6 per payoff processed, or 20 to 30% of recovered money with no upfront fee. Attorneys pay $99 per deficiency audit or a $499 per month subscription. Later, sell aggregated administrator refund-speed benchmarks to dealer groups and regulators.
non_obvious_insight: The consumer refund sites that exist all have the same weakness: they wait for the borrower to show up. The one moment every party knows the loan ended is the payoff, and the lender's payoff desk is the only place that sees all of them. The refund itself comes from the administrator's pool, and the dealer's chargeback is a fight between the dealer and the administrator. The borrower's claim doesn't depend on the dealer cooperating, so the dealer stalling does not need to hold up the refund.
first_30_days: Build the administrator playbook for the 20 largest GAP and service-contract administrators and the 10 highest-population states. Offer 3 credit unions a free retrospective audit of 500 payoffs from the last 12 months and show them the dollar total of unclaimed refunds. Take a 30% success fee on live recoveries. Simultaneously give 5 consumer bankruptcy attorneys the repossession deficiency audit free on their next 3 cases in return for case studies.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. 3. Weaknesses in the idea as written, from reasoning rather than found evidence:
   - The claim that the lender never owned the product is shaky. Under many state retail installment sales acts, and under the FTC Holder Rule, the assignee or holder can carry refund and credit obligations. That helps demand, as a compliance and UDAAP driver, but it changes the pitch from 'find hidden money' to 'reduce liability'.
   - A 20-30% success fee taken from a member's own refund has poor fee optics for a credit union. It also conflicts with the idea's own member-experience rationale.
   - On payoff, the refund goes to the borrower, so the CU gets no direct economic benefit. The CU's incentive is goodwill and compliance, not revenue.
   - CU vendor due diligence and core/LOS integration will make the sales cycle slow.
   - The California SB 766 citation in the idea did not check out. The leginfo summary I fetched for the 2023-24 bill described an unrelated social-worker licensing bill. Do not rely on that cite until it is confirmed.

title: Referee Sampling for Black Mass and Battery Scrap
one_liner: Independent sampling and assay of black mass lots, using Pierre Gy's Theory of Sampling from mining, so scrap sellers and recyclers stop fighting over 5-15% payable swings.
customer: Battery-scrap sellers who are paid by assay: gigafactory scrap desks, EV and ESS dismantlers, and shredder pre-processors in Germany, Poland, the US Midwest, Ontario and Korea. Buyers are hydromet recyclers and trading houses that want defensible acceptance. Whoever needs the settlement pays $1.5-4k per lot or $15-40 per tonne, and often splits it.
problem: Black mass is a worst-case heterogeneous powder: coarse Cu and Al foil flakes, plastic, residual electrolyte, graphite, and a nugget effect for Ni, Co and Cu. Payables are computed on the assay of a few grams. Anyone from mining knows 90% or more of assay error is sampling error (fundamental, segregation and grouping errors), not lab error. Sellers and buyers each sample their own way and get 5-15% differences on Ni, Co and Li. Disputes are settled by splitting the difference or sending to an 'umpire' lab that repeats the same bad sampling. On a $60-150k lot, that swing is $5-15k of pure noise, paid to whoever wins the argument. The industry's chemists treat it like a homogeneous chemical.
solution: Build a containerised, safety-rated sampling and sample-prep station (dryer, rotary divider, splitter, pulverizer, inert handling) and a written ToS-based protocol: incremental sampling from a falling stream or drum auger, particle-size and moisture control, and duplicate-sample bias checks. Send splits to an accredited lab and issue a 'referee certificate' with a stated sampling variance. Provide a two-line settlement clause template that buyer and seller adopt (for example, 'referee result binds') and tie lot IDs to the recycled-content and material-recovery documentation the EU Battery Regulation requires. Extend later to PCB e-waste, catalyst scrap and mixed copper scrap.
why_now: Black mass volumes are ramping with European and US gigafactory ramp-up scrap (often 10-30% early yield loss). EU regulation is pushing black mass toward hazardous-waste treatment and export limits, and Battery Regulation recovery and recycled-content rules are phasing in. Several Western recyclers restructured or were bought out in 2025 (Li-Cycle into Glencore, for example), so sellers now fear counterparty and assay risk. Payables have become the main margin lever as Co and Ni prices swing.
revenue_model: Per-lot referee fee ($1.5-4k) or $15-40 per tonne, annual retainers for large scrap generators, leasing or operating sample-prep stations at recycler gates, and certification and training for recyclers' in-house sampling.
non_obvious_insight: The fight looks like an assay-accuracy problem but it is a sampling problem, and the solution is 1950s-1990s sampling theory that only mining and metallurgy people internalise. Recycling companies are staffed by chemists and process engineers who sample like it is a solution. A person who has been burned by a bad grade-control sample sees the whole market as one giant unsampled stockpile.
first_30_days: Rent time on a commercial sample-prep lab or buy used splitting and pulverizing gear (about $40-60k). Offer a free duplicate-sampling study to three scrap generators or dismantlers: take 10 lots, sample each with the seller's method and yours, and send blind splits to two labs. Show them the between-protocol bias, then sell a 6-month referee retainer. A local mining-lab partner and one senior sampling consultant give instant credibility.

title: Flight simulator drills for county SNAP eligibility workers
one_liner: Short daily drills using synthetic cases built from the state's own error taxonomy, sold to county social-services directors who are about to pay for every eligibility mistake.
customer: County social services / DSS directors and supervisors in county-administered SNAP states (NY, NC, CA, OH, MN, CO, VA) and the state associations of counties. Buyers pay $12k-25k per county per year, or $150-300 per worker. States can buy statewide at $150k-500k.
problem: H.R.1 raises the state/county share of SNAP administrative costs from 50% to 75% starting October 2026. From October 2027, states with payment error rates of 6% or higher must pay part of benefit costs. In New York, St. Lawrence County faces an extra $776,000 in year one, Jefferson County over $1 million and Warren County $415,000. The state's error rate is 13% against a 6% line, a penalty of about $1B statewide, described as 'a missile heading right at New York State'. North Carolina's error rate is 6.69%, with state cost-share exposure of about $140M at 5% and $420M at 15%. The state's advice to counties is 'documenting, documenting, documenting'.
solution: A 15-minute daily micro-drill for eligibility workers: a synthetic household case (pay stubs, shelter costs, household composition changes, address changes) with a realistic case-file packet, where the worker computes eligibility and benefit. The drill feeds back the exact error that federal QC would cite. Cases are generated from the state's policy manual and the public USDA QC error categories (wage reporting, household size, address changes and shelter deductions are the common ones), with no real client data. Supervisors see per-worker error-type heatmaps and a coaching queue. Later: an optional second-look review desk staffed by former QC reviewers that samples a county's real closed cases.
why_now: The error-rate look-back, cost-shift start (October 2026) and penalty tiers (October 2027) create a hard two-year clock. Louisiana is paying cash bonuses to error spotters, Kansas hired an outside consultant, Virginia is buying technology for error checking, and NC is running monthly QC webinars and targeting high-error counties. States are visibly buying error-reduction help, and there is no standard product for it.
revenue_model: Per-worker annual subscription ($150-300) or flat per-county fee ($12k-25k); statewide contracts through the state SNAP office or county association; add-on per-case second-look review at $18-30/case.
non_obvious_insight: A county with a 0% error rate is still penalized if the state averages above 6%, so no county can solve this alone and the real buyer is the state or the association pooling county money. Meanwhile individual county directors are hurting now and have discretionary admin budgets and training budgets they can spend without an RFP. Synthetic cases avoid the PII and system-access barrier that blocks most govtech vendors in benefits programs, so a small team can start selling in weeks, not after a FedRAMP-style review. Evidence: county exposure and 13% New York error rate (https://www.northcountrypublicradio.org/news/story/53929/20260910/snap-cost-shift-pushes-north-country-counties-into-a-financial-bind); NC official on documentation, targeted training and CQI (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9949745/north-carolina/executive/organizations/state-departments-and-agencies/mental-health/developmental-disabilities-and-substance-abuse-services/state-official-urges-counties-to-cut-snap-payment-error-rate-to-avoid-hr1-cost-shares); state remediation tactics such as bonuses, outside consultants and new training (https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/states-scramble-cut-snap-error-214614305.html).
first_30_days: Build 40 synthetic cases across the top error elements from one state's manual, with a scoring engine. Approach the state county association's SNAP resource group and 5 county DSS directors with a free 30-day pilot with a pre/post test on 10 new hires. Publish a 'your error rate in dollars' calculator for county commissioners. Convert the two most engaged counties to paid annual plans priced below their discretionary-purchase limits.

The main threats are structural rather than competitive: (a) the real buyer is the state, which typically owns training (state academies, mandated curricula, training environments in the state eligibility system), and county discretionary budgets may not cover $12k-25k; (b) Maximus or a state's existing LMS vendor could add a practice module; (c) policy variation across states (BBCE, standard utility allowance, county practices) makes per-state case libraries costly to build and keep current; (d) an open-source rules engine (PolicyEngine) lowers the barrier for copycats.

title: Immune-Graded Beef-on-Dairy Calves With Warranty
one_liner: A $1 refractometer reading at day 3-5 predicts whether a $1,400 crossbred calf lives, yet nobody independently verifies it at sale. Own that measurement and the warranty that follows.
customer: Calf raisers, backgrounders and feeder buyers who pay a premium for graded calves (or a subscription for the data), and dairies who pay to have calves graded so they can earn the premium. Later, insurers and MGAs underwriting a mortality warranty.
problem: Beef-on-dairy calf output went from about 50,000 head in 2014 to roughly 3.2M in 2024, with CattleFax projecting 5-6M, and calves have sold as high as $1,500 per head. Calf raisers buy 3-5 day old calves nearly blind and eat the 10-25% loss to scours and pneumonia. The colostrum information stays on the dairy, so raisers blame 'bad calves' and dairies blame 'bad luck'. Each dead calf now leaves a four-figure hole in a heifer pipeline that is short by hundreds of thousands of head.
solution: Independent serum total protein (Brix) testing on every calf at day 3-5, done at the dairy or at pickup by trained techs with digital refractometers and a phone app. Each calf is graded on the published four-tier passive-transfer scale (Excellent, Good, Fair, Poor) and logged with dairy, sire, weight and hydration score, then gets a QR tag or passport that follows the calf to the buyer. Buyers pay a premium for Excellent and Good and discount Poor. Phase 2 uses the accumulated data to price a 30- or 60-day mortality warranty ('we have graded 300,000 calves and know what a Brix 8.4 calf from Dairy X does'). Phase 3 gives dairies a colostrum scorecard that brokers use.
why_now: Crossbred calves are at record values, beef-on-dairy volume is doubling, and the heifer shortage means every lost calf is expensive and hard to replace. Consensus passive-transfer grading standards were published in 2020, digital refractometers are cheap, and buyers are already paying for verified genetics programs, so 'verified immunity' is the obvious next tag that nobody sells.
revenue_model: $4-6 per calf grading fee paid by the seller or split with the buyer, then $10-25 per calf warranty premium once loss data supports underwriting (partner with an insurer or MGA rather than carrying risk), plus a data subscription for larger calf raisers and feedlots.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone argues about sire genetics while the vet knows immune status dominates early death, and calves with failure of passive transfer carry about twice the risk of illness and death. The test is $1 and 60 seconds, but a number only has value when a neutral third party holds custody of it at the point of sale. The business is independent custody of the measurement, not the refractometer, and the resulting dataset becomes the underwriting moat.
first_30_days: Two vet techs, two $150 digital refractometers and a phone form. Offer free grading on 5 dairies' weekly calf shipments to 2-3 calf raisers or brokers. Ask the raiser to report 30-day illness and death by calf tag. After about 60 days, publish graded-versus-ungraded outcomes, then get one raiser to commit to a premium (for example $30-50) for Excellent calves and a discount for Poor, and charge the test fee from that point on.

Competitor check: GAP.
