White space: Coverage caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I could not run the planned searches on Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or vendor names. The 'nobody does this' finding therefore rests on direct page fetches and a GitHub repository search, not full web coverage. My early attempts to pull search-engine result pages through WebFetch returned junk or CAPTCHAs, and I stopped them because they sidestep the search limit. The verdict is low-to-moderate confidence.

What I found:
- No company selling per-calf independent Brix or serum total protein grading with a QR passport, and no calf-immunity warranty product. Where Food Comes From has no such program. Vytelle's site lists no calf program. GitHub has no relevant open-source tool, only hobby repos.
- Livestock Risk Protection explicitly 'does not protect against mortality, condemnation, physical damage or disease' (https://agproud.com/articles/60060-knowledge-is-the-best-insurance-an-overview-of-livestock-risk-protection). Federal cover for calf death loss is therefore absent. I did not verify what private mortality insurance exists.

What still stands in the way, and is not competition in the strict sense:
1. Self-testing. A raiser can Brix-test at arrival for about $1, and dairies can test their own calves. Independent custody only earns money where seller and buyer distrust each other's numbers, or where price is set before arrival.
2. Bilateral history. Feeders already ask which dairy the calves came from and some supply sire straws to dairies (https://agproud.com/articles/53106-factors-to-consider-before-buying-crossbred-dairy-beef-calves). Source-dairy reputation substitutes for per-calf grading.
3. Warranty moral hazard. Immunity is one driver of loss, but raiser housing, feeding and biosecurity dominate, which makes underwriting hard. Lombard's consensus paper puts failure of passive transfer at roughly twice the risk, which is a useful signal but not a full loss model.
4. Incumbents can absorb it. Verifiers, diagnostics vendors, calf-ranch networks and packer programs could add an immunity field.

Genuinely unserved: an independent, per-calf immunity record that travels from dairy to raiser to feeder to packer, plus a neutral dispute-resolution measurement.

title: Chute-Side Cow Counts for Ag Lenders
one_liner: Turn the vet's preg-check clipboard into a borrower-consented, third-party-verified herd inventory that banks can lend against.
customer: Community banks, Farm Credit associations and ag lenders with cattle loan books (they require it or pay per report, usually passed through to the borrower). Secondary payer is the cow-calf or heifer-development operator who wants bigger operating lines or bred-heifer financing on better terms.
problem: Cattle collateral has no VIN. Lenders verify with drive-by counts and borrower-supplied spreadsheets, and prosecutors in 2026 alleged a roughly $9.4M fraud that included a loan of $2.8M against 850 head. Farm loan delinquencies are rising while bred cows trade around $3,000+ per head, so a 500-cow borrower is $1.5M+ of collateral that nobody independent has counted.
solution: A 'Verified Herd Report' generated at the working day the vet is already doing. The vet or tech logs every head with an EID or visual tag scan (a $500 handheld reader plus a phone app), age class, pregnancy status and stage, and location. The vet e-signs and the borrower approves sharing with one tap. The lender gets a portal with timestamped, geotagged counts and year-over-year flags (head count down, pregnancy rate down, tags not matching last year). A second light pass happens at weaning. The vet earns a per-head fee for data they already write down and throw in the truck door pocket.
why_now: Federal EID ear tags became mandatory for many interstate cattle movements in Nov 2024, so per-head digital ID is now normal and cheap. Herd rebuilding at record cattle prices is being financed with debt, lenders entered 2026 carrying operating losses from 2023-2025 (rising delinquencies and restructures), and a fresh cattle-collateral fraud case is making ag loan committees ask for verification. Fall preg-check season is running right now (Sept-Nov).
revenue_model: $2-3 per head per verification, split roughly 50/50 with the vet practice, charged to the borrower or the lender as a loan condition. Add a portfolio dashboard for lenders at $500-2,000 per month once an institution has 100+ verified borrowers. Later, sell the verified inventory and pregnancy data to lenders as an underwriting input (advance rates on verified bred heifers).
non_obvious_insight: The vet is the only independent professional who physically handles every animal in the herd once or twice a year. They count, tag-check and pregnancy-check every cow, and that data dies on a clipboard. Vets refuse to police clients, but they will happily attest to what they handled when the borrower initiates the request, so the conflict-of-interest problem disappears. Honest borrowers are the real buyers: verified bred females can justify higher advance rates, and that cheap capital funds the fee many times over.
first_30_days: Preg-check season is live, so sign up 3 rural practices that each do several thousand head of fall preg-checks. Pitch 3-4 community-bank ag lenders (target the one who has been burned by a herd count before; work through state bankers' association ag committees). Run a pilot on about 10 willing borrowers with a form-based app and a PDF report, charging $2/head. Gather a before and after on what the lender learned that the drive-by inspection missed, then use that to sell the annual program.

Structural weaknesses to be skeptical of:
- Adverse selection: 'borrower-initiated' verification means fraudulent borrowers never opt in. The product only works if lenders make it a loan condition.
- Coverage: a preg-check only counts animals brought to the chute that day, not cattle on other leases or sold or double-pledged since. It does not prove ownership or lien priority.
- Vet liability and willingness: vets may refuse to sign anything that reads as a collateral audit.
- Economics: $2-3/head split 50/50 leaves the vet about $1-1.50/head on top of a preg-check fee that is already several dollars.
- Entry by an existing vendor: IMI Global (WFCF) or Merck/Allflex could add this as a feature.

title: Contingency Hunters for Unbilled Water Revenue
one_liner: Find the 'ghost parcels' and slow big meters that leak revenue out of a utility, using assessor rolls, building footprints, imagery and billing data, and get paid 20-30% of what is recovered so the city risks nothing.
customer: City, county and district water and sewer utilities with 10k-200k connections. The buyer is the finance director or utility director who is facing a council fight over the next rate increase.
problem: Utilities are raising rates 5-10% a year to fund PFAS treatment, lead line replacement and aging pipes, and councils are pushing back on affordability. Meanwhile revenue leaks out in places nobody owns: structures with no water account (unpermitted ADUs on shared meters, converted garages, fire and irrigation taps never billed), commercial compound meters that are 20-30 years old and under-register at low flows, meters swapped without the account being updated, stopped or zero-read accounts that never get investigated, and sewer-only accounts billed off a bad water read. The customer information system, the GIS parcel layer and the assessor roll sit in different departments. Nobody owns the join, and nobody has staff to do it.
solution: Join the utility's account list and consumption history to the assessor roll (building sq ft, units, use code), permits, open building-footprint datasets and aerial imagery (pools, irrigated area, added structures). Build an expected-consumption model by parcel. Rank the mismatches: no account at all, consumption far below expected, sudden step-downs after a meter change, and large meters whose low-flow profile looks wrong. A small field crew and a meter-test partner verify the top leads. The utility gets a documented recovery list with legal-ready evidence, back-billing calculations that respect the state's limits, and a meter-replacement plan. The firm takes 20-30% of first-year recovered incremental revenue.
why_now: Rate shock and affordability politics in 2025-26 make 'recover what we're owed before raising rates' an easy story for council. Open building-footprint datasets and cheap vision AI make expected-consumption modeling accessible to a two-person team, and utilities that finished smart-meter rollouts now have interval data that has never been analyzed for revenue. Contingency work also clears procurement easily because there is no upfront cost.
revenue_model: Contingency of 20-30% on the first 12-24 months of recovered annualized revenue, plus a fixed fee for a meter-testing and replacement plan. Later, a recurring SaaS monitor ($1-3 per 100 accounts per month). Optional referral fees from meter and test vendors.
non_obvious_insight: The leak that matters is not in the pipe. Large commercial meters are about 10-20% of accounts but 40-60% of revenue, and the oldest ones quietly under-register the low flows that hospitals, hotels and factories use all night. The utility never sees this loss because the meter is the thing measuring it.
first_30_days: Pick a county whose assessor roll and building footprints are downloadable and whose utility publishes or will release account addresses (public-records request). Run a free scan and generate 20 named addresses with expected versus billed usage. Cold-email finance directors at five utilities with 'we'll show you 20 unbilled addresses before you sign anything'. Sign the first contingency contract with a city that has a rate hearing scheduled, and verify leads with a hired meter-testing subcontractor.

(2) The metering and analytics incumbents (Itron, Badger, Master Meter, Metron) sell software tied to their own hardware, with no evidence of a ranked, dollar-denominated, legal-ready recovery list or contingency pricing. Ghost-parcel discovery is the weaker half. A structure with no account is rare where permits trigger taps, and an ADU on a shared meter is usually already billed on consumption. Back-billing is politically and legally messy, and some jurisdictions restrict contingency contracts. The larger risk is structural (yield, procurement law, optics), not competitive.

title: Courthouse Tape: Land-Assembly Radar for Infrastructure
one_liner: A daily feed that reads recorded option memoranda, leases and easements to show who is quietly assembling land for data centers, solar and transmission weeks before anyone announces it.
customer: Competing data center, solar, storage and transmission developers' land teams and site-selection consultants; utility and co-op large-load planners; infrastructure and energy funds buying alternative data; and county economic development and planning offices wanting defensive visibility.
problem: Land assembly is a race, and the first public trace is a short memorandum of option, lease or easement recorded at the county. Nobody watches those at scale. The assessor doesn't reflect an unexercised option. The clerk's document-type field is a dropdown chosen by a data-entry clerk, so big deals hide under 'Other', 'Miscellaneous' or 'Agreement'. Developers find out about a competitor's 6,000 acres months late, counties learn from a leaked newspaper story, and everyone pays landmen $300-$600 a day to sit in vaults.
solution: Ingest recorded instruments from county portals and bulk feeds in target corridors. Classify by reading the full image, not the clerk's label. Cluster by grantee, signatory, notary, return-to law firm and mailing address to unmask LLC families. Flag assembly events, such as N option memos within X miles or easement clusters along a line that imply transmission or pipeline. Deliver alerts, a map, and parcel-level chain-of-title and existing-easement packets on demand, with a human landman reviewing the hard ones.
why_now: The 2025-2026 large-load land rush is real: options in Hallam, Nebraska are reportedly worth tens of thousands of dollars an acre, and Hill County, Texas land appraised near $7,100 an acre has been offered about $100,000 an acre. Options are documented only by memoranda under NDA. FinCEN's 2025 decision to exempt domestic companies from beneficial-ownership reporting means LLC unmasking has to come from primary records. LLM vision finally reads messy scanned instruments accurately.
revenue_model: $2k-$8k/month per regional developer or utility seat, $750-$2,000 per tract title packet, and $50k-$150k/year alt-data licenses for funds. Optional revenue share or free access for counties that provide bulk feeds.
non_obvious_insight: The return-to address and notary on a recorded memorandum are the fingerprint of the developer's counsel, and they reveal an assembly weeks before a rezoning hearing. The mislabeled document-type field is why nobody has done this with generic data vendors. Landmen are the recorder's best regulars and know exactly which counties are hot, which makes them the cheapest ground-truth labelers and first customers.
first_30_days: Choose two counties with a rumored project, pull 24 months of instruments, and build the classifier and clustering. Deliver a 'who is assembling where' memo free to 10 site-selection consultants and land brokers, then convert two into $3k-$5k pilots. Check each state's bulk-data commercial-use rules and offer the counties access to the same maps.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ATTOM Data, Reonomy, Regrid, Enverus. White space: The specific product in the idea, a feed that reads recorded option memoranda, leases and easements from county recorders, classifies them from the image rather than the clerk's label, clusters LLC families by notary, return-to firm and address, and alerts on assembly patterns, was not found at any vendor I could read. Everything I could read is adjacent. Parcel and ownership vendors (Regrid, ATTOM, Reonomy) sell deeds, mortgages and LLC piercing but not options or easements. Siting and diligence vendors (Paces, Enverus, GridCARE) help a client find its own site. Project trackers (Cleanview, DC Byte, Heatmap Pro, Data Center Watch) start at permit or public news. Land-management vendors (Pandell, Enverus LandScape) manage a client's own documents. What remains open is cross-county, image-level reading of recorded non-deed instruments to detect other parties' assembly, sold as alerts. It is plausibly protected by the hard part, which is getting recorder access county by county, not the ML. The main structural doubts I could not test are whether developers actually record option memoranda before announcement, and how many counties allow bulk commercial pulls of document images.

title: Air-Permit Unlock for Idle Data Center Diesel
one_liner: Turn the ~55 GW of idle data center backup generators into dispatchable capacity by solving the air-permit problem instead of the hardware problem.
customer: Colo and hyperscale operators in PJM (Northern Virginia, Ohio, Illinois) with 20-500 MW of backup gensets. Secondary buyers are utilities and capacity buyers who need fast MW.
problem: Data centers hold about 55 GW of backup diesel (Virginia alone has about 27 GW permitted), and it runs 10-30 minutes a month. PJM cleared 6.8 GW short and wants large loads to bring their own capacity or be curtailed. Air permits cap non-emergency run hours, so nobody can legally count these engines as capacity.
solution: Fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' packages. They cover a state-specific permit modification strategy (run-hour caps, synthetic-minor limits), engineering and financing for emissions retrofits on the subset of engines that need them, and paralleling/telemetry upgrades. Enrollment in PJM's on-site backup (IRAS-style) and demand-response programs comes with third-party measurement and verification. Runtime is capped at a few dozen to ~100 hours a year, dispatched only in system emergencies, with community disclosure built in.
why_now: PJM's July auction shortfall, the proposed backstop auction (15-year terms, $555/MW-day cap) and the curtailment-or-bring-capacity rule make backup generation valuable for the first time. Turbines are sold out until 2029-30, so this fleet is the only large block of capacity that exists today.
revenue_model: $40-150k fixed fee per site for permit and engineering work, plus 10-20% of the first five years of capacity revenue. At the $325/MW-day cap a 20 MW fleet is worth very roughly $1.5-2M a year after derating, so the fee is easy to justify. Retrofit financing adds a spread.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest big block of new PJM capacity is not new. It is already built and sitting behind a fence, and the barrier is air-permit lawyering that VC-backed hardware companies ignore. A repeatable per-state permit playbook is the moat. Emergency-only runtime is why it works: at under 1% of hours, the capacity value dwarfs the emissions.
first_30_days: Pull public Title V and minor-source permit files for ~30 colo sites in VA, OH and IL. Build a 'permit headroom map' showing run-hour caps and engine tiers. Retain one air-permitting consultant. Offer 25 facility and sustainability leads a $15k fixed-fee dispatch-readiness audit of a 20+ MW fleet and aim to close two paid pilots.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Voltus, CPower, Enchanted Rock (ERock), Trinity Consultants (data center and power team). White space: Verification caveat: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted, so no search-engine, Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or TechCrunch queries could be run. I did about 30 direct page fetches and 2 GitHub searches instead. The GitHub searches found no open-source tool for this. I found no company selling a fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' package for existing data center diesel fleets (permit modification, emissions retrofit financing, telemetry, PJM enrollment and M&V). That is absence of evidence from a constrained search, not proof that none exists.

What appears unserved:
(1) A productized, per-state permit playbook tied to capacity outcomes. Trinity-type consultants sell hourly, per-project permitting. DR aggregators (Voltus, CPower) sell enrollment and revenue share. Generator OEMs and ERock sell hardware. Nobody I found owns the seam between them.
(2) Retrofit financing on the subset of engines that need it.
(3) A permit-headroom dataset across Title V and minor-source files.

The binding constraint is legal, not competitive. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), as summarized from Cornell LII, emergency engines are limited to 100 hours a year for maintenance, testing and emergencies, with at most 50 of those for non-emergency use. The 50 hours cannot be used for peak shaving or non-emergency demand response, and cannot generate income or serve a financial arrangement with another entity. Only narrow exceptions exist, dispatched by local authorities for transmission and distribution limits. Selling emergency-designated diesel as PJM capacity therefore likely requires reclassifying engines as non-emergency, which triggers stricter engine standards (Tier 4 or SCR-type controls), plus state NOx limits and possible major-source permitting. That is why the founder's 'retrofit the subset' step is likely the real cost and risk. It is also why incumbents have stayed away. The wedge exists only where the permit and retrofit math actually closes.

Other risks: PJM DR accreditation rules and limited-duration derating, which I could not verify because the PJM manual fetch returned only a table of contents. Local opposition to diesel. Hyperscalers and utilities choosing gas or battery capacity instead.

title: Grid-Code Models for AI Data Centers
one_liner: Validated dynamic load models and ride-through test packages so data centers can pass the same grid-code exams that generators pass.
customer: Interconnection teams at hyperscalers, neoclouds and colo developers, and their EPCs. Transmission owners and ISOs need the models validated, and the developer pays.
problem: About 1.5 GW of Northern Virginia data center load tripped offline together during a 2024 fault. AI training loads swing tens of MW in seconds, and xAI buys Megapacks largely to smooth them. Texas SB 6 and NERC large-load work now push for ride-through and dynamic models, but no standard model library or test lab exists for GPU cluster, power-supply and UPS stacks.
solution: Build a parametric EMT and PSS/E model library for common facility architectures (UPS topologies, PSU behavior, 800V DC). Validate it with hardware-in-the-loop tests at a partner lab. Sell per-project model packages, ride-through study reports and compliance-ready certification letters. Charge a subscription to keep models current as hardware changes.
why_now: Multi-GW campuses, NERC's large-load task force and Texas and PJM interconnection rules in 2025-26 are turning load models from optional into a gating item.
revenue_model: $75-300k per project for the model and study, an annual model-maintenance subscription, and test or certification fees paid by UPS and power-shelf OEMs.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone frames data centers as demand. The grid now treats them as a dynamic device, like a giant inverter-based generator. Inverter-generator modeling became a consulting industry after events like the 2016 Blue Cut fire, and large-load modeling will follow. The model library is the moat.
first_30_days: Recruit one or two power-electronics engineers from a utility or ISO. Publish an open primer on GPU-load oscillation. Contact interconnection leads at 10 neoclouds and 5 TO planners. Sell a $15k 'large-load model gap analysis'. Sign a university hardware-in-the-loop lab as a partner.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Typhoon HIL (Data Centers solution), OPAL-RT (HYPERSIM, power-HIL), EPRI DCFlex, Emerald AI (Emerald Conductor). White space: Across this session's research I found no direct competitor selling packaged, hardware-validated large-load dynamic models (PSS/E plus EMT) with ride-through study reports and certification letters for GPU-cluster, PSU and UPS stacks. Nobody was seen selling OEM-level type-test certification for power shelves and UPS platforms. Adjacent players cover only pieces: HIL tools (Typhoon HIL, OPAL-RT), generic EMT consultancies, EPRI's flexibility consortium, workload-flex software (Emerald AI), and simulation software vendors with no data center library shown.

Three structural threats need answers:
1. Regulators and EPRI or NERC may publish free generic composite or EMT models, which commoditizes the model library.
2. OEMs (UPS, PSU, NVIDIA) own the confidential control details and may ship their own models.
3. Per-project EMT consulting already exists and is not verified either way for large loads.

The defensible white space is independent, hardware-validated, ISO-acceptable model packages and compliance evidence for the 25-500 MW neocloud and colo developers who lack in-house power simulators. It would be reused across sites through OEM platform type tests, not sold as bespoke studies.

Research limits: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before this task began, so competitor discovery relied on direct page fetches and GitHub search. Startup databases (Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt), news, and NERC or EPRI publication pages were not checked. Several NERC, EPRI and PJM URLs returned 404 or empty content. Treat the 'no direct competitor' finding as moderate-confidence. Verify manually against NERC LLTF outputs, EPRI data center model reports, and WECC or ERCOT model requirements before committing.

title: Contingency Audit of Unbilled Plumbing Materials
one_liner: Reconcile a trade shop's supply-house invoices against its customer invoices and catch both parts that were bought but never billed and quiet supplier price drift, paid a percentage of what gets recovered.
customer: Plumbing, HVAC and electrical shops doing $1.5-15M in revenue with 5-40 techs, running ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro or Jobber plus QuickBooks, buying on account from Ferguson, Hajoca, Winsupply or a local supply house.
problem: Shops lose margin in two places nobody watches. First, parts go out on a supply-house ticket with a job name, or come off the truck stock, and never make it onto the customer invoice. Techs charge the labor from the flat-rate book and forget the $6 valve, the wax ring, the supply lines, the $40 of fittings. In the shops I know, when the office finally reconciles a quarter it is typically a few percent of revenue. Second, supply houses price off list with a contractor multiplier, and list prices have moved several times since the Section 232 copper, steel and aluminum tariffs (50%, working through a long manufacturer-to-contractor lag). Surcharges appear, job-quoted prices are not honored, returns credits are never issued, and no owner has time to read 40 invoices a week.
solution: Shops set up an email forwarding rule for supply-house invoices and statements and give us read access to their field-service software export. An LLM-based line-item parser ties supply-house lines to jobs and POs, then produces a weekly leak list for the office manager: (1) purchased-not-billed by job, (2) price versus the shop's own multiplier and versus the same SKU 30 days ago, (3) unclaimed return credits, (4) pricebook items where cost has risen past the target markup, with a repricing file ready to import. Later add a benchmark ('you pay 9% more than shops your size for PEX-A fittings') built from pooled anonymized invoices, which is the moat.
why_now: Tariff-driven price volatility means flat-rate pricebooks are stale within a quarter, and owners know it. Invoice parsing with LLMs went from a custom-ML project to an afternoon. Field-service platforms expose APIs and exports. The trades are also ahead of everyone else in adopting software but behind in auditing it, so there is no incumbent audit product.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 25% of recovered and newly captured revenue for the first 12 months (no recovery, no fee), converting to a $199-499 per month subscription for continuous monitoring plus the pricing benchmark. Data licensing of the pooled price index to distributors and manufacturers later.
non_obvious_insight: Owners obsess over lead cost and tech hiring while the highest-ROI dollar is sitting in the shoebox of paid invoices. Everything a tech installs was bought on a ticket with a job name on it, so the truth is already in two systems that have never been compared. This is the freight-audit and telecom-audit model, and no one has brought it to the trades because the people who feel the pain are too busy running trucks to build it.
first_30_days: Offer a free 90-day audit to 10 shop owners from a peer group (a PHCC chapter, Nexstar or Service Roundtable style mastermind). Have them forward statements and give a one-time export. Turn each audit around in 48 hours with a single 'found money' number and a list of specific invoices. Convert the shops with the largest number to the contingency contract. A spreadsheet plus an LLM parsing script is enough for the first ten.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ServiceTitan Accounts Payable (bill inbox, 3-way matching, Manage Statements, Manage Credits, discrepancy flags), Kojo, BuildOps (Procurement and Payables), Fergus. White space: Nobody I found offers a contingency-fee, done-for-you recovery audit for trade shops. What remains unserved is the customer-side leak: parts on a supply-house ticket with a job name, or pulled from truck stock, that never reached the customer invoice, plus supplier price drift and quoted-price violations tied back to the shop's own pricebook and markup targets. Existing tools (ServiceTitan AP, Kojo, BuildOps, Ramp) are software the shop must adopt and operate, and they focus on paying suppliers correctly. Three parts are open: (1) shops on Housecall Pro, Jobber, FieldEdge or Simpro, or ServiceTitan shops not using Procurement/AP, who have no PO-to-job workflow; (2) the done-for-you, no-recovery-no-fee commercial model, which no software vendor offers; (3) a cross-shop SKU price benchmark from pooled supply-house invoices. I found no evidence anyone has assembled that for residential and light-commercial trade shops. ServiceTitan's Manage Statements and Manage Credits are the closest overlap with the returns-credit and price-error pieces.

title: Warranty Clock Recovery Audits for Idle Halls
one_liner: A contingency-fee service that finds and files the warranty claims on energized-but-empty data halls before OEM warranty clocks silently expire.
customer: Colocation developers, powered-shell landlords, neocloud operators and enterprise owners with phased or delayed-tenant builds, especially those with halls commissioned 6-14 months ago and not yet loaded. The owner pays a percentage of recovered value, plus an optional per-asset tracking subscription.
problem: Warranty clocks on generators, UPS systems, chillers, CRAH/CDUs, switchgear, and batteries usually start at shipment or startup, not when a tenant loads the hall. With delayed leases and mid-build AI redesigns, halls sit energized and idle for months. Many defects only show under real load (UPS capacitors, chiller compressors, wet-stacking gensets, breaker trip curves, coolant chemistry). By the time the tenant ramps, the warranty has expired. The turnover package is 50,000+ pages of PDFs that ops never reads, the punch-list deferrals are lost, and OEM maintenance records required to keep coverage valid are often missing. Nobody owns the clock.
solution: Ingest POs, OEM warranty terms, startup sheets, Cx reports, shipping documents and maintenance logs with an LLM pipeline to build a serial-number-level warranty ledger with real expiry dates and voiding conditions. Flag anything expiring within 120 days. Run a targeted load-dependent-defect inspection before expiry (thermography, oil and coolant samples, capacitor and battery checks, breaker testing). File claims, negotiate warranty start-date deferrals or extensions with the OEM while leverage still exists, and fix missing maintenance-record gaps. For new builds, sell a PO-stage clause pack that defers warranty start to beneficial occupancy.
why_now: There is a glut of speculative shells and delayed tenant handoffs. Reporting in 2026 shows close to half of planned US builds slipping, with only about a third of 2026 target capacity under active construction. That means many halls are powered, commissioned and idle. Equipment was bought at peak prices with tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper, so each lapsed warranty is worth more. LLMs can now read messy closeout binders cheaply, which was the labor bottleneck for audits like this.
revenue_model: 25-30% of recovered value or avoided cost on claims and negotiated extensions, no fee if nothing is recovered. Optional $150-400 per asset per year tracking subscription. $15K-40K fixed-fee closeout audits for owners who want certainty. PO-stage clause-pack consulting for developers.
non_obvious_insight: The warranty is the only major asset on a data center balance sheet that expires silently. OEMs will defer warranty start dates at PO time, but almost no one negotiates it because the project team is fighting for delivery slots, not paperwork. After the fact, the owner's ops team inherits the docs with no idea when the clocks started. The money is in the punch-list items that were 'to be fixed later' and the load-dependent defects that only appear after the hall is finally used.
first_30_days: Find 3 owner-operators through PM and Cx network contacts with halls energized 8-11 months ago and not fully loaded. Offer a free 10-day scan of their closeout binders in exchange for a contingency agreement on any claims. Build the extraction pipeline on real binders (gensets, UPS, chillers first). Deliver a 'expiring within 90 days' hit list and file the first claims before the first invoice.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ethyco (data center commissioning, warranty-phase support), Anyset AI (agentic closeout / warranty tracking), Nomic (AEC document AI, closeout), Trane delayed start-up warranty (OEM rider). White space: Nobody I found combines all of these for data center MEP: (1) a serial-number-level clock ledger built for idle or deferred-start halls, (2) a pre-expiry loaded stress test using the idle capacity, (3) OEM claim filing and start-date deferral negotiation, and (4) success-fee or fixed-fee pricing sold to the owner or its lender. The pieces exist separately. Anyset and Nomic do doc extraction. Ethyco-style Cx firms do a 10-month warranty review. Wind and solar have end-of-warranty inspection and claims firms. OEMs sell delayed-start riders. Load-bank vendors have the hardware. Data center power and cooling MEP has no dedicated end-of-warranty claims specialist that I could find. Three structural weaknesses limit the wedge. (a) The clocks mostly start at OEM startup, and startup plus IST with load banks already loads equipment in Cx, so the 'idle for 12+ months' exposure is narrower than the pitch implies. It mainly hits gear started early or shipped more than 18 months before use. (b) 'Recovered value' is really avoided repair cost. It is hard to measure and easy for OEMs to dispute, and OEMs can deny on storage or light-load grounds (wet stacking is explicitly excluded, https://cliffordpower.com/wet-stacking-why-its-important-to-load-bank-your-diesel-generator/). A pure 25-30% contingency model will be hard to collect. (c) Documents are the commodity step, so the moat has to be inspection plus OEM leverage, not the LLM pipeline.

title: Pharmacy-Side PBM Ledger for Employers
one_liner: Independent pharmacies hold the half of the PBM ledger that employers never see, which is what the PBM actually paid the pharmacy. Pool it to run spread audits for self-insured employers, and give pharmacies a stay-or-leave calculator for their take-it-or-leave-it PBM contracts.
customer: Two sides. First, independent pharmacies, at $99-199 a month for benchmarking and a network-contract modeler. Second, self-funded local employers, school districts, counties and union funds (from 100 to 5,000 lives), plus the benefit consultants and TPAs that serve them, who pay per audit or a share of verified savings.
problem: The employer sees only what it paid the PBM. The PBM sees both sides and hides one. The pharmacy sees what it was paid and what it paid the wholesaler, but has no benchmark and no idea whether the network offer that arrives every Q4 for January 1 is worse than its peers' terms. Everyone negotiates blind. PBMs threaten a pharmacy with losing about a quarter of its business if it declines, and a plan sponsor cannot verify 'pass-through' claims.
solution: Read-only ingestion of the pharmacy's 835 remittance files and invoice costs from its pharmacy management system (PMS). Output 1) per-drug, per-PBM reimbursement benchmarked against NADAC and an anonymized peer pool. 2) A stay-or-leave model of each 2027 network offer built from the pharmacy's own claims mix. 3) With sponsor consent, a claim-level tie-out of the pharmacy-paid amounts against the employer's PBM claims file. That yields a true spread and rebate pass-through gap in dollars per member, delivered as an audit the employer can use to renegotiate or move to a transparent PBM.
why_now: The contract season for January 2027 is happening right now, which gives a hard deadline and a free entry wedge. Employer fiduciaries are under pressure from ERISA suits over PBM costs, state PBM transparency laws and FTC scrutiny. Pharmacy closures (Rite Aid gone, Walgreens closing about 1,200 stores) have given local officials political will. OCR and LLM parsing of messy remit PDFs now makes onboarding a one-day job rather than a consulting project.
revenue_model: Pharmacy subscription of $99-199 a month, or free in exchange for data. Employer audit fees of about $8k-25k per mid-size sponsor, or 10-20% of first-year verified savings. Data licenses to state employee plans, attorneys general, employer coalitions and consultants at a higher tier.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone in the PBM fight holds half a ledger, and only the pharmacy can prove the gap. Thirty pharmacies in one county reconstruct the local school district's and county government's spread at claim level. Independents will hand this data over willingly because it is the first ammunition they have ever had against take-it-or-leave-it contracts.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 pharmacies through the state independent pharmacy association with the pitch 'we will model your 2027 PBM offers free'. Build parsers for the three biggest PBMs' remit formats (the 835 EDI standard helps). Deliver the first stay-or-leave reports. Hire a healthcare attorney to structure data-use terms, since provider-manual confidentiality clauses and HIPAA de-identification are the main risk. Offer one local school district or county a free pilot spread audit and turn the result into a one-page case study.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Truveris (truAudit / truGuard / Marketplace), Capital Rx (Judi Health), AffirmedRx, SmithRx. White space: Caveat on confidence: my WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before I ran any query in this session. The verdict rests on direct fetches of about 20 competitor and source pages plus GitHub searches, not on a broad landscape scan. It is a provisional 'gap', not a confirmed one.

What I did not find: no company that ingests pharmacy-side remits, benchmarks per-drug, per-PBM reimbursement against a peer pool, models Q4 network offers, and ties pharmacy-paid amounts to an employer's PBM claims file. The employer-side audit market is served: Truveris, benefits consultants, and transparent PBMs that market pass-through. Their audits appear to start from what the PBM hands over, and I found no sign they hold the pharmacy-paid half.

The pharmacy-side gap is plausible. PioneerRx, PQS and CPESN pages show no reimbursement-benchmarking or contract-modeling feature. Not verified: pharmacy services administrative organizations (PSAOs such as Cardinal, AmerisourceBergen Elevate, AAP, Health Mart Atlas) and pharmacy management system vendors may already offer contract review or reimbursement reports to members. Confirm this in customer interviews before building, because the PSAOs negotiate PBM contracts and already hold members' remits.

The specific unserved wedge is a claim-level reconciliation between the pharmacy's actual paid amount and the employer's PBM claims file, delivered as a spread and rebate pass-through gap in dollars per member.

Risks that shrink the white space:
- PBM provider-manual confidentiality clauses and possible antitrust or information-exchange concerns when pooling competitors' reimbursement rates.
- Getting employer PBM claims files with sponsor consent.
- Pharmacy remits are not uniformly 835 files.
- The January 2027 contract window is roughly 3 months away and cannot be met by a product built from scratch.

title: Bridge Loans for Medicare Drug-Price Refunds
one_liner: Fund the 3-4 week float independent pharmacies now carry on Medicare's negotiated-price drugs, underwritten on predictable refund data, before Ozempic joins the list in January.
customer: Independent pharmacies with senior-heavy books, especially those serving long-term care, then 5-50 store groups and PSAOs. Average exposure is estimated at over $27,000 a month per community pharmacy.
problem: Since January 1, 2026, pharmacies pay wholesalers full price for Eliquis, Jardiance, Xarelto, Farxiga, Januvia, Entresto and others, dispense at Medicare's Maximum Fair Price, and wait weeks for the difference to arrive through the Medicare Transaction Facilitator. Estimates put the float at $27k+ a month for the average community pharmacy, over $500M a month industry-wide, on top of wholesalers who still auto-debit weekly. On thin margins that is a real solvency risk. Banks see a pharmacy, not an insured refund.
solution: Start with a reconciliation tool that ingests the pharmacy's PMS claims export and the MTF remittance files and shows late or missing refunds. Then offer a non-recourse advance of about 90% of the expected refund on each week's MFP claims, repaid from the actual MTF payment through a controlled deposit account or sweep. Confirm with CMS and the facilitator what payment-routing options exist, and fall back to a bank-account sweep if third-party routing is not allowed.
why_now: The program only became real on January 1, 2026, and it is already causing cash-flow warnings from pharmacy coalitions. On January 1, 2027, 15 more drugs join, including semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus), which multiplies the float. Wholesalers have not yet solved it and the bank market does not understand it, so there is a window of a few quarters before someone standardizes the answer.
revenue_model: A fee of about 1-1.75% per advance cycle, which works out to roughly 15-25% annualized, plus a $99 a month reconciliation subscription. Contingency of about 10% on missing refunds recovered. Later, sell or syndicate the receivables to a credit fund.
non_obvious_insight: To a bank this looks like distress lending to a struggling small business. In reality it is close to prime paper: the obligor is a drug manufacturer with a statutory duty to pay, routed through a federal facilitator, backed by claim-level data. Only someone who knows how PMS claims map to MFP eligibility, and how a reversal or dispute can claw a refund back, can underwrite it. The free reconciliation report is the wedge that gets the data before any money goes out.
first_30_days: Offer a free 'find my missing refunds' report to 25 pharmacies through state association newsletters and pharmacy owner Facebook groups. Line up a $500k credit line from a regional bank or family office and keep the first ten advances small. Talk to a fintech attorney about commercial-financing disclosure laws by state. Approach one PSAO about distribution.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SpendMend (MFP Rebate Reconciliation), Plenful (MFP Intelligence / MFP Command Center), ScriptPro Financial Advantage, Liberty Software (and other PMS vendors, e.g. PioneerRx, PrimeRx, Redsail). White space: Verdict: gap, and a narrow one. In roughly 27 searches across varied terms (MFP refund advance, bridge loan, factoring, fintech, PSAO program, wholesaler program) I found NO product that specifically underwrites and advances against MTF-remitted MFP refunds. Pharmacy lenders sell generic A/R and MCA lines, and the MFP players only sell reconciliation. The unserved space is a claim-level underwriting and servicing capability for refund dilution risk: 340B lesser-of rejections (RARC N907 inappropriate rejections), reversals, Good Faith Inquiry disputes, and authorized-generic refund amounts. It is most valuable for borrowers whose float is large: LTC/senior-care pharmacies, 5-50 store groups, and possibly 340B covered entities in the HRSA rebate pilot, where the float is $8.9M-$208M a year for hospitals (Health Affairs). It also applies to the January 2027 step-up when semaglutide joins.

The wedge is weak in five ways.
1. The 'free missing-refund report' is already crowded: SpendMend, Plenful ($76M raised), ScriptPro, Liberty, and free Beacon MFP dashboards.
2. A typical independent's float is small, about $11k a week or $27k a month per NCPA. At 15-25% APR that is roughly $4-7k a year of gross revenue per pharmacy, before losses and a cost of funds of 8-10%. Customer acquisition through state associations and Facebook groups will be costly relative to that.
3. Wholesalers control the payment path. Cardinal routes MFP refunds through Central Pay and wholesalers auto-debit weekly, so a lender's sweep sits behind the wholesaler in practice. Cardinal customers cannot easily direct refunds to a lender-controlled account.
4. 'Non-recourse' is hard to deliver. Manufacturers can reverse refunds and CMS's own materials describe reversals when claims prove ineligible, so a lender will need pharmacy recourse or holdbacks. That undermines the 'prime paper' insight.
5. Policy is a moving target. CMS made manufacturers include cash-flow mitigation plans in their MFP effectuation plans (accelerated refunds, self-identification). NCPA is still pushing CMS and manufacturers for faster payment, including in Sept 2026 comments on the 2028 guidance.

Adjacent generic lenders can also just add MFP refunds to a borrowing base.

Caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) ran out, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and open-source sweeps were not fully run. 'No direct competitor found' means not found, not proven absent.

title: Owner-Side Ordering: The Royalty Asymmetry Calculator
one_liner: An advice-only LINE tool that tells franchise convenience-store owners how many fresh items to order and when to mark them down, using the owner's own payoff instead of HQ's.
customer: Franchise convenience-store owners in Japan, especially the many multi-store owners (roughly 55,000 stores nationally, all three chains). They pay a monthly fee plus a share of the waste they cut. First targets are Osaka owners reachable through the franchisee union and owner LINE groups.
problem: The royalty is charged on gross profit calculated as if discarded food never existed. At Seven, HQ absorbs only 15% of disposal cost and the owner absorbs 85%. So HQ's ordering AI and the field counselors (OFC) push order quantities toward what maximizes HQ's royalty, not the owner's take-home. Take a rice ball that costs ¥100 and sells at ¥160. With a 60% royalty on the ¥60 gross profit, the owner keeps about ¥24 when it sells and loses about ¥85 when it is binned. HQ makes about ¥36 on a sale and loses about ¥15 on a discard. The owner-optimal stocking level is far lower than HQ's, and no owner has a tool that shows this. Markdowns would close much of the gap, but staff are reluctant to apply stickers and owners fear the OFC's disapproval.
solution: The owner photographs the daily disposal-scan printout and the hourly sales sheet, or forwards a CSV. The tool never touches HQ systems. Each afternoon it returns a per-category order guide such as 'cut salmon onigiri by 4 at the 16:00 delivery, add 2 tempura udon'. It also gives a markdown clock, for example 'sticker at 20:40, deeper cut at 23:10', calculated from the owner's actual royalty tier, disposal share and sell-through curve. A one-page 'why I ordered less' printout gives the owner data to answer the OFC. Phase two adds an owner-side dashboard showing true hourly wage after royalty and self-labor. It also adds a contract-exit and renegotiation calculator, and anonymized peer benchmarks that owners can use collectively.
why_now: Osaka's minimum wage rises to ¥1,231 on 1 October 2026, up ¥54 after ¥63 last year. Labor is the biggest cost, and waste is the last controllable line item. HQ-side AI ordering is now the default, so owners increasingly follow machine suggestions they cannot audit. Chains have grudgingly allowed markdowns since the JFTC's 2009 order against Seven-Eleven Japan for obstructing them, but owners still lack tools to price them properly.
revenue_model: ¥4,900 per store per month, plus 20-25% of documented waste reduction for the first 12 months. If a store saves ¥80-100k a month, the fee is easy to justify. Multi-store owners get a bundle. Later revenue comes from an owner-benchmark subscription and referrals to specialist franchise lawyers and accountants.
non_obvious_insight: Waste is not a shared problem between HQ and owner. The contract makes it the owner's problem alone, while HQ's revenue is almost indifferent to it. The newsvendor critical ratio for the owner is about 22%, versus about 70% for HQ. Every 'AI ordering recommendation' is optimized for the wrong party's payoff. Nobody built the owner's-side calculator because owners fear retaliation and VCs assume HQ systems are neutral.
first_30_days: Use my three stores as the lab. Photograph two weeks of disposal sheets and hourly sales, then back-test the newsvendor plus markdown model against what actually happened. Build a LINE bot with photo OCR and a spreadsheet engine. Recruit 10 owners from union chat groups and Facebook franchisee groups. Run a free 4-week gain-share pilot with a signed baseline for each store. Publish a one-page 'royalty asymmetry' explainer that spreads owner-to-owner. Convert the pilot to paid at week 5.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Seven-Eleven Japan AI ordering plus HQ-led markdown (Eco da Ne), Lawson AI.CO (ordering plus AI markdown recommendation), FamilyMart AI Recommend Ordering, Sinops (sinops-CLOUD AI markdown) with Sato. White space: No product found that is an independent owner-side payoff engine for Japanese convenience-store franchisees. Searches in Japanese and English returned no startup, SaaS or app that (a) uses the owner's actual royalty tier and disposal-share contract terms to compute order levels, (b) sets markdown timing from the owner's payoff, or (c) audits HQ AI recommendations against the owner's interest. HQ tools (Seven, Lawson, FamilyMart) cover order and markdown outputs but are HQ-controlled and aimed at waste or sales, not owner take-home. Supermarket AI-markdown vendors (Sinops/Sato, Wasteless) sell to retailers, not franchisees. The union and ex-OFC consultants give advice with no calculators or automation. The unserved wedge is: HQ says X, your own contract math says Y, the yen difference is Z, plus contract-aware multi-store economics. Caveats: (1) Seven-Eleven's new contract (announced June 2026, effective autumn 2027) raises HQ's disposal-loss share from 15% to 50% (with a cap), lowers charge to 53%/67%, applies only to newly opened stores with no conversion planned for existing stores (https://www.ryutsuu.biz/strategy/s061915.html, https://www.watch.impress.co.jp/docs/news/2118977.html). At 50/50 the owner critical ratio rises from about 22% to roughly 36%, so the asymmetry mostly fades on new-contract stores but persists on legacy stores for years. (2) Seven's HQ-led markdown push since 2024 partly commoditizes the markdown clock. (3) The 22% vs 70% math checks out for the 85/15 split, but contract terms differ by chain (Lawson subsidy formula is more complex, FamilyMart is about 15%), so each chain needs its own model. (4) Franchise-agreement limits on data use and third-party tools were not verified.

title: Power Passport: Scoring Dead Factories on Amps, Permits
one_liner: A database and paid inspection report that rates shuttered Midwest plants on the things reshoring manufacturers actually need (utility service, slab, crane, transferable air and discharge permits) instead of square footage.
customer: Reshoring manufacturers and their site-selection consultants (first buyer). Industrial listing brokers and sellers of dead factories (they pay to differentiate their listings). Regional economic-development bodies and utility economic-development teams (annual license).
problem: Brokers list buildings by square feet, clear height and dock doors. A reshoring plant needs enough energized 480V/13.2kV capacity, a slab that can carry presses and large CNCs, crane rails, and a transferable Ohio EPA air permit for a paint or wash line. Greenfield permitting and long-lead transformers and switchgear can add 9-18 months before the first good part. Meanwhile data-center developers are hunting the same brownfield shells for their existing utility service, so the buildings that suit manufacturing are disappearing without either side understanding what was in them.
solution: Build a parcel-level dataset of pre-2005 industrial buildings across Ohio, Pennsylvania, Michigan and Indiana by combining public air and wastewater permit records, county parcel data, utility maps, aerial imagery for crane bays and rail spurs, and Phase I history. Score each building on power, permits, structure and contamination risk. Sell a 'Power Passport': a 12-page report with a licensed industrial electrician's walk-through, gear nameplate photos, permit transferability notes and utility will-serve context, delivered in 5 days.
why_now: The 2026 reshoring wave and the data-center land grab are competing for the same shells. Transformer and switchgear lead times are still measured in many months to years. The gap between what manufacturers need and what listings say is at its widest, and brokers have no tooling to fill it.
revenue_model: $1.5k-$3.5k per Passport (paid by the broker or seller, or by the buyer). A 0.5%-1% success fee on closed industrial deals. $25k-$60k per year data licences to economic-development agencies, utilities and site-selection firms. Later, a capital vehicle that buys the best shells and subdivides them into permitted multi-tenant 'factory condos'.
non_obvious_insight: In a dead Ohio plant the building is the cheapest part. The energized service, the paper permits and the crane rails are the asset, and they are invisible to anyone who has not tried to open a factory. Every reshorer I know lost most of a year to power and permits, not to hiring.
first_30_days: Pick one metro (Akron/Canton or the Mahoning Valley). Pull public Ohio EPA permit records and county parcel data to list 150 candidate buildings. Hire an electrician for 20 walk-throughs at about $150 per hour. Cold-call 25 industrial listing brokers offering a free first Passport in exchange for a testimonial and a right to the data. Convert 3-5 into paying $1.5k reports and one economic-development office into a pilot licence.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Brownfield.ai, Scout (ScoutCities), LandGate, Enverus Site & Screen. White space: Nobody I found productises a building-level, physically verified 'inside-the-fence' record for dead Midwest plants. That record would cover the electrician-verified main service size, voltage, gear age and nameplates, spare capacity, slab and crane-rail condition, the state of the existing air and wastewater permits, and a utility will-serve letter, all in a scored, comparable format sold before the deal. The funded players (LandGate, Enverus, GridCARE, Paces) work at the substation and grid level and are aimed at data centers. Utility and state databases (JobsOhio, AEP, FirstEnergy, ZoomProspector) verify sites and utility service, not building gear or permit status. Scout and Brownfield.ai are the closest competitors, but they look desktop- and network-led with no per-building inspection, and I found no evidence they carry electrician-verified data. The genuine gap is a trusted, standardised, seller-commissioned building electrical and permit record, not the parcel-scoring layer, which is already crowded and funded. The idea's weaker points: the Ohio permit-transferability wedge is thin (see evidence), and it is unproven that brokers will pay $1.5k-$3.5k.

title: Outsourced 24-Hour Vulnerability Reporting Desk (CRA)
one_liner: A retainer service that acts as the manufacturer's PSIRT: it watches for actively exploited vulnerabilities in their products' components and files the 24-hour early warning, follow-up notification and final report to the EU platform.
customer: Connected-device makers with 20-500 employees selling into the EU with no 24/7 security team: smart home, e-bikes and scooters, industrial sensors, routers, wearables, toys, EV chargers. Many are non-EU (US and Asian) firms.
problem: CRA reporting obligations began 11 Sep 2026: 24-hour reporting to ENISA for actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents, with fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. Small makers have no on-call rota, no SBOM monitoring and no idea what 'actively exploited' means for their firmware. The briefing found almost no visible tooling aimed at them.
solution: A retainer that ingests each product's SBOM per firmware version, matches it continuously against exploited-vulnerability and threat feeds, triages 24/7 with a pre-agreed decision tree, and files the early warning, notification and final report with text approved by the client's named contact. It also runs coordinated disclosure and advisory publishing, plus quarterly tabletop drills. Software lets one analyst cover 30+ clients.
why_now: The reporting duty went live 17 days ago and the full regime follows in Dec 2027. Firms are discovering that the deadline is a staffing problem, not a document problem.
revenue_model: EUR 1,500-6,000/month retainer, incident surcharges, and EUR 5k annual tabletop exercises.
non_obvious_insight: A 24-hour clock makes this a staffing obligation, which small firms cannot meet alone but a pooled desk can, like outsourced DPO services. Each reported vulnerability also gives a natural upsell into SBOM and technical-file work.
first_30_days: Partner with two or three EU security consultancies or product-safety associations. Sell a EUR 2.5k one-day 'CRA reporting readiness audit' to 20 firms, convert 5-8 into EUR 2k/month retainers, and contract three part-time analysts across time zones.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: TridentSec (PSIRT-as-a-Service), Finite State (managed CRA service), Cybellum (managed PSIRT / incident response service), Patchstack (managed CRA Article 14 reporting for open source). White space: The genuinely unserved piece is a contractually guaranteed 24/7 desk that files as the client's named Assigned Representative on the SRP, priced for 20-500 person device makers.
- Nobody found sells this in that form. TridentSec sells operations with no stated 24/7 and no published price. Finite State and H-X draft the notice but leave filing to the customer. Cybellum's service targets enterprises. CVD Portal, CRA Evidence and other tools stop at timers and packages, and their final filing is a human step by the customer. Patchstack files as AR but only for open source, and free.
- The intake step is also unserved: nobody takes weekend and night hits on 'is this KEV/EUVD entry in our firmware' and makes the call inside the 24h window.

What is not white space:
- The SBOM-to-CVE matching layer is commoditised. CVD Portal's Reporting tier is EUR 99/mo, and CRACI, Zealience, Regulus and ONEKEY sell the same thing.
- Boutiques and large consultancies can add 'PSIRT retainer' as a line item in weeks.
- The idea's claim that there is 'almost no visible tooling' is wrong. The service layer is thin, but the tooling layer is crowded.

Structural problems to plan around:
- The CRA fine exemption for micro and small enterprises on the 24h deadline (Art 64(10), https://cra-facts.com/penalties) removes the sharpest fear driver for the smallest customers. The 72h and 14-day deadlines still carry fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover.
- The SRP requires each AR to use a personal EU Login with MFA (https://www.enisa.europa.eu/topics/product-security/single-reporting-platform-srp/frequently-asked-questions), so named analysts must sit in the loop.
- Liability stays with the manufacturer, and the desk needs professional indemnity cover.
- The 24h clock starts when the manufacturer becomes aware, so a desk that spots an exploit may start the client's clock.
- An actively exploited vulnerability in one specific product's components is a low-frequency event. The retainer therefore risks being seen as insurance that customers only buy under audit pressure.

title: Renewal Radar for Silent AI Exclusions
one_liner: Track carriers' filed AI exclusions and tell brokers, 90 days before renewal, which clients just lost AI coverage, then place the affirmative buy-back.
customer: Independent agencies and regional brokers (10-200 staff) with commercial books, their E&O carriers, and MGAs.
problem: Since January 2026 ISO-style generative-AI endorsements (CG 40 47 and CG 40 48) and far broader carrier forms, such as W. R. Berkley's 'absolute' AI exclusion, are attached at renewal, often buried. Clients use AI in ways they never disclosed. Brokers carry E&O exposure for failing to warn, and no tool maps which of a broker's 300 clients face AI exclusions or what AI each client actually uses.
solution: A rate and form filing scraper (public SERFF filing access) plus an endorsement parser that normalises exclusion breadth: gen-AI only versus any AI, bodily injury versus advertising injury, vendor-supplied AI. It feeds a renewal calendar imported from agency-management CSVs. A 12-question client AI-use questionnaire, optionally backed by an SSO or expense-report scan for AI tools. Output is a one-page 'AI coverage gap letter' plus a list of affirmative AI markets for placement.
why_now: 1 Jan 2027 renewals are the first big cycle after the Verisk endorsements became available, and AIG, Great American and Berkley filings landed through 2026. Affirmative AI capacity now exists (Armilla via Lloyd's, AIUC, Munich Re aiSure), so a gap and its fix can be sold together.
revenue_model: $250-800 per month per agency, $150-600 per gap letter for non-subscribers, 10-15% commission on affirmative cover placed, and $2-5k per month filing-intelligence subscriptions for MGAs and carriers.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is triggered by their own E&O fear, not curiosity about AI. The filings are public but unreadable, so the moat is a normalised exclusion database nobody at a brokerage has time to build. Silent AI cuts both ways: an unexcluded policy is a reason to ask for affirmative cover, so the gap letter also works as a sales tool for the broker.
first_30_days: Scrape SERFF filings in five large states and build the tracker. Start a free weekly 'AI exclusion tracker' newsletter aimed at 500 brokers. Offer 10 agencies a $500 concierge gap audit on their five biggest accounts. Sign one affirmative-AI MGA for placement referrals.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Patra (AI Policy Checking), Quandri, Zywave Apex / Advisor Agent, Testudo. White space: A real gap remains, but it is much narrower than the pitch. Nobody found sells a commercial-lines, broker-facing workflow that (1) takes a book's actual renewal forms schedules, quotes and binders (not just carrier-level filings), (2) detects and normalises AI exclusion breadth for each client, including bespoke wording such as Berkley PC 51380 and unnamed 'AI' language, (3) ties it to a 90-day renewal calendar, and (4) hands the producer a client-ready gap letter and a matched affirmative placement. Pieces exist separately. Patra reads commercial policies for hidden exclusions but is not AI-specific. Quandri and Zywave own the 90-day renewal trigger but show no exclusion-level AI flagging. Testudo and Armilla offer AI-use mapping and placement but only for their own paper.

Three parts of the plan are weak. (a) The SERFF scraper and exclusion database are not a moat. Trades Coverage already compiled 4,078 records for free. Gridex, Certian, Vorp Labs and ShadowLock publish free trackers, and Certian even ships CC BY 4.0 CSV and JSON. (b) A filing shows a carrier adopted a form in a state. It does not show the form is attached to client X's policy, so the real signal is the policy document, not the filing. (c) SERFF filing access covers admitted markets only. Surplus lines is where most E&O, D&O and tech-E&O AI exclusions sit, and it is largely invisible to SERFF.

Wedge that looks unserved: commercial professional-liability and tech-E&O accounts (design firms, law, accounting, software, agencies) where exclusions are broadest and most bespoke, for independent agencies without an in-house risk-advisory team, priced as a renewal-review add-on rather than a filings database.

title: Finish Crew: Stranded Solar Job Completion
one_liner: A completion contractor that takes half-built solar jobs abandoned by bankrupt installers all the way to permission-to-operate, and is paid by the lenders whose loans go bad while the system sits dark.
customer: Solar loan originators and servicers, and TPO sponsors, that now hold stranded projects. The seven finance partners named in the Freedom Forever order are the first buyers: GoodLeap, EnFin, Credit Human, EverBright, Participate, Project Solar and Sunrun. Credit unions and ABS trustees holding 2023-2025 solar loans are the second wave. Homeowners are the beneficiary but do not pay.
problem: When a big installer dies, thousands of systems are left installed but not energized, or half-built. Freedom Forever went Chapter 11 in April 2026 and converted to Chapter 7 on Aug 7, 2026, with about 1,600 layoffs. The borrower stops paying a $30-50k loan on a roof that produces nothing. Lender, homeowner and dead installer each say it is someone else's job. The court let lenders hire new contractors and push systems to PTO, but a lender has no bench of crews and no playbook for doing it.
solution: Run the work as a records-recovery business first and a crew business second. For each stranded job, build a forensic pack: the AHJ permit file, the utility interconnection record, the design set from the dead company's design and CRM tools, equipment serials from distributors and consignment records, and a site photo audit. Sort jobs into tiers: paperwork-only (contractor of record and engineer's stamp need re-issuing), inspection fix, missing hardware, and never started (unwind and refund path). Price each tier at a fixed fee plus a bonus at PTO, and subcontract the labor to licensed local electricians and laid-off installer crews. Give the lender a dashboard of its whole stranded book with cost to cure and expected PTO date.
why_now: Freedom Forever's Chapter 7 conversion (Aug 2026, creditor claims due Oct 16, 2026) and the court order letting financiers step in make this concrete now. Sunnova (June 2025), SunPower (Aug 2024) and 100+ other solar failures came before it. Post-25D volume is down in 2026, so more failures are likely. Lenders have step-in rights but no operating capacity.
revenue_model: Fixed completion fee of $1.5-4k per job by tier, plus a $500 success bonus at PTO, paid by the lender or servicer. Add a monthly stranded-book dashboard subscription. Later, sell a 12-month workmanship warranty on completed jobs, paid by the lender, and a retainer for standby capacity when the next installer fails.
non_obvious_insight: A stranded job is 80% a records and legal-standing problem, not a labor problem. Permits, interconnection applications, engineer stamps and design files sit in a dead contractor's name and portal logins, so nobody can legally finish even though laid-off crews are cheap and plentiful. Also, the buyer is the lender and not the homeowner. The lender's collateral is worthless while the system is dark, it already has contractual step-in rights, and outsiders assume the homeowner is the customer.
first_30_days: Message loss-mitigation and installer-failure leads at 3-4 lenders. Use former installer ops people on LinkedIn to get the introductions. Offer to complete 10 stranded jobs in one metro at cost-plus, with payment on PTO. Recruit 3 laid-off project managers or permit coordinators and 1-2 licensed electrician subs. Write the per-AHJ and per-utility contractor-of-record transfer checklist. Target the first 10 PTOs inside 60 days, with case studies from them.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: GreenLancer (Solar Repair / O&M network), Lender in-house step-in (GoodLeap, Sunrun, EverBright, EnFin, Credit Human, Participate, Project Solar; also Dividend Finance), Atma Energy (installer taking over stranded Freedom Forever jobs), Local rescue and completion contractors (Revival Solar, ECG Solar, Optimus Energy Solutions, Advance Solar, Solar Discovery). White space: The unserved wedge is portfolio-level, event-driven triage, not crews. (1) Forensic records recovery at scale. No competitor found sells a forensic pack per stranded loan (AHJ permit file, utility interconnection record, dead installer's CRM and design files, distributor and consignment serials, photo audit) sorted into cure tiers with a cost-to-cure and expected-PTO dashboard across a lender's whole book. GreenLancer and the local rescue firms all work job by job. (2) Servicers, credit unions and ABS trustees without operations. The seven Freedom Forever financiers have ops teams, and Sunrun and GoodLeap have crews. Solar Servicing LLC (which took over Mosaic's servicing), credit unions, bank holders and ABS investors have no step-in playbook. I found no completion vendor aimed at them. (3) Legacy stranded books. Titan (an estimated 150,000 households), SunPower, Sunnova, PosiGen, Mosaic-financed loans and others. Lenders may not know which loans sit on de-energized systems, so an identify-then-cure offer has little competition. (4) Standby retainer plus pre-negotiated per-AHJ and per-utility contractor-of-record transfer playbooks for the next failure. Not white space: the first-wave Freedom Forever completion work. The stay-relief order dates to about August 2026, so the seven named financiers have probably already picked contractors, and GreenLancer says it already serves seven financiers.

title: Private Road Associations in a Box
one_liner: Turn the neighbors' informal, cash-in-a-coffee-can road fund into a recorded, insurable road association with dues, reserves and competitively bid plowing and grading.
customer: Households on private roads and shared driveways (5-60 homes per road). The urgent buyers are the real estate attorneys, title agents and listing agents whose closings stall without an enforceable road maintenance agreement.
problem: Millions of rural households reach their homes by private roads maintained by handshake. One neighbor plows, some chip in, some free-ride. Washouts and disputes are common. Lenders and title insurers often want a recorded, enforceable maintenance agreement, so sales stall. HOA software assumes an incorporated HOA with a manager, not 12 neighbors and a gravel road.
solution: Fixed-fee formation: map who benefits, draft a state-specific maintenance agreement, record it with the county, and set up a simple legal entity or association where state law allows. Then recurring service: ACH dues collection with reminders and lien-based enforcement where allowed, a reserve fund, standing bids from vetted plow, gravel and grading contractors, a photo log of road condition, and storm-damage documentation packages for county or FEMA requests.
why_now: Post-2020 in-migration put many remote workers on rural private roads. Extreme-weather washouts, such as Hurricane Helene's damage to private roads and bridges in western North Carolina in 2024, showed how many neighborhoods have no entity that can pool money or apply for repair aid. Lenders and insurers keep tightening property-access checks. No vertical software serves informal neighbor groups.
revenue_model: $1,500-3,000 formation fee, paid by the neighborhood or by the seller at closing. $12-25 per household per month for dues administration. A disclosed 5-8% procurement fee on managed contractor bids.
non_obvious_insight: The customer with urgency isn't the neighborhood but the closing. A failed sale costs a seller and an agent five figures, so attorneys and agents will send you deals for a flat fee. Recurring revenue then comes from dues float and admin. At 200 associations you are the largest single buyer of plowing and gravel in a region, which gives you procurement leverage no individual road has.
first_30_days: Pick a state dense with private roads (Maine, Vermont, New Hampshire, or the North Carolina mountains). Get an attorney to draft a reusable agreement template. Partner with 3-5 real estate attorneys and title agents who see failed closings. Sell a $1,500 'closing rescue' formation package. Run 2 pilot associations with free dues collection for 6 months to prove the workflow.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: PayHOA, Mainstream HOA and community-association platforms (Buildium, AppFolio, FrontSteps, Vantaca, CINC and similar), DIY legal templates and local real estate attorneys (Nolo, US Legal Forms, LegalZoom-style forms, local attorney drafting), Public alternatives: state road-association statutes and county road or special-assessment districts. White space: Tentative. Coverage was thin, so absence of a dedicated venture-backed product is not proven. What I found unserved:
1. No product I could find bundles the closing-triggered legal package (state-specific maintenance agreement, county recording, a lightweight entity) with the ongoing administration for informal neighbor groups. PayHOA covers dues admin generically and cheaply; the statutes and the law-firm and forms market cover formation; nobody stitches them together for the 5-60 home private road.
2. Competitively bid, pooled procurement of plowing and gravel across many associations. I found no tool for it.
3. Storm-damage documentation and an organized entity ready for state or FEMA private-road aid. NC's program required a single point of contact, ownership proof and a 50% HOA cost share, so unorganized roads were poorly placed to claim.
4. The transaction-channel distribution (attorneys, title agents and listing agents at a stalled closing) looks unowned by software vendors.

Weak points:
- The recurring $12-25 per household per month is 6-12 times PayHOA's roughly $2 per household.
- Lien-based enforcement is state-dependent. NC's G.S. 136-102.6 only requires disclosure of who maintains private streets, and my Maine excerpt covered assessment authority but not liens.
- Holding dues float triggers trust-accounting and money-handling rules.
- The 5-8% procurement fee creates a conflict of interest.

title: Dry-Hole Atlas for Hydrogen, Helium, Geothermal
one_liner: Re-read a century of scanned well logs and gas analyses, once treated as junk, to find natural hydrogen, helium and hot rock, and sell the resulting atlas to exploration companies by area of interest.
customer: Junior exploration companies and VC-backed developers in natural hydrogen, helium and geothermal (and lithium-brine plays), plus land and mineral-lease advisors who need leads. They pay for subscriptions and area-of-interest data packs.
problem: The US has millions of drilled wells. Old records include gas analyses, bottom-hole temperatures, water chemistry and mud-log shows, mostly recorded as incidental noise by oil and gas operators. They sit as scanned TIFFs and PDFs at state geological surveys and core repositories. New subsurface commodities need exactly this once-discarded information. Oil-and-gas data vendors index hydrocarbon fields, not hydrogen, helium or heat, and small explorers cannot afford to hire teams to dig through archives across 30 state surveys.
solution: A scan-to-structured-data pipeline across public state survey archives. Extract gas composition (hydrogen, helium, nitrogen), bottom-hole temperature and depth, and brine chemistry. Geolocate every record, correct for known temperature-log biases, and publish a queryable map atlas with prospectivity layers per township or section. Sell by area of interest. Offer custom queries such as 'every well within 20 miles of this substation with more than 0.3% helium and temperature above 150 C at 3 km'.
why_now: AI data centers are driving huge demand for clean firm power, and geothermal developers are raising large rounds and signing hyperscaler offtakes. Natural hydrogen exploration has attracted venture money and government attention. Helium supply has been unstable and prices volatile. Vision-language models now extract tables from old scans cheaply, and state surveys are increasingly open to releasing data.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of 15-50k USD per year per company for a basin or state atlas, area-of-interest packs of 5-25k USD, custom data services, and, later, small overriding royalties or success fees on leases won using the data.
non_obvious_insight: The value of data flips when the target commodity changes. A well that reported 'gas contains 40% hydrogen' in 1935 was a dud then, and it is a discovery lead today. Every incumbent data vendor is organized around the old commodity, so nobody re-reads the archive for byproducts. The archives are public and low-margin for the state agencies that hold them, so the moat is the extraction pipeline, cleaning and geological calibration, not data access.
first_30_days: Pick one state survey with well-documented public scans and gas-analysis reports and one target commodity (helium or hydrogen shows are the easiest to demo). Build a proof-of-concept map for one basin using a few thousand well records. Cold-email about 30 junior exploration companies and geothermal developers with the map and one concrete lead they can check. Sell 3-5 area-of-interest packs at around 5k USD each, and ask for pre-payment for the next state.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: USGS/BLM Natural Gas Compositional Analyses Dataset (free), USGS Geologic Hydrogen Prospectivity Map Explorer, SMU / NGDS heat-flow and corrected bottom-hole-temperature database (now on the DOE Geothermal Data Repository), Project InnerSpace GeoMap. White space: The wedge that remains is narrow but real. Nobody found sells page-level, provenance-linked hydrogen, helium and heat evidence extracted from the unstructured parts of old well files. That means mud-log gas shows, drill-stem-test and production-test reports, driller notes such as non-flammable gas, and water-well gas, all at lease-block or section level. The free datasets (USGS/BLM, SMU/GDR, KGS) already cover the structured gas-analysis and corrected-BHT layers, so a paid product cannot rest on those. The USGS roughly 16,000 He-bearing points and the 30,000 corrected BHT wells are a free baseline that any paid product has to beat. The Paris Basin OCR study found only 26 wells with H2 detection out of about 5,000 in the database (0.5%), which suggests few real leads per basin. Unserved specifics: (1) the 20-30 state and provincial archives whose scans are not yet digitized, with a defensible per-record confidence grade (sampling method, air contamination, analytical era); (2) one integrated He, H2 and heat layer, where the players found each cover a single commodity; (3) delivery to small juniors, landmen and lease advisors who cannot fund in-house teams. Koloma, Zanskar, HyTerra and MAX Power already do this in-house, so the addressable buyers are the smaller players (AKAP counts 123 companies in natural hydrogen, Rystad counted 40) plus the lease and land side.

title: Settlement Passports for Florida High-Rise Condos
one_liner: A satellite-radar settlement history for every Florida condo tower, sold as the cheap first page of the milestone-inspection and reserve-study file.
