A rehearsal also works where estate planning fails, because people avoid 'planning' but will attend a scheduled drill.
first_30_days: Recruit 3-5 RIAs through advisor communities and podcasts. Run drills by hand with a spreadsheet and printed binder for each firm's 10 oldest couples. Record time-to-locate-accounts and the number of single-point-of-failure findings. Charge a $2.5K pilot fee and turn the findings into a retention case study the advisor can show prospects.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Empathy (LifeVault + Loss Support), Everplans (Enterprise / advisor channel), Trustworthy (Family Operating System), Wealth.com. White space: Nobody found sells the specific wedge: a facilitated, scheduled couples rehearsal of the first spouse's death, run by the advisor's team. That means simulating each spouse's death in turn with the surviving spouse actually doing the tasks; a survivor-point-of-view audit of titling, beneficiaries, autopays and password single points of failure; pre-agreed day 3/14/45/90 advisor check-ins; and a firm dashboard of drill completion and exposure. Vaults (Empathy, Everplans, Trustworthy) and estate-document platforms (Wealth.com, Vanilla) store information and generate documents, but their pages describe no behavioral ritual, no survivor-POV stress test and no post-death outreach cadence. Independent RIAs at $150M-$2B AUM are also not Empathy's core buyer (insurers, banks and big wealth firms). Caveats: I did not confirm that Empathy lacks scheduled outreach (its Connect page 404'd), and I could not check consultant-led widow-retention programs (see the note under evidence_of_demand). The software layer is commoditized (Trustworthy at $10 per client per year), so the defensible white space is the ritual, the audit method and the outreach cadence, not the vault.

title: Ruling-Backed Tariff Engineering for Product Brands
one_liner: A productized design-and-ruling service that helps mid-market brands legitimately re-spec products across tariff-line boundaries and locks the result in with a CBP binding ruling.
customer: Mid-market consumer and industrial product brands with $10-100M in revenue and at least $1-2M in annual duty spend: footwear, bags, apparel accessories, home goods, hardware, e-bike and powersports parts, and other products with metal components.
problem: Adjacent tariff lines can differ by tens of percentage points, and the 2025-26 regime made the gaps bigger. Section 232 metals lists keep expanding and being recalibrated, and copper smelt-and-cast reporting started July 30, 2026. Yet brokers are asked for a classification only after the tooling is cut and the design is frozen. Product teams never learn that a small change in materials, construction, packaging or set composition can legally change the line. Importers also avoid asking CBP for rulings, assuming it is slow or risky.
solution: Sell two steps. First, a fixed-fee HTS boundary audit: map the top SKUs to the classification tests, spec thresholds and comparable public CBP rulings that determine the line, and list the small design or packaging changes that would legitimately move each one. Second, an engineering sprint with the supplier that documents the changed product and files a CBP binding ruling request under 19 CFR Part 177. The deliverable is a ruling letter, which is a lasting shield for reasonable-care defense. Add a ruling-watch subscription that alerts brands when CBP issues a ruling on competitor or adjacent products.
why_now: The IEEPA reversal shifted the burden to product-specific tariffs (Section 232 and 301) where design details matter. The July 2026 copper reporting and the rewritten 232 valuation rules make product composition a compliance and cost variable. Brands are in a rare window when rate spreads are large enough that redesign pays for itself in one production run.
revenue_model: $4,500 boundary audit for five SKUs; $18-35k per engineering sprint including ruling preparation and filing; optional success fee of about 10% of first-year duty savings, capped. Ruling-watch subscription of $500-$2,000 a month.
non_obvious_insight: Classification turns on physical facts of the article as imported, and those facts are set by designers, not brokers. The most valuable document in a tariff war is a dull letter from CBP's ruling office, and requests cost nothing to file. Tariff engineering is legal when the product really changes, and it requires evidence, which is where a broker's habit of documenting everything matters. Trade lawyers do this ad hoc for large clients, but nobody packages it for mid-market brands at design stage.
first_30_days: Pick two verticals with high design freedom and large rate spreads. Use public CBP rulings to build a boundary map for a prospect's own top SKU as a free sample. Cold-email 40 product, sourcing and COO leads at $10-100M brands with their own sample map. Sell three $4,500 boundary audits and use them to select the first ruling filings. Sign a trade lawyer as reviewing counsel on the ruling requests.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Tarifflo, Flexport (Customs Suite, AI Customs Classification, trade advisory, tariff refund claims), Zonos (Classify), Trademo (Global Trade Management). White space: Verified by fetches, with caveats below. No fetched page showed anyone selling a packaged, fixed-fee, design-stage (pre-tooling) HTS boundary audit for mid-market product brands ($10-100M revenue). None showed a bundled CBP binding-ruling filing with counsel review, or a ruling-watch product built on comparable-ruling analysis.

Software players (Zonos, Trademo, Descartes, Flexport) classify existing products. Tarifflo recovers past overpayments. Big-4 and law firms sell hourly advisory to large clients. A mid-market design-team buyer at the pre-tooling stage looks unserved.

Caveats that cap confidence:
1. The 200-call web search budget ran out before any search ran. Nothing was searched for boutique tariff-engineering consultancies, startups, YC or Crunchbase entries, Product Hunt, or open-source tools.
2. Several vendor fetches failed or returned thin pages: Altana, Avalara, Sandler Travis, Crowell, KPMG, Thomson Reuters, Expeditors and CROSS features.
3. So 'nobody does this exactly' is unproven. A specialist boutique or a well-funded new entrant may exist.

Structural risks that shrink the white space:
- Per 19 CFR 177.2, CBP rulings are limited to prospective transactions and require a full factual statement, samples and photos.
- Per 19 CFR 177.9, a ruling binds CBP only for the addressee and only for identical articles. Third parties cannot rely on it, and CBP can modify or revoke it without notice to anyone else.
- A classification ruling does not protect against Section 232 list changes. The lists are recalibrated and CBP treats sets by their primary classifying article. Redesigning across a line can be undone if the new line is later added to the list.

title: China-Asset Diligence Desk for Pharma BD
one_liner: A bilingual scientist-plus-software sprint that verifies China-sourced drug packages (raw data, GLP and CMC standing, ownership chain) in 72 hours for US buyers.
customer: Pharma BD&L teams, NewCo-building VCs, royalty funds and mid-cap biotechs in-licensing Chinese assets.
problem: About one-third of 2025 licensing spend involved China-sourced drugs (Jefferies) and the pace accelerated in 2026 (Lilly-InnoCare up to $3.35B, Merck-SciBrunch $2.1B). Diligence infrastructure looks thin (inference): data packages are in Chinese formats, raw-data and audit-trail norms differ, and CRO and CDMO GLP or GMP standing is hard to verify. BIOSECURE, enacted Dec 18, 2025, requires OMB to publish the list of biotechnology companies of concern by December 2026 and FAR rules follow, adding an ownership and supply-chain axis.
solution: A fixed-price 'Asset Verification Sprint'. LLM-assisted translation and structured extraction of study reports. Bilingual scientists spot-check raw data and audit trails. Verify CRO and CDMO inspection histories (NMPA, FDA, EMA) and check ownership chains against the BIOSECURE lists. Deliver a Western-format gap analysis for IND-enabling needs (GLP tox acceptability, CMC comparability).
why_now: Deal flow is at record levels, BIOSECURE list publication is due in about three months, and biopharma layoffs (15,000+) free bilingual ex-pharma scientists.
revenue_model: $25-70k per sprint, $150-300k annual retainers for NewCo-builder VCs, and supply-chain mapping as a second product once the BIOSECURE lists land.
non_obvious_insight: The gap is not legal or financial diligence. It is data literacy and tacit standards, for example what counts as GLP-grade raw data, and Western deal associates cannot read the packages. The same team and database serve a second product, supply-chain mapping, when the lists arrive.
first_30_days: Recruit 3-4 bilingual ex-pharma scientists. Price a $20k pilot sprint. Approach 5 NewCo VC platforms and 5 mid-size pharma BD heads. Build a CRO and CDMO inspection database from public regulator records.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Alacrita (biotech consulting network), Patsnap Synapse (AI drug asset due diligence reports), Pharmcube (Yaozhi / Pharma Insight consulting), Locust Walk / Banyan BioInnovations. White space: Nobody found sells what the idea specifies: a fixed-price, bilingual scientist-led verification of a China-sourced drug package's raw data and audit trails, GLP-tox acceptability for a US IND, CMC comparability, and CRO/CDMO standing, delivered as a Western-format gap memo for buyers with no China bench. What exists is adjacent. Data platforms (Pharmcube, Patsnap, Evaluate/Norstella) and AI screening do sourcing and public-data diligence. Investment banks (Locust Walk) and law firms (Sidley, Foley Hoag, Morgan Lewis) do deal access, legal and IP. General biotech consultancies (Alacrita) do generic diligence with no China raw-data focus. Redica sells inspection data. Patsnap's own sample report says binding deals still need source-data review, which points at the wedge. The underserved buyers are NewCo-building VCs below RA Capital or Banyan scale, mid-cap biotechs and royalty funds with no Shanghai presence. Two weaknesses to plan around: (1) the inspection database is a commodity (Redica, and the FDA has promised to publish more foreign-site inspection findings), and BIOSECURE list tracking overlaps with Kharon and Interos, so the moat has to be scientist judgment and trust, not software; (2) seller data access is a bottleneck. Locust Walk's CEO says 'getting data out of the company can be challenging', and China's data-export and human-genetic-resources rules (Morgan Lewis playbook) may block raw-data transfer. The 72-hour promise will be hard unless the seller supplies a data room. Coverage caveat: I could not run WebSearch (session budget exhausted), so I relied on Google News RSS, direct fetches of vendor sites and the YC directory. Stealth boutiques and Big-4 or CRO consulting units were not exhaustively checked.

title: Unwind Desk for California's 3-Day Car Return
one_liner: A per-return concierge that unwinds a cancelled used-car deal (lender, add-on administrators, DMV, sales tax, commissions) inside California's new 48-hour refund deadline. It then turns the return data into a return-risk pool.
customer: California used-car dealers, especially independents and BHPH lots that sell 30 to 200 used cars a month and have no back-office bench. They pay $195 to $250 per return, or a standby retainer. Later, insurers and MGAs buy the underwriting data.
problem: From Oct 1, 2026, SB 766 gives buyers a 3-day right to cancel a used vehicle priced at $50,000 or less. Within 48 hours of cancellation the dealer must cancel the contract and refund the buyer, less only the deductions the law allows for mileage and damage. That is easy to write and very hard to do. The cost of an unwind is the cascade, not the car. The dealer has to reach the lender that has funded or is holding the contract, cancel each service contract and GAP with its administrator, and charge back the F&I commission. It also has to reverse the title, registration and sales tax, refund the down payment and any trade, and document the vehicle condition to justify any deduction. Independents have never done this at volume, and one botched unwind creates a refund violation and a private-plaintiff claim.
solution: Unwind-as-a-service. The dealer forwards the cancellation notice. The desk runs a checklist workflow that notifies the lender, submits cancellations to administrators with the correct pro-rata or full-refund basis, prepares the DMV and tax reversals, calculates the refund and permitted deductions, and produces a compliance file that meets the two-year retention rule. A delivery-day photo and video capture link is bundled, because permitted deductions depend on condition documentation. After 6 months of volume, the desk holds the only dataset on return rates, timing and loss per return in a mandatory-return regime. That data is enough to price a per-unit return-risk cover (roughly $60 to $120 per used unit) through a licensed MGA or insurer partner.
why_now: The law takes effect Oct 1, 2026, so the first returns arrive within days. No US state has had a mandatory 3-day return on used cars at this scale. The 2025 to 2026 run of subprime stress, roughly 30% of trade-ins underwater and repossessions at about 3M a year, means many buyers will discover mid-week that they can't afford the payment. That is the buyer most likely to use the cancellation right.
revenue_model: Flat fee per processed return ($195 to $250). Standby retainer of about $99 per month per store for priority handling. Phase 2: 10 to 20% of premium as an MGA on the return-risk pool. Phase 3: license the cancellation-cascade workflow to DMS and eContract vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody knows the real return rate. Everyone models it on Carvana's 7-day return, but the buyers who return are not typical, because the F&I office sees payment shock and buyer's remorse first. A 48-hour refund deadline is shorter than the time a lender, administrator or DMV normally takes to process anything, so the dealer's exposure is process failure, not vehicle depreciation. Whoever owns the process owns the data, and the data is what makes the insurance product priceable.
first_30_days: Write the cascade checklist by state and by lender for the 20 most common California indirect lenders and 15 administrators. Approach the California Independent Automobile Dealers Association and 10 high-volume independents. Sell a $99 per month standby plan with a guaranteed 24-hour turnaround per return. Handle the first 20 returns manually with a shared spreadsheet and e-sign before writing any software. Log every step's time and dollar cost, since that log becomes the actuarial dataset.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ComplyAuto (exclusively licensed by CNCDA), CDK Global (DMS), CNCDA (California New Car Dealers Association), DealerCenter (DMS for independent dealers). White space: Research limitation: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200), so no searches were run. That means no Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or forum searches, and no search for startups by name. Everything below comes from direct WebFetch of about 30 primary and vendor URLs, with model-generated page summaries. I found NO dedicated 'unwind-as-a-service' for CARS Act cancellations, but I cannot rule out a small startup. Re-run the startup and forum searches before committing.

The idea's premise is weaker than written. Statute text (SB 766, Civ. Code 1784.43, 1784.31(g), 1784.44, as returned by WebFetch and quoted verbatim by the summarizer):
1. The 48-hour duty is only to cancel the contract and refund the buyer. The dealer 'is not responsible for any delays outside the control of the dealer, including delays attributable to the processing of a refund by a bank, credit card company, or other financial institution.' Check payments get a 2-business-day delay. Lender and administrator lag therefore does not create violation exposure. The exposure is the dealer's cash float and its own process failures.
2. The statute lists no duty to cancel service contracts or GAP within 48 hours. The add-on cascade is a business and recovery problem, governed by existing law and contract terms. It is not a statutory deadline.
3. Permitted deductions are formulaic: a restocking fee of 1.5% of price (min $200, max $600), plus $1 per mile over 250 (capped at $150), plus trade-in liens. They are not damage-based. The claim that permitted deductions depend on condition documentation, which justifies the photo and video capture bundle, does not hold up. What does matter is the 400-mile eligibility gate and the trade-in refund rule. If the trade-in is already sold or in title transfer, the refund is the greater of the agreed value, the sale price, or fair market value.
4. Remedies are non-exclusive (1784.22). No explicit private right of action or civil penalty was found. Enforcement runs through DAs, city attorneys and the DMV, plus existing consumer laws.
5. Dealers already run unwinds. California had a 2-day contract cancellation option with a 2-day refund including sales tax (Veh. Code 11713.21), repealed effective Oct 1, 2026. Failed-financing spot-delivery unwinds are also routine (from my background knowledge, not verified here). Buy-here-pay-here lots hold their own paper, so they have no lender cascade at all. The $195 to $250 per-return price competes with a title clerk or F&I manager plus a DMS 'reverse deal' function.

What remains unserved:
(a) Independent, indirect-financed dealers with no back-office bench. Compliance vendors and associations found are aimed at franchised dealers or at pricing, ad and disclosure compliance.
(b) A per-return calculator and checklist: restocking fee, mileage, the trade-in 'greater of three' refund, lender payoff, F&I commission chargeback, and the administrator-by-administrator cancellation basis, with timers and a 2-year compliance file.
(c) Above all, the dealer's economic loss per return. Dealers lost the fee they could charge for the old cancellation option ($75 to $250 or 1%). Restocking is now capped at $200 to $600, against recon, carrying cost and resale loss. Nobody was found pricing or covering that loss.

title: Data Act Broker for Equipment Owners
one_liner: File and operationalize EU Data Act data-access demands so independent service shops can finally read the diagnostics that elevator, heat-pump, forklift and tractor makers lock away.
customer: Independent maintenance and service companies in the EU (starting with elevator/escalator maintainers, then commercial heat-pump installers, forklift and ag-machinery shops). They pay per monitored asset per month. Equipment-owning businesses (building managers, hospitals, logistics sites) are the secondary payer, because they hold the legal right.
problem: Original manufacturers use exclusive access to machine diagnostics and fault logs to keep 60-80% of the lucrative service market. Independents work blind, so they lose contracts to OEMs. The EU Data Act (applicable since 12 Sep 2025) gives the user of a connected product, including a business, the right to get the data the product generates. The user can also have it handed to any third party of their choice. In practice almost nobody exercises the right. The paperwork is unfamiliar, OEMs stall, and the data arrives in a different format from every vendor.
solution: An agency-plus-plumbing service. (1) Sign a user-authorization letter with the equipment owner. (2) Auto-generate and file the Article 4/5 access and third-party-sharing requests to each OEM and track statutory response deadlines. (3) Ingest whatever comes back, whether an API, a file dump or a portal export. (4) Normalize it into one cross-vendor schema per asset class. (5) Give the independent shop a fleet-health dashboard and fault-prediction alerts. Add a public compliance scorecard showing which OEMs comply, and escalate the ones that do not to national enforcement authorities.
why_now: The Data Act became applicable on 12 Sep 2025. On 12 Sep 2026, 16 days ago, its design obligation started applying to newly placed connected products, so data must be accessible by default. The right-to-repair movement is at peak momentum. OEM stonewalling now generates complaints that regulators must act on. No one has industrialized user-side requests yet, so the first mover sets the standard schema and templates.
revenue_model: Setup fee of about 50-150 EUR per asset for the request and integration work, plus 4-12 EUR per asset per month for the normalized feed and health analytics. Add-ons: predictive-maintenance alerts and a white-label owner portal. Later: sell anonymized cross-fleet reliability benchmarks to insurers and asset owners.
non_obvious_insight: A legal right is worthless until someone industrializes exercising it. The Data Act gives the data-access key to the owner, not the repairer, so the winning business acts as the owner's agent and sells the result to the repairer. The moat is accumulated request templates, OEM-by-OEM response knowledge, and one normalized schema. Every OEM refusal also becomes evidence for regulators, which turns compliance friction into marketing.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical and one country pair, for example independent elevator maintainers in Germany and the Netherlands, and reach them through trade associations. Retain a Data Act lawyer for a fixed fee to finalize request templates. Recruit 5 independent shops, get user-authorization letters covering about 50 units, and file the requests. Log every OEM response and format. Charge a pilot fee of about 1-2k EUR per shop for delivered data plus a first fleet report. Publish an OEM response-time tracker to build inbound demand. Expect uneven enforcement, so keep the pilot to OEMs that respond and use the ones that stonewall as regulator evidence.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: High Mobility, agrirouter (cross-manufacturer agricultural data exchange), Jaltest / Cojali (Jaltest Diagnostics and Jaltest Telematics), OEM-owned platforms (KONE API portal; Otis ONE, Schindler Ahead and TK Elevator MAX are from my background knowledge and not verified this session). White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was already exhausted when this check started, so I ran 0 of the 6-12 planned searches. Crunchbase, YC, TechCrunch and Product Hunt were not checked, and Crunchbase returned 403. The verdict rests on direct page fetches and GitHub searches only, so treat 'gap' as moderate-to-low confidence. Re-run with the budget raised before committing money.

Within those limits, I found no product that files Data Act Article 4/5 requests on an equipment owner's behalf, tracks OEM responses, and normalises the returns across OEMs for independent service shops. Every adjacent player is either an OEM platform, cars-only (High Mobility), farmer-facing (agrirouter), on-site diagnostics (Jaltest), or OEM-side compliance code (GitHub kits). Genuinely unserved: (1) the owner-mandate plus request workflow, (2) an OEM-by-OEM response and refusal log, (3) a cross-OEM schema for lifts, heat pumps and forklifts, (4) the independent maintainer as the paying customer.

Structural weaknesses to fix in the idea:
- No fixed response deadline. As I recall Articles 4-5, data holders must respond 'without undue delay'. I could not fetch EUR-Lex to confirm (its WAF blocked me), but the idea's 'track statutory response deadlines' looks wrong.
- Article 5(1) lets 'a party acting on behalf of a user' request data. The independent shop can therefore file the request itself with a signed mandate. The broker's moat is then normalisation and OEM knowledge, not legal standing. Model letters and the Commission FAQ (v1.4, 22 Jan 2026) will commoditise the templates.
- Article 9 lets OEMs charge data recipients reasonable compensation, with a cost cap for SMEs, so OEMs may bill the shops you serve.
- Only 'readily available data' is covered. OEMs will argue that diagnostics are derived data, or invoke trade-secret and security refusals under Article 4(6)-(8). Safety-critical elevators are the likeliest place for a security argument.
- Article 4(1) design-by-default applies only to newly placed products, and old lifts often have no OEM connectivity.
- Tractors and other ag machinery may already have sector-specific repair-information access rules under type-approval law (Reg. 167/2013, from memory, unverified), which weakens ag as a beachhead.

title: Continuity Retainer for One-Licensee Funeral Homes
one_liner: Key-person insurance for funeral homes: a bench of pre-credentialed licensed directors and embalmers who step in within 24-48 hours when the owner is sick, burned out or gone, with a built-in path to succession.
customer: Independent and rural funeral homes with one or two licensed staff (roughly 30-150 calls a year), typically owner-operators aged 55-75. A second buyer is the family of an owner who has died or fallen ill and needs the home kept legal while it is sold.
problem: States require a licensed funeral director or manager-in-charge, and often a licensed embalmer, for an establishment to operate. The owner is on call 24/7/365 and hasn't had a real week off in years. One heart attack, surgery or burnout means the home cannot legally operate, families get funneled to the consolidator down the road, and a business built over three generations is sold at a distressed price. Informal 'relief director' phone lists exist, but there is no bench, no contract, no reciprocity or board paperwork handled, and no guarantee anyone answers at 3 a.m.
solution: Recruit retired and semi-retired licensed directors and embalmers, including many leaving consolidators, and pre-credential them in a target state cluster with background checks and reciprocity filings. Sell continuity retainers that guarantee a set number of coverage days a year (real vacations, weekends off) plus emergency activation within 24-48 hours at a day rate. The company handles the state-board notice of interim manager changes. A succession track lets an interim operator or next-generation licensed buyer convert into a partner or buyer with seller financing, so owners have an alternative to a roll-up.
why_now: Consolidation keeps shrinking the independent pool (SCI alone bought about 22 funeral homes and 2 cemeteries for roughly $101M in 2025). The licensed workforce is aging while mortuary-school pipelines are thin. Rising cremation lowers revenue per case, making full-time second hires unaffordable for small homes. Rural closures are creating 'funeral deserts'. Many states have passed occupational-license recognition laws that make multi-state relief staffing easier.
revenue_model: Retainer of $900-$2,000/month per home including N coverage days. Activation day rate of $800-$1,400 billed to the home, with a 25-30% margin over what the licensee is paid. Per-case fees for trade embalming and prep-room services. A 1-2% success fee on succession transactions.
non_obvious_insight: The real asset of an independent funeral home isn't the building, it's one license holder with a phone, and that is a single point of failure. Consolidators know it and wait. Owners will pay to sleep: this is a wellness and continuity product disguised as staffing, and its best feature is the succession pipeline it creates once a trusted operator is already inside the home.
first_30_days: Recruit eight retired licensed directors and embalmers through state association chapters and retiree groups. Check each state board's rules for temporary manager-in-charge designation. Pitch 20 one-licensee homes in two adjacent counties at a $1,200/month founding rate with a 'test weekend off' guarantee. Sign the first three, and run the first covered weekend within 30 days to produce a testimonial.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: NFDA Funeral Career Hub and NFDA recruiting services, NFDA succession planning member resources and SESCO HR consulting, Selected Independent Funeral Homes (staff recruitment and Selected Transfer Services), American Mortuary Service (trade embalming and removals, Dallas/Fort Worth). White space: Caveat first: this verdict has low-to-moderate confidence. The WebSearch budget for the session was already exhausted (200 of 200), so none of the planned 6-12 searches ran. I did not use WebFetch on a search engine to get around the limit. All I did was fetch about 15 specific vendor and industry URLs. Most guessed domains did not resolve, and the ones that resolved were adjacent players, not direct competitors. "No direct competitor found" therefore means "not found with a very limited method", not "verified absent".

What the limited evidence supports as unserved: (1) A contracted, pre-credentialed, multi-state bench with a guaranteed activation SLA. The only related products I could confirm are a job board (NFDA), an association recruiting and transfer program (Selected), trade embalming vendors (American Mortuary Service) and member-only succession content (NFDA). None of them takes on the license-holder single point of failure. (2) The bundled path from interim operator to succession buyer with seller financing. I found nobody offering it, and it is the strongest differentiator because it turns a cost centre into a deal pipeline.

Risks I could not verify and that could still kill or reshape the idea, all of which come from the idea file and general reasoning, not from research:
- State law. Many boards tie the establishment license to a named manager-in-charge who must be there full-time or on premises, and some have short or no temporary-designation windows. If temporary designation is unavailable in the target states, the 24-48 hour activation promise fails legally. Check this first, state by state.
- Adverse selection and price. $10.8k-24k a year is roughly 2-8% of revenue for a home doing 30-150 calls, and a retainer is bought mostly by owners who feel at risk.
- Liability, insurance and non-solicit exposure when a stranger runs someone else's establishment.
- Supply. A bench of eight retirees has to be dense enough to reach homes in rural counties within 24 hours, so density in one cluster matters more than breadth.

title: Shared-Aide Pods for 55+ Apartment Buildings
one_liner: One on-site aide team serves 6-10 residents in the same building, delivering assisted-living-style help at a fraction of 1:1 home-care cost.
customer: Owners and operators of independent-living and 55+ apartment buildings (market-rate, senior LIHTC and HUD-202 properties). The payers are middle-income residents and their families, who can't afford $75-130k a year and are stuck on waitlists.
problem: Home care is sold as one aide per client per hour ($35 an hour, about $80k a year for 44 hours a week) only because of legacy billing. Assisted living is at 90% occupancy with almost no new supply before 2030. Residents who age past independent living either move out or go without.
solution: A licensed home-care agency subsidiary (or partnership with one) posts 2-3 aides per shift inside the building. They run scheduled 15-45 minute ADL, medication-reminder, meal-setup and toileting visits, plus overnight response. Dispatch software handles acuity tiers and in-building routing (floors, elevators). Residents buy monthly tiers of about $1,800-3,500, and the property gets a retention amenity.
why_now: NIC MAP shows 57 of 99 metros above 90% occupancy, units under construction at a 2012 low, and no meaningful new supply before 2030. Medicaid HCBS is walled off by 15-month waitlists and labor is scarcer after the 2026 visa pause, so stretching each aide across more clients is the only lever left.
revenue_model: Monthly resident subscription by care tier, with a revenue share or amenity fee to the property owner. Later, Medicaid HCBS or managed-care billing for pods in affordable senior buildings.
non_obvious_insight: Aide hours are cheap to make dense (no drive time, no client-hour minimums) but are priced as if they were mobile. The gap between 1:1 pricing and 1:8 cost is the whole business, and only a property-anchored operator can capture it. Assisted-living-without-the-license is a real category nobody has scaled.
first_30_days: Sign a 90-day pilot with one 100-200 unit 55+ property in a tight market. Subcontract to an existing licensed agency to move quickly, staff a two-aide pod, and target 15 residents at about $2,200 a month. Track aide minutes per resident and move-out avoidance.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: National Church Residences (NCR), SASH (Support and Services at Home, Vermont), Selfhelp Community Services (SHASAM), PACE programs (National PACE Association) and PACE-plus-housing projects. White space: Caveat on process: the session's WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200) before I could run any search. I researched only by fetching about 20 known URLs directly and by using prior knowledge. "No scaled startup found" therefore means not found, not verified absent. Rerun 6-8 searches (Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, 'shared aide' and 'cluster care' startup terms) before committing capital.

What looks unserved: (1) A private-pay, tiered, per-building shared-aide subscription in market-rate or workforce 55+ apartment buildings that are not part of a campus. Existing players are either nonprofit coordinator programs (SASH, Selfhelp, NCR), Medicaid or state-licensed programs (PACE, NJ-style ALP), or campus operators (Brookdale). I found no venture-scale company selling this. (2) A dispatch and acuity-tiering software layer for in-building routing (floors, elevators, overnight response). Nothing I fetched showed one.

Serious risks that shrink the white space:
- Licensing. Under Minnesota 144G.08, sleeping accommodations plus any 'assisted living services' (personal care, toileting help, medication reminders, meal setup, safety checks) under contract requires an assisted-living license. Subsidized housing is excluded unless marketed as assisted living, and the statute does not address a property owner that arranges a home-care provider on site. 'Assisted-living-without-the-license' is therefore legally fragile in many states, especially with an owner revenue share and overnight response, which look like 'holding out'.
- Unit economics. Two aides per shift is 17,520 aide-hours a year, about $400-500k loaded at roughly $23-28 an hour. Spread over 15 residents at $2,200 a month ($396k a year) that is break-even at best. At 6-10 residents the cost per resident is about $4,000-5,000 a month, which is above the stated $1,800-3,500 tiers. The idea's own numbers are internally inconsistent (6-10 residents in the one-liner, 15 in the pilot).
- Substitutes. BAYADA and franchise agencies already market to senior-living partners, and NCR and Brookdale could add pods in-house.

title: Remote Second-RN for Rural Night Shifts
one_liner: A pool of remote nurses that acts as the recorded, independent second person on video for narcotic waste, blood checks and high-alert drug double-checks when a rural hospital has three nurses on at 3am.
customer: Chief nursing officers and pharmacy directors at critical access hospitals (25 beds or fewer, roughly 1,300 in the US), plus the malpractice and captive insurers that cover them. Hospitals pay a monthly subscription.
problem: Policy requires a second licensed person to witness controlled-substance waste and to independently double-check insulin, heparin, blood and pediatric doses. At night at a rural hospital that second person is a nurse who is mid-code or mid-admission. Every nurse knows the witness signature is often given without actually watching. That is the most common way nurses divert drugs, and it is also how honest nurses end up with paper trails that would not survive an audit. The hospital cannot prove the witness happened. The other option is waking a colleague from another unit, which delays care.
solution: Start with a $150 tablet-and-camera cart at the dispensing cabinet. A remote RN appears on video within 60 seconds, watches the waste happen, and attests in a portal. The system keeps a time-stamped video clip and an audit log matched to the cabinet's waste records, exported as a PDF for the diversion committee. Then add two-RN blood transfusion verification, independent double-checks for high-alert drugs, and a 'second set of eyes' call for pediatric dosing. Do no EHR integration at first. Matching by timestamp is enough to sell.
why_now: The Bluesight 2026 State of Hospital Pharmacy report says about 63% of health-system leaders reported at least one diversion incident in the past year, and waste is a top diversion method because witnessing is loosely policed. Virtual nursing has become normal since 2024, and the Nurse Licensure Compact now covers most states, so one remote nurse can cover many hospitals. State Rural Health Transformation Program money is flowing, with every state having posted at least one funding opportunity by August 2026, and workforce and quality dollars can pay for this. Whether remote-video witnessing is acceptable is mostly a hospital-policy and pharmacy and therapeutics committee decision, but each state's board of pharmacy and nursing board should be checked before launch.
revenue_model: $1,500-2,500 per hospital per month, plus a per-event fee for transfusion and double-check calls above a set volume. A typical rural ED has 10-25 waste events a night at 2-3 minutes each, so one remote RN can cover roughly 8-12 hospitals per night. Estimated gross margin is 40-50%. A secondary revenue line is a discount arrangement with medical liability insurers, who benefit from the audit trail.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone selling diversion software (analytics, cabinet data mining, waste-testing) tries to detect diversion after the fact. Insiders know the root problem is that no real second person exists at night in a small hospital. You do not need better detection. You need to supply the missing colleague, cheaply and on camera. The service also protects honest nurses, who will therefore support it and not resist it.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 per-diem or retired RNs with compact licenses who want remote night hours at $35-40/hr. Use an off-the-shelf tablet with a recording app and a simple web portal that produces the PDF log. Offer free 30-day pilots to two critical access hospitals through the founder nurse's own pharmacy director and CNO. Get the pilot approved as a policy amendment at the pharmacy and therapeutics committee. Convert to a $1,500 monthly contract after 30 days if the audit log is shown to the diversion committee and the hospital's insurer.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: MIDAS Healthcare Solutions (MidasVIEW / Anytime Witness, aka V.I.E.W.), BD Pyxis Med Link Queue & Waste, Avel eCare, VirtuAlly (with Teledigm Health). White space: Nobody I found sells a shared, pooled, live remote-RN witness subscription to critical access hospitals. The specific gaps are:
(1) Live human supply. MidasVIEW replaces the second person with recorded video reviewed later. Pyxis remote witness still needs a colleague on shift. Virtual-nursing vendors cover admissions, discharges, sitters and documentation. Remote pharmacy vendors cover order verification. Nobody provides a licensed second person on demand at 3am.
(2) Transfusion, high-alert and pediatric double-checks. Asynchronous video cannot substitute for a live independent check before administration. Remote IDC is documented as feasible but under-evidenced, and only a few institutions do it (ONS 2024).
(3) Small-hospital fit. MidasVIEW pilots are at tertiary and children's hospitals. Small facilities lag on diversion controls: only 57% of single facilities actively monitor camera footage, and CAHs lack pharmacy staff to review video the next day.
(4) Insurer-linked audit trail. No diversion vendor sells to liability or captive insurers.
The wedge is narrow and time-limited. Avel eCare, VirtuAlly and the telepharmacy vendors could add a witness line quickly, and MidasVIEW could add live witness routing.

title: Tele-Clearance for Sheriffs' Booking Desks
one_liner: A night-shift nurse-and-NP screening service that lets a rural deputy clear an arrestee for booking from the jail, without spending four hours in the ER while the county goes unpatrolled.
customer: County sheriffs and county commissioners, funded through county risk pools and insurers (for example state association-of-counties liability pools) that pay for jail deaths and lawsuits. Paid per county per month.
problem: Rural jails often have no on-site medical staff, so jail policy requires a hospital 'medical clearance' for any arrestee who is intoxicated, injured or says his chest hurts. At 2am the deputy brings the person to the ER and sits with him for 3-5 hours, sometimes the county's only deputy on duty. The county pays a $2,000-4,000 ER bill and has nobody patrolling. The ER meanwhile holds a bed and a nurse for someone with nothing acutely wrong except being drunk. When clearance is skipped, the risk is a death in custody from alcohol or opioid withdrawal, a head injury or diabetic crisis, which is a lawsuit.
solution: A booking-desk kit (vitals, pulse oximeter, glucometer, breathalyzer, tablet) plus 24/7 on-demand video screening by an RN and NP working from home, using a physician-signed clearance protocol built from ACEP's published best-practice guidance for patients in custody. Dispositions are 'fit for booking with monitoring plan', 'needs ER now', or 're-check in 2 hours'. The service also creates a documented withdrawal-watch checklist, such as sobriety and CIWA-style monitoring, which jails need for liability reasons. The report is time-stamped and defensible.
why_now: Rural hospital and ER closures are lengthening transport times. Prison Policy Initiative reported in October 2025 that about half of incarcerated people are held in rural jails and prisons that risk losing hospital access. Medicaid cuts and the pressure on county budgets are also forcing sheriffs to look for cheaper options, and some already release people on 'medical bond' to avoid ER bills. Telehealth billing and licensure flexibility, together with the Nurse Licensure Compact, make cross-state night staffing workable.
revenue_model: $2,000-3,500 per county per month, including up to about 40 screens. Additional screens are $85 each. Roughly 12 counties would support a team of 6 part-time clinicians. Later, sell an outcome dashboard called 'deputy hours returned to patrol', which is the number commissioners and risk-pool underwriters will care about most.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone frames the problem as ER wait time or inmate healthcare. From inside the ER, the real cost is the deputy who is stuck with us. In a county with one or two deputies on at night, an ER trip is a public safety hole, and the buyer will pay to close it. Also, most 'medical clearances' are defensive medicine that a good screen would make unnecessary. Big correctional health vendors (Wellpath, NaphCare) sell staffing for large jails and are not built for a 12-bed jail on a county road.
first_30_days: Write the clearance protocol with a supervising physician from a rural ER and get it reviewed by one county attorney. Choose one sheriff the founder already knows from ER encounters. Run a paid pilot at $1,500 for 60 days and count deputy hours saved and ER trips avoided. Then pitch the state's county risk pool and sheriffs' association with the numbers.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: NaphCare (STATCare 24/7 telehealth), Wellpath, Southern Health Partners, Turn Key Health. White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before I could run any searches, so this verdict rests on about 14 direct page fetches. That is far short of the 6-12 searches the task called for, and I found no startup-specific evidence either way. I found no vendor whose page shows a tele-clearance product for booking desks, meaning a remote RN/NP screening arrestees before booking with a time-stamped disposition (fit for booking, needs ER now, re-check in 2 hours). Incumbent jail-health vendors (Wellpath, NaphCare, Southern Health Partners) sell on-site staffing or in-custody care. Avel eCare sells 24/7 virtual clinicians to rural ERs and to law enforcement, but only for behavioral crisis. The unserved wedge is a pre-booking, per-county-per-month subscription for jails too small to justify a contracted health vendor, priced against deputy-hours and ER bills. Hospital-run or jail-staff-run tele-clearance programs may already exist locally and I could not check.\n\nTwo structural risks weaken the wedge and need validating early. First, the pitch says the Nurse Licensure Compact makes cross-state night staffing workable, but the NLC covers RNs, not NPs. As far as I know the APRN Compact was not yet operational, so NP staffing likely needs per-state licenses. Second, a remote clinician clearing an intoxicated or injured person on vitals and video alone shifts head-injury and withdrawal liability onto the vendor. That is a malpractice-insurance and clinical-governance problem, and a risk pool may or may not accept it. Revenue is also thin: 12 counties at $2-3.5k a month is roughly $290k-500k a year, with slow county sales cycles.

title: Nonrenewal Cure: Rebutting Insurer Cancellations
one_liner: Nonrenewal notices often cite fixable issues like roof condition, tree overhang or debris. Sell homeowners a fast diagnosis, repair and evidence packet to get re-underwritten instead of dumped on a FAIR plan.
customer: Homeowners in CA, FL, TX, CO, UT and NM who have received a nonrenewal notice, plus independent brokers who lose those clients.
problem: Nonrenewals are at records and homeowners have 30-75 days to react. Carriers are structurally conflicted about helping, and the FAIR plan is pricey with thin cover. Homeowners can't decode the reason code, can't tell which items are cheap to fix, and can't produce the evidence a carrier re-inspection accepts.
solution: Upload the notice. The service decodes the stated reason using state disclosure rules, dispatches vetted local contractors for the fix (patch, trim, vent screens), and produces a time-stamped photo and invoice packet. It files for reinspection or appeal, and gives the broker a clean file to re-market the risk. For wildfire-score cases it documents mitigation credits available under state rules.
why_now: Record nonrenewals, California passed three claims and nonrenewal bills on 2026-09-03, and insurance now rivals mortgage payments. Carriers rely more on aerial-imagery flags that homeowners rarely see or contest.
revenue_model: $149 diagnostic, $250-$500 evidence packet, 10-15% contractor referral fee, and broker referral fees on re-placed policies.
non_obvious_insight: Many cancellations are cheap to cure, but the homeowner has no language, time or evidence, and the carrier won't help. A homeowner who has just been rescued becomes a lifetime referral source for brokers.
first_30_days: Post in local nonrenewal threads and neighborhood groups, and partner with three independent brokers. Handle 20 cases by hand, track how many carriers reinstate, and use the win rate to set pricing.

All findings come from direct page fetches of known sites (regulators, IBHS, competitors, Consumer Watchdog, leginfo). I could not sweep Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or Reddit (blocked or unfetchable). Re-run with a raised CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION before committing.

What looks unserved: nobody found does the execution layer end to end. That means decoding the notice, dispatching a vetted local contractor, producing a carrier-format evidence packet, scheduling the reinspection and handing the broker a clean file. IBHS supplies a checklist and evaluator but no contractors or concierge. State and regulator programs are free but fragmented. Frontline sells one product. ZestyAI and Porch sit adjacent without a homeowner cure flow. Non-CA states (FL, TX, CO, UT, NM) lack an SB 1301-style mandate, and California has a roughly 15-month window before its rules bite.

Important erosion of the pitch as written: CA SB 1301 (Allen), signed 09/27/2026 as Chapter 693, Statutes of 2026 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB1301). Per the bill text, from Jan 1, 2028 insurers must give at least 90 days notice of nonrenewal. They must give a detailed plain-language explanation of remediation that would allow renewal, and at least 90 days to cure. They must hand over all non-aerial imagery and inspection reports within 15 days on request, and may reinspect at their own expense. Protections reach wildfire scores. Consumer Watchdog also says the bill prohibits nonrenewal for roof age alone. That commoditizes the paid diagnose-the-reason step and the time-pressure pain in CA. It leaves the fix, evidence and coordination step, which is the contractor referral and broker-placement revenue, not the $149 diagnostic. The campaign page (https://www.efsurvivors.net/fix-insurance) says six months notice while the enrolled text says 90 days, so treat the exact notice period as unverified. Other weak spots: many flags are area-level wildfire scores or roof age and are not cheaply curable. Contractor lead-gen has thin margins and trust risk. Whether negotiating or filing appeals with carriers needs an insurance producer or adjuster license is unverified and needs legal review.

title: Real-Factory Credentials From Customs Shipping Records
one_liner: Turn public US import records into supplier-owned reputation credentials and audit-ready reasonable-care dossiers that prove a factory is a real manufacturer.
customer: Small and mid-size US importers of record (Amazon and Shopify brands, furniture, hardware and apparel distributors) re-sourcing to Vietnam, India, Mexico and Turkey. Customs brokers are a channel, and factories are the second payer.
problem: The importer of record is investigated first, and liability turns on whether it exercised reasonable care about the supplier's origin claims. In August 2026 the White House published a report on transshipment, a 40% penalty tariff applies, and CBP has expanded inspections of shipments from Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Mexico. Small importers cannot tell a real factory from a trading company or a re-labeller, and sourcing agents' claims are unverifiable.
solution: Supplier Proof. Build a profile per factory from three or more years of US import records (shipper and consignee names, volumes, product codes, ports, cadence) plus corporate registry and location data, flag anomalies such as volume beyond plausible capacity, mismatched product codes or shell-company addresses, and add optional local inspector visits. Factories claim and verify their profile and can consent to name repeat buyers as references. The output is a dossier the importer can hand to a broker or to CBP.
why_now: Tariff enforcement moved in 2025-26 from headline rates to origin verification, and the August 2026 transshipment report has put importer liability on every compliance officer's desk. Sourcing shifts away from China are happening now, so millions of dollars of orders are going to unfamiliar factories.
revenue_model: Importer subscriptions of $149-499 per month, $150-400 per dossier, inspector visits passed through at a margin, and $600-1,200 per year from factories for a verified credential once importers demand it.
non_obvious_insight: Import records are the only unforgeable cross-border reputation ledger for factories, but they are sold as raw rows to analysts. Repackaged as supplier-owned credentials with a reasonable-care wrapper, a data product becomes a compliance product with a real budget line: avoiding a 40% penalty.
first_30_days: Buy 12 months of import records for two categories (for example furniture and hardware from Vietnam and India). Auto-build about 1,000 factory profiles and hand-audit 20. Send 200 emails to sourcing managers and customs brokers. Sell the first 10 dossiers at $250 each and use them to refine the scoring.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ImportGenius, Panjiva (S&P Global Market Intelligence), Descartes Datamyne, ImportYeti. White space: The narrow wedge that appears unserved is a fixed-price, human-reviewed 'reasonable-care file' for a small US importer, sold through customs brokers. The SMB importer (Amazon or Shopify brand, or a $2-50M distributor) needs one factory checked before one PO. Enterprise tools (Sayari, Altana, Tradeverifyd, Trademo, Exiger) are sold by demo and are priced and scoped for large compliance teams. Data tools (ImportGenius, Panjiva, Datamyne, ImportYeti) sell rows and leave interpretation to the analyst. Inspectors (QIMA) and sourcing agents (Sourcify) sell physical checks, not a documentary file that maps to CBP's reasonable-care standard. The part I found nobody offering is a factory-claimed profile with consent-based buyer references, which is a two-sided credential. No visible player runs a supplier-owned reputation credential built on customs ledgers. However, the wedge is thin. (1) ImportGenius already markets 'supplier verification via shipping history' at the same $229-449/mo price band. (2) The raw-data floor is free or near-free. (3) Any one of Altana, Trademo or ImportGenius could add a 'transshipment risk report' feature quickly. (4) The factory-pays credential side has no demonstrated demand and needs a two-sided marketplace. Risks I could not check with the exhausted search budget: whether resale of licensed bill-of-lading data is allowed, that US import records often name the forwarder or trading company as shipper instead of the factory, that importers can request confidentiality under 19 CFR 103.31, and that no CBP safe-harbor exists for third-party dossiers.

title: Vacant-Unit Meter Watchdog and Insurance Vacancy Log
one_liner: Uses utility smart-meter data that owners already have rights to, so PMs can catch squatters, leaks and freeze risk in empty units within hours, without installing any hardware.
customer: Property managers and owners of single-family and 2-to-20-unit portfolios (100 to 2,000 doors). They already pay the utilities on vacant units and carry standard dwelling or small-building policies with a vacancy clause. Buyer is the PM's ops director or the owner. Secondary buyers later are E&S and landlord-program insurers.
problem: When a unit is occupied, the tenant is the sensor and tells you about leaks. When it is vacant you are blind for 20 to 60 days. Water damage, squatters, stolen copper, AC left running and burst pipes all happen in that window. Most property policies restrict vandalism, water damage and theft after roughly 60 days of vacancy, and the claim gets denied or cut exactly when the loss is biggest. Squatter removal is also time-critical: in many states an intruder found on day 2 is a police trespass matter, while the same person on day 30 needs a months-long court eviction. Walk-throughs are weekly at best, and the maintenance tech skips them when busy.
solution: Vacancy Vitals connects to interval electric and water data through owner-authorized utility APIs (Green Button Connect, or aggregators like UtilityAPI). The owner's account is usually the one active during vacancy, so no tenant consent is needed. Rules fire on patterns: continuous 24/7 water flow (leak), electric baseline above the empty-unit norm (someone living there, a crypto miner, a grow), a heating or cooling setpoint far outside range (pipe-freeze or mold risk), and a sudden drop to zero in a unit that should be running HVAC. Alerts go by text to the on-call tech with a one-tap 'send someone' button. The product also generates a time-stamped weekly vacancy-inspection log (data check plus a tech photo check-in) formatted for carriers' vacancy-permit or inspection conditions. That log is what preserves coverage.
why_now: Anti-squatter laws were passed in a wave in 2024 and 2025 (for example Florida and Georgia), which makes early detection more valuable. Smart-meter penetration passed roughly 70% of US electric customers. Insurers have been tightening on water-damage and vacancy exposure for several years. AI-based anomaly detection on interval data is now cheap. (Current state-by-state anti-squatter rules and utility API coverage should be verified before launch.)
revenue_model: $4 to $7 per vacant-unit-month on usage, or a flat $1 to $2 per door per month portfolio subscription. Later, insurer-paid or insurer-discounted programs: the carrier pays a fee per monitored door in exchange for lower loss ratios and a vacancy-clause waiver.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest sensor for a vacant house is the meter the utility already installed, and the account is in the owner's name during vacancy. Nobody in proptech treats owner-account utility data as a security and insurance-compliance feed. They sell $60 leak sensors and cameras instead. The other secret is legal timing. The value is not detecting the squatter, it is detecting them in the first 48 hours, when the law treats it as trespass rather than a tenancy.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 to 5 SFR or small-multifamily PMs, offer a free 'backtest', and pull 12 months of interval data for units that were vacant. Show them the incidents the tool would have caught. These are usually a few leaks, a few unauthorized occupants and several HVAC-left-on units, each worth $1,000 to $15,000. Build a UtilityAPI-based prototype with three rules, text alerts and a weekly PDF log. Charge $99 per month per portfolio during the pilot, then convert to per-unit pricing. In parallel, talk to two independent insurance agents who write landlord programs, to learn the exact vacancy-permit language and to get a warm intro for the carrier channel.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Arcadia (utility data platform), UtilityAPI, Wint Water Intelligence, SmartRent. White space: I found no product that does what this idea proposes: rules on owner-authorized utility interval data to detect squatters, unauthorized occupancy, leaks and HVAC problems in vacant units, then produce a carrier-formatted vacancy-inspection log with no installed hardware. The alternatives are hardware (Wint, SmartRent, Minut, Flume), utility data plumbing (Arcadia, UtilityAPI), or bill-management tools (Conservice, EnergyCAP). None of their pages pitch vacant-unit security or insurance vacancy compliance. Three things are genuinely unserved: (1) electric-baseline occupancy detection in a vacant unit, which the water-focused players cannot do; (2) an inspection log formatted for carrier vacancy-permit conditions; (3) small portfolios of 100 to 2,000 doors, which Wint and SmartRent do not serve well. I could not find how commonly PMs use utility-supplied continuous-flow leak alerts (water utilities with AMI portals, my background knowledge, unverified). Research limits: the WebSearch budget was used up, so no Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or forum searches were possible. The verdict rests on about 20 direct page fetches and background knowledge, and the absence of a direct competitor is not proven. Main risks: (a) UtilityAPI lists $2.40 to $30 per meter per month for scheduled monitoring, so on a $1 to $2 per door or $4 to $7 per vacant-unit-month price, data cost could exceed revenue unless you use free Green Button Connect direct integrations or price higher; (b) interval water data through third-party APIs is thin, because most water utilities have no Green Button Connect, and leaks are the biggest loss, so the water rule may only work in a few metros; (c) each owner must authorize each utility account, a real onboarding cost at 100 to 2,000 doors; (d) I found nothing showing carriers accept a monitoring log in place of a vacancy permit or endorsement, so the 'log preserves coverage' claim is unproven; (e) the '48-hour trespass window' insight is unverified. The Florida HB 621 page I fetched confirms sheriff removal and a July 1, 2024 effective date but gives no time threshold, and Wikipedia confirms Alabama's 2024 24-hour removal law, so statute-specific timing needs a lawyer.

title: Cross-Mine Critical Spares Pool and Inventory Cleanup
one_liner: An AI cleaner for mine SAP materials masters that frees cash from duplicate spares, then turns the informal WhatsApp groups of competing mines' maintenance planners into a contractual, insured rotables pool for mill motors, liners and haul-truck parts.
customer: Supply chain, maintenance and finance heads at mid-size copper and lithium operations, starting in clusters where operators are neighbours: Arizona, Nevada and Utah, Antofagasta, the Arequipa-Moquegua corridor, the Zambian Copperbelt and the Pilbara. They pay a share of freed cash, not an IT budget.
problem: A copper mine holds $30-150M of spares. Materials masters are full of duplicates and near-duplicates (the same bearing under five descriptions), often 20-30% of items, so mines overbuy what is on another shelf. They still stock out on truly critical items (mill drive motors, girth gears, transformers, big castings) with 12-24 month lead times. Meanwhile maintenance planners across competing companies already borrow parts from each other over WhatsApp groups. It works only among friends and has no contracts, insurance, condition guarantees or return terms, so it never scales.
solution: Step one is the wedge. A CSV export of the SAP MM data goes into an LLM pipeline with OEM and aftermarket cross-references, multilingual description normalisation and criticality scoring. It outputs a list of duplicates, surplus and dead stock, plus the freed working capital in dollars. Step two lists surplus and 'insurance spares' on a members-only district board with a standard loan, lease and sale agreement, third-party condition inspection (vibration, NDT), logistics and insurance. It works like airline rotable pooling: three neighbouring mines share one spare mill motor instead of each stocking one.
why_now: Large motors, transformers and castings have longer lead times because of grid and data-centre demand. Steel and copper tariffs make replacement parts pricier. Lithium mines are cash-starved after the price bust, and copper mines face cost inflation and grade decline, so CFOs are hunting working capital. LLMs can now normalise messy multilingual part descriptions at almost no cost, which was not economic three years ago.
revenue_model: 15-25% of freed cash (sales and avoided purchases only, not write-offs), a pool membership subscription ($1-3k per month), and an 8-10% transaction fee on pooled loans and sales, plus inspection and certification fees.
non_obvious_insight: The spares problem is legal and trust-based, not a software problem. The informal swap network is the real supply chain. The biggest saving is not selling dead stock, it is not buying the 'insurance spare' a neighbour already owns. Pooling is an aviation idea that mining has never adopted because competitors will not share data without a neutral third party.
first_30_days: Through ex-colleagues, offer a free 2-week scan of SAP MM exports (CSV) at two or three mid-size mines. Deliver a dollar value of duplicates and surplus and a target list. Sign a success-fee agreement with the first one that shows a big number. In parallel, seed a private 'list before you buy' board among 20 maintenance planners in one district using Signal or WhatsApp, to formalise the network before any software is built.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Verusen, SPARETECH GmbH, SAP (IBP, Store distribution) and IBM Maximo, Partium. White space: Caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted before I could run any queries, so this verdict rests on direct page fetches of known companies. It is not a broad sweep. I could not run forum, Reddit, WhatsApp-group, RFP, Spanish/Portuguese-language or Crunchbase/YC/Product Hunt searches. My 'nobody does cross-company mining pooling' finding is therefore unconfirmed and moderate-confidence.

STEP ONE (SAP dedupe and surplus cleaner) is crowded and should not be the business. Verusen has a live mining case study ($96.8M identified across 17 sites), a listing in the SAP Store, about $33M disclosed funding and enterprise references. SPARETECH does the same dedupe-and-surplus job. Partium and Syniti cover the normalization and SAP-cleansing pieces. The 'LLM cost collapsed, so now it's viable' argument is weak, because Verusen and SPARETECH already do this. The remaining wedge inside step one is small: mid-size mines (roughly $30-150M of spares, one SAP instance, no enterprise budget) below Verusen's Fortune-100 and multi-site-enterprise focus, sold on a success fee. That is a thin, copyable wedge.

STEP TWO (neutral, cross-operator critical-spares pool) is unserved among the players I checked. Verusen's sharing module is intra-company only and has no legal, insurance or inspection layer. Liquidity Services and RB Global sell surplus one-way and offer no loan or lease terms. Grid Assurance proves the pooled long-lead-spares subscription model for utilities, but nobody I found has applied it to mines. The unserved piece is the trust wrapper: a neutral entity, standard loan/lease agreement, third-party condition certification (vibration/NDT), logistics and insurance, and a single-point-of-failure spares register per district.

Risks I could not close out. (1) OEM reman, exchange and consignment programs (haul-truck components, mill liners, motors) are the real substitute for pooling. I could not verify their current terms because the Cat Reman fetch timed out. (2) Competition-law exposure when competing operators share inventory data needs early legal work. (3) The pooled-event frequency is low, so revenue per district is modest, and pooling in Chile or Peru needs local counsel. (4) Verusen could add an inter-company network cheaply; it already lists 'Spare Parts Sharing' and mining customers.

title: ITAR-Safe Identity for New-Space Startups
one_liner: An identity layer that proves a new hire is real, where they actually are and whether they may legally see spacecraft technical data, then feeds that attribute straight into SSO and PLM access controls.
customer: Series A-C launch, satellite and defense-space startups (50-500 staff) and their sub-tier machine shops and avionics suppliers, reached through space-focused investors, accelerators and SpaceWERX/SBIR cohorts. Buyers are the head of security or compliance and the CFO.
problem: Space startups are hiring at breakneck speed, with remote engineers and contractors, into a Golden Dome-driven market (cost estimate raised to $185B) and nine-figure funding rounds. Giving a foreign person access to technical data is an ITAR export violation, and North Korean IT-worker schemes have reached 70 to 100+ US companies. Standard IDV proves someone is real, not whether they are a US person, and HR and ATS tools do not carry export-control eligibility as an access attribute. Fake suppliers and counterfeit parts add a second exposure.
solution: (1) Verify person and US-person status using document and injection-resistant liveness (partner with an existing IDV vendor rather than building it). (2) Check presence over time (VPN and laptop-farm signals). (3) Write 'US person, permitted data categories' into Okta or Entra groups and PLM and repo permissions through SCIM. (4) Supplier onboarding with KYB, sanctions and counterfeit-part red flags. (5) An auditor-ready evidence pack for CMMC Level 2 assessments and export-compliance reviews.
why_now: The DoD's CMMC rollout reaches its second phase on 10 Nov 2026, when third-party Level 2 certification starts appearing in contracts, and small suppliers are scrambling. North Korean worker prosecutions in Apr and May 2026 put hiring fraud on boards' agendas, while 3-second voice cloning and virtual-camera injection attacks defeat casual video interviews.
revenue_model: $60-120 per verified person per year, $1-3K per month platform fee, and $250 per supplier onboarding. Add a paid $2K 'ITAR access audit' as an entry product.
non_obvious_insight: In space the compliance object is not employee identity but nationality-scoped access to technical data. The unbuilt gap is attribute-based access control fed by identity proof into CAD and PLM systems. These startups fear DDTC and DoD audits and investor diligence more than hackers, so they buy compliance evidence rather than security.
first_30_days: Build a 'verified US person to Okta group' integration on an off-the-shelf IDV API. Sell a $2K ITAR access audit (export the Drive, GitHub and PLM permission lists and flag foreign-person exposures) to 5 startups via investor and accelerator introductions in Colorado Springs, Los Angeles and Huntsville. Convert audits to per-seat subscriptions before the Nov 2026 CMMC milestone.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: archTIS NC Protect, Persona (Candidate Verification), Incode Candidate Verification, Socure (workforce and candidate verification). White space: Verdict is gap, and a narrower one than the pitch implies. No product found does the specific loop the idea describes: proof of US-person status, the attribute written to an IdP through SCIM, enforcement in Drive, GitHub and PLM, and continuous drift detection. Four things fill the space today. IDV vendors (Persona, Incode, Socure, Nametag, CLEAR, Entra Verified ID) prove someone is real but do not assert or record ITAR eligibility. archTIS NC Protect enforces nationality-based access but only inside Microsoft 365 and file shares, and it trusts whatever attribute it is given. Managed-service shops (BEMO at about $4,800/month, ATX CMMC Space plus $30/user/month) deliver it as consulting with 8-month timelines. PLM vendors enforce access to an admin-typed attribute that no one has proven.

What is genuinely unserved:
- A lightweight, startup-priced system of record for US-person and permitted-data-category status, with the Empowered Official sign-off, that syncs to Okta, Entra and Google Workspace groups.
- Continuous deemed-export exposure scanning across the Drive, GitHub, Slack and PLM permission lists that startups actually use. Many are on commercial Google Workspace, which is not ITAR-compliant, and they cannot afford a GCC High or enclave migration.
- A managed workflow for licensed or TAA-scoped foreign-person exceptions, which is where hiring friction really sits.

Parts of the pitch that are not white space:
- Supplier KYB and counterfeit screening is owned by Exiger, Kharon and Sayari.
- CMMC evidence packs are owned by Secureframe, Vanta and Drata.
- Candidate and DPRK fraud detection is crowded and moving fast (Persona, Incode, Socure, Nametag, Endorsed).

Biggest structural risks:
1. The 'why now' is broken. DoD suspended CMMC Phase 2, due 10 Nov 2026, on 13 Jul 2026 and launched a 60-day reform review. Phase 1 self-assessments remain. Do not build the go-to-market around a Nov 2026 CMMC cliff.
2. Legal and product risk. The Clifford Chance settlement ($132K) shows DOJ IER penalizes employers who over-apply ITAR into citizenship discrimination. ITAR does not require hiring only US persons. Under INA 274B, employers cannot demand specific documents or run citizenship checks unevenly. A biometric 'US person' scanner sold to HR is legally delicate. Verifying green-card, asylee and refugee status by document scan is harder than a citizen passport check, and the I-9 already exists as the system of record.
3. Easy DIY. An IT admin can put an I-9-derived flag into an Okta group, so the paid value must be audit and drift detection plus the exception workflow, not the attribute itself.
4. Coverage limit. WebSearch is US-only and Crunchbase and YC searches surfaced nothing, so a stealth or very early startup on this exact wedge cannot be ruled out.

title: IEP Chief of Staff for Special-Ed Parents
one_liner: Rich parents win school disputes with a paid educational advocate and paper trail; for $20/mo, give parents of the roughly 7.5M US students with IEPs a chief of staff who watches the legal clocks and logs every missed service minute.
customer: Parents of children with IEPs (autism, ADHD, dyslexia, speech and language delay), sold through state and local special-ed parent groups, parent training centers, pediatric practices, disability law clinics and credit unions.
problem: Districts arrive with a team; wealthy families bring an advocate ($150-400/hr) and an attorney. Federal enforcement was hollowed out (mass OSEP layoffs in October 2025, and reported moves of oversight to HHS and civil-rights enforcement to DOJ in June 2026), so parents are effectively on their own. Most violations are procedural (late evaluations, missing prior written notice, services not delivered) and go unnoticed because nobody keeps the clocks.
solution: Parent uploads the IEP and evaluations. The system builds the legal calendar (evaluation timelines from consent, meeting-notice windows, annual and triennial reviews, progress-report cadence), drafts records requests, creates a one-page pre-meeting brief (top asks plus data), and sends a same-day 'memorializing' follow-up email with prior-written-notice requests after meetings. It logs service minutes delivered vs promised, quantifying missed minutes for a compensatory-services claim, and scans the IEP for defects (no baselines, unmeasurable goals). Advocates are on-demand at $75 per 30 minutes, with a path to state complaint and due process.
why_now: The federal special-ed enforcement vacuum is documented and new as of late 2025 and mid-2026. IEP counts are rising, and LLMs can parse messy IEP PDFs and draft procedurally precise letters. Parent communities are organized on Facebook and Reddit and actively looking for help.
revenue_model: $20/mo per family; $75 advocate sessions with a revenue split to a vetted advocate co-op; $3-6 per member per month from parent centers, pediatric groups and credit unions; district-facing analytics sold only with parent consent, later.
non_obvious_insight: What the rich buy is not better argument but continuous procedural pressure: dated, written, specific requests. The subscription funds clock-watching and documentation, not advice. Parents who log service minutes turn 'I feel they're not delivering' into a quantified claim, and the paper trail is the evidence in any later dispute, so value compounds over time.
first_30_days: Publish a free IEP clock calculator and letter templates. Partner with admins of 10 state-level special-ed Facebook groups and concierge 30 families manually, measuring violations found. Convert those families to $20/mo and recruit 5 advocates for the on-demand tier.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: IEP Advocate.ai, ChatGPT and general LLMs (endorsed by CADRE's parent guide), Parent Training and Information Centers (PTIs/CPRCs), Wrightslaw. White space: Confidence is moderate-low. The WebSearch budget hit 200/200 before I could run the planned 6-12 searches, so I found competitors mostly by fetching guessed and known URLs. More direct competitors probably exist that I did not see, and this should be re-run once the search limit is raised.

The core pitch is NOT white space. Deadline extraction, procedural letter generation, meeting prep briefs and state-complaint drafting are already live at IEP Advocate.ai for $30/mo. Free ChatGPT covers much of the rest. A $20/mo 'AI IEP chief of staff' would be a cheaper copy.

Specific gaps I could not find served in the pages I reached:
1. A service-delivery ledger. This means logging minutes promised vs delivered per IEP service line and turning the shortfall into a compensatory-services claim packet. IEP Advocate.ai's fetched pages do not describe service-minute logging or comp-ed calculation.
2. Human-in-the-loop verification. CADRE and K-12 Dive document AI-drafted complaints with fabricated case law and wrong IDEA readings. A product that combines grounded output with vetted advocate or attorney review, at $75 per 30 minutes, is unserved. IEP Advocate.ai has no human tier.
3. B2B2C distribution through parent centers, disability law clinics, pediatric practices and credit unions at $3-6 per member per month. IEP Advocate.ai lists only individual pricing. The channel is unproven.
4. Evidence-grade record keeping. Time-stamped, tamper-evident logs that a hearing officer will accept, rather than chat history.

title: Placement Proof for Workforce Pell Providers
one_liner: A verified job-placement and completion ledger that makes short-term training programs (CDL, CNA, welding, HVAC, medical assistant, cosmetology) audit-ready for the governor and Secretary approvals that Workforce Pell requires.
customer: Small proprietary career schools, community college workforce and continuing-education units, and employer-training nonprofits running 8-15 week programs. The program owner or director pays. State workforce boards are a second buyer because they were given no new resources to verify placement.
problem: The Workforce Pell final rule (published May 19, 2026; effective July 20, 2026, with early implementation from July 1) covers programs of 150-599 clock hours and 8-15 weeks. A program must show 70% completion and 70% job placement, measured over the 12 months before it applies and annually after that. The governor must first certify the program as high-skill, high-wage or in-demand, then the Secretary approves. Providers must submit completer lists and the information needed to verify placement. Commenters flagged burden for small providers and noted states got no new resources to run the framework. Separately, the earnings-premium rule (effective July 1, 2027) strips Direct Loan access from programs that fail in two of three consecutive years. The Department estimated 93% of cosmetology programs would fail under the proposal.
solution: At completion the system automatically sends completers and employers text and email verification requests at 30, 90 and 180 days. It collects pay stubs, employer confirmations and consent for state wage-record matching, and reconciles them to the rule's placement definition. It produces the governor's application packet (completer list, placement evidence, tuition versus earnings benchmarks) and the annual recertification. It also scores each existing program's exposure to the earnings-premium test using public program-level earnings data so owners can decide what to keep, fix or convert into a short-term program.
why_now: The 12-month look-back means a provider that is not tracking verified placement now cannot apply in 2027. The earnings-premium test takes effect July 1, 2027 and is already being scored on 2021 completers' 2025 earnings.
