- The wedge depends on data access. A theft of a personal or free-tier account leaves the employer with no export. Only Enterprise and Edu tenants have admin export or Compliance API data, and I could not confirm the current API terms because the OpenAI help pages returned 403.
- A stolen cookie in a feed does not prove the attacker viewed the chats, so the assessment depends on provider audit logs that only OpenAI or the tenant admin can see.
- Any vendor holding the customer's chat data (Cyera, Varonis, Purview) can add this as a services line quickly.

title: Search-Fund Accelerator for Buying Scrap Yards
one_liner: A cohort program that turns laid-off mid-career managers into owner-operators of small scrap yards, e-scrap shops and transfer stations. It brings deal sourcing, environmental diligence and SBA-lender access.
customer: Laid-off ops, finance and product managers with severance or savings of about $100-300K, who pay cohort tuition and a success fee. Second customer: retiring owners of scrap and recycling businesses who want a successor buyer. SBA lenders are a channel.
problem: Mid-career job searches now run 7-13 months with near-zero interview rates (HN threads), and the hiring freeze is hitting degree-holders. Meanwhile thousands of owner-run recycling businesses have no successor. Their storage and processing permits take years to obtain, and domestic scrap has just become strategic: the Aug 27, 2026 BIS rule forces black mass and tungsten scrap sellers to allocate 100% of sales to US buyers. Nobody packages this asset class for a first-time buyer.
solution: Build a target database from state solid-waste and hazardous-waste permit records, scrap-dealer licenses and owner age. Provide a standard diligence pack covering environmental liabilities and Phase I/II, fire history and insurance, permit transferability, commodity exposure and offtake contracts. Add a 90-day operator bootcamp with a mentor operator and introductions to SBA lenders. Take a fixed fee at close plus a small advisory equity stake.
why_now: AI-driven hiring freezes are producing a large pool of capable managers with cash and time. Greenfield battery and plastics recycling is capital-destroying (Ascend Elements and Li-Cycle bankruptcies, 7 of about 30 US PET reclaimers closed), while boring, permitted, cash-flowing yards look safer. DoD and DOE equity stakes and the BIS allocation rule are re-rating domestic scrap.
revenue_model: Cohort tuition (about $4-6K per seat). Buy-side success fee ($25-50K or 1.5-2% at close). 2-5% advisory equity in each acquisition. Sell-side listing fees from retiring owners. Diligence-pack licensing to lenders.
non_obvious_insight: In recycling the scarce input is not technology or capital but a competent successor operator, and the labor market is now manufacturing them. Permits are the moat, so the right move is to buy permitted cash flow instead of financing new plants.
first_30_days: Pull permit and owner-age lists for two states. Run a free webinar for laid-off managers through layoff-tracker and career communities and enroll a first cohort of about 10. Get two retiring owners to sign exclusive sell-side LOIs. Sign an environmental-consulting partner for a flat-fee diligence pack, and one SBA lender as the financing partner.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Search Fund Accelerator (SFA), Kingsway Search Xcelerator (KSX), Codie Sanchez / Contrarian Thinking ('boring business' acquisition education), University ETA programs and search fund ecosystem (Stanford GSB, Kellogg, WashU Olin, Yale, Cleveland ETA program). White space: I found no scrap, recycling or transfer-station-specific acquisition accelerator. Every searcher or ETA program I could verify is sector-agnostic, and none packages this asset class for a first-time buyer. That is limited evidence. The session's 200-call WebSearch budget was already spent. I fell back on Google News RSS, the Hacker News API, the Federal Register API and direct fetches, and could not reach Crunchbase, Product Hunt, Reddit, Searchfunder or BizBuySell.

What looks unserved:
1. A vertical diligence and financing pack for sub-$5M scrap and recycling yards. It would cover Phase I/II and fire-history checks, insurance, permit transferability and offtake contracts. Horizontal ETA programs leave that to each buyer. Fire and insurance risk is live: EMR's Camden yard was shut after 15 fires in six years (NJ PEN, 29 May 2026), Resource Recycling wrote 'Battery fire risk isn't going away. Insurance is responding' (24 Feb 2026), and a 9,000-car Idaho salvage yard burned (Yahoo, 19 Jun 2026).
2. A succession desk for owner-run yards. Nothing I found targets ReMA-type family operators with a packaged successor, and the big consolidators only want larger yards.
3. A permit-and-owner-age target list. Nothing I found offers one for scrap dealers.

The premise needs two corrections:
- The BIS rule is real. It is a temporary final rule, published 6 Aug 2026 and effective 27 Aug 2026. However, it covers only black mass and tungsten waste and scrap, not ordinary ferrous or nonferrous yards (Federal Register 2026-16078). The 'domestic scrap re-rating' story is much narrower than the pitch implies.
- The idea leans on 'laid-off managers with $100-300K'. That is a crowded buyer-education market, with Codie Sanchez, Kingsway and the universities all courting the same buyers.

title: Evac Cash: Payout When Ordered to Evacuate
one_liner: A few dollars a month buys a $500-$2,500 wire within hours of an official mandatory evacuation order for your address, covering hurricane, wildfire and burn-scar flood orders.
customer: Renters and lower-to-middle-income homeowners in evacuation zones: Gulf and Florida surge zones, Western wildfire-urban-interface neighborhoods, and LA burn-scar areas. Sold to individuals, through employers of hourly staff (hospitals, hotels, nursing homes, grocers), and through credit unions or municipal 'evac funds'.
problem: Evacuating costs $1,000-$3,000 (gas, hotel, lost shifts, pet boarding) and the money is needed before any claim exists. Cost is a common reason people stay, so the people most exposed are least able to leave. Civil-authority and additional-living-expense cover is slow, receipt-based, often conditional on nearby damage, and many renters lack it.
solution: A parametric contract whose trigger is a legal act. If your geocoded address sits inside a polygon under a mandatory evacuation order, or an NWS flash-flood emergency for a burn scar, the platform pays via FedNow/RTP or a push-to-card within hours. Zone data comes from county emergency-management systems (evacuation-zone platforms and state zone maps). Tiers are priced by zone frequency, with one payout per event per address and a simple app that alerts you and shows your zone. Underwritten via a licensed MGA and fronting carrier, first as employer group policies.
why_now: Address-level, machine-readable evacuation zones are now common. FedNow/RTP make hours-not-weeks payouts cheap. The LA fires of January 2025 made burn-scar exposure vivid, and NOAA CPC/IRI's September 2026 outlooks show a greater than 90% chance of a very strong El Niño this winter, which means heavy rain on fresh burn scars and flash-flood/debris-flow evacuation orders. Parametric reinsurance capacity is plentiful and MGAs want small-ticket distribution.
revenue_model: Premium of roughly $3-$15 per month depending on how often each zone is ordered out (about 1.3-1.5x expected payout), or $1-$3 per employee per month on group plans. The company keeps an MGA commission of 15-25%, plus municipal, nonprofit and employer-funded policies for vulnerable residents. Later it can sell zone-frequency data to emergency managers.
non_obvious_insight: The best parametric trigger is a legal act, not a physical measurement. An evacuation order is binary, public, address-specific and timestamped, so basis risk nearly vanishes. Paying people to leave also changes behavior and saves lives, which makes employers and governments willing co-payers, so the product has two buyers instead of one.
first_30_days: Sign a parametric MGA and fronting carrier. Build the polygon match and instant-payout flow on public evacuation-zone data. Pilot a group policy for about 200 hourly workers at one Gulf hospital or hotel employer and one credit union serving a LA burn-scar community. Offer emergency-management agencies a free 'what zone am I in' tool for distribution. Goal: 500 covered addresses before peak rain season.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Arbol, FEMA Individuals and Households Program (Serious Needs / Displacement Assistance), Homeowners and renters ALE / civil-authority coverage (State Farm, Assurant, Lemonade and other carriers), Jumpstart (parametric earthquake, California). White space: Verification is incomplete, so treat this as a provisional gap verdict, not a confirmed one. I found no product that pays a flat cash amount to an individual within hours because a mandatory evacuation order covers their address. Every adjacent player triggers on something else. Parametric platforms use physical measurements. FEMA and GiveDirectly pay after the event and need an application or a declaration. Homeowners and renters ALE and civil-authority cover is receipt-based. The unserved wedge is the legal-act trigger, paid out as a flat amount before the trip, to renters and hourly workers, funded by someone other than the individual (county or state emergency management, Medicaid and Medicare Advantage plans, landlords or property managers, credit unions, philanthropy). That funder-pays model is the specific space I found nobody in. Main risks: a carrier could add a flat 'evacuation expense' rider to renters policies, and evacuation-zone data is held by vendors and counties, some under licensing terms that were not checked.

title: Orphan Fleet Depot for Bankrupt-Maker Electric Buses
one_liner: Sustainment-as-a-service for school districts and transit agencies stuck with electric buses whose manufacturer went bankrupt, using the military's orphan-platform playbook (salvaged parts pool, configuration control, depot repair, availability guarantees).
customer: School districts, regional education service agencies and small transit agencies that own buses from failed OEMs (Lion Electric US buses, Proterra, and similar EV truck and bus makers), plus state grant administrators and cooperative-purchasing bodies that want the taxpayer-funded fleets running.
problem: When Lion Electric went through bankruptcy and its new owner voided prior U.S. warranties, districts were left with buses nobody would service. Some sourced parts themselves, some sidelined buses, and some went back to diesel. Proterra's transit business went through a similar handoff. Grant-funded buses that sit idle are a political and audit embarrassment. Dealers cannot fix proprietary battery, inverter and charge-port faults, and there is no parts channel.
solution: Run it like a military orphan-platform sustainment program. (1) Buy the bankruptcy estate's remaining parts, tooling and diagnostics at liquidation. (2) Build a per-VIN configuration database and a reverse-engineered diagnostic library. (3) Stand up a regional depot and a mobile repair van for line-replaceable units: contactors, DC-DC converters, charge ports, battery management modules and pack modules. (4) Buy sidelined orphan buses cheaply as cannibalization donors. (5) Sell a fixed annual sustainment contract per bus that guarantees a morning-route availability rate, backed by a shared spares pool across districts sized with readiness-based sparing math.
why_now: Lion's sale voided U.S. warranties (reported late 2025), so the 2025-26 school year is when the pain became real. The installed base of grant-funded EV buses is large and aging out of warranty, and subsidy rollbacks (the federal commercial clean vehicle credit ended for vehicles acquired after Sept 30, 2025) make further OEM failures likely. The parts estates of failed makers are cheapest to buy right now, before anyone else sees their value.
revenue_model: Annual sustainment contract of roughly $4-8k per bus with an availability guarantee, plus time-and-materials for depot repairs, spares-pool membership fees for districts that want priority access, and salvage and refurbished battery pack sales. Sold through cooperative purchasing vehicles so districts do not each run a bid.
non_obvious_insight: Orphaned does not mean unfixable. In most orphaned fleets, 5-10 recurring line-replaceable units cause most of the downtime. A small shared spares pool plus a configuration-controlled baseline can lift availability from a coin flip to about 90%. The right buyer is not one district's bus garage but a state agency or regional service center pooling many districts, because the sparing math only works at fleet-of-fleets scale. Military sustainers call this the DMSMS problem and solved it by owning the baseline instead of waiting for the OEM.
first_30_days: Build a list of about 20 districts that took Lion or similar deliveries in 2022-24 from press coverage and grant award lists. Offer one district a free 'orphan health check' on a stranded bus using generic diagnostic tools and an EV-experienced transit mechanic. Register as a bidder in the relevant bankruptcy and liquidation processes and ask for the parts inventory lists. Hire 1-2 retired transit or heavy-duty EV technicians. Sign three districts to a per-bus quarterly pilot and use their fault logs to identify the top recurring failure modes.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Highland Electric Fleets, Hyroad Energy, Phoenix Motor (Phoenix Motorcars) / Proterra transit, Lion Bus (post-bankruptcy Lion Electric). White space: Not found in this research: any player selling a brand-agnostic, per-bus sustainment contract with an availability guarantee and a pooled spares inventory for orphaned electric school buses. Highland offers a guarantee for buses it deploys and Hyroad does the estate-buying for hydrogen trucks, but neither was found serving orphaned Lion buses. Herscher CUSD (IL), Winthrop (MA) and Yarmouth (ME) are paying ad hoc 'alternate vendors' or have parked buses, and the Electrek piece names no third-party service provider. The wedge is Lion's US-orphaned school buses. That is a small installed base, described only as 'dozens of districts', and its sizing was not verified. Multi-district pooling through a state agency or regional service center is also unserved. Caveats: this verdict comes from a thin evidence base, because the WebSearch budget ran out (200 of 200) and only about a dozen direct page fetches worked. No search of Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or open-source tools was possible. Small independent EV repair shops, dealers or school-bus contractors may already do this informally and would not show up in homepage fetches. Weaknesses in the idea: (a) the 'buy the estate cheaply now' premise looks partly stale, since Lion's US facilities were divested by mid-2025 and its Chapter 15 dates to Dec 2024, so the parts and tooling may already be sold; (b) Proterra transit has a successor OEM in Phoenix Motor; (c) battery, BMS and inverter repair on reverse-engineered buses carries fire and liability risk, given the EPA investigation of Lion bus fires and Quebec pulling Lion buses out of service; (d) the buyer pool is small and public budgets are slow.

title: GLP-1 Palate Panel for Food R&D
one_liner: A managed panel of GLP-1 users and their households that food and restaurant companies rent to test products, portions and health claims.
customer: R&D and insights teams at mid-size CPG (protein, snacks, frozen), restaurant chain menu teams, foodservice for hospitals and senior living, and supplement brands that need claim substantiation ($25-150k per study).
problem: 73% of GLP-1 users report taste changes and 70% lose joy in eating, so 'just add protein' fails. About 70% change what the household eats, and non-users adopt 30-50% of the changes, so the affected base is ~50% larger than the user count. Food companies are reformulating and launching 'GLP-1 friendly' labels on general-population panels and conflicting forecasts.
solution: Recruit and maintain a segmented panel (drug, dose, weeks on therapy, aversion profile, household makeup). Run sensory, portion and format tests plus home-use tests and 8-12 week muscle and satiety claim studies. Deliver 'aversion maps' (which textures and smells trigger nausea at which dose) and household spillover models.
why_now: Households with a GLP-1 user doubled from ~11% to 22% in under 3 years. Pills launched in 2026 broaden the base. CPG is mid-reformulation, and FTC claim scrutiny makes 'evidence-backed' labels valuable. Purchase-panel incumbents see what is bought, not why.
revenue_model: $25-150k per study, plus $40-100k/year data subscription for 'aversion map' updates.
non_obvious_insight: The 'GLP-1 consumer' is 5-6 sensory segments that shift with dose and week on therapy, not one persona. Forecasting from sales data cannot separate them, but a panel can. The picks-and-shovels of a reformulation wave are the testers, not the brands.
first_30_days: Recruit 300 panelists from subreddits and Facebook groups with a $25 incentive, verified by photo of the pharmacy label. Publish a free 'taste change' survey report for press. Cold-email 30 CPG insights leads and land a first paid pilot of about $25k.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Circana (GLP-1s and Consumer Behavior insights hub), Numerator (GLP-1 People Groups and GLP-1 Custom Analysis), The Hartman Group - 'GLP-1s: Seizing Opportunity in a New CPG Landscape', Tastewise (GLP-1 CPG Playbook, TasteGPT). White space: Limited to what I could check: I found no vendor, on the pages I fetched, that runs a managed, longitudinal panel of verified GLP-1 users segmented by drug, dose and weeks on therapy. I also found none that does physical product testing on that panel (sensory, portion and format tests, home-use tests) or maps aversions by texture and smell against dose. The players found are all survey, signal or purchase-data based: Circana and Numerator show what GLP-1 households buy, Hartman sells a one-off $10k survey report, and Tastewise sells AI trend signals. Nothing found covers household spillover modeling tied to a panel. Nothing found offers claim-substantiation studies (8-12 week muscle and satiety) for 'GLP-1 friendly' labels. Big gaps in my evidence: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so I could not run general web searches and relied on direct fetches of vendor pages. I did not check startups, YC or Crunchbase entries, sensory CROs (Sensory Spectrum showed no GLP-1 content; Tragon and Eurofins fetches failed), generic panel vendors (Cint, Toluna showed no GLP-1 content; Dynata unchecked), telehealth companies (Ro, Noom, WeightWatchers) that could monetize their own user bases, or flavor houses (Givaudan, Kerry and dsm-firmenich showed no GLP-1 content on the pages retrieved; IFF returned 403). Any of these could already offer a GLP-1 screener or a similar service, so treat the gap verdict as medium-low confidence.

title: Family Bank: Bank of Mom and Dad, Papered
one_liner: A family office's real job is governance and records, not investing; for $20/mo, give ordinary parents and adult children a promissory-note, autopay and sibling-fairness ledger for the money that already flows between them.
customer: Parents aged 55-75 who lend or give money to adult children (down-payment help, car, tuition, debt payoff, business start), sold as a pair with the adult child (28-45). Elder-law attorneys, mortgage brokers and credit unions are referral channels.
problem: Family lending is handshake-based. Zero-interest loans over $10k invite imputed-interest questions. Gifts above the $19,000 annual exclusion (2026) need Form 709 filings. Medicaid's 60-month look-back treats gifts and forgiven loans as transfers. Mortgage lenders want documented gift letters. Siblings fight at inheritance over who got what because nobody kept records. NAR's 2025 profile shows the median first-time buyer is 40 and 22% received a gift or loan from relatives or friends.
solution: A guided flow decides gift vs loan and generates a note at or above the AFR (August 2026: 4.10% short, 4.35% mid, 4.92% long). ACH autopay collects and pays, and both sides get annual interest statements. A December 'forgiveness engine' forgives up to the exclusion with proper letters. A sibling ledger records every advancement so estates can equalize. Flags fire for Form 709 and Medicaid look-back exposure, and there is a mortgage-ready gift-letter generator plus one-click export to the family's estate attorney. Attorney review is an add-on.
why_now: Median first-time buyer age hit 40 (a record), housing costs push more family help, and long-term-care costs make the Medicaid look-back a live worry for boomer parents. Instant-payment and bank-linking rails make autopay cheap. The 2026 federal estate exemption is $15M, so for most families the value is peace and records, not tax planning.
revenue_model: $20/mo per family (up to 3 active loans); $49 document packs for the free-to-paid funnel; $149 attorney review add-on with referral fees; optional servicing fee; later, a pooled family reserve product.
non_obvious_insight: The killer feature is not the loan, it is the sibling ledger. Most family money fights are about unequal treatment nobody can prove, and family offices solve this with an advancement ledger that ordinary families never get. The loan-vs-gift label is also the pivot point for tax and Medicaid consequences, so classification is the paid moment.
first_30_days: Ship a free AFR calculator and note generator aimed at 'family loan agreement' searches, and sell $49 document packs. Convert 5% to the $20/mo servicing tier. Line up 3 elder-law attorneys who receive leads and review notes. Target 50 paying families.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: LoanBack, FamZoo, Wealth.com, Vanilla. White space: Research was limited: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200) before any planned search ran, so I worked only from direct fetches of specific pages. I did not search Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, forums or RFPs, and I could not check LegalZoom, Rocket Lawyer or Nolo because those URLs returned 404 or 403. What the evidence shows: (1) The document layer is already commoditized. LoanBack sells a note plus amortization schedule for $15 to $30 and has 10+ years of traction, so the free AFR calculator and $49 note pack in the 30-day plan would compete head-on with it. (2) Nothing I found does the parts that are the real product. I checked LoanBack, FamZoo, Wealth.com and Vanilla, and none advertises these: real ACH autopay between parent and adult child; annual interest statements for both parties; a December forgiveness engine that applies the annual gift exclusion; a gift-vs-loan classification flow tied to Form 709 and Medicaid look-back flags; a mortgage gift-letter generator; a sibling advancement ledger that estates can equalize from; a one-click export to the family's estate attorney. (3) The sibling ledger and the classification audit trail appear genuinely unserved for ordinary families. The advisor-only estate tools (Wealth.com, Vanilla) do not sell to a 62-year-old parent or her adult child. (4) Coverage gap: I could not confirm the absence of niche competitors. Private-note servicers, small startups and attorney-firm tools may exist that my fetches missed.

title: Supervised-Hours Bench for Counselors and Social Workers
one_liner: A managed group-supervision network and hour-logging platform that lets clinics fund the thousands of post-degree supervised hours gating counseling, MFT and social-work licenses.
customer: Group therapy practices, community mental-health agencies and school districts hiring associate-level counselors and social workers; the associates themselves.
problem: Counseling, psychology and social work were excluded from the higher federal loan cap. Licensure typically requires 2-4k supervised hours after the degree, and associates often pay $50-150 an hour out of pocket for supervision that is scarce and tracked on paper. Clinics cannot hire associates faster than supervisors can be found.
solution: Certified supervisors, often semi-retired licensed clinicians, deliver state-compliant group supervision by video. The platform logs hours in board-ready format and enforces state ratios and rules. Clinics pay per associate per month to onboard associates who can bill insurance under supervision.
why_now: The July 2026 loan caps squeeze students in excluded fields and push them toward employer support. Behavioral-health demand is high, and telesupervision is widely permitted in many states after the pandemic.
revenue_model: $150-300 per associate per month from the clinic, supervision delivery margin, and hour-logging SaaS. Optional share of billed associate revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The scarcest input in the credential chain is not the degree but post-degree supervision, and the payer is the employer, not the student, because associates bill insurance and become revenue-positive once supervised.
first_30_days: Pick one large state that permits telesupervision. Recruit 5 licensed supervisors. Sign 3 group practices with about 10 associates in total. Run the hour logs in spreadsheets first and charge $200 per associate per month. Verify board rules before selling.

The competitor list therefore comes from direct fetches of known and guessed vendor sites, not systematic search. It is likely incomplete, and "nothing found" is weak evidence.

What the fetches showed. Hour logging is commodity: Time2Track is an incumbent, and Supervaise, clinicalsupervision.com and Supervision Studio show the product is easy to build, so the SaaS layer is not a business. Supervisor matching and group supervision are sold to the associate by small regional operators (Licensure Supervision LLC in Oklahoma) and by Supervaise as a marketplace feature.

Not found in any fetch: a company selling employer-paid, managed supervision capacity (a certified supervisor pool, supervisor-of-record contracts, liability coverage and state-rule enforcement) priced per associate per month to clinics, agencies and school districts. Every competitor sells to the associate or the supervisor, or sells software. The unserved wedge is the employer-side service: practices, community mental-health agencies and school districts with associates on staff but no board-approved supervisor. I did not verify whether large group practices such as LifeStance or Thriveworks already staff supervision in-house, so treat the wedge as unconfirmed.

Risks to verify before building (from general knowledge, not confirmed this session):
- Many states restrict who may supervise and whether outside supervisors qualify.
- Many commercial payers do not credential associates, which weakens the "associates become revenue-positive under supervision" claim.
- Third-party supervisors take on liability.
- The July 2026 loan cap reduces future degree enrollment and does not directly raise today's supervision cost, so the why-now is weaker than the pitch suggests.

title: Well Covenant Trustee for Rural Data Center Counties
one_liner: A neutral program administrator writes, monitors and runs a county-mandated, developer-funded private-well protection covenant, where excess drawdown versus upgradient control wells triggers in-kind remediation with no lawsuit and no sensor sales.
customer: Wedge: county attorneys and planning directors in rural, private-well counties that are already drafting developer-funded monitoring and neighbor-escrow language (Franklin County IN draft v3.0, Shenandoah County VA, and similar counties in GA, PA and IN). Payer: the independent developer of a 50-500 MW campus in that county, which funds the covenant because the county makes it a permit or development-agreement condition. Not hyperscalers with in-house community teams.
problem: Dry or silted wells are what actually produce lawsuits and hearing revolts (Meta / Newton County GA: neighbors say wells went dry, Meta's own study says groundwater flows away, families sued in Sept 2026). Nobody can separate data-center drawdown from drought or other pumping, so developer-commissioned studies are not believed and neighbor claims cannot be proven. Counties are drafting escrow and monitoring language from scratch, with no tested trigger, no neutral administrator and no legal structure. The parent's sensor-baseline product is a crowded, commoditizing layer (KETOS, Aethair, Envirosuite, consultancies), and its automatic cash payout risks being classed as insurance or read as an admission of liability.
solution: Sell trusteeship of a well covenant, not sensors. (1) A paste-in Covenant Kit for county attorneys: development-agreement rider, trust instrument, enrollment rules, and a published trigger protocol. (2) Trigger design: 8-12 upgradient control wells outside the cone of influence, a 12-month pre-construction regression of each enrolled household well on the control wells, and the developer's metered pumping records shared with the panel. A trigger fires only on sustained deviation beyond the control-adjusted trend (for example >5 ft and >2 standard errors for 30 days), so the developer pays for excess drawdown and not for drought. (3) Remedy is in kind, not cash indemnity: emergency water hauling in 24-48 hours, then pump lowering or well deepening by a pre-qualified local driller at a fixed rate card. The developer is the obligor and a corporate trustee (a regional bank trust department) holds the escrow. We are administrator and data steward and never hold the money. That structure is closer to a remediation trust or warranty than to an insurance policy, and a counsel opinion is the gate. (4) Governance: a 3-person technical panel with one member appointed by the county (ideally from state extension or the geological survey), one by the developer and one by a residents' council. (5) Hardware and labs are bought from KETOS, Eno Scientific, Kunak-type vendors. Noise, PM2.5 and voltage are paid add-ons later.
why_now: Permit politics moved to governors in 2026 (NY Executive Order 62 on July 14, Texas TCEQ permit halt on Sept 21), and counties are writing the rules now. Franklin County's draft already contains developer-paid monitoring wells, a licensed-hydrogeologist assessment and an escrow for 24-hour potable water to impacted neighbors. Shenandoah County officials back applicant-funded third-party testing, and St. Louis's permit requires a developer-funded hydraulic study. Ordinances get copied county to county, so a ready, legally vetted kit written this quarter can become the template. The Newton County lawsuit (Sept 2026) shows what a baseline-less well dispute costs.
revenue_model: Paid by the developer through the county-mandated covenant. Illustrative program of 500 enrolled households: $1,000 per household setup (mostly hardware pass-through, about 25% margin) = $500k; $480 per household per year for telemetry, QA, lab checks and reporting = $240k per year at about 55% gross margin; administrator fee of 1% per year on a $1.5M remediation reserve (about $2,500 per household) = $15k; $500 per adjudicated claim. Extensions add per-household noise, air and voltage modules. Later: license the trigger protocol and dataset to state agencies and insurers. Assumptions to test: expected remedy claim rate of 5-10% of wells over 10 years, and $8-15k per remedy.
non_obvious_insight: The real buyer is the county attorney, not the developer. Because the county imposes the covenant, the developer's objection to volunteering a payout (an implied admission) disappears, and the county gets an instrument it cannot write itself. The economics are also better for developers than the alternative: NorthPoint offered $10k to each of 4,500 households ($45M) and was accused of bribery, while an in-kind covenant reserve for the households that could plausibly lose water is a small fraction of that and is credible because a neutral panel decides. Attribution is fixed in the design (control wells and pumping records), not argued afterward.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: get Franklin County IN's draft v3.0 and the Shenandoah County notes, call the county attorneys and planning directors, and offer to draft the covenant and trust instrument free in exchange for being named in the draft. Days 3-14: retain a land-use or insurance-regulatory lawyer for a written view on insurance characterization (remediation trust, developer as obligor, in-kind remedy); recruit a land-grant extension hydrogeologist and two regional bank trust departments as prospective corporate trustee. Days 10-30: run the parent's 10-neighbor-well pilot in a county with a pending hearing, but with control wells and the regression trigger back-tested on 12 months of public USGS or state well data, and bring the term sheet plus live dashboard to the hearing. Kill gate at 90 days: one developer or county puts a funded escrow in writing and counsel signs off; otherwise stop.

title: Home Equity Assurance for Data Center Neighbors
one_liner: A neutral calculation agent runs a county-approved, developer-funded home-value guarantee for houses near proposed data centers, using pre-announcement baselines and public sale records with no sensors, and unspent escrow reverts to the developer, which makes it cheaper than $10k checks and more credible.
customer: Payer: independent data center developers and their CFOs and general counsel, especially those that have already tried lump-sum checks or buyouts and got 'bribe' coverage (NorthPoint-type offers, Mason County-type buyouts). Co-signer: county commissions that put the guarantee into a development agreement. Distribution partners: title and escrow companies, mortgage lenders and local realtors in the impact radius, who deliver claims at the point of sale. Beneficiaries: owner-occupants within roughly 1-3 miles.
problem: Residents' biggest fear is not a sensor reading, it is the value of their house. Developers are already spending on this fear in the worst way: NorthPoint's $10k-per-household offer ($45M across 4,500 households) was called a bribe, and Propmodo expects future offers to move to 'utility bill credits or property value guarantees rather than lump sums'. A check pays 100% of households for a risk that only touches the minority who sell at a loss, buys no trust, and leaves the price question unresolved. Home-value anecdotes are contested (a 4-bedroom listed 15-18% lower next to a Northern Virginia hyperscale site; the NAR 2026 Data Center Impact Report and local reporting disagree on how far effects reach), so both sides are arguing about a number nobody has pre-agreed.
solution: Product: a Property Value Assurance Program administered as a contract, not insurance. The developer is the obligor and funds an escrow (illustratively $3-5k per eligible household, against $10k of certain checks) with a corporate escrow agent at signing of the development agreement. We are the neutral calculation agent, the way a calculation agent works in a structured contract. Mechanics: (1) Freeze a reference value for each enrolled home at the date of first public disclosure of the project, using an AVM plus a broker price opinion (about $300), with a full appraisal only if disputed. (2) Publish a county-wide control index (repeat-sales or hedonic, plus matched control neighborhoods) so market moves are separated from project effects. (3) If the owner sells at arm's length within 10 years (listed 60+ days, arm's-length buyer), we pay from escrow the shortfall between the net sale price and the control-index-adjusted reference value, up to a cap (for example 20% of reference). (4) Unspent escrow reverts to the developer at year 10, or is split with a community fund. (5) No sensors: the trigger is a price versus a pre-agreed formula, so there is no argument about causation, only about arithmetic. Adverse selection and gaming are handled with the arm's-length rule, an exposure cap and a three-appraiser tie-break (already the norm in Mason County buyouts).
why_now: In 2026 lump-sum neighbor payments went mainstream and drew immediate backlash (NorthPoint, September 2026 coverage), while moratoria in NY (July 14) and Texas (Sept 21) plus local pauses give developers a reason to look for a structure that survives a hearing. Data-center adjacency is now a mainstream real-estate question: Realtor.com counts 108 ZIP codes with a large data center by June 2026, up from 12 in 2015, and NAR and HousingWire are publishing on it, so buyers and lenders already ask. AVMs, MLS and deed data are cheap and standardized. Wind developers have used property-value guarantees as permit conditions, so counties and lawyers recognize the form.
revenue_model: Paid by the developer from the program budget. Illustrative 3,000-household program: $300 per household enrollment (AVM, BPO, lien check, portal) = $900k; 1% per year of a $12M escrow = $120k; $1,500 per adjudicated sale claim; optional 50 bps share of escrow yield (T-bill yield on $12M is meaningful float for the agent-of-record bank to share). Roughly $1M+ of year-one revenue per program, about 10x the parent's $75-150k sensor setup, with software-like margins after the model is built. Second revenue line: sell the control-index and price-effect research to counties, lenders and appraisers. Assumptions to test: 10-25% of homes sell within 10 years and only some at a shortfall; expected payout 10-30% of escrow.
non_obvious_insight: A guarantee is cheaper for the developer than a check and more persuasive to the neighbor, at the same time: the expected payout is only the shortfall on homes that actually sell at a loss, and unspent money returns, while residents receive the thing they said they wanted (protection of value, per Propmodo) instead of hush money. It also sidesteps the attribution trap that hurts the parent, because the trigger is a formula on public deed data, not a causal claim about a well or a hum. And it aligns incentives: every year the facility runs quietly is a year the developer's escrow is not drawn, so neighbors and developer want the same outcome. Making the developer the obligor also removes the insurance-law problem the parent's escrow payout faced.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build the price-effect model on deed and MLS data around 3 existing clusters (for example Loudoun and Prince William VA and one Georgia or Texas site) using difference-in-differences against matched control neighborhoods, and publish 'what data centers actually do to nearby home prices' (this is both lead generation and the expected-payout estimate). Days 10-20: write a 2-page term sheet and a development-agreement rider; call the government-relations and general-counsel offices of 8-10 independent developers that have publicly offered checks, buyouts or community funds. Days 15-30: pitch two county attorneys with pending hearings; line up a corporate escrow agent and one title company. Target: a letter of intent for a 300-household pilot with a $1M escrow. Gate at 90 days: one signed pilot or one county condition, plus a counsel view that the developer-obligor structure is not insurance in that state.

title: Neutral Registry and Standard for Neighbor Baselines
one_liner: An independent, vendor-agnostic registry and open protocol that notarizes pre-construction baselines from any sensor vendor or consultant, gets referenced in county ordinances and a model presumption statute, and becomes the title-plant-style record that insurers and lenders underwrite against.
customer: Three payers, sequenced. (1) Sensor vendors and developer-hired consultancies (KETOS, Aethair, Kunak resellers, TRC and Salas O'Brien-type firms) that need a neutral stamp so counties will believe their data. (2) Data center developers who must file a baseline to satisfy an ordinance or a hearing (50-500 MW campuses in contested counties). (3) Later, insurers, lenders and state agencies buying registry data and certification. Counties and regulators are the standard's adopters, not payers.
problem: Every county and agency is inventing its own baseline rules: a 48-hour ambient sound survey here, monitoring wells and a hydrogeologist there (Franklin County IN, Chadds Ford PA, Shenandoah VA, St. Louis, Virginia DEQ's five Kunak sensors in Loudoun). Developer-hired consultants produce the data, so residents distrust it; opposition-side groups produce competing data, so developers distrust that. Nothing makes a baseline tamper-evident, comparable across sites, or legally meaningful. Unlike Pennsylvania's Act 13 for oil and gas (operators pay for pre-drill tests, and a rebuttable presumption applies when no baseline exists), no data-center equivalent creates a legal reason to buy, which is the parent's biggest unproven assumption.
solution: Build the audit-firm layer for baselines, in four steps. (1) Protocol v1, open and free: sensor siting rules, control-site design, QA/QC, minimum 90 days pre-application, chain of custody and data schema for wells, noise, PM2.5 and voltage, written with a land-grant university hydrogeologist and an acoustician. (2) The registry: any vendor submits raw data through an API, and we run automated QA, protocol audit and dual-key custody (a university library or state geological survey as second custodian, plus RFC 3161-style public timestamp logs, no token). The output is a Registered Baseline certificate with tamper-evident, first-in timestamps and a public read-only view. (3) The adoption engine: a one-page ordinance rider ('baseline must be registered under an independent public-benefit protocol') sent to every county drafting rules, and a model bill for the January 2027 legislative sessions (TX and NY are the pressure points) that adapts the Act 13 logic: a registered baseline lets a developer rebut unsupported claims, while no registered baseline shifts the presumption to the operator. (4) Governance: a public-benefit board with county, university, developer and resident seats, so no vendor controls it. Year 2-3 balance-sheet option: once 30+ campuses are registered, use the loss-relevant data to launch a developer-owned risk retention group or mutual for neighbor-harm guarantees, with the registry as its underwriting file. The same registry then extends to other large-load neighbors (battery storage, fabs, lithium, hydrogen).
why_now: The moratorium wave (NY EO 62 on July 14, Texas TCEQ halt on Sept 21, local pauses) means regulators must define 'what evidence counts' before lifting pauses. State legislatures convene in January 2027. Counties are copy-pasting bespoke baseline language right now, so an early standard can be the copied text. Public-sector baselines are starting (Virginia DEQ's Loudoun air sensors since Feb 2026) and need tamper-evident custody, and the Newton County lawsuit (Sept 2026) is a live example of dueling studies. Sensor prices collapsed, so the scarce input is now trust, not data.
revenue_model: Registry filing fee of $15-25k per site (protocol audit, QA, dual-key custody, certificate) plus $3-6k per year custody for 10 years; vendor and assessor certification of about $10k per firm per year for the registry-verified listing; data and API licences to insurers, lenders, state agencies and researchers; later, a premium share if a mutual launches. Bottom-up sketch: 150 new registrations per year at $20k = $3M; 500 custodied sites at $4.5k = $2.25M; 60 certified firms at $10k = $0.6M; about $6M per year by year 3 from data centers alone, with the upside from adjacent industries and underwriting data. Sales-cycle proxy: a filing is a line item in a permit budget, not a new budget.
non_obvious_insight: The incumbents are the channel, not the enemy. Developer-hired consultants and sensor vendors already produce the baselines but cannot be believed, and their best sales asset is a credible neutral attestation, exactly as companies prepare their own books but need an independent auditor to be trusted. So the registry sells to the competitors' customers through the competitors, and vendors pay to be certified because counties will ask for it. The moat is a cornered resource (first-in timestamped pre-construction baselines cannot be recreated after a site is built), network economies (cross-site data improves control models and expected-loss estimates) and switching costs (10-year custody), backed by counter-positioning (a vendor cannot be neutral without giving up its own product). The lever that decides everything is the legal presumption, which is why the model bill and ordinance rider are part of the product, not lobbying on the side.
first_30_days: Days 1-14: draft Protocol v0.1 with a land-grant extension hydrogeologist and an independent acoustician; publish it CC-BY with a one-page ordinance rider. Days 10-25: send the rider to the county attorneys behind Franklin County IN, Shenandoah VA, Chadds Ford PA and 10 other counties with open drafts; ask to be named as an acceptable registry. Days 15-30: sign 3-5 letters of intent from sensor vendors and consultancies to submit pilot baselines for the Registered Baseline certificate; book calls with two state association-of-counties or legislative staff on presumption language for TX and NY. Sell the first two filings ($12-18k pilot pricing) to developers with hearings in the next 60-90 days. Six-month target: 10 registered sites, 3 vendors certified, one ordinance or permit condition naming the registry, $150-250k of fees. Gate: if no county or regulator will reference the protocol within 6 months, fall back to selling attestations as a service inside the well-trustee model (offspring 1).

title: Scribe-Adjusted EBITDA: Privileged Diligence for Physician Deals
one_liner: A fixed-price, 10-business-day, counsel-engaged report that tells private equity buyers how much of a scribe-enabled physician group's revenue is real, and what the rest could cost them.
customer: Deal partners and VPs at lower-middle-market PE funds and MSOs buying 20-150 provider specialty groups (dermatology, orthopedics, ophthalmology, GI, urology, behavioral health, primary care) that adopted an ambient scribe in the last 18 months. The engaging party is the buyer's healthcare transactions counsel, so the work is privileged. Quality-of-earnings accounting firms are channel partners, not rivals.
problem: Buyers pay a multiple of EBITDA that now includes scribe-era E/M uplift, and drift dollars fall through at near-100% margin. Illustration (assumptions to validate): $30M revenue, 40% E/M, 6% scribe uplift gives $0.72M, about 14% of a $5M EBITDA, or roughly $8M of enterprise value at 11x. A stock deal also inherits overpayment liability, and the 60-day return rule starts once a problem is identified. Nobody in the deal team can answer the question. QoE accountants have no coder bench. Regulatory counsel runs generic billing samples. Seller materials and scribe vendor 'AAPC-verified' claims are self-serving. The parent's own research flags that the drift may be legitimate documentation catch-up, so buyers cannot tell whether to discount it or trust it.
solution: Deliverable is a 'Scribe-Adjusted Run-Rate Report', engaged through deal counsel under a privilege-preserving engagement letter. (1) Causal drift estimate: 24-36 months of claims from the data room plus each provider's scribe go-live date from the seller's admin console. Because rollouts are staggered, non-adopters and late adopters in the same group form a built-in control group, so a staggered difference-in-differences replaces a naive before/after. (2) Coder-signed sample: 150-300 stratified encounters from the highest-drift providers, reviewed by certified coders on MDM and time statements. This splits drift into 'supported catch-up' and 'at-risk narration'. (3) Outputs: a scribe-adjusted EBITDA range, an extrapolated overpayment exposure with a confidence interval, and recommended escrow, specific indemnity or price adjustment language. It also includes a 100-day post-close remediation and refund plan. (4) Later: the same report sold sell-side ('prove your uplift is clean before you go to market') to cut re-trades.
why_now: Scribes went mainstream across groups in 2025-26, so the first wave of PE deals with 12-24 months of scribe-era claims is closing now. The FCA enforcement climate makes successor liability a live diligence topic. There is no historical playbook, because this diligence item did not exist in 2023.
revenue_model: $20-45k per buy-side report, priced by provider count and data volume. $8-15k for a sell-side readiness version. Optional 100-day post-close monitor at $4-8k per month. Direct cost is roughly $3-5k per report (30-45 coder hours plus senior review), so gross margin is about 80%. Two people can deliver one to two reports a week. Second, EBITDA leverage makes a $30k report protect about $8M of price, so it is priced against the deal, not against a compliance budget. The same report is also valuable to a seller with clean documentation, which makes it a two-sided product that gets better as deals accumulate.

title: Scribe-Safe Billing: White-Label Audit for Billing Companies
one_liner: Outsourced billing companies buy a per-provider, coder-signed drift monitor and quarterly attestation letter, then resell it to their small-practice clients as 'scribe-safe billing'.
customer: Mid-size outsourced billing and RCM companies (roughly 40-500 providers under management, spread across 5-50 small groups, for example HBMA members) that bill for practices using a mix of scribes. Later channels: practice-management and EHR marketplaces, and IPAs.
problem: The bulk of scribe adoption in small practices is cheap or low-cost tooling with no compliance officer behind it. The billing company sees every claim across many clients and scribe vendors, is paid a percentage of collections (so scribe uplift raises its own fee), and can be exposed as a party that caused false claims. Its contract says the client owns documentation, but that does not stop a payer or DOJ from asking the biller what it did. Enterprise audit platforms are priced and sold for organizations with in-house compliance staff, so this segment gets nothing. Small groups also lack the resources to appeal payer downcodes.
solution: 'Scribe-Safe' program the biller white-labels. (1) Claims-only monitor across the biller's whole book, with no EHR access: per-provider E/M and modifier drift versus specialty peers, plus the payer downcode rate from 835 remits (CARC 150, 'payer deems the information does not support this level of service') as a leading signal. (2) Quarterly coder-signed review of about 8 encounters per flagged provider, focused on MDM and total-time statements. (3) A signed quarterly attestation letter per practice that the biller can show a client, payer or auditor. (4) A contract addendum plus a refund workflow so findings reach the practice's designated contact and can be acted on within the 60-day overpayment rule, so the biller never sits on an identified problem. (5) Cross-book benchmark by scribe vendor and specialty returned to the biller as a sales asset.
why_now: Small groups adopted low-cost scribes in 2025-26, payers' automated downcoding programs are now hitting the small groups least able to appeal, outsourced billing keeps growing, and billing companies compete on differentiation as AI coding commoditizes their core work. Law-firm commentary warns that 'the AI suggested it' is not a defense. Billing companies now need something independent to point to.
revenue_model: Wholesale $12-20 per provider per month; the biller resells at $25-40 or bundles it for retention. $25 per encounter for extra coder reviews. A 300-provider biller is about $45-70k a year, so 25 billers is roughly $1.1-1.75M ARR. Coder time is about $7 per provider per month at 8 reviews per quarter of about 6 minutes each with an AI pre-read, giving 55-65% gross margin. Land through a 60-day paid pilot at $4-6k per biller.
non_obvious_insight: The payer's own downcode rate is a free, externally labeled audit signal. A jump in CARC 150 adjustments for one provider after go-live means the payer's model has already flagged the notes, before any human looks. The billing company is also the only actor with a cross-client, cross-scribe view, and it buys cover more than detection: an independent signature is the product, which is why more AI coding automation is not a substitute.
first_30_days: Contact HBMA chapter leaders and 40 billing-company owners on LinkedIn. Offer a 60-day paid pilot ($4-6k) that starts with a scan of the biller's aggregated 12-month 837/835 book, structured under the biller's counsel and with the findings routed to practices, not left with the biller. Recruit 2 CPC/CPMA contractors and a healthcare lawyer to draft the addendum and refund workflow. Deliver a provider watchlist and 30 coder-signed reviews to each pilot. Goal: 3 signed pilots and 1 conversion to a per-provider contract.

title: The Reference Panel: Neutral Ruler for E/M Levels
one_liner: A neutral, triple-blind coder-and-physician panel that measures how reliable any E/M level really is, and sells that measurement to scribe vendors, payers and providers who are now fighting over it.
customer: Three sides. First payer: health-system and large-group compliance and counsel with contested encounters (payer record requests, downcode appeals, OIG inquiries). Second: scribe and coding-AI vendors that need independent validation. Third: payers running automated downcoding, which face state laws and regulator scrutiny on human review. Auditors and RCM firms become licensees.
problem: E/M level is a judgment, not a fact. Published studies show weak agreement even among trained coders: one study had five experienced certified coders assign codes to six notes and only one code was unanimous, and another found 36% inter-rater reliability among eight research nurses across 4,137 visits. Yet three AI systems now assign levels (scribes, autonomous coders, payer downcoders) and contradict each other. Each treats its own output as truth, and extrapolated overpayment demands multiply one reviewer's noise across a whole claims universe. Nobody publishes the noise floor, so the dispute goes to whoever has more lawyers.
solution: An independent panel of certified coders plus a physician advisor labels encounters blind against the 2021 MDM and time rules, with adjudication and published agreement statistics (Krippendorff's alpha by specialty and level). An AI pre-read and single coder handle easy cases and only disagreements escalate to a three-person panel, so the average is about 1.6 reviews per encounter. Product ladder: (a) 'Panel-Certified Level' files for contested encounters, giving a level, a confidence and dissent notes, at $60-90 each; (b) annual validation of a vendor's or payer's AI against a held-out panel-labeled set with a published scorecard, $75-200k a year; (c) noise-floor benchmark subscription and consortium membership at $25-50k; (d) later, a licensed evaluator model trained on the adjudicated labels. Governance rules that make it credible: published methodology, physician advisory board, no vendor equity, no single side above 30% of revenue.
why_now: In 2025-26 three sets of AI systems are assigning and contesting E/M levels at scale. Payers' automated downcoding (Cigna's nationwide policy from October 2025) is reported, as are state downcoding laws in Arkansas and Virginia, with more pending. Scribe vendors are advertising 'audit-ready' and 'verified' accuracy. The 'coding arms race' is in the literature. Each side needs a ground truth it can cite, and the trailing 12 months are when disputes and vendor procurement turn to evidence.
revenue_model: Contested-encounter certification at $60-90 per encounter is the first revenue, with cost near $15-25 including adjudication, so about 70% gross margin. Vendor and payer validation at $75-200k a year. Benchmark and consortium memberships at $25-50k a year. Later licensing of the evaluator model. Revenue mix goal is roughly a third from each of providers, vendors and payers to keep neutrality.
non_obvious_insight: The product is the disagreement rate. Once you can say 'certified coders disagree on this specialty's level-4 encounters 30% of the time', a single-reviewer downcode or a single-reviewer audit finding falls inside the noise floor, and an extrapolated overpayment should shrink, which is worth real money to providers. It also turns every incumbent into a customer. VMG, MDaudit, Healthicity, Charta and the AI coders can each validate against or license the panel, so none of them needs to see it as an attack. Credibility is the moat and scales with every adjudicated encounter.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 CPC/CPMA coders and one physician advisor. Approach two health-system compliance teams that have open payer record requests or downcode disputes and offer to triple-blind review 100 contested encounters each at a pilot rate ($8-15k). Publish a 6-page methodology paper and the first anonymized agreement statistics. Offer two scribe or coding-AI vendors a 200-encounter validation on the understanding that results are only published with consent. Aim for one paid pilot and one vendor letter of intent.

title: Lead Line Photos Taken During Meter Swaps
one_liner: Add a 90-second, three-photo service-entry protocol with on-device AI to the water-meter change-out crews a utility already sends into basements, and sell it to the utility as a $10-14 per line change order.
customer: Mid-size water utilities (30k-150k connections) in the Northeast and Great Lakes that have inside-set meters, an active or planned meter or AMI replacement program, and more than 30% 'unknown' service lines in their inventory. Two budget owners: the AMI/meter program manager (capital project change order) and the lead program manager (compliance budget). The meter-installation contractor is the channel and co-beneficiary. Wedge account: a utility whose meter contractor has not yet mobilized, so the protocol goes into the statement of work.
problem: Unknown lines stay unknown because access is the hard part. Mailer self-ID reaches 10-25% of owners, and absentee landlords and LLCs almost never answer. The parent idea's paid-photo network has three weak points. First, opportunistic supply (home sales, water-heater swaps) is thin per utility. Second, the state may treat photos from third parties as self-ID-grade evidence, because the rule appears to require identification by 'water system personnel' (verify by state). Third, inspectors may not accept the liability of calling a pipe lead. Meanwhile utilities are paying crews to enter the very same basements and stand within about 3 feet of the service entry for every inside meter swap. Those crews record a meter serial and nothing about the pipe.
solution: An app or SDK for the meter crew. Photo 1 shows the pipe where it enters the wall, upstream of the meter valve. Photo 2 is a scratch and magnet close-up, using a $0.50 test card in the installer's kit. Photo 3 shows the meter serial and pipe together, which ties the evidence to the account. On-device checks reject blurry or ambiguous shots while the tech is still standing there ('retake, pipe not visible'). A vision model classifies the pipe as copper, galvanized, lead, plastic or unresolved. Low-confidence cases go to human QA and, for unresolved or mixed-material lines, to a probe or pothole queue. The tech never labels a pipe, which removes the liability concern. Output is a reconciled inventory feed in the state portal format, pushed into the utility's Esri layer, plus a dashboard showing unknowns falling by ZIP. Techs get a small per-verified-set bonus so they don't skip the step.
why_now: Meter fleets from the 2000s-2010s AMR wave are hitting battery and end-of-life, and cellular sunsets have pushed utilities into funded AMI change-outs (verify local schedules). These are the few funded programs that put a utility contractor inside every home in a specific neighborhood. State inventory updates and the 10-year replacement clock (federal details are still being litigated and revisited, and several states have their own statutes) mean unknowns carry real cost and a deadline. On-device vision models now catch bad photos at capture time, so the crew does not have to be an expert. SRF and infrastructure-law money rewards utilities that shrink unknowns before applying for replacement funds.
revenue_model: Per-line fee of $10-14 billed as a change order to the meter deployment contract, or as a per-utility deployment license of $60-150k. Change orders in that size range often clear without a council vote. Rough unit economics per line: installer bonus $2-3, kit $0.50, AI and QA $2-3, hosting and support about $1, leaving about $5-6 gross margin (roughly 45%). A 40k-inside-meter deployment is about $480k of revenue. Add-ons: inventory reconciliation SaaS, and later a resell of the same feed to meter contractors as a bundled 'verification-ready' option in their bids.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not a photographer, it is legal access. Every water tariff already makes meter access a condition of service, and utilities enforce it with repeat visits and shutoff notices, so meter crews reach exactly the absentee-landlord and LLC homes that no self-ID portal can reach, at a marginal trip cost of zero. The crew is also water system personnel or contractor, so the evidence sits in the strongest evidentiary class the state rule seems to allow. And the pipe at an inside-set meter is usually the same pipe the lead rule cares about, a few feet from where the crew is already working. A separate paid-photo marketplace has to build access, supply and trust. This borrows all three from the utility's own procurement.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: list every utility in two states that has inside meters, an announced meter or AMI program, and a public inventory over 30% unknown. Call the AMI program manager and the lead program manager at 15 of them. Also call three meter-installation contractors and ask whether they'd add a photo step for a per-set bonus. Days 10-20: get one state drinking-water program to say in writing whether a visual verification by utility-contracted personnel can reclassify an unknown. Prototype the capture app with real-time retake prompts and a scratch and magnet card. Days 20-30: run a 300-home pilot inside one utility's existing swap route, priced at cost as a change order. Validate the classifier against 100 lines the utility already knows (historical records, prior replacements) and against 20-30 potholes. Publish the accuracy and per-line cost, and propose a full-route contract at $12.

competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: BlueConduit, VODA.ai (Lead Finder / Lead Zero / Lead Management Dashboard), Trinnex leadCAST (used by Durham, NC), Esri ArcGIS Lead Service Line Inventory solution. White space: Nobody I found runs the specific thing proposed: a paid supply-side network of trade professionals (inspectors, plumbers, water-heater installers) who photograph the service entry under a fixed protocol, with vision-AI classification, tamper-evident geo-verification, human QA, and export to state inventory formats, sold to utilities per verified line. Players fall into four groups. (1) Predictive modelers (BlueConduit, VODA.ai) reduce digs statistically but still need ground-truth field samples, and Texas does not accept predictive modeling for official inventories. Caveats: (a) my WebSearch budget ran out after 4 searches, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and GitHub sweeps were not done and a stealth or very early startup in this niche could exist; (b) the search snippet says physical identification methods 'must be conducted or overseen by water system personnel' (state-dependent), so third-party photos may only count as self-ID-grade evidence unless the utility or state accepts contractor verification; (c) the idea's own note that regulatory details are from memory still applies; (d) per-utility supply is limited to home sales and water-heater swaps, so density per utility could be slow; (e) inspectors may resist liability for calling a pipe lead (my recollection, unverified); (f) Trinnex or Esri could add a 'contractor submission' role cheaply. | How this version avoids them: BlueConduit and VODA.ai predict statistically and still need ground truth. This produces deterministic evidence for 100% of the homes the crew visits and can be sold to them as calibration data. RCAP door-to-door inspections, Electro Scan probes and Echologics/Mueller acoustic tools all need a dedicated visit or crew per line. This rides a trip that is already paid for. Trinnex or Esri adding a contractor role would not reach into the meter-deployment workflow, which the installers and utilities own. The parent's inspector network is dropped as the primary channel, which removes the cold-start, the liability objection and the third-party evidence problem.

title: Independent Audit Samples for Modeled Lead Inventories
one_liner: Become the independent auditor of predictive lead-line inventories: sell engineering consultants and state reviewers a statistically designed sample of 60-150 photo-verified lines that proves a model's error rate, paid per ground-truth point plus an annual attestation fee.
customer: Regional engineering and environmental consulting firms (50-500 staff) that win lead-line inventory work as prime contractor, license or run a predictive model, and must defend the classification to a state reviewer. Wedge: firms holding three or more utility inventory contracts in a state whose drinking-water program requires field validation of modeled non-lead classifications, or in a state that rejects pure modeling (Texas is reported not to accept predictive modeling for official inventories, verify before selling). The state reviewer is the second beneficiary, and the utility is the eventual budget owner.
problem: Predictive modelers and consultants classify tens of thousands of unknown lines statistically, but a regulator or council will ask 'what is your error rate?' The consultant's current answer is a field crew, a subcontractor or potholing, priced at hundreds of dollars per point, with no independence from the party selling the model. Vendors that sell both prediction and verification are grading their own homework. In the parent idea the buyer was a utility that needed tens of thousands of lines cleared, which made low homeowner response and thin supply fatal. An audit needs far fewer points.
solution: An audit-sample service. We draw a stratified random sample from the utility's modeled bins (predicted non-lead, predicted lead, low-confidence), so the sample design is ours and can't be steered by the modeler. Homeowners get a utility-letterhead notice with a $25-30 incentive. A panel of 20-40 licensed plumbers and inspectors in the state visit and capture the three-photo protocol plus scratch and magnet test. Each point goes through AI classification, human QA, and tamper-evident geo-verification. Deliverables: (1) an evidence pack in the state inventory format; (2) an error-rate report with confidence intervals, including a non-response follow-up on a subset to measure bias; (3) a signed attestation the consultant can attach to the inventory submission. Where the state requires water-system oversight, the utility designates panel members as its agents in writing or witnesses by video. The sampling math is what makes it small: if 60 randomly sampled 'non-lead' lines are all non-lead, the true lead rate in that bin is below 5% with 95% confidence, and 150 clean lines bounds it below 2%.
why_now: First-round inventories leaned heavily on models, and reviewers, litigants and journalists are now questioning the unknown and 'non-lead' bins. The next inventory update cycle (around late 2027 under the federal rule, verify) is when models get challenged. Consultants are under fixed-fee pressure and want to avoid running field crews. Vision models plus tamper-evident capture make a small distributed audit panel cheaper than centrally staffed crews. Predictive modeling has reached the point where the constraint is credibility, not accuracy.
revenue_model: Wholesale price of about $140 per ground-truth point, against a cost of roughly $85-95 (panel payout $70-85, homeowner incentive, QA). An audit of one bin (60-150 points) is $9-21k, and a mid-size utility with three bins is a $30-40k engagement that fits under many small-purchase limits. Sold through the consultant as a pass-through with markup, or directly to the utility when the state reviewer requests it. Recurring revenue comes from an annual drift attestation ($10-15k per utility) as inventories are updated. A later product is a labeled, consented evidence dataset licensed back to modelers to retrain.
non_obvious_insight: A buyer that needs a sample, not a census, changes everything the judges worried about. Sixty to a few hundred points per utility means a 10-25% response rate is fine, thin opportunistic supply is fine, and per-point price can be $140 instead of $40. Every clean point vouches for thousands of predicted lines, so a sample point is worth far more to the buyer than a census point. The valuable thing to sell is independence: the model vendor cannot audit its own model, and the consulting firm that sells hourly field crews has no reason to keep the audit small.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: interview 10 regional consulting firms and 3 state drinking-water programs. Ask what evidence the state wants to accept a modeled non-lead bin, and whether a third-party photo sample with utility authorization counts. Pick one state and one consultant with at least three active inventory contracts. Days 10-25: recruit 20 licensed inspectors and plumbers through local chapters and pay a launch rate. Draw a random sample of 60 from one predicted non-lead bin the consultant has already produced. Mail notices with the incentive and contact until 60 are visited. Days 25-30: deliver the evidence pack and a one-page error-rate memo at cost or free, and submit it to the state reviewer through the consultant. Ask for a paid audit of the next utility's three bins.

competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: BlueConduit, VODA.ai (Lead Finder / Lead Zero / Lead Management Dashboard), Trinnex leadCAST (used by Durham, NC), Esri ArcGIS Lead Service Line Inventory solution. White space: Nobody I found runs the specific thing proposed: a paid supply-side network of trade professionals (inspectors, plumbers, water-heater installers) who photograph the service entry under a fixed protocol, with vision-AI classification, tamper-evident geo-verification, human QA, and export to state inventory formats, sold to utilities per verified line. Players fall into four groups. (1) Predictive modelers (BlueConduit, VODA.ai) reduce digs statistically but still need ground-truth field samples, and Texas does not accept predictive modeling for official inventories. (2) Customer self-ID portals (Trinnex leadCAST, Esri Survey123, Cognito Forms) collect photos and reach only the 10-25% of owners who respond, and absentee landlords and LLCs almost never do. (3) Hardware probes (Electro Scan, Echologics) need a utility crew at each line. (4) Door-to-door inspection programs (RCAP, engineering firms) are staffed centrally and slowly. The unserved wedge is professional-grade evidence for the non-responding, owner-absent lines at about $30-60 per line, collected by people already inside the building. Two sub-gaps stand out: states that reject modeling but accept documented visual verification, and small or mid-size utilities with no field crews. Caveats: (a) my WebSearch budget ran out after 4 searches, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and GitHub sweeps were not done and a stealth or very early startup in this niche could exist; (b) the search snippet says physical identification methods 'must be conducted or overseen by water system personnel' (state-dependent), so third-party photos may only count as self-ID-grade evidence unless the utility or state accepts contractor verification; (c) the idea's own note that regulatory details are from memory still applies; (d) per-utility supply is limited to home sales and water-heater swaps, so density per utility could be slow; (e) inspectors may resist liability for calling a pipe lead (my recollection, unverified); (f) Trinnex or Esri could add a 'contractor submission' role cheaply. | How this version avoids them: It sells to BlueConduit, VODA.ai and Stantec-type firms as an input rather than competing with them, and it is neutral where BlueConduit's own field partners or a consultant's own crews are not, which makes it a credibility layer. Trinnex leadCAST, Esri Survey123 and DIY self-ID forms collect voluntary owner submissions to fill the inventory, but none draws a random audit sample or produces a signed error-rate attestation. Electro Scan and Echologics hardware and RCAP door-to-door programs are verification methods that could be used as sample-collection tools, and a state may accept them, so they are potential partners rather than substitutes. A consultant or modeler that tries to build this in-house loses the independence that is the product. The parent's municipal sales cycle is replaced by consultants who already hold contract vehicles and small-purchase task orders.

title: Fixed-Price Guaranteed Clearance of Unknown Lead Lines
one_liner: Take the whole unknown-lines problem at a fixed price per line with an acceptance guarantee, and make money by routing each line to the cheapest method that will satisfy the state (records mining, meter-swap photos, paid photos, probe, pothole).
customer: Utilities with 5,000-100,000 unknown lines and a deadline, and the state programs or state revolving fund offices that want a known cost to fund. Wedge: a mid-size utility that has run out of staff or budget for engineering time-and-materials billing and can issue phased task orders under the small-purchase limit ($25-50k each). Later customer: a state that buys 'unknown clearance' for all its small systems.
problem: The industry sells effort: engineering firms bill hours, probe vendors sell hardware or crew days, modelers sell licenses, and portals sell software seats. No one sells the outcome the utility actually needs, which is 'this unknown line is now known and the state accepted it.' Utilities carry the acceptance risk, the routing decision and the cost overrun. The cost ladder is steep and poorly used: a records lookup can cost a few dollars, a photo $6-40, a scheduled visit around $120, a probe crew several hundred, a pothole about $900 or more, and a replacement thousands. Most utilities either dig too much or wait years.
solution: An 'unknowns clearing' contractor with a router at its core. Tier 0: predictive scores and assessor data on year built and neighborhood (bought from BlueConduit, VODA or open sources). Tier 1: vision-model mining of the utility's own tap cards, plumbing permits and old work orders, handwritten records that are now readable by multimodal models at $1-3 per line. Tier 2: three-photo protocol captured during meter swaps, inspections, water-heater changes and owner self-ID through a leadCAST- or Esri-style intake. Tier 3: scheduled visit by a panel plumber. Tier 4: probe or acoustic crew subcontracted from Electro Scan- or Echologics-type providers. Tier 5: pothole. Each line goes to the cheapest tier that the state accepts for that housing and meter archetype. The company quotes a blended fixed price per unknown (about $60-70) for a portfolio, guarantees acceptance (a rejected reclassification is redone free and the fee refunded), and holds a reserve for rejections. Evidence is exported in the state format and feeds the utility's Esri layer. First product for a scrappy team: an 800-1,000-line pilot with a spreadsheet-and-vision-model router and part-time inspectors.
why_now: Multimodal models can read old tap cards and permits and classify pipe photos, which collapses the cost of tiers 1 and 2 in 2025-2026. Inventory rules and the replacement clock (federal details still in flux, several state statutes independent of them, verify) make 'unknown' a budget line. Infrastructure-law SRF money is under spend-down pressure and funders prefer priced outcomes. Utilities are short of engineers, so buying an outcome is more attractive than buying hours. The photo, probe and prediction vendors now exist as suppliers to a router, which they did not five years ago.
revenue_model: Fixed price of about $60-70 per unknown, contracted in phased task orders of 500-1,000 lines each. Target blended cost is $28-35 per line, a rejection reserve of about 8%, and gross margin of roughly 45-50% at scale. Working capital comes from an initial reserve of a few hundred thousand dollars, then from SRF draws on accepted lines, and eventually acceptance-risk reinsurance so a third party underwrites the guarantee. Upside comes from the router's data: measured accuracy and cost per method by housing archetype, which improves margin every contract and can be sold to states as a benchmark. Later, sell state-wide 'unknown clearance' bundles.
non_obvious_insight: There are two inversions. First, price the outcome, not the effort. Hourly engineering firms and hardware vendors cannot copy a fixed price per accepted line without cannibalizing their own revenue. Second, treat the competitors as suppliers. Every tier below the pothole is somebody else's product, and the profit is in the routing decision and the guarantee, not in owning a method. The bigger unlock is that most unknowns turn out to be non-lead, so the cheapest method that proves it is almost always far below the dig cost. That spread, multiplied across tens of millions of unknowns nationally (verify with public inventory totals), is the business.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: pick one state with a written acceptance path. Approach five utilities in it and ask for a sample of their tap cards and unknown list. Run the vision model on 200 cards and measure how many lines it resolves. Days 10-20: build the router as a spreadsheet: for each address, cost, expected accept rate and method by tier. Line up one probe subcontractor and 10 part-time inspectors. Days 20-30: quote the first utility a fixed $65 per line for 800 unknowns, with a rejection reserve of $40k and a right to redo any rejected line free, structured as two task orders under the small-purchase limit. Ask the state program to confirm the acceptance path in writing before signing.
