title: Dark Roof Capital: Buy, Cure, Re-Perform
one_liner: Invert the parent. Instead of being paid a $3k fee to cure other people's stranded solar loans, buy those loans at dark-roof prices, finish the systems with a proprietary per-AHJ cure playbook, and keep the full value uplift as a re-performing loan pool.
customer: Sellers: credit unions, banks, servicers and ABS trusts or controlling-class holders that want dark and forbearance-stuck solar loans off their books. Capital side: distressed-credit funds, family offices and NPL buyers who want a new niche but cannot cure a roof. Homeowners are offered a cure and a payment reset in exchange for reinstating payments.
problem: Dark solar loans are an orphan asset class with broken pricing. NPL desks discount them to zero collateral value because they cannot fix the system. Lenders will not cure at scale and cannot collect on a roof that produces nothing. A cure costs perhaps 10-15% of the loan balance yet restores most of its value, but a $3k cure fee captures only about 10% of the $20k+ of value created. The holder of the loan keeps 90%, and today nobody who can cure holds the loan.
solution: Use the forensic pack from the parent as an underwriting engine. Sell a Bid Desk: audit a seller's dark loans, then quote a purchase price within 10 days. First 6 months: sell a zero-upfront cure-share product to a credit union (we finish the jobs, and take about 25% of restored loan value once PTO is achieved and payments resume), funded by a small working-capital line. Then buy pools through an SPV with a licensed sub-servicer. Cure with the playbook and offer borrowers a reset (a rate or principal modification in exchange for reinstatement). Hold or resell re-performing pools. Longer term, securitize re-performing solar loans, as mortgage RPL funds do. Purchases are limited to loans where the borrower is engaged and in forbearance, with reps and warranties and a seller-funded holdback for claims.
why_now: Freedom Forever, Sunnova, SunPower and PosiGen mean a growing pool of dark loans now exists, with forbearance windows expiring. Post-25D, lenders are shifting from origination to workout and want clean books. Mortgage NPL and RPL buyers already exist and are looking for new asset classes in a higher-rate world. Cheap agentic records recovery makes the per-loan diligence cost low enough to bid on small-balance loans.
revenue_model: Phase 1 (0-6 months): cure-share, about 25% of restored loan value, with zero upfront cost to the seller. Phase 2: spread on purchased loans. Illustration only: buy a $35k loan at about $11k (roughly 32% of balance), spend about $3.5k to cure, and a re-performing loan is worth about $24-28k, giving a $10-13k gross uplift before servicing, legal and default haircuts. Investors in the SPV pay roughly a 1.5% management fee and 20% carry above an 8% preferred return. The operating company also earns cure and coordination fees. Phase 3: RPL securitization fees.
non_obvious_insight: Fee-for-service captures the wrong slice of value, and whoever can cure at the lowest cost can bid the highest and still make money. Pure NPL funds cannot cure, lenders will not, and cure contractors have no balance sheet, so the buyer with the best per-AHJ playbook has a structural cost advantage. Dark solar loans also carry a specific hidden liability for buyers. Under the FTC Holder Rule, a homeowner can raise installer misconduct claims against whoever holds the loan. Curing the system removes the basis for most of those claims, so the cure is also the de-risking step, and buyers who cannot cure are pricing that risk at its maximum.
first_30_days: Use the audit engine to build a bid model on 50-100 loans from a friendly credit union or servicer under NDA, and price them. Get a commitment letter from one distressed-credit family office for a $1-2M first-loss pilot. Commission a legal memo on the Holder Rule, state lender and servicer licensing, and rescission risk, and identify a licensed sub-servicer. Sign one cure-share deal (no purchase) covering about 30 loans to measure real cure cost per tier and how many borrowers reinstate. Write a one-page pool teaser for investors. The riskiest assumption is borrower willingness to resume payments and rescission exposure, so measure reinstatement rates before buying anything.

title: Appraisal Workfile Trustee for Retired and Deceased Appraisers
one_liner: A neutral custodian that holds a retiring or deceased appraiser's workfiles for 10 years, proves they were never altered, and answers subpoenas, board letters and lender QC requests so the retiree or widow never has to.
customer: Wedge: sole-proprietor certified residential appraisers aged 62+ who have just gone inactive or announced retirement in 3-4 states (TX, OH, PA, CO), plus heirs and executors of appraisers who die or become incapacitated. These people usually already hold a free LIA or OREP retirement tail, so the money risk is covered and the missing piece is the defense file. Scale payers: E&O administrators and state appraiser associations (loss-control benefit). Requesters (attorneys, lenders, boards) pay production fees where rules allow.
problem: USPAP requires workfiles to be retained and retrievable for at least 5 years (or 2 years after a judicial proceeding ends), and regulators can act later. A retiree's copy sits on an aging laptop, a USB drive or a software subscription that lapses. The free tail pays defense costs but does not preserve or produce the file, and a workfile with no independent proof of when it was finalized is easy to attack as backfilled. When an appraiser dies, board letters and subpoenas land on a widow with no idea what a workfile is. Nobody answers a subpoena on the retiree's behalf: software vendors store files, they do not act as agent.
solution: Product v1, 'Seal and Hold': (1) A 60-minute import from a la mode, ClickFORMS or ACI exports or a drive image. Every file is hashed and stamped with a third-party RFC 3161 timestamp, kept in write-once encrypted storage with an index by date, client and address. (2) A custodian agreement naming the Trustee as records custodian and agent for production, plus a notice letter to the state board. (3) A production desk that handles subpoenas, board requests, lender QC and repurchase requests and E&O carrier requests, notifies the retiree or estate, and bills the requester. (4) An estate trigger: named heirs, a death or incapacity switch and pre-filled paperwork. (5) Retention beyond the minimum, with legal-hold extension. Deliberately excluded: trainees, client transfer, earn-outs, tail brokerage.
why_now: UAD 3.6 becomes mandatory Nov 2, 2026 and is pushing veterans to quit rather than relearn. WorkingRE's 2026 survey says 31% plan to leave within 3 years and 57% are over 60, so a predictable wave of exits is starting. Free LIA and OREP tails have made the money side a solved problem, which leaves the file as the remaining exposure. Immutable cold storage and third-party timestamping are commodity-cheap, so intake per retiree is under an hour of ops time.
revenue_model: $695 one-time for 10-year custody including 3 productions (or $19/month). $995 estate or heir rush plan. Extra productions at $195-450, requester-pays where state rules permit, otherwise billed to the retiree or estate. Group license to E&O administrators and associations at roughly $8-15 per insured per year as loss control (needs validation). Cold storage for about 100 GB costs around $1 per month, so gross margin is 85%+ and the real cost is the production desk and counsel. A two-person team breaks even around 500 custodies a year (assumption).
non_obvious_insight: The free tail pays the lawyer, but a claim is won or lost on whether the appraiser can produce a file that provably existed in that form on that date. A retiree's own drive cannot prove non-alteration, while a neutral custodian with hash chains and third-party timestamps can. So this is closer to a notary or escrow than to storage, which is why software vendors paid by the user cannot credibly sell it and why insurers, estates and boards have reasons to care. Once the custodian is named in the retiree's board and carrier paperwork, moving away means new attestations, which creates switching costs.
first_30_days: Week 1: retain counsel for the custodian agreement and a state-by-state memo on retention, board notification, subpoena handling, and confirmation that we are not acting as an appraiser or AMC and no fee-splitting rule applies. Pull public rosters for TX, OH, PA and CO and flag licenses that went inactive or expired in the last 24 months and active licensees licensed 25+ years. Week 2: call 20 of them and pre-sell at $695 with a refund guarantee, then concierge-deliver the first 5 by hand (import 5 years of workfiles, timestamp, issue a custody certificate). Kill rule: fewer than 6 of 20 pay means pivot to insurer-funded only. Week 3: ask LIA and OREP claims managers, two independent E&O agents and one state appraiser association how workfile requests reach them today and whether they would co-brand or fund it as loss control. Meet 3 estate-planning attorneys. Week 4: run a 'What happens to your files when you retire' session through Appraisal Institute chapters and appraiser forums and target 15 paid custodies.

title: Community Lenders Pool Orders to Keep County Appraisers
one_liner: Sell rural credit unions and banks a pooled, multi-year county 'appraisal continuity compact', where their combined order flow plus a fixed capacity retainer makes a retiring appraiser's territory viable for a supervised successor.
customer: Payer: the 4-8 community banks and credit unions that originate mortgages in a rural county cluster whose appraiser is retiring, each paying about $3-8k a year, bought through state credit union leagues, bankers associations and their service arms or CUSOs. Beneficiaries: the retiring appraiser (paid a fixed stipend), a mid-career certified appraiser from an adjacent county acting as supervisor, and 1-2 career-changer trainees (agents, inspectors, adjusters).
problem: A rural lender places 30-100 appraisal orders a year. No single small lender can sustain a trainee, and none is big enough to make an out-of-county appraiser drive 60 miles. When the county's only appraiser retires, orders go to distant AMC panel members, closings slip and purchase loans are lost. Trainee programs like Valligent's assume one lender commits volume. The retiree's book was stable because 15 direct lenders each sent about a dozen orders, so each lender was individually too small to replace it.
solution: 'County Compact': (1) Diagnose at-risk counties by joining board rosters (active certified appraisers and license age) with HMDA originations by lender and county. (2) Sign a 3-year compact among 4-8 lenders in the county: pooled first-look on local orders (lenders still order directly and independently, with no link to value conclusions or loan approval), a turnaround SLA such as 7 business days, and a fixed annual capacity retainer paid to us. (3) Recruit and equip the continuity team: a certified supervisor plus 1-2 trainees, with desk QC and UAD 3.6 tooling. (4) Pay the retiree a fixed 12-month knowledge-transfer stipend for the recorded local-knowledge interview, adjustment grids, neighborhood boundary notes and lender introductions. The retiree does not sign reports and gets no percentage of anything. (5) Give each lender a quarterly turnaround and quality report for their compliance and board files. Money flow: borrower pays the appraisal fee through the lender at the customary fee, 100% to the appraiser firm with no skim or split. Lenders pay us the retainer. We pay the retiree a fixed stipend and the supervisor a per-trainee capacity stipend. Counsel to confirm the retainer is independent of order outcomes and that we stay under state AMC registration thresholds (roughly 15 appraisers per state, to verify) because lenders order directly.
why_now: UAD 3.6 goes mandatory Nov 2, 2026 and veterans are choosing to quit. ABA Banking Journal and CSBS have documented rural appraiser shortages in 2026. The AQB exposure draft that drops the college-degree requirement widens the trainee pool. EO 14393 signals regulators want more appraiser supply. State leagues and bankers associations already sell shared services to small members, so the channel exists.
revenue_model: Capacity retainer of $3-8k per lender per year scaled by originations, so about $30k a year for a 6-lender compact, on 3-year terms. Add-on lender-paid collateral QC or desk review at roughly $45 per report. 10% distribution share to the league or CUSO. Rough economics (assumptions): year 1 costs are about $10k retiree stipend, $10k supervisor and trainee capacity stipends and $5k ops and QC, leaving a thin margin. Years 2-3 drop the retiree stipend, giving about 45-50% gross margin at steady state. 50 compacts is about $1.5M a year.
non_obvious_insight: Small lenders are each below the minimum viable volume for any successor, but pooled they equal the retiree's book. The compact re-creates that pool contractually. Lenders are not paying for appraisals, which borrowers still cover, but for the option value of local capacity, priced like a rural fire district. A single delayed or lost purchase loan costs a lender more than its share of the retainer, so 2-3 saved closings a year pay for it. Paying supervisors a capacity stipend funded by the pooled retainer solves supervisor scarcity without taking a cut of trainee fees, so fee-splitting rules are avoided.
first_30_days: Build a county risk map for TX, OH, PA and CO from board rosters and HMDA and NCUA/FFIEC lender lists, and shortlist 15 counties with an aging appraiser and 4+ community lenders. Call appraisal or ordering managers at 20 credit unions and banks and ask which orders were delayed or unplaceable in the last 12 months and what each cost. Offer two state leagues or bankers associations free county risk maps for their members as the door-opener and ask for a pilot. Recruit 2 supervisors and 4 trainees. Get a signed letter of intent for 2 pilot compacts of 3+ lenders each. Commission one counsel memo on appraisal independence and AMC thresholds.

title: Rural Sales Commons: Pay Retiring Appraisers for Comps
one_liner: Invert the idea: instead of retirees paying to leave, pay them for their verified sales books and build the private sales-price registry that non-disclosure states lack, sold first to practicing rural appraisers and later to AVM, lender and assessor buyers.
customer: Supply (paid): retiring and retired certified residential appraisers in roughly a dozen non-disclosure states (for example TX, UT, ID, MT, WY, NM, KS, LA, MS, ND), starting with Texas. Demand: practicing rural appraisers first (subscription), then AVM and hybrid-valuation vendors, rural lenders' collateral-risk teams, county assessors for ratio studies, and eventually programs expanding alternative valuations.
problem: In non-disclosure states, sale prices are not in public deed records. For non-MLS rural sales (FSBO, family transfers, auctions, seller-financed land-with-house), the only record of price is often an appraiser's own phone-confirmation notes and comp files. When the appraiser retires, that sales book is thrown out or dies on a hard drive. Practicing appraisers then struggle to find defensible comps, AVMs and desktop valuations are weakest exactly there (hypothesis to test), and human appraisers stay indispensable and scarce.
solution: Wedge product: a 'Rural Comp Finder' subscription for practicing appraisers in one region, built from a paid capture program. (1) Sales Book Capture: a 2-day white-glove engagement in which we ingest the retiree's comp libraries (a la mode or ClickFORMS exports, spreadsheets, paper binders) with LLM parsing. We keep only transaction facts (date, price, terms, property characteristics, verification source and method), plus the retiree's own adjustment grids and market-area notes. Client and borrower identities never enter the system, and MLS-derived fields are tagged and excluded. The retiree signs a license and certifies what is theirs. (2) Product: county-level search showing each verified sale with provenance (who confirmed, how, when) and a confidence grade, plus a paired-sales adjustment library. (3) Contributor loop: active appraisers who add confirmed sales get a discount, so the commons refreshes after the retirees are gone. (4) Later products: API and data licenses to AVM and hybrid vendors, lenders and county assessors, positioned as ground truth for validating AVMs and alternative valuations.
why_now: About 6-7k appraisers a year are expected to leave (31% of a roughly 65k workforce within 3 years per WorkingRE), and each exit destroys a sales book permanently. UAD 3.6 (mandatory Nov 2, 2026) pushes the industry toward structured data. EO 14393 expands alternative valuations, which need ground truth in thin markets. LLM extraction of messy comp files (old exports, PDFs, handwritten binders) became cheap enough in 2025-26 to make capture affordable.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of $39-59 per month per region for active appraisers (contributors pay less). Data licenses of about $25-120k per state per year to AVM and hybrid vendors and lenders, and $15-40k per year to assessors (all unvalidated). Retirees are paid $1,500-3,000 upfront plus a 20-25% royalty pool shared by verified contribution, and that payout is our main cost of goods. Rough plan (assumptions): 20 retirees x about $2,000 is $40k to acquire perhaps 50-100k verified records. 300 subscribers by month 12 is roughly $210k ARR before any data licenses.
non_obvious_insight: The parent asks retirees to pay, but a retiree is a supplier with a ticking clock. Each exit permanently deletes an asset that no later entrant can recreate, and scraping cannot reach it because the value is provenance: who confirmed this price, how and when. First to sign the last generation of phone-confirming appraisers cornered a resource competitors cannot buy once it is gone. Practicing appraisers contributing new confirmed sales gives the commons a network effect that outlasts the retirees. The moat is the counsel-designed data model (provenance tagging, MLS exclusion, client stripping), which turns legal risk into a barrier to fast followers. Because retirees are paid, the parent's unproven willingness-to-pay problem disappears and no earn-out or client transfer is needed.
first_30_days: Gating step: a counsel memo on MLS license terms, the USPAP Confidentiality Rule, GLBA and state board views, and stop or redesign if the extractable data set is too thin. Interview 15 retirees and 15 active appraisers in Texas and ask to see their comp books. Buy 5 sales books at $1,500 as paid pilots, parse them with an LLM pipeline, and tag provenance and MLS-derived rows. Run a blind coverage test on one rural county: how many verified non-MLS sales in the last 5 years the commons holds versus what an active appraiser or an AVM can find. Show the test to 3 AVM or hybrid-valuation vendors and 3 rural lenders and ask for letters of intent. Pre-sell a $39 per month beta to 30 active appraisers. Because the web-search budget ran out, also verify in week 1 whether Cotality, ATTOM or any appraiser comp-sharing group already sells verified non-MLS sales in non-disclosure states.

title: Nonrenewal Desk for Colorado Independent Agencies
one_liner: An agent-side triage-and-evidence service that starts when a Front Range nonrenewal or score-disclosure notice lands, and charges most of its fee only when the policy is saved.
customer: Owner-principals of independent insurance agencies in Boulder, Jefferson, Larimer, El Paso and Douglas counties. Each has 150+ wildland-urban-interface homeowner policies, is appointed with 6 or more carriers so it can re-market, and has received several nonrenewals or surcharge notices since January 2026. Colorado only. California is dropped until AB 75 is confirmed enacted.
problem: When a nonrenewal or score disclosure arrives, the agent has about 10 days to get an acknowledgement and about 30 days to a decision (HB25-1182). The agent has no verified evidence, and the free homeowner kits (FireRisk.ai, Defensible Space Score) only produce letters. A corrected score may not move the premium, because insurers can meet the law with a manual mitigation discount and do not have to accept third-party imagery. The agent loses the commission and the bundled auto and umbrella policies, roughly $600 a year or more per WUI household.
solution: The agent forwards the notice PDF and gets three things within 48 hours. (1) A Lot Ledger: dated 15-50 cm imagery and public lidar canopy and clearance measurements set against each feature the insurer disclosed. Each feature is marked contradicted, confirmed or unknowable. (2) A Credit Map: for each carrier the agency is appointed with, which filed mitigation credits or underwriting-exception paths the evidence supports, so the pack asks for the premium or retention outcome and not just a score change. (3) A carrier-formatted pack timed to the 10 and 30 day clocks, plus a re-marketing shortlist when the appeal is weak. The desk declines to file when the evidence does not contradict the score. That keeps the concession ledger clean and makes carriers trust the packs. After trust is built, the same imagery layer is run across the agency's whole WUI book to flag likely errors before renewal.
why_now: HB25-1182 has been in force since July 1, 2026, so disclosures, appeals and the 10/30-day clocks are now real for every Colorado WUI policy. Independent agents are the ones absorbing the nonrenewals. Public regional aerial flights, USGS-style lidar and cheap commercial archives mean the first appeals need no imagery licence. I did not verify that insurer appeal desks are unprepared, so the plan does not rely on it; the trigger is the notice itself.
revenue_model: $249 per month per agency, including 5 triage runs and a book scan of up to 300 WUI policies. Extra packs are $149 each. A flat $300 success fee applies per policy retained or re-marketed within 90 days of a pack. There is no percentage of premium, to avoid producer-compensation and rebating problems. At 20 agencies, that is about $60k in subscriptions plus roughly $90k in success fees, around $150k ARR, with gross margin above 70% once imagery is bought per filed case only.
non_obvious_insight: The product is a decision about what will actually change the outcome: fix the input, harden the house, or re-market it. It is not a rebuttal letter. Honest triage is the moat, because a desk that refuses weak cases gets a higher concession rate, and a concession ledger keyed by carrier, vendor, input error and evidence type becomes something carriers cannot get elsewhere. Carrier-side vendors like Zesty, Nearmap and Cotality cannot sell against their own customers' scores. That is counter-positioning.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 Front Range agencies through a Colorado independent-agent association or by direct outreach to principals. Run concierge delivery by hand with an analyst using public imagery, lidar and QGIS, with no licensing. Give the first 5 files per agency free and charge $99 from file 6. Aim for 40 real notices and 20 filed appeals with outcomes tracked. Send agencies a private weekly concession scoreboard as the sales asset.

White space: Nobody found sells imagery-based, parcel-level, insurer-format rebuttal evidence, and nobody sells an agent or HOA 'scan the whole book for likely score errors' workflow. What exists is (a) free or $99 homeowner letter and template kits with no imagery (FireRisk.ai, DefensibleHome, Defensible Space Score), (b) slow on-site certifications (IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home, Wildfire Partners), (c) contractor evidence packets sold with hardening jobs (Road Home Exteriors), and (d) carrier-side imagery scoring (Zesty, Nearmap/Betterview, Cape, Cotality, Verisk) with at most a compliance 'framework' for appeals. Specific unserved wedge: multi-date 15-50 cm imagery that shows a lot's actual condition (irrigated, gravel-scaped, recently cleared) against a 30 m coarse-layer score, formatted for Colorado's 10-day acknowledgement and 30-day decision clock, delivered to independent agents who carry many clients. Genuine caveats that shrink the gap: (1) The premise for California looks broken. AB 75's status page shows it 'held under submission' in Appropriations on 08/29/2025 and no source found shows it enacted (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB75). The CA DOI's own report reportedly says there is no formal appeal process. So the 'statutory appeal right' in CA is unverified and Colorado is the only confirmed regime. (2) Colorado HB25-1182 (signed 28 May 2025, effective 1 July 2026, https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb25-1182) requires disclosure of the score, range and a plain-language explanation of features. It does not clearly require raw model inputs (fuel class, vegetation density), and it does not require insurers to accept third-party imagery. The 'pull the disclosed model inputs' step may be thin, and DOI enforcement is only that the Commissioner may request a copy of a denied appeal. (3) Insurers can satisfy the law with a manual mitigation discount, so a score correction may not change the premium. (4) Free and $99 substitutes cap willingness to pay for $149-299 per file. (5) Zesty, Nearmap and Cotality hold the same imagery and the carrier relationships, so the durable moat is the concession database, not the imagery. | How this version avoids them: FireRisk.ai and DefensibleHome sell homeowner letters and templates with no imagery and no verification. This sells verified evidence and a decision to agents, who buy per book and not per household. The Defensible Space Score is free and self-reported, and the desk is what an agent uses when self-reports fail. IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home and Wildfire Partners are slow on-site certifications, and they become a channel later. Road Home Exteriors bundles packets with hardening jobs and does not scan books or work the clocks. Zesty, Nearmap, Cape, Cotality and Verisk are carrier-side and conflicted, and the desk does not compete with their scoring. The risk that one of them bolts on a policyholder module is met by locking in agency distribution and the concession ledger early, and by considering a data partnership with one of them.

title: Insurable-at-Closing: Pay-on-Closing Insurability Sheets for WUI Listings
one_liner: Listing agents order a 48-hour parcel evidence and carrier-routing sheet before a wildfire-zone home goes to market, and the seller pays a flat fee at closing only if the sale closes.
customer: Listing agents and brokerages selling wildland-urban-interface homes in Front Range and mountain markets such as the Boulder foothills, Evergreen and Conifer, Estes Park, Black Forest and the Colorado Springs foothills. Title and escrow officers are the channel, and the seller pays through the settlement statement. A licensed WUI-specialist independent agency is the placement partner.
problem: A lender will not close without a bound homeowners policy. In WUI sales the bind often fails late: the buyer's quote is declined on a score cutoff and the contract clock is running. Neither the seller's nor the buyer's agent can say in advance which carriers will write the lot. No statute helps at that point, because the new-business decline is not a nonrenewal appeal. Free homeowner appeal kits do not touch this moment.
solution: When the home is listed, the agent orders an Insurability Sheet. It is a one-page PDF and a data file with a lot condition ledger from dated imagery and lidar, a ranked list of pre-closing fixes with cost and time to complete, and a carrier route showing which carriers' models see this lot accurately and have a human exception path. The partner agency supplies indicative appetite and quotes. At contract, buyers' agents can re-run the sheet in 24 hours. The lot evidence goes to underwriters as an exception referral at carriers that read it, and away from carriers using coarse 30 m models that will decline the same lot on a raster.
why_now: Colorado WUI homeowners' rates roughly doubled in 2020-2025 (per the parent research) and carriers keep retreating, so insurance availability is now a closing risk. HB25-1182 disclosures mean sellers can now hold a score but not a plan. Cheap high-resolution archives make a 48-hour turnaround affordable. I could not verify local closing-fall-through statistics or new pre-listing tools in this pass, so check both first.
revenue_model: A $395 flat fee on the settlement statement, due only if the sale closes; $150 upfront if the agent prefers. A $75 rapid re-run for buyer-side agents. A placement technology fee or revenue share from the partner agency on policies bound (about 10-15% commission on roughly $5k premiums, renewing yearly), structured with counsel around RESPA and producer-compensation rules. At 8% of roughly 6,000 annual WUI sales in the five focus counties, that is about $0.2M in fees in year one. Expanding across the Western WUI markets lifts this to the low tens of millions.
non_obvious_insight: The same lot gets very different treatment from different carriers. The parent research cites identical Class A homes receiving discounts of 0.7%, 12% and 41%. That suggests the profitable move is routing the lot to the carrier whose model sees it correctly, and not rebutting a score. Routing needs no statutory appeal right, so it works in California, Oregon and Washington where the Colorado law does not apply. The moat is a bindability database of carrier appetite by parcel features and actual bind outcomes. Score vendors see scores, not who binds, and agents see only their own quotes.
first_30_days: Sign one Front Range WUI-specialist independent agency as the licensed placement partner. Recruit 2 title or escrow offices and 5 listing agents. Run 20 listings with the fee contingent on closing and track policy-bound-before-closing rate, days saved and deals rescued. Get a written RESPA and producer-compensation review before any fee reaches a bank account. Turn the results into one case study for brokerage sales meetings.

What exists is (a) free or $99 homeowner letter and template kits with no imagery (FireRisk.ai, DefensibleHome, Defensible Space Score), (b) slow on-site certifications (IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home, Wildfire Partners), (c) contractor evidence packets sold with hardening jobs (Road Home Exteriors), and (d) carrier-side imagery scoring (Zesty, Nearmap/Betterview, Cape, Cotality, Verisk) with at most a compliance 'framework' for appeals. Specific unserved wedge: multi-date 15-50 cm imagery that shows a lot's actual condition (irrigated, gravel-scaped, recently cleared) against a 30 m coarse-layer score, formatted for Colorado's 10-day acknowledgement and 30-day decision clock, delivered to independent agents who carry many clients. Genuine caveats that shrink the gap: (1) The premise for California looks broken. AB 75's status page shows it 'held under submission' in Appropriations on 08/29/2025 and no source found shows it enacted (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB75). The CA DOI's own report reportedly says there is no formal appeal process. So the 'statutory appeal right' in CA is unverified and Colorado is the only confirmed regime. (2) Colorado HB25-1182 (signed 28 May 2025, effective 1 July 2026, https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb25-1182) requires disclosure of the score, range and a plain-language explanation of features. It does not clearly require raw model inputs (fuel class, vegetation density), and it does not require insurers to accept third-party imagery. The 'pull the disclosed model inputs' step may be thin, and DOI enforcement is only that the Commissioner may request a copy of a denied appeal. (3) Insurers can satisfy the law with a manual mitigation discount, so a score correction may not change the premium. (4) Free and $99 substitutes cap willingness to pay for $149-299 per file. (5) Zesty, Nearmap and Cotality hold the same imagery and the carrier relationships, so the durable moat is the concession database, not the imagery. | How this version avoids them: FireRisk.ai, DefensibleHome and the Defensible Space Score serve homeowners disputing an existing score and have nothing for the sale moment or for carrier routing. IBHS and Wildfire Partners are on-site programs that take weeks, and they do not fit a 30-day contract, though they could later validate a sheet. Road Home Exteriors sells evidence with hardening jobs, not before a sale. Zesty, Nearmap, Cape, Cotality and Verisk score for carriers and do not see the buyer's bind attempt. Possible new rivals are quote-at-offer tools and portals with climate scores; they quote from their own models with no lot evidence and no multi-carrier routing. I could not check for those in this pass.

title: Notarized Mitigation Records: The Evidence Standard for Wildfire Credits
one_liner: A score-agnostic verification layer where contractors capture signed photos that are cross-checked against imagery and issued as portable machine-readable Verified Mitigation Records, which carriers and certifiers accept.
customer: First, Front Range defensible-space crews, roofers, ember-vent installers and drone inspectors, who pay per job. Then wildfire certification programs (Wildfire Partners, IBHS-style programs) that pay per avoided inspection. Then carriers' appeal desks and underwriters, who read the record through a free API and later pay for ingestion. HOAs and fire-safe councils are the bulk channel.
problem: Homeowners spend $5k-$30k hardening a house and cannot prove it in a way an insurer will accept. Photos and photo-log templates are easy to fake, and AI image generation makes unverified photos worth less each year. HB25-1182 obliges insurers to credit documented mitigation but sets no evidence standard, and on-site inspection capacity is the bottleneck. Contractors cannot promise an insurance credit, so hardening jobs stay unsold.
solution: A web app (PWA first) for contractors and homeowners with guided capture: a checklist of shots for Zone 0/1/2, vents, roof and gutters, taken with signed capture (C2PA-style content credentials, device attestation, GPS, time and heading). The system cross-checks each claim against archived and new imagery and lidar, for example that vegetation was cleared between two dated images or that a roof is Class A. It issues a Verified Mitigation Record as an open-schema JSON file plus a PDF, versioned and portable across carriers. The schema is published under an open licence and co-developed with a fire-safe council. Carrier and certifier readers are free, and acceptance outcomes feed a per-carrier acceptance dataset. The capture layer would use an existing signed-capture SDK, not a new one.
why_now: Generative image tools have made unverified photo evidence untrustworthy. Signed-capture standards and SDKs are now commodity. HB25-1182 turned documented mitigation into a legal object with no format. High-resolution archives and public lidar are cheap enough to act as the independent witness. This is also the inversion of the parent idea: instead of proving a model wrong about the house, prove the house right and let any score-maker read it.
revenue_model: $49-$89 per notarized job, paid by the contractor and passed through in the quote. $40-$120 per avoided on-site reinspection from certification programs. $15-$60 per accepted record from carriers via subscription or API. Agents from a rebuttal desk buy per file. At 300 contractors doing 40 records a year at $65, that is about $0.8M, and the carrier and certifier layers scale it much further.
non_obvious_insight: The reason insurers can decline third-party imagery is that they cannot trust or parse it, not that they are hostile. Give them evidence with provenance, in a schema they can auto-ingest, and the cost of handling an appeal falls. The parent's moat, the concession database, then extends into a network: contractors, homeowners and carriers all gain from a shared format, as with ACORD forms or the Uniform Appraisal Dataset. Because the layer describes the house and not the score, it holds up when Zesty, Cotality or Verisk change their models, and it is neutral in a way a scorer can never be.
first_30_days: Sign 5 Boulder and Jefferson County defensible-space and roofing contractors on a free pilot. Ship the guided-capture PWA with the imagery cross-check. Notarize 60 real jobs. Ask 3 agencies to submit those records in real credit requests and log carrier responses. Propose a 10-file remote pre-verification pilot to Wildfire Partners. Publish schema v0.1 on GitHub.

title: 48-Hour Verify List for Independent Floorplan Lenders
one_liner: A daily, capacity-capped list of the specific floored VINs an independent lender's auditor should physically verify in the next 48 hours, built from listing disappearance plus the lender's own payoff ledger, with a disposition classifier and per-dealer baselines that fix the noisy-signal problem.
customer: Head of collateral or audit (CRO as signer) at independent used-car floorplan lenders with roughly $30M to $500M outstanding across 100 to 1,500 independent and buy-here-pay-here dealers, plus credit unions and community banks with dealer floorplan lines. It deliberately excludes franchised new-car dealers, where captives already get retail delivery reports and can build this in-house. Secondary channel is regional floorplan audit firms that dispatch for-cause audits.
problem: An independent lender has a handful of auditors and hundreds of dealers, so the Monday question is not 'is there fraud' but 'which 12 VINs at which 4 dealers do I visit this week'. The judges' flaws map onto this. (1) A raw 'VIN left the website' flag is noisy, since the car may be wholesaled, transferred to a sister lot, in recon or never listed. (2) A fixed 7 to 10 day payoff window misfires on slow-funding but honest dealers. (3) A standalone radar dashboard is one more screen for a team with no data scientists. (4) The $15 to $30 per dealer price is unvalidated. (5) It misses double-flooring, which was most of Sky Auto Mall.
solution: Data need is one file: the lender's daily list of active floored VINs (VIN, dealer, floor date, advance), exported as a flat file from any core system. A VIN dropping off that file means it was paid, so no payoff-event integration is needed. Listing history comes from a licensed feed (a MarketCheck-type source scanning 100k+ dealer sites daily), plus a crawl of only the lender's own dealers' public sites, which the lender's dealer agreement can require them to permit. (a) A disposition classifier sorts every vanished floored VIN into transfer to a sister store, appears at auction or wholesale, relisted, or 'retail-sale signature' (gone, no reappearance, often after a pending or price-change state). Only the last type with an open balance enters the queue. (b) Each dealer gets its own baseline lag distribution of delist-to-payoff days learned over 90 days, and the flag fires on deviation from that dealer's own pattern, not a fixed window. (c) The output is capped to the lender's audit capacity, for example 'you have 3 auditor-days: here are the 12 VINs at 4 dealers with the highest expected loss', with a timestamped listing-history evidence pack and a one-click verify request that can go to the lender's own auditors or an audit vendor. (d) An optional second signal is title or lien-release data where lawfully obtainable, but v1 does not depend on it.
why_now: Tricolor and PrimaLend (Sept 2025) and the Sky Auto Mall litigation (Ford Credit and Stellantis, March 2026) made every lender's risk committee ask what they know between audits. Inventory sits near 88 days' supply with floorplan at SOFR plus 200 to 400 bps, so dealers lean harder on lines. Licensed daily dealer-site listing history now exists off the shelf, and LLM extraction makes normalizing messy dealer pages cheap for a team of three. Vero's April 2026 content says bank dealer-services teams want to 'automate audit triage and SOT reporting', which confirms the buyer's framing.
revenue_model: Platform fee of about $1,500 to $3,000 per month per lender, sized to dealer count and booked against the audit budget, plus a catch fee of about $250 per VIN later confirmed unpaid-sold by the lender's own ledger and caught before its next scheduled audit. A backtest-based 'retro-scan' is priced at $5k and credited against year one. A lender with 300 dealers pays roughly $40k to $60k per year. A first-two-years target of 40 to 60 lenders and credit unions implies roughly $2M to $3.5M ARR. These are assumptions to validate, not findings.
non_obvious_insight: The lender's payoff ledger is free data hiding in plain sight: a VIN leaving the daily floored-VIN file is the payoff event, so the product needs one CSV, not a core-system integration. The real product is dispatch, not detection. Auditors only pay for a signal that changes whom they visit this week, and the noise is tamed by comparing each dealer to its own delist-to-payoff habits rather than to a global threshold, and by refusing to alert unless the disposition looks like a retail sale.
first_30_days: Weeks 1 to 2, backtest on public cases (Sky Auto Mall filings and a few others) using historical listing data to show fire dates versus discovery dates. In parallel, interview five lender audit or risk heads to confirm the ranked list would change their audit order. Weeks 2 to 4, sign three small independent floorplan lenders or credit unions to a free retro-scan. They send 12 months of daily floored-VIN files plus their known SOT events. Report recall, false alerts per 100 dealers per week and median days of lead time over their actual discovery. Offer a free 60-day live shadow run, converting to platform plus catch fee only after at least one real catch. Also ask two audit firms for a for-cause dispatch partnership.
lineage: mutation of I0218 ('Sold-Out-of-Trust Radar for Floorplan Lenders'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: In-house 'website VIN vs floorplan VIN' comparison (SAS Global Forum paper, 'PROC HTTP: Using the Web to Combat Fraud in Auto Finance During a Global Pandemic'), Vero Technologies (VeroOS), SBS Digital Audit (SBS Software), LotCount. White space: Among the products I could find, none sells the specific signal in this idea: an external-behavior signal (a floored VIN vanishing from the dealer site or marketplaces) checked against the lender's own payoff ledger on a running clock, with a ranked daily queue. Existing offerings cover other things. Physical or photo audits (CSI, LotCount, SBS Digital Audit, Netresult) are periodic and dealer-cooperative. Platforms (Vero, Solifi, Alfa, SBS servicing) analyze the lender's own payment and title data. Bank-data tools (Plaid-style) watch dealer cash. DRN covers location. The unserved wedge is mid-size and small lenders that lack data-science teams: independent floorplan companies, credit unions and community banks with dealer lines, and third-party audit firms that need risk-based audit targeting. It is strongest for used-car and buy-here-pay-here dealers, where captives' retail-delivery reports do not exist. Caveats that shrink the white space: (1) captives see retail deliveries within days and can build the signal in-house, and the SAS paper suggests at least one lender did; (2) Vero, SBS and Cox/NextGear could bolt on the signal; (3) a listing that disappears is a noisy signal (wholesaled, transferred, in recon, or the dealer never lists), so precision must be proven; (4) marketplace scraping has terms-of-service risk, so a licensed feed such as MarketCheck is likely needed. | How this version avoids them: SAS-paper in-house build: large lenders can do this, but independents have no analytics team, and the product adds what a conference method lacks (disposition classes, per-dealer baselines, evidence packs, dispatch capping). Vero, Solifi and other platforms analyze the lender's own payment data and have no outside-world signal, so they are integration targets or distributors (export in, module out). SBS Digital Audit, LotCount, CSI and Netresult are periodic, dealer-cooperative physical audits, and this product sends them where to go, so audit firms gain premium for-cause work and become the channel. MarketCheck is the supplier, not a rival, and licensing removes scraping ToS risk. DRN is a physical-location alternative, and MOBI is a captive-only non-commercial pilot. NextGear and Cox is the latent threat, but independent lenders that compete with NextGear are unlikely to hand their book to a Cox-owned vendor. Double-flooring stays out of scope here (it is the seed of a later cross-lender feature), so precision claims stay honest.

title: Independent Collateral Verifier for Warehouse Lenders
one_liner: Sell the same listing-vs-ledger signal not to the floorplan lender but to the lender's lender: credit funds and banks that fund floorplan and subprime auto lenders and get a borrower-supplied VIN tape they have never been able to check, delivered as a signed monthly verification certificate that borrowers pay for through facility fees.
customer: Portfolio-monitoring and credit officers at credit funds, banks and specialty-finance desks that provide warehouse or revolving lines to independent floorplan companies and subprime or BHPH auto lenders. The chooser is the warehouse lender, and the payer is usually the borrower via a monitoring fee written into the facility, the way custodian and backup-servicer fees already are. The law firms that draft these credit agreements are a second influence channel.
problem: After Tricolor and PrimaLend (Sept 2025), the lender's lender is exposed to collateral that is self-reported by the party with the strongest incentive to overstate it. It receives a VIN-level borrowing-base tape weekly or monthly. It has no auditors and no view into dealers, and field exams are annual, sample-based and weeks stale. It holds the tape but has no line of outside data to check it against. Existing floorplan-side tools are bought by the borrower, so they cannot be independent by construction.
solution: Tape-in, verification-out. The warehouse lender (or borrower on its behalf) forwards the borrowing-base tape it already receives and we return a weekly exceptions report and a signed monthly Borrowing Base Verification Certificate. (1) VIN-level reconcile of every tape VIN against listing history and the borrower's reported paydowns and collections, flagging vanished-from-listing with no paydown. (2) A borrower-level Collateral Integrity Index covering percent of tape VINs vanished-unpaid by age bucket, listing coverage ratio, and trend, benchmarked against the warehouse lender's other borrowers. (3) Because noise averages out at portfolio level, precision required is far lower than for per-VIN dispatch, and low listing coverage is reported as its own finding, not hidden. (4) Escalation: a 'for-cause exam recommended' trigger with a shortlist of dealers for a partner field-exam firm. (5) Contract language kit: a standard 'independent verification agent' covenant and fee schedule for law firms to drop into new facilities and amendments.
why_now: Sept 2025's Tricolor and PrimaLend collapses put verification failure in front of every warehouse lender and investor. Private credit funds now hold large slices of specialty-auto warehouse exposure with small monitoring teams. Facilities are being re-papered and re-underwritten, so a verification covenant can go in now instead of waiting for a renewal cycle. Cheap licensed listing history and LLM tape parsing make a weekly external check a software job instead of an exam-firm engagement.
revenue_model: Monitoring fee of about $3,000 to $6,000 per facility per month ($36k to $72k per year), paid by the borrower through the facility's fee schedule or by the lender directly, plus a $15k to $25k onboarding backtest. Add-ons include a 10 to 15 percent referral fee from partner field-exam firms on for-cause exams, and licensing the anonymized Collateral Integrity Index to ABS investors and surveillance teams. If a niche of 100 to 150 specialty-auto warehouse lenders with 3 to 5 facilities each adopts it, the ceiling is roughly 300 to 600 facilities, or $15M to $30M per year before expanding to retail-auto tapes. These figures are assumptions to test.
non_obvious_insight: The funding-side buyer already owns the one input the product needs (the VIN tape) and has never had a single external data point to check it against. Verification fees are set by the chooser but paid by the borrower, who benefits from an independent stamp that supports better advance rates, so the payer wants it even when the chooser only tolerates it. Once written into facility documents, a fee line like custodian and backup servicer is sticky and renews automatically, which is a switching-cost moat that a per-dealer SaaS tool never gets.
first_30_days: Days 1 to 10, list 40 warehouse lenders and credit funds active in specialty auto from trade press and deal announcements, and line up conversations with two or three finance law partners who draft these facilities. Days 10 to 30, run 10 calls with portfolio monitoring heads and offer a free one-facility 'shadow verification' using a tape they already hold. They email it, and within five business days we return a one-page findings memo covering coverage ratio, vanished-unpaid VIN count and peer benchmark. Also sign a partner field-exam firm for for-cause follow-ups. Success is one lender agreeing to a paid quarter and one law firm agreeing to circulate the covenant language.

title: Day-Zero Payoff Bridge for Floorplan Dealers
one_liner: Invert the radar: instead of catching dealers who fail to pay the floorplan lender, wire the payoff directly to the lender the day the car sells and get repaid when the retail contract funds, turning sold-out-of-trust risk into a short, fully secured receivable with data-driven underwriting.
customer: Independent and franchised dealers that sell through third-party indirect finance and get squeezed when contracts in transit, stips or unwinds stretch funding beyond the floorplan payoff window. Pilot referral partners are two or three independent floorplan lenders. Capital comes from a credit fund or family-office vehicle buying short-dated receivables. Dealer pays a per-deal fee, and the floorplan lender shares in it and saves audit cost and risk.
problem: SOT often starts as a timing gap, not fraud. The dealer has delivered the car, the retail lender has not yet funded, and the floorplan payoff clock is running. That is why honest and dishonest dealers look identical in the books for a week or more, and it is how a small cash squeeze becomes fraud. Detection tools (including the parent) only tell the lender after the timing gap has already turned into a loss or a phone call. Floorplan lenders then hold reserves and audit constantly because they cannot see the cash in transit.
solution: When a floored car sells, the dealer requests a bridge with the payoff quote, bill of sale and contract or funding-approval docs (LLM-parsed). We verify the sale with the listing signal (retail-sale signature) and cross-check the payoff quote, then wire the payoff directly to the floorplan lender, so cash never touches the dealer and cannot be diverted. We are repaid when the retail lender funds the contract, through a lockbox or deposit-account control agreement, or a notice of assignment where the retail lender allows it. The risk is receivable dilution (an unwound or charged-back contract from a creditworthy obligor), not dealer fraud. Underwriting uses obligor identity, the dealer's payoff-lag history, the dealer's unwind and chargeback record, and the listing check. Rollout runs in three phases. (1) A free dealer-side 'Unpaid VIN clock' built on the radar signal is the top of funnel and lets aged sold-not-paid VINs self-select. (2) A capped concierge bridge of up to $25k per unit. (3) Floorplan lenders name Day-Zero as an approved payoff method, in return for lower reserves and audit frequency, and receivables are sold forward to credit funds so the startup stays capital-light.
why_now: Inventory near 88 days' supply and floorplan at SOFR plus 200 to 400 bps tighten dealer cash. Contracts in transit stretch a week or more. After Sky Auto Mall, lenders have less tolerance for late payoffs. Private credit is searching for short-duration, self-liquidating receivables at high gross yield. LLM document parsing plus listing signals make per-deal verification cheap enough to underwrite $150 fee deals, which was not economical with a human ops desk.
revenue_model: A fee of about 0.5 to 0.7 percent of the payoff per roughly 9-day bridge, which is about 25 percent annualized gross, plus a 10 to 20 percent referral share to the floorplan lender, capital from a credit fund at about SOFR plus 6, and the startup keeping servicing fees and a first-loss or excess-spread slice. Illustration (assumptions): a dealer bridging 15 deals a month at $22k averages about $100k outstanding and pays about $2.1k a month. 5,000 dealers at that size is roughly $500M outstanding, about $125M of gross yield and perhaps $50M to $60M net after capital cost and losses. A $99 to $199 per dealer per month clock subscription is the top-of-funnel product.
non_obvious_insight: The listing-disappearance signal is too noisy to accuse a dealer but precise enough to underwrite a nine-day secured advance, because a false positive costs a declined bridge and not a false fraud allegation. Paying the floorplan lender directly makes the lender's SOT exposure structurally zero for bridged deals, so the lender is a willing distributor and co-subsidizer, and no lender integration is needed at the start because the dealer supplies the payoff quote. Detection was always a workaround for a timing mismatch that capital can simply remove.
first_30_days: Ask two independent floorplan lenders to name their 10 dealers with the most aged, late payoffs for timing reasons and to introduce us. Draft a term sheet with one credit fund or family office for a $500k to $1M pilot facility. Engage commercial-finance counsel on state licensing (some states license commercial lending and receivables purchases). Build the dealer-side Unpaid VIN clock as a landing page plus a manual crawler for the pilot dealers' sites. Aim to sign LOIs with 5 dealers and one capital source, and run the first three concierge bridges by hand to measure dilution, decline and cycle time.

NextGear and Cox is the real latent competitor because it owns floorplan plus Dealertrack contract flow, but it can serve only NextGear dealers, while independents will not send their dealers to a Cox product. The parent's research did not cover contract-in-transit funding or dealer factoring providers, so checking those incumbents is step zero. Regulatory and capital risks are the main reasons this is the highest-variance offspring.

title: Smoke Report Autopsy for Policyholder Advocates
one_liner: An adequacy auditor that scores any carrier-side smoke, ash and soot report against a public, versioned sampling grid. It then drafts the AB 1795 deficiency letter and supplemental sampling plan, and sells to public adjusters and plaintiff attorneys in the Eaton and Palisades zones.
customer: Wedge: 15-25 licensed public adjuster firms working standing-home smoke claims in Altadena, Pasadena, Pacific Palisades and Malibu, plus 3-5 plaintiff firms running the Ghazarian-style class actions against carrier-retained hygiene vendors. Later: homeowners buying direct at about $295, then carrier claims-legal teams running pre-flight audits on their own vendors.
problem: Every standing-home claimant holds a carrier-vendor IH report saying 'clean' or 'minor'. Neither the public adjuster nor the attorney can tell quickly whether it was under-sampled. Carrier-retained hygienists reportedly take about 10 samples in 3,000 sq ft, skip attics, wall cavities and HVAC, and compare results to urban background dust. A CIH second opinion costs $2k-$4k+ and takes weeks from a scarce pool. Purdue's free review is capacity-limited and does not produce claim-ready output. From Jan 1, 2027 AB 1795 makes insurers pay for testing that is 'necessary', but only if someone shows what is necessary and missing.
solution: Upload the IH report and lab PDF. LLM extraction with human QA pulls sample count, locations, media (wipe, tape lift, air, bulk), comparison basis, detection limits and skipped zones. It scores them against a public 'Adequacy Grid' built from AIHA's wildfire guide, IICRC/RIA/CIRI, 40 CFR 745.227 and 8 CCR 1529, with every criterion cited. Within 48 hours the customer gets a 2-page scorecard listing what was not sampled, a statute-cited deficiency letter for the PA or attorney to send, and a supplemental sampling plan that a partner CIH-of-record can sign, with a priced quote from a partner testing firm. The plaintiff tier ingests hundreds of reports in batch for pattern analytics (share with zero attic samples, samples per 1,000 sq ft by vendor). The grid is versioned so it re-maps when DTSC publishes standards in 2028-29. We do not sample, employ technicians, or give expert opinions.
why_now: AB 1795 was signed 9/15/2026 and takes effect 1/1/2027. It creates a 30-day inspection duty and a duty to pay for necessary testing, and it presumes smoke, ash and soot in a standing home came from the fire. Class actions over vendor sampling were filed in Feb 2026, LA County sued State Farm on 8/31/2026, and 13,000+ standing homes with smoke damage are in play. Cheap LLM document extraction makes a 48-hour, hundreds-of-dollars audit feasible where it used to be a $3k CIH engagement.
revenue_model: Public adjusters pay $395 per audit, or $2,500 a month for up to 10 active files. The CIH-signed supplemental sampling plan costs $900, split 50/50 with the partner CIH. Plaintiff-firm pattern analytics run $40k-$150k per engagement, for example a 300-report batch. The partner testing firm pays a flat referral fee on supplemental sampling it wins, or we take none if that raises fee-splitting concerns. Phase 2 sells carrier claims-legal teams a $2k-$5k per-vendor-report pre-flight audit. Bottom-up: even 15% of 13,000 homes at $395 plus a few analytics contracts is about $1.5M-$2.5M in year one, so the wedge is small and the dataset is the asset.
non_obvious_insight: The unit of leverage is the omission list, not the test result. AB 1795 obliges the insurer to pay for necessary testing, and a scored list of what was not sampled and why it matters converts a fuzzy fight into a checklist the adjuster must answer in writing. Every audit also writes one structured row (vendor, square footage, samples, comparator, zones skipped), so the tool quietly builds the largest labeled dataset of how carrier vendors sample. Counter-positioning is real: HygieneTech, Rimkus and Safeguard cannot sell a tool that indicts carrier-side sampling without alienating their own clients.
first_30_days: Week 1: collect 25 real IH reports with consent from EFRU volunteers, two public adjusters and one attorney. Sign two CIHs at about $150/hr to review the rubric, and a toxicologist as advisor. Weeks 2-3: build Grid v0.1 as a spreadsheet plus extraction pipeline, targeting over 90% field-level accuracy on the 25 reports. Run free 48-hour audits for 10 PA files. Track whether the deficiency letter gets the carrier or FAIR Plan to authorize additional testing. Week 4: start charging $395 from audit #11, aiming for 30 paid audits and one attorney LOI for a 100-report batch pilot at about $25k. Before day 15, confirm from the chaptered AB 1795 text that there is no qualified-person or licensure rule that blocks a non-CIH from drafting a sampling plan for CIH signature.

We sell no sampling, so EHS and Home BioTesting become the partners who fulfil the supplemental plans and gain lead flow. Purdue's free review is bounded by grad-student capacity and has no claim-language deliverable, SLA or batch mode; we cite its method and offer a data-share and donation instead of competing. Safeguard's 'defensible framework' is a carrier-side essay, whereas ours is a scoring engine aimed at the policyholder side. title: Loss-Draft Clearance Standard for Mortgage Servicers
one_liner: Mortgage servicers and portfolio lenders pay a per-loan fee for verified smoke clearance. That verification gates the final release of insurance loss-draft funds and the end of forbearance on smoke-damaged standing homes. Lenders, not carriers, become the enforcer of a defensible standard.
customer: Loss-draft and disaster-recovery departments at mortgage servicers and subservicers with concentrated Altadena, Pasadena and Palisades books, plus community banks, credit unions and CDFIs around Pasadena and the Westside. Secondary buyers: escrow and title officers on standing-home sales. Homeowners and their PAs are the delivery channel, not the payer.
problem: Servicers hold insurance proceeds on mortgaged, smoke-damaged homes and typically release them in staged draws with a final holdback against completion inspections. For destroyed homes the milestones are objective (foundation, framing). For smoke there is no completion gate: the contractor says 'cleaned', the carrier's vendor says 'clean', and the owner says the house still makes the family sick. EFRU's roughly 50 remediated homes showed 63% with elevated lead and one third with asbestos, so a lender that releases the last draw on an unverified cleaning is funding continued collateral impairment. A servicer that withholds gets complaints and unhappy borrowers paying a mortgage plus rent. I have not verified how servicers handle this today, so this is the riskiest assumption to test first.
solution: A one-page, servicer-adoptable 'Smoke Clearance Acceptance Standard' covering sampling grid, threshold basis, chain of custody and lab accreditation, tied to AB 1795, AIHA and IICRC/RIA/CIRI references and versioned for DTSC's 2028-29 standards. Alongside it, a portal where the borrower's hygienist or remediator uploads results. We verify them (automated checks plus partner CIH-of-record review) and issue a machine-readable Clearance Verification (pass, fail, or specific deficiency list) that the servicer's loss-draft workflow accepts to release the final draw or convert a forbearance. A book-level ledger shows every loan in the burn perimeter, joined to parcels, with status: not tested, tested, remediating, cleared. Testing stays paid by the insurer under AB 1795 or by the borrower from claim proceeds. The servicer pays only for verification and monitoring.
why_now: AB 1795 (effective 1/1/2027) forces insurers to pay for testing and bars ALE termination before clearance, so a verified clearance event now exists in statute and can be a lender milestone. 13,000+ standing homes with smoke damage in the LA fires, many mortgaged, are hitting the remediation and final-draw stage through 2027. Meanwhile the state standard will not exist until 2028-29, and servicers adopt vendor standards faster than agencies write them.
revenue_model: Servicers pay $250-$450 per loan verified, usually recoverable as an inspection or protective-advance line they already charge, plus $2-$5 per loan per month for ledger monitoring on flagged loans. Community banks and credit unions pay a flat $15k pilot. Hygienists and remediators can pay $50 to have their evidence pack pre-checked against the standard, since a fail costs them time. Honest sizing: LA alone is roughly 13,000 homes x about 55% mortgaged x $350 x 1.5 verifications, or about $3.7M. The business is the repeatable template for post-disaster loss-draft verification (hurricane mold, flood, wildfire) across the US, not California smoke alone.
non_obvious_insight: The party with real power over whether a smoke repair is 'done' is not the carrier or the state. It is whoever holds the last check. Servicers already control disbursement, already buy standardized inspection work in bulk, and do not need to win the sampling-design argument. They need a pass/fail they can rely on. Lender incentives also align with policyholders (impaired collateral) and with carriers (fewer reopened claims and bad-faith suits), which neutralizes the parent's buyer conflict. If five servicers and credit unions accept the same evidence package, contractors and hygienists will produce to it, so the de facto standard is set by lenders.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: ask 5 public adjusters which servicers are sitting on their clients' checks, then hold 25 calls with loss-draft and disaster managers at about 10 servicers and 10 Pasadena-area banks and credit unions. The one question is what evidence would let you release the final draw on a smoke claim. Days 10-20: draft the one-page acceptance standard and get two CIHs and one toxicologist to endorse it publicly. Days 20-30: agree a paid pilot of 15-30 loans at about $300 with one credit union or servicer, and pre-check evidence packs for 10 borrowers referred by PAs. If no servicer says smoke draws are actually stuck, kill or pivot to escrow and title on resale.

title: Lab-Sourced Smoke Contamination Benchmark and Loss Index
one_liner: A give-to-get data cooperative that captures post-fire dust wipe, tape lift and air results directly from accredited labs, whoever ordered them. It returns percentile benchmarks to hygienists and adjusters for free, and sells the resulting contamination-prevalence and remediation-cost index to reinsurers, cat modelers, rating agencies and reserving actuaries.
customer: Payers: catastrophe and reserving actuaries at wildfire-exposed carriers, the California FAIR Plan, reinsurance brokers' analytics teams and cat-model vendors, and rating agencies. Contributors, who get the service free: IH firms, public adjusters and 2-3 AIHA-accredited environmental labs. Free-licensed users: DTSC, CDI and LA County, so the index becomes the citable reference.
problem: AB 1795 turns smoke on a standing home into a presumed covered loss with a 30-day clock, yet nobody knows contamination prevalence by distance, home age, construction, HVAC or plume. The only public dataset is EFRU's roughly 50-80 homes (63% elevated lead, one third asbestos, post-remediation). Carrier-vendor data sits in privileged silos. Cat models are built around destroyed structures, and I did not verify whether any vendor has a smoke-on-standing-homes module. Reinsurance and reserving for 2027 must price a blind tail: 13,000+ standing smoke-damage homes in LA alone, with ALE running until clearance. Every hygienist also argues about the comparison basis (urban background dust versus thresholds), and Purdue reports consultants using wrong comparators. No one has a defensible background distribution.
solution: The chokepoint is labs, not reports. Every sample, carrier-side or policyholder-side, runs through a handful of accredited labs. The co-op gives labs a differentiator: a structured electronic data deliverable plus a consent checkbox on the chain-of-custody form ('de-identified results may be contributed to the benchmark'). Contributors get a free percentile report, for example 'kitchen floor wipe lead at the 92nd percentile of 1,400 homes 0.5-1 mile from the perimeter, built 1950-79', plus a neighborhood background-dust distribution that answers the comparator fight. Buyers get a parcel-level contamination probability by contaminant, and an expected remediation-scope and cost distribution calibrated on consenting claims. Delivery is by API, CSV and annual studies, versioned, with a free license to state agencies. Public data (Cal Fire DINS, assessor year built, DTSC soil results) fills the gaps. The model generalizes to CO, OR, HI and any WUI fire.
why_now: The signing of AB 1795 on 9/15/2026 converted smoke from an adjuster judgment into a legislated, presumed, time-boxed loss. Reinsurance and carrier reserving for 2027 must now price the distribution. State standards are two to three years away and the regulators will borrow the largest population dataset available. Labs are commodity businesses hungry for differentiation, and structured data plus LLM tooling makes lab-level ingestion cheap for a small team.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of $40k-$120k a year per reinsurer, cat modeler or carrier. Bespoke reserving studies at $75k-$150k. A data-processing fee of $15-$25 per sample, paid by labs or contributors, for the percentile reports. A later licensing revenue share with cat-model vendors. Balance-sheet option once the index is trusted: a parametric smoke-remediation trigger calibrated on the co-op's data, built with a licensed MGA and reinsurer capacity. That is a 2029 step and needs admitted-carrier or surplus-lines structuring.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone assumes data comes from adjudicated claims and reports. Labs are the only neutral point that sees both carrier-side and policyholder-side samples, and the percentile report solves the hygienist's biggest weakness, defending the comparison basis, so contributors have a selfish reason to opt in. The hard problem is selection bias: policyholder-side samples skew dirty, and carrier vendors sample thinly and shallowly. The co-op only earns trust if it corrects for who ordered the sample, ideally with at least one carrier's vendor data, or with a randomized sampling frame in one neighborhood. Solving that bias is the scientific moat, and it is exactly what a regulator or actuary will test first.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: pitch 3 accredited labs handling fire-zone samples on a consent-based structured feed, aiming for one signed LOI. Request EFRU's dataset and Purdue's reviewed reports under a data-sharing MOU. Days 10-20: assemble the public layer (DINS perimeters and damage inspections, assessor year built, DTSC soil data, CDI task-force figures) and publish a free 'Eaton Fire Smoke Background Dust Benchmark v0' from the EFRU sample (n of roughly 50-100) to seed usage. Days 20-30: sell two paid $15k-$25k 'Smoke Reserving Briefs' to a carrier cat or reserving team and a reinsurance-broker analytics team ahead of renewals. Sign 5 IH firms as contributors. Kill test: if no actuary will pay for a brief built on public and EFRU data, the reinsurer thesis is wrong.

title: Cavity ID: Tool-of-Origin Evidence via Counsel
one_liner: Expert-grade 'which tool made this part, and when' reports, built from parts the brand already holds in the US and sold through China-facing IP law firms to brands whose ex-supplier is selling their product.
customer: Wedge: branded hard-goods companies ($10M-$150M revenue: housewares, pet, fitness, hand tools, juvenile, small appliances) that sell injection-molded or die-cast products on Amazon/Walmart/Target, hold a design patent, trade dress or registered mark on the part, and ended a China supplier in the last 18 months. Buyer of record is their outside China/IP counsel (15-25 boutique cross-border firms), who engage us as a consulting expert so the work is privileged. The brand's GC or COO signs off on the disbursement.
problem: The brand sees look-alike units of its own product on Amazon, Temu and 1688 at 30% below its price, and suspects the ex-supplier is running its steel on a third shift. Today its lawyers can send a cease-and-desist built on suspicion, and the supplier answers 'that is a copy, not ours'. Marketplace takedown vendors produce screenshots and listings, not proof of which tool made the part or that it was made after the orders stopped. Without that proof the brand loses the negotiation over tool release, and losing it costs six or seven figures in tooling and margin.
solution: One product, the Tool-of-Origin Report, with no China operations and no extraction business. (1) Baseline: macro-image 30-60 retained parts per SKU, taken from the brand's own US inventory, returns and QA samples across different lots and dates. Build a cavity signature library (cavity ID marks, gate vestige, ejector-pin witness marks, parting-line and texture flaws) plus a wear-over-time curve, since tool wear is monotonic and dates the tool's state. (2) Attribution: test-buy 5-10 suspect units, match them to a cavity and tool state, and report a forensic-style likelihood ratio, including whether the tool state postdates the last PO. (3) Counsel-ready pack: chain of custody, methodology and a signed declaration from a retained independent molding-process engineer, formatted for the Amazon Report-a-Violation and APEX flows, the Alibaba IP platform, CBP recordation, a demand letter or litigation. Monitoring is bought or white-labeled from an existing vendor. Field capture in China is subcontracted, and only in a later pre-exit 'baseline while the supplier is still cooperative' tier.
why_now: The 2025 tariff whiplash and the Feb 2026 IEEPA ruling (per the parent research) have produced a wave of supplier breakups. Formal-entry bulk imports rose after the end of the US de minimis exemption in 2025, which makes overrun sellers easier to reach through CBP and marketplaces. Cheap macro-imaging plus modern vision models make tool-mark statistics feasible at SMB prices, where a forensic lab used to cost $30k+ per case.
revenue_model: Baseline $4,500 per product family. Test-buy attribution report $6,500 per case (up to 10 samples). Expert declaration or testimony $350/hr through counsel. Optional 'Overrun Watch' retainer $1,500/month per family, with two attributions a year included and monitoring white-labeled. Counsel buys the report as a disbursement and marks it up under its own billing, so there are no referral fees, which avoids fee-sharing ethics problems. Target 60 clients at about $14k blended annual spend, roughly $0.85M ARR, by month 12. Gross margin about 65% (assumption). Bottom-up reachable market is roughly 1,500 qualifying brands (assumption to validate).
non_obvious_insight: The evidence a lawyer needs is not 'this is a copy'. It is 'this was made on your steel after you stopped ordering'. Tool wear is a clock: edges round, texture erodes, flash grows, and repairs leave dated marks. So parts you already own in a US warehouse from 2022, 2024 and 2025 reconstruct the wear timeline without ever visiting China. Routing the work through counsel also makes it privileged, and it moves the spend from a marketing or brand-protection budget to a legal-dispute budget that is bigger and less price-sensitive.
first_30_days: Weeks 1-2: interview 12 China-facing IP lawyers and 8 GCs, asking what evidence they wish they had at the demand-letter stage and whether they would buy at $6.5k. In parallel, run a blind validation. Buy multi-cavity molded parts from known sources across 2-3 tool states and test whether our imaging plus statistics assigns cavity and tool state correctly (target above 95%). Publish the methodology memo. Retain one independent molding-process engineer as expert of record. Weeks 3-4: sell 3 paid $2,500 Overrun Audits (test-buys plus a one-page verdict), qualified on the client owning enforceable IP on the part, through one law-firm co-marketing partner. Kill signal: fewer than 3 of 12 lawyers say they would buy, or blind accuracy below 90%.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Harris Sliwoski (China Law Blog), Alitheon (FeaturePrint), Red Points, Corsearch (Zeal 2.0, Investigations 360, Distribution Control). White space: Coverage caveat: the WebSearch quota (200 per session) was already used up when I started, so I could not run the planned 6-12 searches. I also could not check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or open-source repos. The findings below come from about 25 direct page fetches, so treat 'nobody does this' as unproven. The vendors most likely missed are the many small China-based QC and sourcing agents that sell 'mold audits' and 'mold relocation', plus PI and investigation firms (Kroll-type). Do a manual pass on those before committing.

What I found: I found no productized, US-facing service that bundles (a) a serialized tool census, (b) cavity-level physical fingerprints, and (c) marketplace test-buy attribution of overruns to a specific tool. The problem is documented and treated as an unproductized legal-advice problem: Harris Sliwoski tells clients to keep an inventory form and audit quarterly, and never mentions a third-party vendor for it. Marketplace monitoring and takedown (Red Points, Corsearch, Alibaba's free IP platform) is commoditized and crowded. Object fingerprinting exists (Alitheon) but is aimed at electronics, aerospace and gray-market diversion, not tool-mark attribution.
