title: Tooling Title Diligence for Small-Brand Acquirers
one_liner: A fixed-fee, 5-day report that tells buyers of $2M-$50M product companies which molds the target legally owns, where they physically sit, and whether the factory is already selling the target's product.
customer: Buyers of physical-product brands and small manufacturers with China-made tooling: search-fund and ETA searchers, independent sponsors, lower-mid-market PE platforms and SBA 7(a) acquirers. The channel is business brokers (Quiet Light, Empire Flippers, FE International-type firms), M&A attorneys and SBA acquisition lenders. The payer is the buyer, at the LOI-to-close stage. Secondary payer is the seller, who pays for a pre-listing 'tooling-ready' file.
problem: In a small-brand acquisition the molds are the asset that everyone values at zero. The QoE accountant sees an expensed PO line, the lawyer sees a boilerplate 'all assets used in the business' rep, and the seller often cannot say whose name the tools are in or whether a bill of sale exists. If the factory holds the tools, the buyer has bought a business that the supplier can hold hostage for a 30% price hike, and the buyer also cannot move production, which matters more now that tariff rules keep changing. Nobody in the deal owns this question: brand-protection vendors sell to the brand, not to the buyer, and audit firms do not cover tooling.
solution: 'Tooling Title and Leakage Report', delivered in 5 business days. (1) Tool schedule: every tool, its location, its condition, and who holds title (bill of sale, PO language, tool-ownership clauses, supplier confirmation letters). (2) Leakage test, which is the parent's $2,500 overrun audit repurposed: buy 10 units from 1688, Alibaba, Temu and Amazon third-party sellers, and compare them with the golden sample and lot codes to say whether the supplier is already selling the product. (3) Portability score: what it would cost and how long it would take to move each tool or re-cut it, with quotes from a US or Mexican molder. (4) Deal remedies: draft closing conditions, a tool bill-of-sale assignment, custody and release agreements, and a holdback or escrow sizing suggestion for the buyer's lawyer to use. The on-site audit is optional and subcontracted, passed through at cost, and only for deals over $10M.
why_now: The searcher and ETA wave and retiring owners are pushing more small manufacturers and brands to market. The Amazon aggregator unwinding put many product brands up for resale with tooling and supplier problems. Tariff volatility (the Feb 2026 IEEPA ruling per the parent research) makes 'can this brand switch factories?' a live diligence question, where in 2019 it was rarely asked. Remote marketplace scanning has become cheap enough to fit inside a fixed fee.
revenue_model: $4,900 per report, paid by the buyer, usually as a closing cost. Seller pre-listing file $2,500 through brokers. Post-close '100-day tool sovereignty plan' $12k (title cure, fingerprint baseline, second-source quotes). Portfolio monitoring for PE sponsors $2,000/month per physical-product company. Model: 240 reports a year at month 12 is about $1.2M, plus a 25% attach rate on the plan (60 plans at $12k) is about $0.7M. Reachable market is assumed at roughly 1,500 physical-product deals a year, to be validated with brokers. Lenders or brokers might pay for reports on deals that later close.
non_obvious_insight: This is the same asset as the parent idea, but a far better moment to sell it. A breakup victim only hires you once they are already hurt and have already lost leverage. An acquirer is at peak willingness to pay, because they are about to wire $5M, and the report's cost is rounding error on the deal. The finding also turns straight into money: a missing bill of sale becomes a closing condition, a holdback or a price cut. A short-lived supplier concentration risk becomes a negotiating chip. Diligence is also the top of a repeat-customer funnel, since a sponsor with 6 platform companies buys monitoring on all of them.
first_30_days: Build a redacted sample report from public listings and a mock data room. Pitch 6 brokers and 3 searcher communities, offering 3 free reports on live deals, in exchange for testimonials and a written referral agreement, since a diligence step that reduces buyer fear helps brokers close deals. Then sell 5 paid reports at an introductory $3,500. Get one M&A attorney to endorse the closing-condition language. Line up two China audit contractors by referral for the on-site option. Kill signal: brokers refuse to introduce the report to buyers, or no buyer will pay $3.5k.

title: Tool Passport: Molds That Report Themselves
one_liner: An OEM-owned, tamper-evident magnetic cycle counter and registry that makes every mold or die report its own location and shot count, so an unauthorized overrun shows up on the owner's screen and, in time, verified tools can be financed and insured.
customer: Wedge: US OEMs and PE-owned manufacturers ($50M-$500M) that have just moved, or are moving, tools out of China to US, Mexican, Vietnamese or Indian molders and never want a second breakup. Second user: the receiving nearshore molder, who installs the tag to earn 'verified' status with skittish customers. Later payers: tooling lenders, insurers and procurement teams that require a Passport.
problem: Even after reshoring, the OEM's tools sit in someone else's building with no independent record of how many shots they have run, on which press or when. The molder's own counters and MES data are self-reported. Enforcement is all after-the-fact forensics, which is expensive and easy to dispute. Because tools cannot be verified, they are worth nothing as collateral, cannot be insured on custody, and force OEMs into blunt contracts with minimum order quantities and amortization games.
solution: Phase 1 product, 'Tool Heartbeat', is a magnet-mount IP67 tag with an accelerometer that counts mold-open and mold-close cycles from vibration signatures, geofences the tool, detects removal, stores and forwards data over LTE-M, and reports to a per-tool 'passport': QR plate, serial, photo and fingerprint baseline, custody chain, shot ledger versus POs. Silence is contractually a breach. A model 'Tool Passport Addendum' for MSAs, drafted with a China-facing law firm, gives the OEM tag access and audit rights. Phase 2 uses the ledger as the meter for pay-per-shot billing and escrow, so the molder is paid per verified shot and proves innocence. Phase 3 is the registry as a standard: a VIN-and-Carfax for tools that lenders accept for collateral and underwriters use for custody cover. Phase 4 is Passport-backed tooling finance and custody insurance, where the balance-sheet upside sits. Tools still in China get the Census-and-forensics service from the parent, not tags, until SIM roaming and consent barriers are solved.
why_now: Reshoring has created thousands of just-moved tools whose owners are motivated to prevent a repeat. LTE-M and NB-IoT modules with IMUs now cost roughly $25-45 in BOM for a 3-5 year tag. EUROMAP 77 / OPC UA 40077 machine interfaces make molder-side data available to cross-check the independent witness. The tariff-driven wave of moves in 2025-26 (per the parent research) means a stock of new supplier relationships where the tag can be built into the contract from day one.
revenue_model: Hardware $150 per tag (roughly 60% margin at scale), $10 per tool per month for the ledger and alerts, and $1,000 per site onboarding (QR plates, fingerprint baseline, custody paperwork). A 60-tool OEM pays about $22k in year one and $7k a year after. Reaching $1M ARR takes about 140 OEM-sites, so the early business is small. The upside is in the standard: verified-tool finance fees and custody insurance premiums, plus a 'Passport Verified' seal for molders. This is a longer-dated bet, and the near-term money rests on services and hardware.
non_obvious_insight: The parent asks how to prove theft afterward. The inversion is that a tool is the only expensive asset in manufacturing that reports nothing about itself. A cycle count is a signal the tool already produces every 30 seconds through its own vibration, and no one owns it as a customer-side record. Once an independent meter exists, the honest molder benefits as much as the OEM, because it settles quantity disputes, proves clean custody and lets the molder offer pay-per-shot pricing. That aligned incentive is what makes a standard plausible, where a policing tool would not spread.
first_30_days: Weeks 1-3: build 10 prototype tags from an off-the-shelf LTE-M module and IMU (Blues Notecard-class) in a magnetic housing, about $3k. Validate cycle-count accuracy (target within 1%) on 2-3 presses at a friendly Ohio molder who gets free tags and 'Passport-ready' status. Weeks 2-4: pre-sell 3 OEM pilots at $2,400 for 10 tags plus a year of service with a refundable deposit, using the Reshoring Initiative and Ohio plant-manager networks. Draft the Addendum with one law firm. Use the $2,500 Marketplace Overrun Audit as the top-of-funnel cross-sell. Kill signal: vibration counting cannot reach 98% accuracy across press types, or fewer than 2 of 10 OEMs will sign a pilot.

title: Recall Drills: State QC Findings Become Worker Training
one_liner: A recall-notice system for SNAP errors: every finding from a state's own QC review and every H.R.1 rule change becomes a dollar-tagged synthetic drill within 14 days, delivered through the state's CQI field staff to new hires in its highest-error counties, with an audit trail for corrective-action plans.
customer: Wedge: North Carolina's SNAP continuous-quality-improvement (CQI) unit. Its staff are former county workers who visit each of the 100 county departments monthly, plus the counties the state has already flagged as high-error. NC's 6.69% rate sits 0.69 points above the 6% cliff, and the parent research puts crossing it at about $140M a year. Payer: the state SNAP director's training/CQI line. Users: CQI specialists and county supervisors. Next states: Louisiana (7.61%) and any state within about 1.5 points of a 6/8/10% tier line.
problem: QC findings reach workers months after the case action, as webinars and memos. H.R.1 rule churn (work-requirement, noncitizen and utility-allowance changes) creates fresh errors faster than classroom training absorbs them. New hires learn on live caseloads, and Kansas cites turnover as an error driver. Counties are told 'documenting, documenting, documenting' but have no per-worker evidence trail. A handful of CQI staff cannot be in 100 counties every day.
solution: Three pieces. (1) An error-to-drill pipeline: CQI staff upload a QC finding at element level (stacked shelter deduction after a rent change, biweekly pay-stub conversion, household member who left). Within 14 days we return a synthetic twin case, scored with PolicyEngine as the oracle and hand-checked against the state manual, and push it to the assigned counties. (2) A 30-day new-hire certification track over the top three error elements, with pre/post scores and time-to-competency. (3) A CQI console with per-county and per-worker error-type heatmaps and a one-click 'CAP evidence packet' PDF (assigned, completed, score trend) that counties attach to corrective-action documentation. Drills test the input and verification decisions workers actually make (what to verify, which income to budget, which old entry to close), not the arithmetic the eligibility system already does.
why_now: The FY2027 QC sample year opens Oct 1, 2026. It is the first year measured under the new rules and it sets the FY2030 cost share (FY2029 and later use the rate from three fiscal years earlier). FY2028 exposure is effectively locked to the state's better of FY2025 or FY2026, so the next lever is FY2027 onward. The 75% state/local admin cost share also starts Oct 1, 2026. USDA published FY2025 rates on June 24, 2026: 41 states are above 6% and the national rate is 10.62%, and states above 6% must file remediation plans. States are visibly buying: Alabama DHR posted a QC assessment and training RFP, and NC's one-click 'close old deduction' prompt has been used more than 20,000 times, which shows targeted micro-interventions get adopted.
revenue_model: Year-1 state pilot of $60-90k for 12-15 named counties (verify it sits under each state's small-purchase limit). This expands to statewide at $250-400k a year. Counties outside the state contract pay $150-300 per worker, and new-hire certification is $250 per hire. All prices are unvalidated, so get the budget line from the CQI director before writing case #13. Realistic ceiling is about $10-20M ARR across the roughly 40 states above the threshold, so this is the modest-ceiling, fast-to-cash version.
non_obvious_insight: The product is closing the lag, not teaching skill. States already hold the scarcest asset, their own QC findings, and lose months turning it into training. A recall loop (finding, twin drill, completion evidence) cannot be copied by a vendor that only has the generic USDA taxonomy. It is one data-sharing MOU with a state QC unit away, and US Digital Response reports such agreements take 3 weeks to 3 months. Pick the launch state by distance to a cliff times benefit dollars, not by pain: NY at 13% needs a 3-point cut just to reach the 10% tier, while NC at 6.69% can plausibly cross 6%. A 0%-error county is still charged for the state average, so the state CQI unit, not the county, is the customer.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: 20 calls with NC CQI staff, county DSS directors and the state county association, asking who owns a budget line for this and what the last training tool cost. Days 5-15: build 12 drills from public sources only (H.R.1 rule changes, the publicly described stacked-shelter-deduction failure, biweekly wage conversion, household-member removal), and script the 14-day finding-to-drill workflow. Days 15-25: run a 3-county new-hire pre/post pilot with CQI staff as co-facilitators. Days 25-30: hand the state a CAP evidence packet sample and a one-page letter of intent with a price, and ask the CQI director to name the budget line.

title: Federal-Agreement Lab for State SNAP QC Reviewers
one_liner: Sell calibration drills to the small, high-leverage group whose findings set the official error rate, the state QC reviewers, scoring them against a federal answer key and putting part of the fee at risk on the state-federal disagreement rate.
customer: State SNAP Quality Control unit directors and the state SNAP directors who sponsor them, in the 41 states above 6% that must now file remediation plans. Each QC unit is a few dozen reviewers. Warm lead: Alabama DHR, which posted an RFP for 'SNAP Quality Control review assessment and training'. Check who won and at what scope. Targets: states within about 1 point of a tier line, once the FY2025 state table is pulled.
problem: The official rate is not the state's own number. USDA re-reviews a subsample and adjusts (regresses) the state's findings, and disputed differences go to arbitration. Rates are cliffs (6/8/10%), each worth tens to hundreds of millions in state benefit cost. A state QC reviewer who under-calls errors gets corrected upward by federal re-review. One who over-calls inflates the state's own rate. QC units are small and turnover-prone, and the FNS 310 handbook is dense. Today that calibration happens ad hoc, in meetings or through occasional consultants.
solution: A library of about 200 synthetic completed-review packets: case file, interview notes and an 'as-reviewed' finding, with planted misses and planted false alarms. Answer keys are adjudicated by retired FNS and state reviewers and cite FNS 310 sections. Reviewers find the errors, and we score agreement with the key by element (income, household composition, shelter, resources, ABAWD/H.R.1 rules), by reviewer and by supervisor. We add weekly live calibration sessions run by the retired reviewers, and an arbitration-readiness checklist. We do not perform QC reviews. We train and score, which keeps us clear of the federal oversight rules for third-party QC contractors (verify against the 2018 Farm Bill provisions). Method is symmetric: the goal is agreement with the federal standard, not lower error counts.
why_now: FY2025 rates came out June 24, 2026: 41 states above 6% and a 10.62% national rate. FY2026 rates finalize through federal re-review and arbitration into mid-2027, and states can use the better of FY2025 and FY2026 for FY2028. The FY2027 sample opens Oct 1, 2026 and sets FY2030 cost share. H.R.1 made every QC finding a budget line, so QC directors now have executive attention and remediation-plan deadlines. The Alabama RFP shows states already buy QC-side assessment and training.
revenue_model: $90-250k per state QC unit per year: about $2.5-4k per reviewer seat, a packet-library license and quarterly calibration sessions. 20-25% of the fee is at risk, refunded if the state-federal difference rate on FNS re-reviewed cases does not narrow. FNS measures that outcome, not us. 41 states at 40% penetration is about $5-8M ARR, so the ceiling is small but each logo is high-value and fast to close. Expansion: Medicaid eligibility-error programs (H.R.1 adds payment reductions starting around FY2030, verify), plus a per-case add-on for arbitration memo review. Prices are unvalidated assumptions.
non_obvious_insight: Dollars at stake per trained head is 100-1000x higher for QC reviewers than for eligibility workers. A 30-person unit's calibration can swing a tier cliff worth $100M+, and a county worker's cannot. The regressed rate turns under-calling into a hidden tax, not good luck. Unlike eligibility policy, which varies by state, QC review method is national (FNS 310), so one packet library serves every state. That fixes the parent's per-state case-library cost problem. The buyer population is tiny, homogeneous and reachable through a few networks.
first_30_days: Days 1-5: pull the Alabama RFP, announcement and results documents to learn the winner, scope and price. Recruit 2 retired state or FNS QC reviewers as adjudicators at $100-150 an hour. Days 5-18: write 25 planted-error packets from the public FNS 310 handbook and published arbitration guidance. Days 10-30: reach 15 QC directors through APHSA payment-accuracy contacts and FNS regional liaisons. Offer a free blind 10-packet test for 5 of their reviewers and return an agreement-gap report within a week. Convert 1-2 to $25-40k pilots via simplified procurement.

Code for America and PolicyEngine are flow and rules tools with no review-standard content. Kognito-style simulation had no dollar-weighted outcome or federal answer key. The Alabama RFP winner is the one real competitor to profile in week one.

title: Unit Tests for Benefit Law: Eligibility System Conformance
one_liner: Invert the drill: aim the same synthetic households and adjudicated answer keys at the eligibility software itself, selling H.R.1 conformance test packs to states and system vendors, with an aim to become the standard test suite that state RFPs cite.
customer: State SNAP and Medicaid policy directors and eligibility-system program managers (the people running user-acceptance testing), then the system integrators that build the systems and the AI-tool vendors selling into agencies. First buyers: 2-3 states whose H.R.1 system releases are due between Oct 2026 and Jan 2027 and that already have a UAT process.
problem: The most expensive error is one the system makes identically thousands of times, which no worker training can fix. NC's eligibility system stacked shelter deductions when caseworkers updated rent, and a one-click prompt fixed it and has since been used more than 20,000 times. H.R.1 forces reprogramming everywhere at once (SNAP work-requirement, noncitizen and utility-allowance rules, Medicaid work requirements and six-month renewals due around Jan 2027) under a 75% state admin share and a 6% error cliff. Vendors test their own work. States rarely have independent, boundary-case test data with signed-off expected outcomes.
solution: H.R.1 Conformance Pack v1: about 250 synthetic households aimed at the edges of each changed rule (income at the threshold, mixed-status households, month-boundary changes, shelter and utility interactions), each with an expected outcome and a citation trail to statute, USDA guidance and the state manual. The state's own policy staff sign off the answer key, so we test state policy against state system and do not have to settle federal ambiguity. Where state policy and federal guidance conflict, we flag it as a second deliverable, a QC-risk memo. Delivery fits existing UAT: scenario scripts and machine-readable fixtures with expected results, plus a divergence report. Later: a regression subscription refreshed on every guidance change, vendor pre-certification, and household-level evaluation sets for AI intake and caseworker-assist tools.
why_now: Every state must change its SNAP and Medicaid eligibility logic within months of each other, and Medicaid work requirements and six-month renewals land around Jan 2027. AI tools are entering benefits workflows and agencies have no household-level ground truth to test them against. USDA's FY2025 numbers (41 states above 6%, 10.62% nationally) make a systemic logic bug politically and financially radioactive. Open-source rules engines (PolicyEngine) and LLM-assisted drafting cut the cost of building cases, so adjudication, not authoring, is now the scarce step.
revenue_model: Per-state pack at $40-120k per major rule change, and a regression subscription at $100-250k a year per program per state. Vendor certification runs at $15-50k and AI-tool evaluation runs at $10-30k. Bottom-up: 50 states x 3 programs x about $300k, so $30-60M ARR is a plausible ceiling, and more if state RFPs cite the suite as an acceptance criterion. Much of the spend can draw federal IT matching funds in system-change budgets (verify per program). Prices are unvalidated assumptions.
non_obvious_insight: Independence is the product, in the way UL or a ratings agency is. Vendors cannot credibly grade their own homework, and states cannot staff independent test authorship, so the cornered resource is the adjudicated, state-signed answer key: expert time that compounds across states and rule changes. Testing the machine reaches a bigger error source than training people, and the same answer-key corpus later powers worker drills, QC calibration and AI evaluation. A standard is reachable because states already buy test scripts and would rather cite a neutral suite than write their own.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: pick 12 H.R.1 SNAP provisions from USDA implementation memos and write 60 boundary-case households. Run them through PolicyEngine and through 2-3 states' public online benefit screeners, which needs no system access. Days 10-18: send each state policy director a private divergence report with 3-5 mismatches and an offer of the full pack. Days 15-30: sign 1-2 paid $25-40k UAT-pack pilots with a state policy or IT lead, and start talks with a system integrator's state account team about pre-certification. Recruit 2 ex-state policy and ex-FNS adjudicators to sign keys.

title: Site-Control Check for Utility Large-Load Queues
one_liner: A neutral 48-hour report on whether each large-load applicant really controls the land it names, sold to the utilities that must now screen speculative data center requests and billed through to the applicants.
customer: Large-load and interconnection managers, plus regulatory counsel, at G&T electric co-ops, municipal utilities and mid-size wires companies. Wedge: Texas co-ops, munis and mid-size TDUs (about 150 entities), then SPP and MISO states. The buyer is the utility. The applicant pays through the study-fee schedule.
problem: Utilities are buried in large-load requests, and many are speculative. The same parcel is shopped to several utilities. 'Site control' is often an applicant-supplied PDF or a non-binding LOI. The utility has to decide which requests get $100k+ studies and reserved capacity. A wrong guess strands capital or pushes cost onto ratepayers. Regulators and commissions now expect screening, but staff have no independent way to check control of land beyond what the applicant says.
solution:
The utility requires the applicant to list its parcels, and we do the rest.
1. Pull recorded instruments on those parcels and their neighbors from county portals, targeted per parcel with a landman fallback, so no bulk licence is needed.
2. Classify by reading the image rather than the clerk's label, and resolve the LLC family by notary, return-to firm and address.
3. Deliver a one-page Site-Control Report graded Recorded, Partial, Unrecorded or Conflicting. It shows acreage under recorded control against the acreage the claimed MW implies, option expiry dates, competing claimants, and duplicate-request flags across utilities through an opt-in hashed-parcel index.
4. Upsell a monthly territory sweep, which is the original Courthouse Tape, for assemblies that have not filed a request yet.
A human landman reviews every Partial or Conflicting result.
why_now: Utilities are being pushed to prove large-load requests are real. Texas SB 6 (2025) reportedly requires 75 MW+ applicants to show site control, disclose duplicate requests and pay study fees. Other utilities have added financial-commitment tariffs. ERCOT's large-load queue is reported at well over 200 GW, far beyond any buildable amount. LLM vision now reads messy recorded instruments accurately. FinCEN's exemption of domestic companies from beneficial-ownership reporting means LLC unmasking has to come from primary records. Verify the SB 6 details before quoting them to customers.
revenue_model: $1,500-$3,000 per Site-Control Report, added as a pass-through line to the applicant's study-fee schedule. $60k-$150k a year per utility for the territory sweep, unlimited reports and a regulator-ready audit pack. Bottom-up: 60 utilities at about $80k is $4.8M ARR in Texas and neighboring states. 500 utilities nationally is about $40M ARR. Later add-on: applicants buy a neutral verified-site-control certificate to speed their queue position.
non_obvious_insight: Verification is much easier than detection. Because the utility can compel the parcel list, we skip the hardest parts of the parent: not knowing where to look, statewide bulk scraping, and false positives. A missing or unrecorded instrument becomes a finding in its own right, which also dodges the doubt that developers may not record option memos before announcement. Only a utility-side neutral can build the moat. Developers shop the same parcel to many utilities, and no utility will share its queue with a vendor that also sells to developers. A cross-utility duplicate-parcel index is therefore a network effect that Enverus or Paces cannot build without losing the trust of their own developer customers.
first_30_days: Take Texas. Call 25 co-op and muni large-load contacts through the Texas Electric Cooperatives and Texas Public Power Association networks and the NRECA circuit. Offer a free retrospective audit of each utility's last 10 requests using only recorded instruments. Report what share had no recorded control, duplicate claims or expired options. Convert two utilities to $20k-$30k paid pilots on new requests. In parallel, confirm which county portals allow per-parcel commercial retrieval and line up two landmen for offline counties.

title: Holdout Ledger: Landowner-Side Assembly Intelligence
one_liner: The landowner's half of the courthouse tape. It shows farm families and heirs in an assembly corridor who is buying around them, how close the buyer is to finishing, and how much leverage the last holdouts have, paid on closing.
customer: Owners of 100-2,000 acres in counties where recorded options and easements cluster, reached through ag and land-use attorneys, county farm bureaus, rural lenders and direct mail. Wedge: heirs, tenants-in-common and absentee owners who get anonymous offers under NDA. The payer is the landowner, on a contingent fee, plus subscribing law firms.
problem: Each landowner is approached alone by a landman working for an anonymous LLC. NDAs stop neighbors comparing notes. The developer sees the whole assembly and the owner sees one offer. Owners sign early and cheap, or hold out blindly, and cannot tell whether their parcel is a keystone or an afterthought. Landmen work for the buyer, local lawyers rarely have county-wide data, and county officials learn of the project from a leaked story.
solution:
1. 'Neighbor Check': enter a parcel or address and get a map of recorded instruments within about 5 miles, classified from the image. It shows the LLC family behind them, the share of the plausible footprint already recorded, whether the parcel sits on a critical path (contiguity, road access, a line crossing), expiring options, and a plain-English read of what the pattern usually means.
2. Owners in a cluster can opt into a negotiating pool, like the mineral-owner associations in oil and gas leasing. A licensed land broker or attorney partner represents them. We supply the analytics and take a success fee on closing.
3. We sell a group map subscription to ag and land-use law firms and farm-bureau chapters.
why_now: The 2025-26 large-load land rush has put anonymous NDA'd offers in front of thousands of rural owners, and local fights over data center land deals are widely reported. Owners can now see the buyer's footprint because public recorded memoranda can be read at scale with LLM vision. FinCEN's exemption for domestic companies means owners cannot ask who is behind the LLC and get a federal answer, so primary records are the only route. Reported prices such as roughly $100k an acre offered near Hill County, Texas, make the information gap worth real money to owners.
revenue_model: Free lookup as lead generation. $149-$399 for a full parcel report. A contingent success fee of 1.5%-3% of total consideration at closing, collected through a licensed broker affiliate. Example: a 300-acre owner closing a $4M option-plus-lease package yields $60k-$120k. $300-$800 a month per law firm or farm-bureau seat. Ten closed deals in year one is roughly $500k-$1M, at very low marginal cost after the data pull.
non_obvious_insight: The developer's own recorded memoranda reveal how complete the assembly is, and holdout value peaks in the last 20-30% of parcels. That is the moment owners are least informed. Every existing vendor's paying customer is the developer, so none can serve the counterparty without alienating buyers. That is counter-positioning in Helmer's sense. Landowners are numerous, each needs the service once, and assessor rolls are public, so mail reaches them cheaply. The demand is one-shot and high-stakes, which suits a contingent fee better than SaaS. The data burden is also small: a few dozen instruments per cluster, pulled per parcel, with none of the statewide bulk-ingestion risk.
first_30_days: Pick one county with a visible assembly. The parent's method of pulling 24 months of instruments gives the pattern. Mail 400 landowners within the cluster a letter with a QR code: 'Three LLCs using the same law firm recorded options on X acres within 4 miles of your land.' Offer a free Neighbor Check, then a $199 report. Sign a referral and co-marketing agreement with one licensed land broker and one ag attorney. Get 5 owners into a pooled negotiation and 20 paid reports. Before launch, have counsel confirm the broker-licensing and fee-sharing rules in the state (lawyers generally cannot split fees with non-lawyers), and use only public records. We are never a party to any NDA.

title: Recorder Rails: County-Funded Clean Index of Instruments
one_liner: AI re-indexing and compliance scans that counties buy from their own records-modernization funds. In return we hold the cleaned, entity-resolved index of every non-deed instrument, which becomes the data layer for assembly alerts and much else.
customer: County recorders and clerks (about 3,100 counties), who pay first, starting with mid-size rural and exurban counties in data-center and energy corridors where economic development offices also want the assembly view. Downstream buyers are the parent's developers, utilities and funds, plus ag lenders and title-adjacent firms.
problem: The parent's product depends on county-by-county recorder access and on document types that are often wrong ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'Agreement'). Ingestion is a grind, bulk commercial-use rules vary, and the good data is scattered. Counties have their own pains: aging archives, mandated redaction of sensitive data, covenant-review requests and property-fraud pressure, all with thin staff. They already spend on indexing and digitization from earmarked funds. Nobody owns a clean cross-county index of non-deed instruments.
solution:
1. Sell the county a fixed-price Hidden Instruments Audit. AI reclassifies its mislabeled and 'Other' instruments from the images, corrects grantor and grantee indexing, flags sensitive-data and statutory items such as discriminatory covenants, and gives the county a corrected index and an economic-development view of large instruments.
2. In the agreement, the county gives bulk access to the images and index at cost, and we keep the right to publish the derived classification and entity graph. The underlying records are already public.
3. Publish an open taxonomy for non-deed instruments, in the manner of MISMO for mortgages, so counties and vendors can adopt it.
4. Keep the labeled corpus and the LLC-family graph proprietary and build products on it: Courthouse Tape alerts, the utility site-control check, landowner tools, alt-data licences and collateral-encumbrance alerts for ag lenders.
why_now: LLM vision has collapsed the cost of reading a scanned page, so a re-index that once cost a labor-intensive vendor per-page fees is now cheap. Counties are under fresh mandates to review archives: covenant-removal laws in a number of states, and reportedly some large counties have already run AI covenant scans (verify which). Property-fraud concern is high. FinCEN's exemption of domestic companies from beneficial-ownership reporting makes primary-record entity resolution more valuable. The large-load land rush gives the resulting index an immediate paying use. Rural counties facing data center proposals want visibility into assembly.
revenue_model: County audits at $9k-$40k per county, fitted under small-purchase thresholds and paid from records-modernization or technology funds, then $5k-$20k a year to maintain. Data licences to funds at $50k-$150k a year. Downstream product revenue per the parent: developer or utility seats at $2k-$8k a month and title packets at $750-$2,000. A plausible year-three target is 300 counties at about $25k, or $7.5M, plus $5M-$10M of licences and subscriptions. Gross margin on data products should exceed 70% once ingestion is standardized.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is county cooperation, not the classifier. So invert who pays. Instead of buying access from counties, we get paid by them to solve a problem they already fund, and the by-product is the corpus. A county that gets a corrected index and a free economic-development dashboard has little reason to block a downstream data feed, and other counties will copy the arrangement. This is a cornered resource plus switching costs that build county by county. Incumbents face asymmetry: indexing and digitization vendors earn from labor-based per-page work, so AI re-indexing at a fraction of the price undercuts their own revenue. Title plants index for title, not for cross-county assembly detection.
first_30_days: Run an offline proof on two rumored-project counties. Pull 24 months of instruments, reclassify 'Other' and 'Agreement' filings, and count how many option memoranda were recorded before the announcement. If that count is low, shift the wedge to easement and transmission detection. Show each recorder the result: 'We found N large instruments mislabeled as Other.' Offer a $9,500 audit to three counties, and separately sell the free 'who is assembling where' memo to 10 site-selection consultants to fund the corpus. Check each state's rules on commercial use of bulk records and on data-sharing agreements, and get county counsel comfortable.

title: Ship-Date Cliff Audits for Phased Campuses
one_liner: A fixed-fee clock-map, rider-negotiation and proof-test sprint for developers of multi-phase data center campuses whose pre-bought gensets, UPS and chillers were shipped long before the halls they serve, so the OEM 18-months-from-ship outer limit expires before startup.
customer: Wedge buyer: the VP of procurement or construction director at colo developers and neoclouds building multi-phase campuses (100MW+, with phases 2-4 not yet energized) that accepted long-lead MEP deliveries ahead of the shell. Start with generators, then UPS. Secondary buyer: the lender's technical advisor asking for an equipment warranty schedule at draw or refinancing.
problem: The judges and the competitor check both found that the parent's premise is too broad. Startup plus load-bank IST already loads most equipment, so the 'idle hall' exposure is narrow. The clean exposure is different. OEM terms run to the earlier of about 12 months from startup or 18 months from factory ship (Cummins, Eaton and Trane terms in the research). Developers buy gear in blocks for phases 2-4 to lock lead-time slots and pre-tariff prices, and take delivery into yards or spare rooms. When a phase slips, the outer limit lapses before the unit is ever started. Storage voiding conditions (heaters, battery freshening charges, engine exercise) are usually undocumented, so an OEM can also deny on those grounds. Procurement has moved on, the ship date lives in a bill of lading nobody rereads, and ops inherits the unit with no idea the clock ran out.
solution: 1) Cliff calendar. Per serial number, extract ship date (bill of lading, delivery ticket), planned startup, outer-limit date and voiding conditions. The LLM pipeline is an internal tool; the deliverable is a one-page dated list of cliffs. 2) Rider sprint. Before each cliff, negotiate a written start-date deferral or delayed-start rider with the OEM. Package it campus-wide, because the owner's phase 3-4 orders are the leverage a single-unit rider buyer lacks. 3) Storage-compliance repair. Fix missing exercise, heater and battery-charge logs so the OEM loses its easy denial grounds. 4) Proof test. For installed units 6-9 months before the cliff, run a staged load test using a load-bank rental partner, then file claims with OEM-grade evidence while the OEM is still liable. Contingency is not the lead model.
why_now: Long-lead power gear (gensets, transformers, switchgear) is being bought years ahead of buildings, and phase slippage is widespread in 2026 reporting. Tariffs make each unit more expensive, so each lapsed warranty is worth more. LLMs make serial-level extraction from delivery documents cheap. Delayed-start riders exist (Trane), so the ask is normal to OEMs but rarely made.
revenue_model: $30-60K fixed fee per campus phase for the cliff calendar plus rider negotiation. $60-120K per year campus retainer that keeps the calendar live as phases progress. Load-test pass-through with a 15% markup, plus a referral fee from the rental partner. Success fee of 20% of OEM-accepted claim value, measured by the OEM's claim number or credit memo, and 10% of the discount won on riders versus list. Assumption to validate: about 30 campus programs at roughly $80K per year is about $2.4M ARR with 2-3 people.
non_obvious_insight: The exposed population is defined by shipment date versus startup date, not by whether a hall is idle. That makes it provable from documents and public filings before any owner talks to you. It also makes the contingency-collection problem disappear: a signed deferral or an OEM credit memo is a countable outcome, unlike 'avoided repair cost'. The leverage is future orders across the campus, which the owner has and a one-off rider purchase does not.
first_30_days: Build a target list from public state air-permit filings for backup diesel generators, which typically list unit counts and models by phase, cross-referenced with press releases and county filings. Rank 40 campuses where permitted units far exceed operating ones. Email the procurement lead a one-page teaser: 'if your gensets shipped in Q3 2025, the OEM outer limit lands in Q1 2027'. Land three owners who hand over POs and delivery tickets for a free 5-day clock map. Use the first dated cliff to open a rider conversation with the OEM before any invoice. This also answers the parent's unresolved question of whether clocks are truly running out on unstarted equipment.
lineage: mutation of I0229 ('Warranty Clock Recovery Audits for Idle Halls'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ethyco (data center commissioning, warranty-phase support), Anyset AI (agentic closeout / warranty tracking), Nomic (AEC document AI, closeout), Trane delayed start-up warranty (OEM rider). White space: Nobody I found combines all of these for data center MEP: (1) a serial-number-level clock ledger built for idle or deferred-start halls, (2) a pre-expiry loaded stress test using the idle capacity, (3) OEM claim filing and start-date deferral negotiation, and (4) success-fee or fixed-fee pricing sold to the owner or its lender. The pieces exist separately. Anyset and Nomic do doc extraction. Ethyco-style Cx firms do a 10-month warranty review. Wind and solar have end-of-warranty inspection and claims firms. OEMs sell delayed-start riders. Load-bank vendors have the hardware. Data center power and cooling MEP has no dedicated end-of-warranty claims specialist that I could find. Three structural weaknesses limit the wedge. (a) The clocks mostly start at OEM startup, and startup plus IST with load banks already loads equipment in Cx, so the 'idle for 12+ months' exposure is narrower than the pitch implies. It mainly hits gear started early or shipped more than 18 months before use. (b) 'Recovered value' is really avoided repair cost. title: Warranty Gap Desk for MEP Contractors
one_liner: Sell to the electrical and mechanical contractors who promise owners a warranty from substantial completion while their OEM warranties run from shipment or startup, and fund the service from the contractors' own warranty reserves.
customer: The warranty manager, contracts VP or CFO at mid-size to large electrical contractors, mechanical contractors and construction managers building data centers who furnish the MEP equipment themselves (colo, enterprise and neocloud jobs, not owner-furnished hyperscale). They give the owner a 12-24 month warranty and carry a warranty reserve on the balance sheet.
problem: The parent assumed the owner feels the pain. The party actually squeezed between two clocks is the contractor. The OEM warranty passes through on an OEM calendar (startup or 18 months from ship). The contractor's promise to the owner runs from substantial completion or Tier certification, and owner-side counsel are actively advising developers to push warranty commencement to certification (the law-firm guidance in the parent's evidence). Every month of delay widens the gap, and in that gap the contractor pays for defects out of pocket. Estimators price it as a flat percentage, project managers do not track it, and closeout binders bury the OEM terms. Contractor warranty reserves are real P&L items the CFO wants released, which gives a budget line the parent never had.
solution: 1) Bid-stage gap pricing. Read the subcontract warranty clause and the OEM quotes, compute gap-days by equipment line, and price it into the bid instead of a flat reserve. 2) Deferral riders on the contractor's own POs. A contractor buying hundreds of units per year has leverage the owner lacks, and the desk pools rider purchasing across contractor clients for discounts. 3) Pre-expiry proof test and claim filing on installed gear so the OEM, not the contractor, pays for defects (load-bank partner does the physical work). 4) Reserve-release package at contract end: a documented file showing what OEM claims were accepted and what exposure remains, so the CFO can release reserve early.
why_now: Owner counsel now push warranty starts to Tier certification while long-lead delivery and phase slippage stretch the shipment-to-certification interval. Data center MEP backlogs are large, so contractors have more warranty exposure on more sites than ever. Extraction of PO, contract and OEM terms into gap-days used to require a warranty analyst per job and is now nearly free.
revenue_model: Program fee per project, roughly 0.03-0.08% of MEP contract value (about $120-320K on a $400M scope), which is a small share of a typical reserve. Assumption to validate: reserves of around 0.5-2% of contract value. Plus 20% of OEM-accepted claims that would otherwise have been borne by the contractor. Plus a rider-pooling margin or referral fee from OEMs and rental partners. Renewals follow the contractor's project pipeline, so revenue is recurring across projects.
non_obvious_insight: The contractor is the only party in the chain holding an unhedged, quantifiable, budgeted warranty liability, and it is growing because of owner-side contract trends. Selling to the contractor also flips the leverage problem: one contractor buys from OEMs at volume, and a desk representing several contractors can win start-date deferrals that no single owner could. The buyer is a CFO with a reserve, not an owner's ops team with no budget.

Confirm the key assumption early, which is what share of their data center equipment is contractor-furnished.

title: Load-Proven Warranty Wrap for Data Halls
one_liner: Invert the parent: instead of chasing OEMs for owners as warranties expire, run a standardized load-proof test before expiry, fix what the OEM owes for free, then sell a capacity-backed warranty wrap that covers the post-expiry tail, priced from a proprietary fleet failure database.
customer: First buyers: owners and lenders' technical advisors of energized data halls approaching OEM warranty expiry, asking for a standardized Load-Proven test and certificate (a covenant-friendly document for refinancing or ABS). Later buyers: the same owners buying multi-year coverage for gensets, UPS, chillers and liquid-cooling CDUs. The capacity provider (a specialty insurer or reinsurer) is a third party in the money flow.
problem: The parent's contingency model is hard to collect and OEMs can deny on storage or light-load grounds. Behind that is a bigger issue: once OEM warranties lapse, owners of AI halls with dense power and liquid cooling carry an unpriced failure tail, and nobody has independent load-tested failure data on these systems. OEM service contracts cover a single vendor's gear and are priced generically. Lenders financing GPU-era assets see equipment residual risk with no standard way to test or rate it.
solution: Phase 1, within 6 months: sell a standardized Load-Proven protocol. It is a 3-5 day staged load test (gensets, UPS and battery, chillers and CDUs, breakers), thermography, oil, coolant and battery diagnostics, using a load-bank rental partner and NETA-type testing subcontractors. Each test outputs a certificate and, where a defect shows, an OEM claim package while the OEM is still liable. Every test feeds a proprietary failure and degradation database. Phase 2, months 6-18: place multi-year tail coverage for tested gear through a broker or MGA partner on a quota-share basis with an insurer or reinsurer. Only gear that passed the test is bound. Defects surfaced by the test are repaired at the OEM's cost first, so the wrap covers a cleaner tail. Phase 3: become the MGA, and push the test protocol into loan covenants and insurer schedules as the standard.
why_now: AI halls introduce liquid-cooling and high-density power gear with immature public failure data, so generic pricing is either too expensive or blind. Data center lending and ABS need equipment-condition standards. Phase slippage means a large group of halls will pass through OEM expiry without ever having been stressed. Cheap LLM extraction of test logs and maintenance records lets a small team standardize reports across sites.
revenue_model: Phase 1: $60-120K per hall for the Load-Proven test (much of it load-bank pass-through), plus any claim-based fee. Phase 2: broker commission, then MGA ceding and profit commission on premium. Assumed pricing to validate with capacity providers: coverage at 1-2% of covered equipment value per year, and a 50 MW hall carries roughly $50-80M of gensets, UPS, chillers and switchgear, so about $0.5-1.6M of annual premium per hall and roughly $100-300K of commission to the MGA. That is on the order of 5-10x the parent's audit fee per hall.
non_obvious_insight: The inspection is both the revenue product and the underwriting filter, and the two feed each other. Defects found pre-expiry are paid by the OEM, which reduces adverse selection, and the resulting data is a cornered resource: independent, fleet-level, load-based, across OEMs. The parent treated the warranty as an asset to recover. The bigger business treats post-warranty risk as an asset class to price, using the only thing OEMs cannot easily replicate, which is neutral cross-vendor test data.
first_30_days: Draft a two-page Load-Proven protocol with a load-bank rental partner and a NETA-type test firm. Get one data-center-finance law firm or lender's technical advisor to review a one-page covenant template. Pitch three owners with halls approaching OEM expiry and one lender with a delayed-lease loan. Meet two equipment-breakdown or specialty warranty MGAs and ask what data they would need to quote a quota-share on tested MEP gear. Goal: one paid pilot test signed and one written indication of appetite from a capacity provider.

title: Keep-the-Amps: Electrical Carve-Out for Plant Liquidations
one_liner: A 3,000-dollar electrician-verified 'in-place value memo' sold to industrial liquidators, trustees' counsel and corporate closure teams, so the switchgear and transformers are carved out of the equipment auction and sold with the real estate as a powered shell.
customer: Wedge: the 15-30 mid-size Midwest industrial liquidation auctioneers, and the panel trustees, receivers' counsel and corporate-real-estate disposition managers who hire them when a plant with at least 2 MW of service goes dark in OH, PA, MI or IN. Not manufacturers, not brokers.
problem: A plant liquidation has two teams that never talk. The equipment auctioneer sells presses, CNCs and often the switchgear, bus duct and transformers as used-equipment or scrap lots. The real-estate side lists square feet and dock doors. The energized service is the scarce asset (large transformers run about 128 weeks, switchgear 44-90+ weeks, so a buyer who has to replace them loses a year or more), and it is destroyed or stripped in the gap between the two teams. The trustee or seller has a fiduciary or financial duty to maximise proceeds but no document showing what the gear is worth in place versus removed. A secured mortgage lender and an equipment lender may also be fighting over what is a fixture.
solution: Sell one fixed-scope deliverable, the 'Powered-Shell Memo', in 8 days: (1) licensed electrician's one-day walk-through with one-line diagram, nameplates, gear age, thermography and spare capacity; (2) a carve-out schedule marking every item of electrical infrastructure as 'stays with the building' or 'safe to sell', with in-place value (replacement cost plus lead-time cost) against scrap and used-lot value; (3) utility service status (energized, disconnected, minimum-bill exposure) and a one-line check of air and wastewater permit status (shutdown, fees current, notification-only transfer), demoted to a checkbox because Ohio EPA transfer is easy; (4) a buyer-agnostic data-room cut that a data-center, battery, cold-storage or manufacturing buyer can underwrite. The fee is a flat cost line in the auction budget, paid from proceeds at closing, so the estate needs no upfront cash.
why_now: Buyers are paying for existing energized shells (TeraWulf/Anthropic's $19B lease on a shuttered aluminum plant, the former Goodyear plant in Akron running about 150 MW), and transformer and switchgear lead times are still measured in years. Plant closures and manufacturer distress continue in 2026, so supply of dead plants is steady. Before the AI-power scramble a stripped switchgear lineup was worth scrap; now it is worth a year of a buyer's schedule.
revenue_model: $3,000 flat per plant (electrician cost about $1,300, analyst about 4 hours, roughly 55% gross margin), paid at closing or as a budgeted line in the liquidation. Add-ons: $1,200 buyer-ready data-room cut, $9,000 for multi-plant corporate closures (3-5 sites), and a $6k-$12k annual retainer for auctioneers who want a standing right to use the memo in their pitches. No percentage of sale price and no brokerage, which avoids the licence problem and the conflict the parent's success fee had. Later: license the anonymised gear-and-value dataset. Bottom-up: 150 to 250 qualifying Midwest industrial disposals a year at $3k-$4k is about $0.5M-$1M of report revenue for one small team before retainers, which is enough to fund the next two offspring-style expansions, not a venture-scale market by itself.
non_obvious_insight: The thing that destroys the power asset in a dead plant is the equipment auction itself, not neglect. The liquidator is paid to turn gear into cash quickly, the real-estate broker never sees the gear list, and nobody owns the question 'is the switchgear worth more bolted to the building?'. The memo is not a report on the building, it is a decision document that changes what goes in the auction catalogue, and it gives the trustee defensible cover for keeping it out.
first_30_days: Week 1: pull 24 months of WARN closure notices for OH/PA/MI/IN, PACER Chapter 7/11 filings by manufacturers with real property, and county receivership dockets, and cross-check against Ohio EPA facility status to list about 60 dark plants with 2 MW or more. Week 2: call 15 regional liquidation auctioneers and 10 trustee counsel with one offer, a free first memo on their next live liquidation in exchange for a written case study and permission to anonymise the data. Weeks 3-4: hire one electrician for two walk-throughs at about $150 per hour; deliver memos; ask one secured mortgage lender to accept a memo as a fixture-line exhibit. Success test: at least one auctioneer pulls electrical gear from a catalogue, and two of the next three mandates pay $3,000 at closing.
lineage: mutation of I0820 ('Power Passport: Scoring Dead Factories on Amps, Permits'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Brownfield.ai, Scout (ScoutCities), LandGate, Enverus Site & Screen. White space: Nobody I found productises a building-level, physically verified 'inside-the-fence' record for dead Midwest plants. That record would cover the electrician-verified main service size, voltage, gear age and nameplates, spare capacity, slab and crane-rail condition, the state of the existing air and wastewater permits, and a utility will-serve letter, all in a scored, comparable format sold before the deal. The funded players (LandGate, Enverus, GridCARE, Paces) work at the substation and grid level and are aimed at data centers. Utility and state databases (JobsOhio, AEP, FirstEnergy, ZoomProspector) verify sites and utility service, not building gear or permit status. Scout and Brownfield.ai are the closest competitors, but they look desktop- and network-led with no per-building inspection, and I found no evidence they carry electrician-verified data. The genuine gap is a trusted, standardised, seller-commissioned building electrical and permit record, not the parcel-scoring layer, which is already crowded and funded. The payer is the seller side at the moment of disposition, which none of them serve, and JobsOhio, AEP and FirstEnergy databases are free but verify sites and service, not gear or carve-out decisions. PCA and electrical inspection firms give buyers a compliance-style ampacity line; nobody gives a seller a valued in-place versus scrap schedule tied to the auction terms. The permit-transferability wedge that was thin in the parent is reduced to a checkbox, and the success fee is dropped.

title: Load Recovery for Municipal Utilities and Co-ops
one_liner: Sell the verified dead-plant record to the municipal electric utilities and rural co-ops that lose money every month the anchor plant sits dark, priced as a package plus a bonus tied to the load they get back.
customer: Municipal electric systems, rural electric co-ops and their joint-action agencies or statewide associations (for example American Municipal Power and the state municipal electric associations) in OH, PA, MI and IN, where an anchor industrial plant has closed and the utility's own economic-development or general manager decides. Wedge: 8 utilities in the Mahoning Valley, Akron/Canton and western PA with an idle plant of at least 2 MW in their territory.
problem: When a plant with several MW of load closes, a small public utility keeps paying its fixed wholesale power, transmission and substation costs but spreads them over fewer kWh, so rates rise for homes and shops and the remaining industrial customers get nervous (an assumption to validate with 10 utility managers). These utilities have no economic-development staff, are ignored by the investor-owned-utility databases and grid-analytics vendors, and cannot tell a data-center or battery developer what is actually inside the fence of their dead plant. Meanwhile the plant's energized service, which the utility itself installed and meters, is the one asset that could replace the lost load.
solution: A 'Load Recovery Package' per idle plant: (1) electrician-verified one-line diagram, gear nameplates, spare capacity and slab/crane condition; (2) the utility's own historical interval load and substation loading, which only the utility holds, turned into a stranded-load scorecard showing what re-energizing 2, 4 or 8 MW would do to fixed-cost recovery and rates; (3) a pre-cleared economic-development rate rider and a written will-serve position, drafted with the utility's engineer, which is the hardest input in the parent's product and is free when the utility is the customer; (4) outreach to a curated buyer list (manufacturers, battery and cold-storage operators, small data-center and inference developers) with the record as the data room. Later, a member-services version sold through a joint-action agency to all members.
why_now: Buyers with real money now want existing energized industrial shells, so a dead plant in a small utility's territory has more than one class of possible buyer for the first time in decades. Large-load tariffs and interconnection queues at the big investor-owned utilities push developers to look for capacity elsewhere, and roughly 128-week transformer lead times make existing service worth years. Ohio's 125+ local data-center moratoriums are a problem for pure data-center strategies, so a buyer-agnostic pitch to friendly municipal utilities is safer.
revenue_model: $9,500 per Load Recovery Package paid from the utility's economic-development budget; $18,000 per year retainer covering up to five sites, buyer outreach and a rolling record refresh; a capped performance bonus of about 10% of the first-year demand-charge margin from re-energized load (cap around $60k), structured as an economic-development services fee from the utility and not a commission on a property sale (have Ohio counsel confirm the real-estate licence question before signing). Channel: a joint-action agency or state association licenses the tool to members at $40k-$80k per year. Bottom-up: about 100-150 qualifying utilities in four states at an average $12k in year one is $1.2M-$1.8M, with 70-plus percent gross margin after the electrician cost on the package.
non_obvious_insight: The utility, not the broker or the manufacturer, is the party that already holds the two hardest inputs, years of interval meter data on the dead plant and the ability to say in writing what it would take to re-energize it, and it is also the only party that loses money every month the plant stays dark. Sell to them and the will-serve letter that costs the parent weeks of chasing becomes something the customer hands you. Small public utilities are also unserved by every funded competitor, which all chase hyperscalers and the big investor-owned utilities.
first_30_days: Week 1: build a list of every municipal electric system and co-op in northeast Ohio and western PA (from state association member lists) and match each to idle plants using Ohio EPA and county parcel data; shortlist 20 with a dark plant of at least 2 MW. Weeks 2-3: call 20 general managers and superintendents; pitch a free 'stranded-load scorecard' on their dead plant using their meter data. Get three to share interval data and access. Week 4: deliver one scorecard plus a paid quote of $9,500 for the full package, and pitch a 20-minute slot at a state municipal electric association meeting. Success test: one utility signs the $9,500 package or a letter of intent, and one association agrees to a member pilot.

title: Keep-Warm: Preserving Power in Idle Plants
one_liner: Invert the database: instead of scoring dead plants once, sell a monthly service that keeps their electrical service alive and monitored, then turn 200 preserved shells into a right-of-first-offer inventory and, later, a balance-sheet powered-shell bank.
customer: Wedge: banks, special servicers and lenders holding real-estate-owned industrial plants, plus corporate owners of mothballed plants and county land banks, in the Mahoning Valley and Akron/Canton first. Later buyers: data-center, battery and manufacturing developers who pay for shells certified 'energized-ready'.
problem: An idle plant's electrical system is a wasting asset on a clock. Standard commercial property policies limit cover for vandalism, theft, water damage and sprinkler leakage once a building has been vacant for about 60 days (an assumption to verify with an insurance broker), copper theft and roof leaks wreck switchgear, utilities can pull service or reclassify accounts on idle meters, oil-filled transformers degrade, and permit fees and reports lapse. Residential-style property-preservation firms winterize and change locks, but nobody is paid to preserve amps. Owners find out the plant is worth far less than it was only when a buyer's electrician opens the gear two years later.
solution: Two tiers. 'Watch' at $650 per month: baseline electrician record (the Power Passport becomes the set-up fee), a $600 sensor kit (humidity, temperature, door, current clamps on the main service, cellular camera), quarterly thermography, and an insurer-facing monthly report. 'Warm' at $2,200 per month: monthly electrician visits, keep-energized management with the utility including minimum-bill and account status, annual transformer oil sampling, dehumidification, theft-alarm response and permit fee and report compliance. The continuous data produces an 'energized-ready' score, days to first power, and a verified time series no one-off inspection can match. Marketing and right-of-first-offer rights are bundled into the contract for owners who want a sale.
why_now: Low-cost cellular sensors and cameras collapsed to tens of dollars a unit. Vision models now read nameplates and gear photos cheaply, which cuts analyst hours per building. More industrial shells are going idle while buyers now pay a premium for existing power, so, for the first time, preserving the electrical system has a positive return.
revenue_model: Recurring: $650 or $2,200 per building per month plus a $2,500 baseline record; a carry-cost comparison shows a 300k sq ft idle plant costing an owner roughly $15k-$40k per month, so the service is 3-8% on top of existing carry. Gross margin about 50-55% at 10 buildings per electrician route. Insurer angle: partner with a vacant-property insurance managing general agent to turn monitoring into a rating credit, which can pay for itself. Scale path: 200 buildings on Warm and Watch is about $4M-$5M annual recurring revenue; the contract's right of first offer gives inventory to sell to buyers on a fee basis; a later fund of $50M-$100M exercises options on the best 20 shells, subdivides them into permitted 'factory condos' or powered shells and sells or leases at a premium. First 6 months: 5-8 paying buildings.
non_obvious_insight: The same service that stops the asset dying also builds the only dataset that matters: a time series of load, temperature, humidity and access on hundreds of idle industrial buildings, and exclusive access to a pipeline of them. That combination is a cornered resource plus a switching cost, defended by contracts and data history and not by scoring algorithms anyone can copy. The parent is a snapshot; this is the movie, and a monthly bill is a better business than a report.
first_30_days: Week 1: list 40 idle plants owned by banks, special servicers and land banks from county auditor and REO data in two metros; contact 8 REO and asset managers. Week 2: call two vacant-property insurance brokers and one managing general agent to test whether monitoring earns a premium credit or a vacancy-clause endorsement (the riskiest assumption). Weeks 3-4: sign three 90-day pilots on Watch at a waived set-up fee in exchange for a case study and marketing rights, install kits, and deliver the first insurer-facing report. Success test: one lender converts to $650 per month paid and one insurer or broker confirms a written premium credit or vacancy accommodation.

That record would cover the electrician-verified main service size, voltage, gear age and nameplates, spare capacity, slab and crane-rail condition, the state of the existing air and wastewater permits, and a utility will-serve letter, all in a scored, comparable format sold before the deal. The funded players (LandGate, Enverus, GridCARE, Paces) work at the substation and grid level and are aimed at data centers. Utility and state databases (JobsOhio, AEP, FirstEnergy, ZoomProspector) verify sites and utility service, not building gear or permit status. Scout and Brownfield.ai are the closest competitors, but they look desktop- and network-led with no per-building inspection, and I found no evidence they carry electrician-verified data. The genuine gap is a trusted, standardised, seller-commissioned building electrical and permit record, not the parcel-scoring layer, which is already crowded and funded. The idea's weaker points: the Ohio permit-transferability wedge is thin (see evidence), and it is unproven that brokers will pay $1.5k-$3.5k. | How this version avoids them: None of the parent's competitors monitor or preserve anything. Brownfield.ai, Scout, LandGate, Enverus, GridCARE, Paces and ZoomProspector sell data or listings, and JobsOhio and the utility databases are free lists. PCA and electrical inspection firms sell a one-time report, and residential property-preservation and big facilities-management firms cover occupied, high-value assets or locks and lawns, not energized-capacity preservation. The business is recurring service revenue with a proprietary time series, so a funded data competitor would have to hire electricians and sign owner contracts to copy it, and the exclusive marketing rights become a cornered resource.

title: Pooled Calendar Reporters for Limited-Scope Family Lawyers
one_liner: One physically present reporter sits an entire family-court calendar and sells the record by the matter, about $110 per 15-minute hearing, so each lawyer pays roughly 75% less than a half-day pro tem while the reporter earns more than a normal pro tem day.
customer: Wedge: limited-scope (unbundled) and solo family-law attorneys who appear on DVRO, custody and support calendars in ONE high-volume California courthouse, plus the non-indigent 'missing middle' litigants they represent, who fail the fee-waiver test but cannot spend $450 on a record. Not indigent litigants (the FVAP ruling moves them to a court-paid record) and not the court.
problem: About 7 in 10 civil, family and probate hearings in California have no verbatim record, and appeals of custody and restraining-order rulings fail without one. Courts tell litigants to 'arrange your own' reporter, but a private pro tem costs $450-500 for a half day, and no one pays that for a 12-minute item. The parent's fix (remote reporters dialing in) is barred by Gov. Code 69959 and by the 69959.5 pilot limits, so it cannot launch as written. The parent also has no proof that anyone will pay $95, and the ruling shrinks the legal-aid segment.
solution: Drop remote reporting and prediction. A reporter is physically in the department for the whole morning or afternoon calendar, which is the lawful 'bring your own reporter' route. Attorneys book a matter slot the day before at $110 for up to 15 minutes, plus a per-page certified transcript (about $8/page) only if they order one. Booking is all-or-nothing, like a crowdfund: the reporter goes only if at least 6-8 matters are booked by 5pm the day before, otherwise everyone is refunded. That kills the dead-time problem without any duration model. Each party gets only its own matter's transcript, and other matters on the reporter's notes are never released. Cross-department hopping and duration prediction come later, once the manual logs give real data. Unit economics (assumptions to test): 2 sessions/day x 8 matters x $110 = $1,760 gross. The reporter keeps about 60% ($1,056) versus $900-1,000 for two half-day pro tem bookings, and the company keeps about $700 per reporter-day before ops.
why_now: FVAP v. Superior Court (Aug 10, 2026) put the 70% no-record gap in every family lawyer's inbox. It also makes courts serve only indigent litigants, which leaves a large paying middle. Courts are already telling family litigants in writing to arrange their own reporter. The reporter shortage (about 5,500 short by 2030) means freelancers can choose better-paying days, so a higher-yield day is a real recruiting pitch.
revenue_model: $110 per matter slot for up to 15 minutes, $8/page for certified transcripts, and prepaid 5-packs ($500) for cash up front. The reporter keeps about 60% of slot fees, the platform keeps about 40% (about 35% gross margin after the payment and ops costs of a services business). Year-2 add-ons: a subscription for attorneys who book 8+ hearings a month, and referral-funded 'record scholarships' from DV appellate nonprofits.
non_obvious_insight: Once the first attorney in a department triggers the reporter's presence, every other matter that day costs roughly nothing extra, so the price can fall 75% while the reporter's day pay rises. Limited-scope attorneys are the right buyer because they bill flat per hearing and can pass the record fee through as an itemized line, while a full-service litigator does not think of the record as a per-hearing line item. The tipping-point booking rule replaces the prediction model the parent needed.
first_30_days: Week 1: one-week legal check with a court-reporter licensing attorney and the clerks of the 2 target departments (private pro tem in the room, multiple parties sharing one reporter, closed-hearing rules, and any court-reporting-firm registration). Weeks 1-2: pick the single biggest family courthouse in one county, recruit 3 physically local pro tem reporters, and pre-sell 5-packs to 15 limited-scope attorneys from the family-law bar and unbundled-services listservs. Weeks 3-4: run the first 10 calendars with a Google Sheet, Stripe links and a group text, using the booking threshold, and log booked-matter density and actual call order per department. Offer FVAP and one DV appellate nonprofit free slots for cases they flag as appeal-bound.

White space: Nobody offers flat-fee coverage of 15-minute California family-law hearings. That is because the core mechanic, private reporters dialing in from anywhere, is currently barred. Gov. Code 69959 says 'Remote court reporting shall not be used by courts to make the record of any court proceedings' and defines it as a stenographer not present in the courtroom (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959/). The only exception, Gov. Code 69959.5, allows remote reporting only by 'full-time official reporters ... employed by the participating superior court', physically in a court facility, in 13 pilot counties, capped at 10-20% of reporters (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959-5/). Court reporter unions opposed AB 3013 and are a political headwind. | How this version avoids them: Steno, DirectDep, StenoScout and the agencies (Veritext, Esquire and others) sell a whole appearance to one buyer, mostly depositions, so every buyer pays the full minimum, and their half-day minimum is structural. We sell the matter, split one appearance across many paying parties, and stay lawful without remote reporting. We serve paying litigants in any county and do not compete for the court-employed slots. eScribers and Verbit transcribe recordings, which fits the court's indigent fallback but not an attorney who wants a stenographic record, live and immediate. The moat, if the wedge works, is proprietary calendar density and call-order data per department, and reporter loyalty from the higher day yield, which points to a cornered-resource advantage in one courthouse before any scale.

title: Record-on-Request Desk for Superior Courts
one_liner: A managed compliance service that lets a superior court answer any indigent litigant's request for a verbatim record with one certified record per request, priced per record delivered and using the cheapest lawful method, whether steno or electronic recording.
customer: Court executive officers and presiding family/probate judges of small and mid-size California superior courts, especially those outside the AB 3013 pilot or above its 10-20% cap. Self-represented litigants and DV legal aid are the users, but the court is the payer.
problem: FVAP v. Superior Court (Aug 10, 2026) gives indigent litigants a mandatory right to an official verbatim record on request, through court-paid pro tem reporters or electronic recording. Courts have no reporters and hiring freezes, and they cannot staff for requests that could arrive any day. Their real gap is a defensible request-to-record workflow: intake, indigency check, method selection, delivery of a certified appeal-ready record, and reporting. The 3 million hearings without a record are already a Judicial Council-visible metric. Half-day pro tem minimums make each request cost $450-500 or more.
solution: A per-request desk, priced by outcome. The litigant or facilitator files a request when they set the hearing, so the desk usually gets 2-7 days of notice, which turns random demand into schedulable demand. The desk picks the method: (a) the court's own recording plus a certified transcript on demand (subcontracted to an eScribers-style vendor), or (b) a physically present steno reporter from a pooled roster that covers several requests in the same courthouse (the offspring-1 network) when a steno record is required or the department has no recording. The court pays only for records delivered and certified. A dashboard shows requests, turnaround and no-record rate by department, ready for Judicial Council reporting. The desk is offered at no retainer with a quarterly spend cap, sized to the court's own budget.
why_now: The Supreme Court decision is Aug 2026 and the court decision names the compliance routes, so every court now needs a plan, and no incumbent has packaged one. Reporter budgets and vacancy savings exist because courts cannot fill positions, and CA has already sent dedicated funding to court reporters (verify the current allocation and whether vacancy savings can be redirected). Verbit's Judicial Council master agreement for captioning from July 1, 2026 shows courts do buy court-tech through master agreements, which gives a path from single-court pilots to statewide.
revenue_model: The court pays a flat $150-250 per hearing record delivered (up to 30 minutes), certified transcripts at a per-page rate, and no retainer. Pricing sits below a $450-500 half-day pro tem and far below an idle full-time reporter. Steno requests use pooled reporters, and audio requests use subcontracted transcription, so gross margin is about 30-40%. Year 2: annual subscription for the dashboard and intake software, and a statewide master-agreement bid. Legal aid and foundations can fund 'request navigators' who file requests for litigants, which lifts volume.
non_obvious_insight: The court does not need reporters. It needs a defensible answer to a request, so the method is irrelevant, and the biggest threat (electronic recording) becomes a supply input to a desk that will choose it. Requests that arrive at intake instead of at the courtroom door are what make pooled steno economical, because notice converts unpredictable demand into a schedule. Outcome pricing ('pay only when a certified record is delivered') is the contingency that lets a risk-averse court say yes without a retainer.
first_30_days: Week 1: one-week legal check with a court-reporter licensing attorney, plus reading the ruling's list of lawful compliance routes. Weeks 1-3: ask FVAP and 2-3 DV legal-aid groups to introduce court executives of two counties with the highest no-record rates. Build the intake form and an eScribers-style subcontract, and sign 3 physical pro tem reporters in one county. Weeks 3-4: offer one family department a no-cost, at-cost 60-day compliance pilot (about 20-40 requests) with a weekly report. Aim for an under-threshold purchase order or sole-source urgent-compliance pilot within 90-120 days. The 30-day success test is a signed pilot letter from one court and a design-partner agreement with FVAP.
