title: Courtroom ETA: Call-Time Network for Family Court
one_liner: A 'FlightAware for family court calendars' that texts litigants, lawyers and freelance reporters and interpreters their predicted call time, giving the queue away and selling the same feed to the professionals who lose half-day minimums waiting.
customer: Start: DV survivors and family litigants (free, via legal-aid and DV org sponsors) and solo family-law attorneys ($29/month). Paying side by month 6: freelance court reporters, interpreters and appearance attorneys who buy call-time alerts to hop between hearings. Later: courts, which pay for staggered 'time-certain' calendars.
problem: Family calendars run on the 8:30 cattle call: 30-40 matters set at one time and called in an order nobody can see. Parties, including survivors who may wait near their abuser, sit in a hallway for hours. Attorneys burn billable time (a solo lawyer's 2-hour wait costs $400-600, an assumption to verify). Reporters, interpreters and appearance counsel price by the half day because no one can predict a 15-minute call time. The parent's dispatch model needed that prediction but assumed it was a feature, when it is the missing infrastructure for every short-hearing service.
solution: Inverted product: prediction first, services second. Month 1-6 product: an SMS bot for two departments in one courthouse. A litigant or attorney texts a case number and gets 'about 45 minutes; you are 9th of 34'. Data comes from the public daily calendar, historical durations by hearing type and judge, and check-ins: people text 'called' or 'out' from the hallway (not from inside the courtroom, where phones may be restricted), plus paid spotters logging call order at $18/hour for the first 20 court days. Publish a per-department 'wait report card' as press and leverage. The same feed then powers a services layer, with reporters, interpreters and appearance attorneys buying alerts and booking one hearing at a time, which turns the parent's marketplace into the second product. Endgame: the call-time index becomes the standard that courts license to stagger calendars.
why_now: After the FVAP decision the gap in recorded hearings is public news. Courts, legal aid and press now treat family-court process failures as a story. Cheap SMS, LLM-based calendar parsing and speech-to-text make the data layer nearly free, while calendar data has been public but unused for years. The reporter shortage forces reporters to hop to survive, and the shortage gives them an incentive to pay for the ETA.
revenue_model: Free for litigants (sponsored by DV legal aid, foundation and IOLTA-type grants). $29/month for attorneys. $99-299/month per reporter, interpreter or appearance attorney for alerts and hop scheduling, plus a booking fee (10-15%) once the per-hearing marketplace exists. Courts pay for calendar analytics and a staggering tool ($20-60K per court per year, an assumption) after the wait report cards create pressure. Bottom-up illustration to test: 40 family departments x 30 matters x 2 parties is about 2,400 party-attendances/day in one large county.
non_obvious_insight: The reporting shortage is a symptom of an information problem: half-day minimums exist because the call time is unknowable. Give the information away to the crowd and charge the people who can turn it into utilization. Each check-in improves the ETA for everyone else in the department (network effect), so density in a courthouse is the moat, and the data is a cornered resource no reporter agency can copy without the crowd. It also fixes the parent's legal flaw: it needs no remote reporting, only public calendars and voluntary check-ins.
first_30_days: Week 1: choose the two busiest family departments in one large county, hire two spotters (retired court watchers or paralegal students) and log call order and durations for 20 court days. Week 2: build a Twilio SMS bot with a manual ETA rule (calendar position x median duration by hearing type). Week 3: recruit 10 solo attorneys and 2 DV legal-aid groups as first users, and 3 freelance interpreters or reporters as paying alerts customers. Week 4: publish the first department wait report card and test whether hallway wait shrinks and whether any reporter will pay $99/month. Day 180 target: 300 active attorneys and litigants in one courthouse, 20 paying professionals, and a second courthouse.

title: Camp-Road Closing Rescue Plus Resale Toll
one_liner: A Maine-only, attorney-supervised service that runs the statutory neighbor meeting, records an enforceable assessment-lien covenant, and then issues a paid road-status letter on every future sale on that road.
customer: Wedge: closing attorneys and title agents handling lake-camp, second-home and rural sales in Maine's lakes region and midcoast (start with the 5 to 8 firms that do the most camp closings). The payer at the table is the seller, or the buyer via negotiated credit. Out-of-state second-home buyers and their lenders are the ones who insist on a maintenance agreement. Listing agents are a secondary channel in the Oct-Feb off-season, when they prep camps for spring listing.
problem: Maine Title 23 section 3101 (text re-checked today) lets as few as 3 parcels petition a notary to call a meeting, lets a majority vote set assessments, and shields board members from civil liability. It contains no lien or collection remedy. The parent research counted 4 parcels, but the fetched text says 3 parcels held by 3 different owners. So the statute is a vote without teeth, and nobody runs the vote. No closing attorney will chase 14 owners for proxies at a flat closing fee, so the sale stalls or closes on a handshake. The parent's own flaws sit on top of this. Its $12-25 per household per month is 6 to 12 times PayHOA's price anchor. Holding dues float triggers trust-account rules. A 5-8% procurement fee is a conflict of interest. Its plan to have attorneys send deals for a flat fee is a RESPA Section 8 trap, because 12 CFR 1024.14 bars referral fees and unearned fees in federally related mortgage transactions and permits payment only for services actually performed.
solution: Sell 'Meeting-in-a-Box' as a fixed-scope, attorney-supervised package. We do the non-billable grunt work: map benefiting parcels from the registry of deeds and county GIS, serve statutory notice, run the notary-called meeting (in person plus absentee and proxy ballots), keep minutes, collect the officer slate and a treasurer, take a baseline road-condition photo log, and handle recording. The supervising attorney, either the closing attorney or our contracted Maine counsel, owns the legal instrument: a recorded covenant that adds what the statute lacks (assessment lien running with the land, successor obligation, reserve requirement, estoppel-letter mechanism). We build no dues software and hold no money. Each association opens a bank account with a treasurer, and we hand over a checklist plus a PayHOA or plain-ACH setup guide. After formation we run one annual notice-and-meeting cycle and issue a road-status letter (dues current, no open assessments, maintenance agreement on record) whenever a house on the road sells. This works like the HOA resale certificate. No referral fees are paid to anyone. Attorneys bill their own legal work, and our fee is a disclosed third-party service line.
why_now: Maine's statute already exists, so formation is process work rather than a legal breakthrough. Post-2020 in-migration put many out-of-state buyers on camp roads they do not understand. Housing turnover is historically low (roughly 3-4% a year, an assumption to confirm), so every stalled closing costs a seller and an agent real money. Hurricane Helene's NC private-road program showed that aid and repair money flow only to an organized counterparty with a named contact, which makes 'pre-formed association' a sellable feature. Oct-Feb is slack season for Maine camp closings, so attorneys have time to try a new workflow before spring listings. Cheap document automation and e-signature make proxy and absentee ballot logistics a small cost rather than a paralegal week.
revenue_model: Formation: $1,400 flat per road, paid at closing from seller proceeds or by the neighborhood, disclosed as a third-party service. Attorney legal review is billed separately by the attorney at roughly $300-500. Recurring: $200 per association per year, flat rather than per household, for annual notice, meeting, officer changes and records. Transaction toll: $175 per road-status letter, paid by the seller at each future sale. With about 9 coordinator hours plus recording fees per formation, gross margin should be near 60-65%. Rough year-1 target is 40 roads, or about $56k formation plus $8k recurring. At 300 roads with about 18 homes each and 3-4% turnover, resale letters add about $35k a year. That makes a real but modest Maine business, and the scalable asset is the state-by-state playbook plus the registry.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing in Maine is not the entity, since the statute lets neighbors make one, and not the legal template, which is a commodity. It is the person who runs the meeting and the recorded covenant that gives assessments teeth. The first closing buys the association, and every later closing pays a toll, so a formed road becomes a perpetual, transaction-priced revenue stream. That toll avoids the PayHOA per-household price anchor and sits where the money is, in seller proceeds. Because the attorney does the legal work under supervision and is never paid to refer, the attorney channel is RESPA-clean and the attorney stops being the substitute. Over time title agents learn to ask for our letter, which creates switching costs because the association's officer and records live with us.
first_30_days: Week 1: retain a Maine real estate attorney on a flat $3-5k engagement to draft the covenant with lien language, the estoppel-letter form and the meeting script. Have that attorney confirm the lien is enforceable when drafted as a recorded covenant and confirm the RESPA-safe fee structure. Weeks 1-3: hold 20 calls with lakes-region and midcoast closing attorneys and title agents and ask which of their last 12 months' closings hit a road issue, what happened, and what they would pay to have it handled. Weeks 2-4: run 2 pilot roads (one tied to a live or stalled closing) at a $600 pilot price, and measure owner participation rate, days to majority vote, and hours per road. By day 30, get 3 firms to sign a one-page agreement to route their next road problem to us at $1,400. The riskiest assumption to kill early is whether attorneys will buy outsourced meeting logistics rather than absorb it.
lineage: mutation of I0048 ('Private Road Associations in a Box'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: PayHOA, Mainstream HOA and community-association platforms (Buildium, AppFolio, FrontSteps, Vantaca, CINC and similar), DIY legal templates and local real estate attorneys (Nolo, US Legal Forms, LegalZoom-style forms, local attorney drafting), Public alternatives: state road-association statutes and county road or special-assessment districts. White space: Tentative. Coverage was thin, so absence of a dedicated venture-backed product is not proven. What I found unserved:
1. No product I could find bundles the closing-triggered legal package (state-specific maintenance agreement, county recording, a lightweight entity) with the ongoing administration for informal neighbor groups. PayHOA covers dues admin generically and cheaply; the statutes and the law-firm and forms market cover formation; nobody stitches them together for the 5-60 home private road.
2. Competitively bid, pooled procurement of plowing and gravel across many associations. I found no tool for it.
3. Storm-damage documentation and an organized entity ready for state or FEMA private-road aid. NC's program required a single point of contact, ownership proof and a 50% HOA cost share, so unorganized roads were poorly placed to claim.
4. The transaction-channel distribution (attorneys, title agents and listing agents at a stalled closing) looks unowned by software vendors.

Weak points:
- The recurring $12-25 per household per month is 6-12 times PayHOA's roughly $2 per household.
- Lien-based enforcement is state-dependent. NC's G.S. 136-102.6 only requires disclosure of who maintains private streets, and my Maine excerpt covered assessment authority but not liens.
- Holding dues float triggers trust-accounting and money-handling rules.
- The 5-8% procurement fee creates a conflict of interest. | How this version avoids them: PayHOA: we build no dues product and do not compete at about $2 per household. We price per association and per sale, and PayHOA is a setup option we recommend, so it is a partner rather than a rival. Buildium, AppFolio, FrontSteps, Vantaca, CINC: they serve incorporated associations with managers, whereas we create the legal counterparty they cannot. DIY templates and local attorneys (Nolo, LegalZoom-style forms): a template gives no notice, vote, proxy, minutes or recording service, and the attorney is our channel and supervising counsel rather than a substitute, because we take the work they cannot bill profitably. Maine statute: we productize it and plug its missing lien with the recorded covenant. NC Private Road and Bridge Program: a demand signal, and our 'pre-formed association with a named contact' is exactly what such programs require. Local road-association managers and bookkeepers (unidentified): they sell ongoing bookkeeping, not closing-triggered formation, and could be subcontractors for annual administration.

title: Town-Paid Private Road Census and Formation Bounty
one_liner: Sell New England towns (and their municipal insurance pools) a four-week census of every private road's legal status and emergency-access risk, then earn a per-road bounty for each neighbor group converted into a recorded association with a named point of contact.
customer: Town managers, road commissioners and fire chiefs of small and mid-sized Maine towns (2,000-15,000 residents), then NH and VT. Multi-town buyers: regional councils and planning commissions, and municipal risk pools that fund loss-control services for member towns (Maine Municipal Association's risk program, NH Primex, Vermont VLCT PACIF, all from prior knowledge and unverified here). Secondary payers: developers, via a road-association setup line on the town's subdivision application fee. Residents co-pay a small share.
problem: Every town has dozens to hundreds of private ways with unknown legal status. The town usually cannot spend public money on them (varies by state, to be confirmed per state), yet it is blamed when an ambulance or plow cannot pass a failed culvert, when a subdivision road approved on the condition that a road association be formed decays years later, or when residents petition the town to accept a broken road that would cost six figures to rebuild to town standard. After a storm, state aid wants an organized counterparty. NC's post-Helene private-road program (verified) required a single point of contact and proof of ownership, plus a 50% cost share. The town has no inventory to hand over. Neighbors are stuck in a collective-action deadlock, because nobody wants to be the one who calls the meeting.
solution: Step 1, a fixed-price Private Road Census, roughly $6,500 per town. We ingest parcel GIS, E911 road-name files, registry-of-deeds documents and any culvert or bridge inventory the town has. Language models read the recorded instruments to flag whether a maintenance agreement exists and what it says. For each private way we output parcels served, recorded instrument yes/no, whether an active association exists, contact if any, single-access and stream-crossing flags, and a fire-truck-passability risk score reviewed with the fire chief. The town gets a ranked list, map and memo. Step 2, activation. The town mails a letter on its own letterhead to the top 40 roads with a pre-filled petition for the statutory meeting. In Maine a few owners can petition a notary, and the town letter breaks the who-goes-first deadlock. We run the meetings, and an attorney-supervised covenant is recorded. The town pays a $600 bounty for each completed association (recorded instrument plus officers and point of contact), and residents co-pay about $500. Step 3, a registry subscription at about $2,400 per town per year. It keeps contacts, insurance certificates, reserve attestations and condition photos current, and yields a disaster-ready roads list for the state emergency agency after a storm. Step 4, the town adds a setup fee to subdivision applications so new roads get an association and reserve schedule at approval.
why_now: The cost stack collapsed. Reading recorded instruments for 120 roads used to mean about 120 title searches at hundreds of dollars each. With document extraction plus human QA it is roughly a tenth of that, which is what makes a fixed-price census possible. Storm events keep exposing the same gap, and NC's $175M program (verified) shows states will pay for repair but only through an organized counterparty. Parcel GIS and E911 layers are now open in most New England states. Municipal risk pools are always looking for loss-control programs to justify member subsidies (hypothesis to test). The disaster-aid windows (NC applications closed Feb 2026) show that the next program will again favor roads that are already organized.
revenue_model: Census $6,500 per town, or a regional-council package of 10-12 towns at about $55-65k. Formation bounty $600 per association from the town, plus a $500 resident co-pay, or about $1,100 per road. Registry $2,400 per town per year. Developer setup fee about $1,200 per new subdivision, collected through the town. A town with 120 private ways where 60% are informal has about 70 candidates. If 40% convert in year 1, that is 28 roads, about $31k in bounties and co-pays, plus census and registry, or about $40k per town in year 1. 25 towns would be about $1M. Conversion rate is the key hypothesis. Risk pools could subsidize the census for members, making the insurer a second payer.
non_obvious_insight: The town is not buying road repairs or software. It is buying a legal counterparty for roads it cannot touch, plus a defensible record that it knew about the risk and acted. That is liability hygiene, an easier budget line than subsidizing private roads. The official letter is the cheapest neighbor-activation channel that exists, because it dissolves the who-goes-first deadlock that makes formation so slow closing-by-closing. One buyer delivers dozens of roads, which inverts the parent's per-road CAC. The census data, once assembled across towns, becomes a state-level inventory that emergency agencies, lenders and title underwriters would pay for.
first_30_days: Pick one pilot town with open parcel GIS and online registry access, ideally a lakes-region Maine town of about 4,000 people. Build a free 30-road slice of the census in 10 days from public data. Walk it to the road commissioner, fire chief and town manager, and ask them for the 5 roads they fear most. Ask to mail an official letter to 10 pilot roads and run 2 statutory meetings within 30 days. In parallel, call 3 regional councils and the risk-management teams of the Maine, NH and Vermont municipal associations to test whether they would subsidize census work as loss control. Target one signed $4,500 first-town census (typically under small-purchase thresholds, to be confirmed) and one pilot association recorded. Riskiest assumptions: town willingness to pay a per-road bounty, and letter-to-meeting conversion above 25%.

title: Contractor-First Road Billing, Then Repair Lending
one_liner: Invert the parent: sell to plow and gravel contractors who each serve dozens of handshake roads with a get-paid rail that binds every household to its share, then use the payment history and recorded covenants to become the lender for culvert and washout repairs no bank will touch.
customer: Wedge: independent plow, gravel and excavation contractors serving 15-80 private roads and shared driveways each, starting in one snow-belt county in Maine or NH. Later payers: road associations as borrowers, and community banks, credit unions and CDFIs as capital partners who buy participations in the loans we originate and service.
problem: A contractor plows a 12-home road on a verbal 'we'll split it'. He bills one neighbor, who fronts the money and chases the others. After one or two free-riders the fronting neighbor quits, so the contractor drops the road or absorbs the loss. Contractors also front fuel, labor and equipment for a season and are paid unevenly. When a culvert or bridge fails, a $30-150k repair has no borrower, since there is no entity, no assets and no financials. NC's post-Helene program (verified) demanded a 50% cost share, a single point of contact and proof of ownership, so roads that could not front cash and had no organization were shut out. Both sides of the road are cash-starved for the same reason, which is no legal counterparty.
solution: Phase 1, sold this October to be live by first snow. RoadPay for contractors: the contractor enters a road's seasonal price. Each household receives an e-sign Road Service Agreement (pro-rata formula, driveway-level opt-in, dispute rule) with autopay via Stripe Connect direct charges, so we never hold funds. The contractor gets one dashboard across all roads, automatic reminders and statements, and monthly payouts. Phase 2, winter: Season Advance. We advance 60-80% of a signed road's seasonal contract to the contractor, funded by a small credit line, and repay ourselves from the households' autopay through April. We underwrite at the road level using percent of households on autopay, contractor history and driveway geometry. Phase 3, year 2: Graduation. Roads with two clean seasons are invited to record an assessment-lien covenant (through the closing-rescue-style formation service), because it lowers their borrowing rate. Phase 4: Repair and cost-share bridge loans. $25-150k loans to the association for culverts, regrading and bridge repairs, repaid over 5-10 years from assessments, funded by CDFI and community-bank participation with us as originator and servicer. The same facility can bridge the up-front 50% of state reimbursement programs.
why_now: Winter 2026-27 seasonal contracts get signed in October and November, about six weeks from today. That gives a hard deadline and a full season of data inside a six-month window. Embedded payments are now a commodity (Stripe Connect handles onboarding, split payouts and money-movement compliance), which is the Wardley shift that makes a two-person team viable. Post-Helene aid design (verified) teaches that organized counterparties get capital and unorganized roads do not. Document extraction makes reading recorded covenants cheap enough to underwrite each road. Contractor cost inflation since 2021 plausibly makes non-payment more painful (hypothesis to test in interviews).
revenue_model: Phase 1: 4% of billings collected, paid by the contractor (no per-household fee, so the PayHOA $2 anchor never applies). Phase 2: 3-5% fee on advances, turned several times per season. Phase 4: 2-3% origination plus about 1.5% servicing on loans sold to bank partners, plus net interest on any retained slice. Illustration: 100 contractors x 40 roads x $3,000 is about $12M of billings, so about $480k of rail revenue. If 5% of roads borrow $60k a year, that is about $12M of loans and roughly $300-500k of origination and servicing. Early revenue is small. The business becomes large only if the payment history and lien-backed collateral become the standard underwriting file for private roads, which is the 10x claim.
non_obvious_insight: The party with the best data and the strongest incentive is the contractor, not the neighbors. He knows every road's parcels, who pays, and which culvert is about to fail, and one phone call reaches 40 roads. His invoice is a high-frequency touchpoint neighbors already accept, whereas a formation package is a rare, compliance-flavored purchase. The legal entity stops being a product and becomes collateral. Neighbors will sign a recorded covenant to cut their repair loan rate from, say, 14% to 8%, which they would never do for 'compliance'. It also removes the parent's conflict of interest, since the contractor is the customer rather than a party we take a procurement fee from.
first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 plow and gravel contractors in one county through local snow-removal and excavation groups, feed and hardware stores and Facebook groups, and offer free first-season setup on their 3 most annoying roads. Have an attorney spend $2-4k reviewing a generic Road Service Agreement and consumer-ACH disclosures. Build a no-code MVP in 2 weeks (contractor form, e-sign page, Stripe Connect autopay, manual reconciliation sheet). Convert at least 25 roads before first snow and measure the household sign rate (target 75% or better), autopay success and contractor willingness to pay 4%. Open a conversation with one CDFI or community credit union about a $250k participation for advances. Riskiest assumptions: whether households sign a contractor-issued agreement, and how to handle free-riders on a shared road, since the contractor can skip non-signers' driveways but not the common road. Also confirm lending and money-transmission licensing with counsel before Phase 2.

title: Daubert-Ready Sample Audits for Litigation Surveys
one_liner: A neutral data-quality auditor that gives survey experts and litigators a signed, control-calibrated audit of the respondent sample behind a Lanham Act, false-advertising or damages survey, or a teardown of the other side's sample.
customer: Wedge: the 30-60 US testifying survey experts and boutique survey-litigation consultancies who field likelihood-of-confusion, secondary-meaning, deception and conjoint-damages surveys, plus the IP and false-advertising litigation partners who retain them. Later: in-house counsel at CPG and pharma companies that run claim-substantiation surveys for FTC or NAD challenges.
problem: A litigation survey is only worth what survives cross-examination and a Rule 702 challenge. Until recently 'we removed speeders and failed attention checks' was an adequate answer on sample quality. Agents now pass those checks (99.8% of 6,000 trials in the parent's evidence), so the standard defence is hollow. Opposing experts can attack the panel, and the amended Rule 702 (Dec 2023) makes the proponent show reliability by a preponderance. Survey experts have no neutral way to show their sample is clean, and rebuttal experts have no fast, credible way to quantify contamination in the other side's produced respondent data. The fee is small next to the $50k-$300k+ a litigation survey costs (from background knowledge, to be verified in calls) and the case value behind it.
solution: Two case-driven products. (1) Proponent audit: before full fielding, insert canary and honeypot items (with the expert's sign-off) and run a pilot. Ingest detection signals licensed from dtect, Verisoul or DQC rather than building an ensemble. Field the test and control cells on a 150-300-complete slice of a licensed address-recruited panel (NORC, Ipsos or Verasight-style, resold, not built). Deliver contamination-adjusted net-effect estimates with bounds, a sensitivity table ('conclusion holds up to X% contamination') and a hash-timestamped chain-of-custody field log. A named academic methodologist signs a declaration that can be attached to the expert report. (2) Rebuttal teardown: a fixed-scope 10-business-day analysis of the opposing side's produced respondent-level data, built to fit rebuttal-report deadlines. The firm never opines on the merits (confusion, deception, damages). It only certifies or attacks data quality, so it is a supplier to every expert rather than a competitor.
why_now: Agents that pass attention checks (2025-26) killed the old defence. Pew's Aug 2026 finding of 18% bogus respondents in opt-in samples, with trap questions and Sentry disagreeing on who is bogus, gives opposing counsel a citable, public source. The Dec 2023 Rule 702 amendment gives judges an explicit mandate to scrutinise reliability. The first contested Daubert motion where an expert cannot rebut agent contamination will spread fast through the small survey-expert community.
revenue_model: $12-40k per case engagement (proponent audit or rebuttal teardown), billed to the law firm as consulting-expert cost and passed through to the client. $60-120k/yr retainers for survey-expert firms that run 8-15 surveys a year, covering unlimited pilots and field-log stamps. $2-5k per survey for a hash-stamped field log as a low-touch add-on. Later, a $25-50k/yr library subscription for in-house claim-substantiation teams. Gross margin is mostly the licensed control slice (about $3-8k per engagement) plus methodologist hours.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not paying for truth. The buyer is paying, with the client's litigation budget, for insurance against cross-examination, so willingness to pay is set by case value and not by the $/complete price that caps every other idea in this space. The test-versus-control design used in litigation surveys also means random-answering bots hit both cells and pull net confusion toward zero. Contamination therefore tends to hurt plaintiffs and help defendants, so both sides have a reason to buy: proponents to insulate, opponents to attack. Once a court admits or credits the method, it becomes citable precedent. That is process power and switching cost that no detection API can copy.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: list every survey expert named in published Lanham Act opinions of the last five years and 40 IP litigation partners. Run 10 price-validation calls (5 experts, 5 partners) and stop if fewer than 4 say $15k+ is reasonable. Days 10-25: buy about 300 completes each from 4 panel vendors on a classic Eveready-format and Teflon-format design, plus a 150-complete control slice from a licensed address-recruited panel. Measure how many bots it takes to swing net confusion by 5 points. Days 20-30: publish 'How many agents does it take to flip a confusion survey?' as a white paper and CLE talk proposal. Offer two free rebuttal teardowns on public-record survey data in exchange for permission to cite. Sign one academic survey methodologist as chief methodologist and testifier.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Data Quality Co-op (DQC), Verasight, Verisoul, CloudResearch (Sentry, Engage, Bot Olympics). White space: Detection is crowded and getting cheap: Verisoul, Roundtable, dtect, CloudResearch, Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, ReDem and CleanID all sell it, some at cents per respondent. Cross-supplier scorecards already exist too, since Data Quality Co-op is a neutral clearinghouse. Building a detection ensemble or a generic vendor scorecard would be a fifth-to-tenth entrant against funded players.

What I did not find anyone selling:
1. A per-study ground-truth calibration. This means running a slice of the same questionnaire on a verified, address-recruited human control group and then reporting contamination-adjusted estimates with error bounds. Every vendor I found detects and removes. None quantifies how much bias survives the cleaning, and none re-estimates the result against a known-real reference. Pew's finding that voter-file matching removed valid respondents and made the error worse suggests 'remove the flagged' is itself a source of bias.
2. A neutral buyer-side referee that owns no sample. dtect is neutral but only sells entry-time detection. DQC is neutral but does not audit individual studies or supply a control sample. Verasight owns verified humans but sells sample.
3. Independent, third-party verification of the vendors' own accuracy claims. CloudResearch and Verisoul each claim 100% agent detection from internal or self-run tests. The Bot Olympics is MIT-judged but tests CloudResearch's own system.

The missing piece for a startup is the control panel. Building an address-recruited, device-attested panel of about 2,000 people is slow and expensive. The likelier route is to partner with or license an existing one (Verasight, NORC, Pew or Ipsos-style panels), not recruit from scratch.

This conclusion has limits. My WebSearch budget ran out at 200 calls, so I could not run the Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt checks or search for a second wave of small startups. I also could not confirm funding for DQC, Roundtable, dtect or Verasight. | How this version avoids them: Detection vendors (Verisoul, dtect, Roundtable, CloudResearch, ReDem, CleanID) sell entry-time filtering to panels at cents per complete and produce nothing a court can use. They are input suppliers here. Data Quality Co-op's scorecard and Data Trust Score describe suppliers in general and do not give a case-specific, testifiable declaration. Verasight owns verified humans but sells sample, so opposing counsel would call it conflicted. Pew and NORC publish the methodology for free but not per case, and not in expert-report form. Panel-owner stacks (Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, Pori) are the self-grading problem that Daubert challenges target. Existing litigation-survey consultancies field surveys and testify on merits, so they are customers, not rivals.

title: Contingency Recovery for Contaminated Survey Sample
one_liner: A freight-audit-style recovery firm that finds contaminated and duplicated completes in the survey sample buyers already paid for, files credit claims against panel vendors, and keeps 25-35% of what it recovers.
customer: Wedge: mid-size full-service market research agencies (about 100-500 staff) that buy $1-10M a year of third-party online sample on fixed-fee client projects and absorb the reruns. Second wave: procurement teams at CPG, pharma and financial-services firms that already run recovery audits on freight, telecom and cloud spend but have never applied one to research sample.
problem: The parent idea asks insights teams to pay for a quality audit, and the research found no evidence anyone will pay $3-15k for one. Buyers do pay for money back. Kantar says post-field reconciliation (rejected sample) rates are up about 300% in three years, with some clients rejecting up to 40% of data (a vendor source). Contaminated completes that pass screening are paid for and used. The same panelist or device is also resold through several exchanges, so buyers pay twice for one human. Agencies eat the rerun cost, procurement never sees data quality, and nobody has respondent-level evidence strong enough to make a vendor pay. Vendors also fight individual rejections because their detector disagrees with the buyer's.
solution: Zero-upfront retrospective audit. The buyer gives read access to 12-24 months of respondent-level files, vendor IDs, invoices and MSAs. The firm runs LLM-assisted open-end forensics, cross-vendor duplicate detection (hashed device, IP and open-end similarity) and paradata review. It ingests detection flags from dtect, Verisoul or DQC where the buyer already has them. A 300-500-complete verified-human control cell per major vendor calibrates a population-level contamination estimate with error bounds. The firm then files claims for replacement completes, credits or refunds, citing the contractual quality clause. Claims argue that a vendor's batch exceeded the SLA (e.g. above 5% invalid, 95% CI) rather than fighting each flagged complete, which is where vendors dispute. Fee is 25-35% of value recovered, with no recovery meaning no fee. Stage two is prospective: a payment-hold or escrow layer where vendor payment for a batch releases after a control-calibrated pass, and a monitoring subscription.
why_now: Agents passing attention checks mean the largest share of contamination is now undetected at entry, which is exactly the paid-for-but-invalid pool that recovery targets. The cost stack collapsed: reading 10 million open-ended answers used to need human coders at dollars per complete, and LLMs now do it at fractions of a cent, so a contingency model works even on mid-size invoices. Pew's Aug 2026 study and NORC's fraud review give claim letters a public, credible methodology to cite. Buyers are already 'auditing suppliers, bringing sampling in-house and demanding accountability' (Greenbook), so procurement is primed.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 25-35% of recovered value. Illustrative unit economics, which are assumptions to test: $3M annual sample spend, 5-10% recoverable ($150-300k), 50% recovered, 30% fee, so $22-45k per customer per year. That is lower than the parent's $50-150k programmes but has almost no sales friction. Add-ons are a prospective monitoring subscription ($2-4k/month) and escrow at 1-2% of sample spend. Roughly 150-250 agencies and 30-60 enterprise buyers as a bottom-up serviceable market gives a $10M+ ARR business without ever selling 'quality' as a line item.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody budgets for data quality, but everyone has a process for accounts receivable. Turning 'is my sample clean?' into 'how much money are we owed?' moves the buyer from the insights head, who has no budget and no pain, to finance and procurement, who have both. The scarce asset is the same verified-human reference as in the parent, but used differently. It is needed only in small doses (a few hundred humans per vendor), which removes the 2,000-person panel problem and lets it be licensed instead of built. Population-level SLA claims also sidestep the detector-disagreement fight that makes per-complete rejections so contentious.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: post to insights and procurement communities and DM 20 agency founders and heads of ops. The offer is 'send one vendor's last quarter of respondent files, we tell you the recoverable amount, you pay nothing unless we recover'. Days 5-15: have a contract lawyer review 10 sample sample-vendor MSAs and SOWs to extract quality, replacement and dispute clauses, and draft a standard claim letter. Days 10-25: build the pipeline (open-end similarity, hashed-device dedupe across vendors, control-cell comparison) and buy 300 completes each from 4 major vendors as baseline. Days 20-30: sign 3 contingency agreements and file the first claim. Success is the first $50k recovered by day 90. Kill if, after 5 audits, recoverable value is below 2% of spend or vendors refuse every claim.

title: Independent Answer Key for Synthetic Respondents
one_liner: Invert the referee: a neutral scoring authority that holds fresh, verified-human ground truth, and scores synthetic-respondent and digital-twin vendors against it in quarterly pre-registered, sealed-prediction benchmarks.
customer: Two-sided. Vendors: synthetic-respondent, persona and digital-twin startups and the survey platforms adding synthetic boosts. Buyers: CPG, pharma and financial-services insights and innovation teams and research agencies being pitched 'AI respondents' and unsure whom to believe. Later: AI labs that need uncontaminated human-opinion evals.
problem: Synthetic-respondent vendors claim high accuracy on self-chosen benchmarks. Backtests against old polls leak, because published polls and concept-test norms are in the models' training data, and vendors can cherry-pick questions. Buyers have no neutral way to tell which claim is real before betting a launch decision on it. The parent evidence that agents pass 99.8% of attention checks shows LLM personas mimic humans on surface features, which cuts both ways: it enables fraud and it makes synthetic research plausible. Nobody holds fresh verified-human answers on questions asked after model cutoffs, with the vendor's predictions locked in beforehand.
solution: A predict-then-reveal benchmark. Each quarter, the firm and a buyer advisory board write about 80 novel questions and concepts, including anonymised buyer concept tests under NDA. Vendors submit hash-committed sealed predictions of the answer distributions for named demographic targets. The firm fields the items to 1,000-3,000 verified humans, address-recruited and device-attested, licensed from partners (NORC, Verasight, Prolific or a university survey centre) so no one panel controls the answer key. It scores distribution error, rank-order of concept winners, subgroup fidelity and calibration of stated uncertainty, and publishes a leaderboard. Vendors pay for private diagnostics and for a licence to cite their scored accuracy, never for placement. Buyers pay for full reports and for a 'bake-off as a service', running a shortlist of 3 vendors on 10 of the buyer's own concepts against 400 verified humans. Endgame: the growing library of pre-registered human ground truth becomes shared infrastructure. It calibrates hybrid human-plus-synthetic samples, is licensed to AI labs as fresh opinion evals, and feeds the original bot-audit business off the same panel.
why_now: Synthetic-respondent and digital-twin companies raised large rounds in 2025-26 and are getting enterprise pilots (specific rounds not verified in this session, so check). Model releases every few months make static benchmarks stale and leaky, which turns a benchmark into a recurring re-fielding business. Pew's Aug 2026 study is a public design template for benchmarking against address-recruited samples. Buyers who lived through the panel-fraud scare now ask 'how do you know it is right?' by reflex.
revenue_model: Vendors pay $8-25k per quarterly private diagnostic and $30-100k/yr for an audited accuracy-claim licence. Buyers pay $10-25k/yr for full reports and $20-40k per bake-off. Founding-member pre-sales fund wave 1: 8 buyers at $15k covers a 1,000-human wave. Later, AI-lab dataset licences of $100-500k/yr. Control-panel cost is the main COGS at about $10-40 per verified complete, which suggests 60-70% gross margin once pre-sales cover each wave.
non_obvious_insight: The verified-human panel is worth more as the answer key for AI than as a shield against AI, and the business wins whichever way the synthetic-research bet goes. If synthetic respondents work, everyone needs a scorer and a calibration anchor. If they fail, buyers need proof and a return to human samples. Fraud and progress both raise demand for the reference. The product is not data but a commitment protocol (sealed predictions, then reveal), which solves the training-data leakage that no static dataset can. Refusing to be scored becomes a signal of weakness, which is the flywheel that turns a benchmark into a standard, the way MLPerf-style or leaderboard-style evaluators gained authority.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: write the protocol and scoring spec (sealing method, metrics, no pay-for-placement rule) and publish it openly. Recruit 5 founding buyer-side advisors (CPG or pharma insights heads) at $5k pilot memberships. Days 5-20: invite 6-8 synthetic-respondent vendors to a free founding wave slot in exchange for submitting sealed predictions. Days 15-30: finalize 40 novel questions, hash-commit vendor predictions, and field wave 0 to 600-1,000 verified humans from a partner for roughly $10-20k. Publish the first leaderboard by day 45. Kill test: fewer than 4 vendors willing to submit, or fewer than 3 buyers who say they would pay for the results.
lineage: mutation of I0716 ('Independent Referee for Survey Panel Data'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Data Quality Co-op (DQC), Verasight, Verisoul, CloudResearch (Sentry, Engage, Bot Olympics). White space: Detection is crowded and getting cheap: Verisoul, Roundtable, dtect, CloudResearch, Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, ReDem and CleanID all sell it, some at cents per respondent. Cross-supplier scorecards already exist too, since Data Quality Co-op is a neutral clearinghouse. Building a detection ensemble or a generic vendor scorecard would be a fifth-to-tenth entrant against funded players.

What I did not find anyone selling:
1. A per-study ground-truth calibration. This means running a slice of the same questionnaire on a verified, address-recruited human control group and then reporting contamination-adjusted estimates with error bounds. Every vendor I found detects and removes. None quantifies how much bias survives the cleaning, and none re-estimates the result against a known-real reference. Pew's finding that voter-file matching removed valid respondents and made the error worse suggests 'remove the flagged' is itself a source of bias.
2. A neutral buyer-side referee that owns no sample. dtect is neutral but only sells entry-time detection. DQC is neutral but does not audit individual studies or supply a control sample. Verasight owns verified humans but sells sample.
3. Independent, third-party verification of the vendors' own accuracy claims. CloudResearch and Verisoul each claim 100% agent detection from internal or self-run tests. The Bot Olympics is MIT-judged but tests CloudResearch's own system.

The missing piece for a startup is the control panel. Building an address-recruited, device-attested panel of about 2,000 people is slow and expensive. The likelier route is to partner with or license an existing one (Verasight, NORC, Pew or Ipsos-style panels), not recruit from scratch.

This conclusion has limits. My WebSearch budget ran out at 200 calls, so I could not run the Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt checks or search for a second wave of small startups. I also could not confirm funding for DQC, Roundtable, dtect or Verasight. | How this version avoids them: Every competitor in the parent's research defends human samples against bots (Verisoul, dtect, Roundtable, CloudResearch, Kantar Qubed, PureScore, ReDem) or sells verified sample (Verasight), or writes standards without testing (GDQ). None scores synthetic respondents. CloudResearch's Bot Olympics grades detectors on its own turf and is not neutral. Verasight's replication of Pew shows its own panel is cleaner, so it sells sample and could not be an arbiter between vendors that compete with its product. DQC is neutral but aggregates fraud signals. It does not run sealed-prediction tests against fresh human truth. Pew and NORC could field this, but a non-profit research org will not run a recurring commercial scoring service. Academic synthetic-survey benchmarks exist but are static and leak into training data. I could not verify whether a commercial neutral scorer already exists because the web-search budget ran out, so check before building.

title: Outsourced Large-Load Intake Desk for Co-op Pools
one_liner: A stage-gated, applicant-paid intake administrator and cross-utility duplicate registry for G&T co-op pools outside ERCOT, so 5-person planning staffs only ever see evidence-backed projects.
customer: Wedge: one mid-size G&T (or state co-op association planning group) outside ERCOT, in SPP, MISO or the Mountain West, that fields 8+ large-load inquiries a year and has 1-2 planners eating the load (Central Electric Power Cooperative's lead spends about 40% of his time on data centers). The G&T adopts the desk by board resolution, and the applicant pays through a filed fee schedule, following Great River Energy's bill-the-petitioner model. Second ring: the G&T's 20-40 distribution co-ops, then neighboring G&Ts.
problem: The judges' central worry was right. Collateral, study fees and site-control rules are making applicants self-prove, so a 12-point memo shop sells checks the applicant will soon hand over anyway. Equipment slots and financing letters are also confidential, and real developers often call the utility before they order equipment. Meanwhile the co-op still has no staff to run intake and no way to see that the same 300 MW is being shopped to five utilities. Regulators are absorbing LLC transparency at the state level (Texas audit, Pennsylvania's Aug 18 order for projects over 25 MW), which weakens any pure-LLC-lookup product.
solution: Run intake as an operated service, not a memo. (1) Evidence ladder tied to money release. Gate 0 (intake fee paid): public-record checks only, which is what any real developer already has: LLC principals across states, recorded deed or option, air-permit pre-application and generator count vs. claimed MW, water and stormwater filings, and claimed energization date vs. published transformer and switchgear lead times. Gate 1 (study deposit released): named references (OEM, EPC, tenant, lender officer) verified by phone, with a signed attestation and a misrepresentation clause that forfeits the deposit. Gate 2 (ESA signature): redacted OEM order acknowledgment and financing confirmation. Early gates test only what an early-stage real project has; unobservable items are pushed to the gate where money is at risk. (2) Consent clause: the application form has the applicant consent to share LLC, principals, parcel APN, POI substation, MW ask and status with a pooled registry, which solves the confidentiality problem. The registry matches on parcel, substation POI and principal, not company name, because shells rename themselves but land parcels and substations do not. It returns hits like 'this parcel and principal appear in 3 other territories.' (3) Outputs are structured records that drop into GridUnity or PowerClerk as the pre-queue front door.
why_now: Tariffs and collateral rules are landing (Texas SB 6 final rule due by 12/31/2026, AEP Ohio-style deposits), and Exelon's pipeline fell about 40% and AEP Ohio's more than half once fees and collateral arrived. Every co-op now has to decide what its intake rules are, and most have no staff to run them. About half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or canceled, so boards are burned. Cleanview-class permit data has made the public-record layer cheap to assemble and license. Nobody yet runs a duplicate registry outside ERCOT, where SB 6 mandates duplicate disclosure only inside the state.
revenue_model: $20-30K one-time G&T setup (intake policy, fee schedule, ESA rider, board presentation). Applicant-paid intake fees scaled by MW, $10K under 100 MW up to $40K over 500 MW, plus a $15-30K Gate 1 verification fee. The utility keeps a 15% admin share and the desk keeps 85%. A $36K/yr G&T floor retainer covers slow quarters. Registry seats at $12K/yr for utilities outside the pool later. Bottom-up: 3 G&Ts x about 25 paid intakes x about $20K is $1.5M in year 1 at about 80% gross margin, with the registry as the compounding asset.
non_obvious_insight: The fee and the gates are themselves the phantom filter. Shell LLCs will not pay $15K to be verified, and real developers spending $2B+ will not blink. So the desk's real product is converting scarce planner hours into a queue that carries only evidence-backed projects, and detection is a side effect. The staged ladder fixes the 'real developers come before they order equipment' flaw by demanding equipment proof only at the gate where the utility's money is at risk. And the registry keys on parcels and POI substations, physical objects a phantom cannot rename, which is why it holds up even as LLC-disclosure rules improve.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: get the last 10-15 inquiries from two co-op contacts via a state association or G&T planning group. Back-test them to show how the ones that died would have scored at Gate 0 and Gate 1. Stand up scrapers for air-permit databases in 4-6 states and deed and Secretary of State records in 2-3 territories, and license Cleanview-style permit data instead of rebuilding it. Days 10-20: write the 2-page intake policy, fee schedule and misrepresentation-clause template. Present the back-test and template to the G&T planning head and ask for a 90-day pilot that starts fees on the next new inquiry, free for existing ones. Days 20-30: interview 5 developers with real projects to test that they would pay $10-15K at intake. Close 1 G&T pilot and process the first paid intake. Kill test: if no G&T will let applicants be billed, or 0 of 5 real developers accept the fee, the applicant-pays thesis is dead.
lineage: mutation of I0079 ('Phantom Load Vetting Desk for Rural Utilities'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: GridUnity, Clean Power Research (PowerClerk), Enverus, LandGate. White space: I found no direct competitor. No startup, consultancy or association was selling a utility-side, per-inquiry 'is this developer physically real' memo with a recommended collateral amount and milestone-gated study structure. The gap is real but narrow.

What is unserved: (1) External physical-trail verification for small utilities, meaning air-permit generator counts vs claimed MW, recorded deeds and options, LLC principal cross-checks, and OEM or EPC evidence. GridUnity and PowerClerk track applicant-supplied data but do not verify it. Enverus, LandGate and GridCARE serve the developer side. (2) A cross-utility duplicate-request registry. Texas SB 6 mandates duplicate-request disclosure only inside ERCOT. Outside ERCOT there is no pooled registry. Developers do file the same project with several utilities (Latitude Media, Utility Dive). (3) Packaging for 5-person co-op engineering staffs: I found no NRECA vetting checklist or tool, and no small-utility-specific vendor.

Serious weaknesses the founder must address:
- Regulation and tariffs are substituting for vetting. Collateral, study fees and site-control mandates make the applicant self-prove. Exelon cut its estimates about 40% after stricter collateral. AEP Ohio's pipeline fell by more than half after study fees of up to $100K (https://techstartups.com/2026/09/01/ai-data-centers-request-700-gw-of-u-s-power-but-much-of-the-demand-may-be-an-illusion/). Once a co-op requires a deposit, site control and a signed LOI, much of the 12-point test becomes documents the applicant hands over.
- Texas SB 6 / 16 TAC 25.194 applies only in ERCOT (https://www.dlapiper.com/en-us/insights/publications/2026/03/texas-proposes-new-interconnection-standards-for-large-electric-loads). The 'small utilities in neighboring states get the displaced phantoms' claim is plausible but I found no evidence for it.
- Several tests may not be observable by an outsider. OEM order acknowledgments and financing letters are confidential, and real developers often approach the utility before ordering equipment.
- Regulators are absorbing the LLC-transparency piece. Texas ordered an audit requiring true-ownership disclosure, and Pennsylvania issued an August 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW.
- Big engineering consultancies could add this as a service line. I could not verify whether they already do. My web-search budget ran out before I could check. | How this version avoids them: GridUnity and PowerClerk are workflow tools built on applicant-supplied data. The desk verifies and feeds them as a front door, so it is a complement to sell alongside, not a rival. Enverus, LandGate, GridCARE and ZEG sit on the developer side or in forecasting, and this desk works for the utility and is adverse to the applicant. Cleanview is a public tracker and cannot hold confidential cross-utility inquiry data, so it becomes a licensed input rather than a competitor. NRECA offers free checklists but cannot run a fee-collecting, data-holding, liability-bearing intake operation, so its state associations are the resale channel. Hourly consultancies (Burns & McDonnell and similar) could copy the checks but not the pooled registry economics. Memos were the entry product; the pooled registry across co-ops is the business, and it gets better with every co-op added.

title: Phantom Pipeline Audits for Utility Rate-Case Intervenors
one_liner: Sell to the ratepayers who pay for phantom load, meaning industrial customer groups and state consumer advocates in IRP, CPCN and large-load-tariff dockets, a testimony-ready audit of how much of a utility's confidential data-center pipeline is physically real.
customer: Buyer: counsel and expert budgets of (a) industrial customer intervenor groups (steel, paper, chemicals) that fear being left with stranded data-center infrastructure costs, and (b) state consumer advocate offices, in dockets where the utility's generation or transmission request rests on a data-center pipeline. Later: county and city governments facing abatement votes ($15-30K packs), and utility credit and equity analysts who subscribe to a Phantom Ratio Index. The sales path is through the law firms and staff attorneys who run these dockets.
problem: Utilities are asking commissions to approve gigawatts of gas plants and transmission justified by 'signed' large-load pipelines. The pipeline exhibits are confidential or anonymized ('Customer A, 400 MW'). Intervenor experts can only critique them top-down with econometrics, because nobody checks entries one by one against the physical trail. The evidence that pipelines are inflated is broad: an EPRI survey found none of 10 utilities with requests of 50%+ of peak expected actual 5-year load above 35% of peak, and Exelon's estimates fell about 40% after stricter collateral. But the intervenor cannot show which megawatts are fake, and a project shopped to two utilities is counted twice.
solution: A 'realization audit' delivered through counsel. Under the docket's protective order, the desk takes the utility's pipeline exhibit (MW, county or substation, in-service date, status). It scores each entry against the public trail: air permits and generator counts, deed or option and rezoning agenda items, water and stormwater filings, principal and LLC cross-matching across states, and whether the claimed in-service date is feasible given published equipment lead times. The output is a probability-weighted realized MW by year with confidence bands, a list of duplicate-counted megawatts across utilities, and a testimony-ready exhibit sponsored by a credentialed expert witness (a retired utility planner or former commission staffer on retainer). Where entries are fully anonymized, the audit triangulates from county-level permit and land-use activity and asks the commission to compel the identities under protective order. The same work product seeds a quarterly Phantom Ratio Index by utility and state.
why_now: Electricity affordability is a live political issue in the November 2026 midterms, and data-center load forecasts are the key contested input in a wave of 2026 large-load tariff, IRP and generation-certificate dockets. Regulators are already moving on transparency (Texas ownership audit, Pennsylvania's Aug 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW), so intervenors now have standing to ask for pipeline detail. Cleanview-style permit trackers plus OCR'd county records have made the public-trail checks cheap enough to run per docket at a fixed fee.
revenue_model: $40-120K fixed fee per docket engagement, covering the audit, exhibit and expert sponsorship, paid from intervenor budgets and industrial group dues. $15-30K county and municipal packs. A $25-60K/yr Phantom Ratio Index seat for credit analysts, muni and equity desks and hedge funds. Year-1 target: 6-10 dockets ($600K-$900K) plus early index subscribers, with about 60% gross margin because the expert and analyst time is billable.
non_obvious_insight: The parties who lose most from phantom load are not the utility's five planners but the other ratepayers, and they already have lawyers, a procedural calendar and an expert budget. The docket schedule sets the deadline, so no procurement cycle is needed. The natural competitors, utility-aligned engineering consultancies, are conflicted when the audit target is their client's pipeline, which makes an adversarial audit counter-positioned rather than just different. And duplicate-counting is only visible from outside: each utility sees only its own queue, but an auditor working in four states sees the same project in three pipelines. The adversarial work therefore seeds the national duplicate registry from a side no utility-aligned vendor can reach.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: list every live docket in 6-8 states where a large-load pipeline is in dispute, using public commission dockets, and note testimony deadlines in the next 60-120 days plus who the intervenors and their counsel are. Days 10-20: build a free 2-page 'public trail check' of one utility's publicly disclosed data-center announcements, using licensed permit data plus deeds and permits, and send it to 15 intervenor counsel and consumer advocate staff. Recruit a credentialed expert witness (retired planner or ex-commission staff). Days 20-30: close 1-2 paid engagements at about $40K, one with an industrial group and one with a consumer advocate. Kill test: if counsel will not pay $40K for a per-entry audit because their econometric expert already covers it, the intervenor thesis is dead and the index is the fallback.

title: Megawatt Credit Bureau with Bonded Collateral
one_liner: Invert the vetting desk: real developers pay to be rated, utilities accept the rating for lower deposits, and the company eventually underwrites large-load security bonds off the physical-readiness data, so regulators' collateral rules become the market instead of the threat.
customer: First payer: mid-size and regional developers with real sites and real equipment slots (powered-land developers, ex-bitcoin-miner sites converting to AI, regional colo builders) that are in 10-30 utility queues and being asked for $50K/MW collateral or up to $100K per study in each. Accepting side: co-op and municipal pools that agree to recognize the rating. Capital side: a specialty surety or insurance carrier and reinsurer that provide bond capacity through an MGA structure.
problem: Collateral regimes (Texas proposes $50K/MW, AEP Ohio-style deposits) treat every applicant as a phantom. A real 300 MW project must lock up $15M in cash or letters of credit per utility, and re-submit the same package to each co-op. Hyperscaler-backed developers have the balance sheet and shells do not, so thinly capitalized developers with real projects get squeezed or forced to sell to bigger players. Surety and LC markets price the principal's balance sheet, not the project's physical readiness, so there is no credit signal between a hyperscaler guarantee and a shell LLC. Utilities cannot tell the difference either.
solution: Phase 1 (months 0-6): the 'Verified Ready' dossier for $15-25K. The developer hands over what real projects have (air permit, deed or option, OEM slot confirmation, EPC contract, tenant LOI, financing letter), and the desk verifies it through public records and direct confirmation calls. It issues a dated, registry-anchored readiness rating (R1-R5) that pilot co-op pools accept as satisfying Gates 0-1 and as grounds for a 30-50% deposit reduction or study priority. Utilities pay nothing. Phase 2 (months 6-18): a bonded-collateral program, meaning surety-style 'large-load security bonds' written by a specialty carrier through an MGA, priced off the rating and posted to the utility as obligee in place of part of the cash or LC collateral. Phase 3: publish the methodology as an open standard and lobby tariffs and regulators to reference it, e.g. 'rated applicants may post bonds or reduced collateral.' The registry accumulates milestone-hit data on who actually energizes, which becomes proprietary loss data no one else has.
why_now: Texas SB 6 (final rule due by 12/31/2026), AEP Ohio-style minimum-demand tariffs and study fees of up to $100K created a huge new collateral requirement that did not exist 18 months ago, and each dollar of required cash collateral creates demand for a cheaper substitute. Transformer lead times of 3-5 years and switchgear sold out into 2028 make equipment evidence a cheap, hard-to-fake readiness signal that a rating can be built on. Roughly half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or canceled, so utilities and lenders are hunting for a credible signal.
revenue_model: Rating fee $15-25K (up to $75K per GW) per developer per accepting utility set, plus $5K/yr renewals. Bond premium of 2-3% a year on the security amount, with the MGA taking about 20-25% commission plus profit share and the carrier taking the risk. Later, registry data licences to lenders and utilities. Illustrative: 40 rated projects in year 1 is about $800K. At 100 bonded projects a year with $15M average security, that is $1.5B of security, about $37M of premium and about $9M of MGA revenue. It rises further if regulators adopt the rating in tariffs.
non_obvious_insight: Regulators' collateral rules look like the death of a vetting business, but they are the birth of a substitute market, and a substitute needs an underwriter that can price physical readiness. The paying base self-selects to real projects because phantoms will not pay to be scrutinized. The classic conflict of interest of issuer-paid ratings is solved by having the MGA and carrier carry loss exposure, so the rater has skin in the game, unlike a ratings shop. Finally, the segment nobody serves is the thin-balance-sheet developer with real equipment slots, whose risk is legible only in the logistics trail. The rating therefore turns a compliance cost into a moat: loss data on who energizes.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: interview 15 mid-size developers, sourced from the 384 developers on Cleanview's tracker, powered-land brokers and LinkedIn, asking how many co-op queues they are in, how much collateral is posted and how many times they have re-submitted. Days 10-20: pre-sell 3 dossiers at a $10K founding price, refundable if no co-op accepts. Use the free co-op back-test as the lead magnet to sign an MOU with one G&T pool to accept the dossier for deposit relief. Draft methodology v0.1 and publish it openly. Days 20-30: talk to 2 commercial surety brokers or MGAs that already place utility deposit bonds and get term-sheet-level interest, not a binder. Deliver the first dossier. Kill test: if no G&T will trade a rating for lower deposits, the utility-acceptance leg fails and the bond phase never starts.

My web-search budget ran out before I could check. | How this version avoids them: GridUnity and PowerClerk are utility workflow tools, and the rating is a credential they can ingest. Enverus, LandGate and GridCARE help developers pick sites or find capacity but do not verify readiness or produce a rating a utility will accept for lower deposits. Cleanview is a public tracker with no verification or credential. ZEG is advisory consulting. NRECA is a distribution channel that can endorse the standard but cannot underwrite. A two-sided credential (developers pay, utilities accept) that later carries insurance-backed loss data has network and data economics none of them touch, and the parent's own problem, that collateral rules substitute for vetting, is turned into the demand driver.

title: Independent Auditor for AI-Paid Pet Claims
one_liner: A read-only shadow adjudicator plus a cross-carrier duplicate registry that independently re-checks every auto-paid pet claim against the policy's own clauses and produces the validation records state examiners now ask for.
customer: Head of claims and the compliance officer at US pet-insurance MGAs and small carriers paying roughly 100k-400k claims a year that already auto-adjudicate through a vendor platform or in-house LLM triage. The channel is the fronting carriers whose binders give them claims-audit rights over those MGAs. Narrowest wedge: MGAs that announced automation in the last 18 months and write in the 25+ states that have adopted the NAIC AI bulletin.
problem: Once claims are auto-paid, the insurer is accountable for the model's output but cannot see inside it, and the vendor selling the automation is marking its own homework. Two failures are invisible. One is silent overpayment: excluded lines paid (exam fees, cremation, prescription diets, supplements), wrong deductible, co-insurance, annual-limit or waiting-period math. The other is wrongful denial, which means complaints and market-conduct exposure. No single carrier can see the same PDF invoice filed with two insurers, or an altered invoice that looks fine in isolation. The parent's price-based edits add a third problem: reductions land on owners as balance bills, with no vet contract behind them, so mid-size insurers will not fund them.
solution: Read-only nightly export of invoice, policy form and adjudication decision, with no workflow replacement. (1) Normalize every invoice line to a canonical code (start from VeNom, so there is no taxonomy to defend). (2) Extract each policy form's exclusions, limits and waiting periods into clause-anchored rules once per form, human-verified. (3) Re-adjudicate independently and return agree or disagree per claim with a clause citation, sorted into three queues: likely overpaid, likely wrongly denied, and duplicate or tampered (PDF metadata, font and amount forensics). (4) Produce a monthly exam-ready validation pack with sample testing, drift and complaint linkage, which is what examiners request under the bulletin. (5) Cross-carrier registry: carriers contribute only hashed fingerprints (clinic, date, total, pet identity hash, line hashes) and get match alerts. Price benchmarks appear only as informational flags. They become a reason to reduce a payment only where the policy form has reasonable-and-customary language and the carrier opts in.
why_now: NAIC's AI model bulletin has been adopted by 25 states plus DC as of July 2026, and a 12-state examiner evaluation-tool pilot runs through September 2026. Under it, insurers stay accountable for vendor model outputs, and 'we cannot see the model internals' is not accepted. Pet premiums grew about 19% in 2025 on 6.98M insured US pets, and carriers are racing to automation (Five Sigma at Odie, Lassie at about 60% automated). LLMs make clause extraction from policy forms and PDF invoice reading cheap enough for a two-person team.
revenue_model: Annual platform fee of $45k-$120k by claim volume (about $0.15-$0.30 per claim scored), including monthly exam-ready packs. Registry-only tier of $12-25k for small carriers and TPAs. Optional 15% contingency on documented overpayments prevented on contract-clear lines. Sales math, assuming a $350 average paid claim: a 200k-claim MGA pays about $70M a year in claims, so an $80k fee breaks even at about 0.11% of claim dollars. Month-12 target: 6 MGAs at $80k plus 6 registry-tier customers at $15k, roughly $570k ARR. The registry then extends to all US carriers at a per-lookup fee, an ISO-ClaimSearch-style utility for pets.
non_obvious_insight: Regulation has turned automation from a cost saver into a liability, and the vendors selling automation are structurally unable to vouch for themselves, the way an accounting firm cannot audit its own consulting work. Independence is the product, and it is a budget line that exists (compliance, delegated-authority audits) rather than one that has to be invented. Duplicate and tamper detection is the only kind of edit that gets more valuable with every carrier that joins and never requires fighting a vet or a policyholder. State anti-fraud immunity statutes generally permit sharing suspected-fraud data with anti-fraud organizations, which makes a hashed registry lawful to seed on day one.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: map which MGAs and small carriers have publicly announced automation, and list the NAIC-bulletin states each writes in. Recruit an ex-claims QA manager as design partner. Days 7-21: build the clause extractor on 10 public policy forms and the invoice normalizer on about 500 sample invoices. Days 14-30: cold-approach 25 heads of claims and compliance with a free 'exam-readiness shadow audit' of 2,000 of their auto-approved claims from the last 90 days. The deliverable is a one-page count of overpaid lines, likely wrongful denials and duplicates. Convert the best results to a $25k, 90-day paid pilot. Success is 3 signed pilots by day 90 and a registry seeded by those pilots' fingerprints.

Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: VetControl (Illingen, Germany), Five Sigma (Clive AI claims adjuster), Sirma (custom ML for PetsBest, now under Synchrony), FairVet. - VetControl is the only true direct analog, and it is German, GOT-based, a services-plus-software hybrid, and shows no US customers.

Avoiding price-based reductions removes the balance-bill risk that the parent's research flagged.

title: UK Vet Price Panel for Investors and Insurers
one_liner: The first normalized, ownership-linked, time-series panel of UK vet prices, built from the price lists the CMA now forces every practice to publish, and licensed as a data feed to equity and credit investors, pet insurers and independent-practice bodies.
customer: Three payers with different budgets. (1) Buy-side and sell-side analysts and credit or private-equity funds with exposure to listed and sponsor-owned vet consolidators (CVS Group, Pets at Home/Vets4Pets, IVC Evidensia, Medivet, VetPartners, Linnaeus). (2) Pricing, claims and panel-strategy heads at UK pet insurers and their reinsurers. (3) Independent-practice trade bodies such as FIVP, which need to benchmark independents against groups. The first buyer to target is the analyst covering CVS Group, because alt-data budgets are large and the purchase decision is one person.
problem: Consolidators keep local practice brands after acquisition, so almost no one can build a clean same-practice, before-and-after price series by owner. The CMA found consolidated practices had about 5% higher claim values and 9.2% higher prices within four years, but insurers, lenders and analysts still cannot track drift by group or postcode. Insurers hold itemised claim lines but no market panel to compare them to. Investors underwrite price-led same-store growth with anecdotes. The official RCVS comparison data will not reach approved third parties until late 2027.
solution: Crawl and normalize the published price lists monthly, keeping history. The CMA order requires 36 standard items across six patient categories (216 prices per practice), written estimates over GBP 500, itemised bills, and ownership disclosure. Map each practice to its ultimate owner using the mandated ownership statements, Companies House and the RCVS register. Deliver: (a) a monthly group-level price index and same-practice change series, (b) a practice-level API with postcode reference ranges, (c) an alert feed when a group re-prices a category. Extension beyond the 36 routine items: insurers contribute itemised estimate and invoice lines above GBP 500 in exchange for a discount, which extends the panel to orthopaedics, oncology and emergency work. Apply to become an RCVS approved third party the day that channel opens, so the RCVS feed becomes an input rather than a threat. US extension later from insurer-contributed claim lines.
why_now: The CMA's final report (March 2026) became an order with RCVS undertakings accepted on 22 September 2026. Large groups' first transparency duties start 23 December 2026, and smaller practices follow through 2027. RCVS's enhanced Find a Vet is due by 22 June 2027, with business data supply later in 2027 and sharing with third parties under restrictions. That gives a 9-12 month window in which a normalized, owner-linked panel from the start of publication is the only structured source, and history cannot be back-filled later. Cheap LLM extraction handles the mess of 5,000 differently formatted price pages.
revenue_model: Data licences. Investor feed at GBP 30-60k a year. Insurer and reinsurer feed at GBP 20-50k, with a 40-50% discount for contributing itemised claim lines. Trade-body and independent-practice benchmarking at GBP 5-15k. Month-12 target of about GBP 550-600k ARR from 8 funds at 45k, 6 insurers at 30k and 3 bodies at 15k. Marginal cost is close to zero after the crawler exists. Year-2 upside comes from extending to US insurers' claim lines (US premiums grew about 19% in 2025) and to dental and specialty procedures.
non_obvious_insight: The CMA did not only mandate price disclosure. It mandated ownership disclosure, and that is the join key nobody had. A price series linked to owner is worth far more to an investor than a price list is to a pet owner, so the buyer with the deepest pocket is not the insurer or the consumer. The panel is also a cornered resource in time: every month a rival waits is history they can never buy. The parent's canonical-code thesis still holds, because regulation just created the first common procedure list and this business maps to it before anyone else. Insurers' claim lines then extend that list into severity territory that the 36 routine items cannot reach.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build crawlers for the six largest groups' price pages and 300 independents, and load the 36-item by six-category schema. Many practices already publish some prices ahead of the deadline. Days 10-20: build the ownership graph from the mandated ownership statements, Companies House and the RCVS register. Publish a free Pre-Order Baseline note on group price levels to draw inbound from analysts and journalists. Days 20-30: pitch 15 named buyers (5 analysts covering CVS Group and Pets at Home, 5 credit or PE funds with vet exposure, 5 insurer pricing heads) on a founding-subscriber annual deal at GBP 24k with a price lock and input on the index. Target 3 signed letters of intent by day 60 and the first live index the week after 23 December 2026.
