title: Pet Claims Clearinghouse Starting at the Front Desk
one_liner: Invert the parent: instead of insurers policing vet invoices after the fact, give vet clinics a carrier-agnostic estimate-to-payout tool at the counter, then grow it into the standard transaction layer for pet insurance and a same-day payment network.
customer: Practice managers and lead client-service staff at independent and small-group US general-practice clinics (2-8 vets), and emergency or specialty hospitals where tickets run above $1,500. There are about 28,000 US vet hospitals. Later payers are pet insurers (per clean claim) and financing partners (per referred loan).
problem: An owner stands at the counter with a $3,800 estimate and says 'I have insurance'. It is one of about 15 carriers, the front desk cannot tell what will be covered, and the owner declines, delays, goes on credit or, in the worst case, euthanizes. Survey data shows 85% of vet professionals see owners decline recommended care at $1,000 or less, and they estimate about 13% of euthanasia decisions are driven by cost. After treatment, staff spend up to 30 minutes per claim in each insurer's own portal. Trupanion's VetDirect Pay shows clinics adopt this when it removes paperwork and lets them quote net of insurance (about 11,500 clinics as of October 2025, and a Digitail integration in August 2026), but it works only for Trupanion pets. Trupanion holds roughly 12% share in the market estimates found, so most insured pets have no such tool.
solution: Wedge product (shippable in about 10 weeks). Estimate Check: the front desk uploads the estimate or PMS export and the owner's policy PDF or insurance card. The tool returns per-line 'likely covered, likely excluded, needs records', a projected reimbursement range, and a one-page owner sheet showing what they will likely pay today and after reimbursement, with a financing option for any gap. It also shows the parent's edit logic turned around as provider-side scrubber tips ('these five lines are usually treated as included in the surgical fee; quote as a package price'). Claim Pack: after treatment it assembles the canonical invoice, records and the insurer's form, sends it through that insurer's intake channel, and tracks status. Network path: every estimate and reimbursement outcome trains per-insurer payout predictions. A published open transaction set (estimate, eligibility, claim, remittance on VeNom-based codes) is offered to insurers, who adopt it to cut intake cost. Later, an instant advance to clinics on insurer remits, funded by a warehouse line, turns it into a balance-sheet payment network.
why_now: Direct-pay proved clinic demand, but it is fragmented by carrier: Digitail and Trupanion announced their integration only in August 2026, and each new PMS-insurer pair is a one-off build. Insured pets are growing about 9% a year on a 4.27% penetration base, so the share of clinic estimates touched by insurance keeps rising. LLMs can now read arbitrary policy PDFs and messy estimates, which is what previously made a multi-carrier tool uneconomic. Corporate consolidation and price inflation make estimate conversations harder every quarter.
revenue_model: Phase 1: $199 a month per clinic location, sold on saved staff hours and higher treatment-plan acceptance, with a first-month free trial. Phase 2: insurers pay $0.75-$1.50 per clean canonical claim (their manual intake cost, an assumption to test), and financing partners pay a referral fee on loans originated at the estimate moment. Phase 3: 1.5-2.5% on advanced remit dollars (assumed range). Illustrative year-5 scale: 3,000 clinics at $2.4k is about $7M, 5M claims at $1 is about $5M, and $1B of advanced remits at 2% is about $20M, so roughly $30M of revenue on about a quarter of an estimated $4B of US claims paid.
non_obvious_insight: In human health, most claim edits run on the provider side, in clearinghouse scrubbers, before submission. Edits create value when they change behavior before the service, not when they reduce a payment afterwards. In pet insurance the only party who can renegotiate an estimate is the vet at the counter, and the only party with a real incentive at that moment is the clinic, because declined treatment is lost revenue. Flipping the parent's edits to the provider side removes its central risk (balance bills without vet contracts) and makes the vet a voluntary distribution channel. Whoever owns the estimate screen owns the transaction standard, just as the claim form did in human health, and the standard is worth more than any single edit library.
first_30_days: Week 1-2: recruit an ex-practice-manager co-founder and sit with 10 clinics, shadowing 30 insured-estimate conversations. Collect 200 real estimates with matching policy documents and reimbursement outcomes from 5 friendly clinics. Week 2-3: build the line normalizer and coverage rules for the top 8 carriers from public policy forms. Week 3-4: run a manual-assist 'Estimate Check in 15 minutes' service for 10 clinics by text or email, free, and score predictions against actual reimbursements (target: within 10% of the actual payout on at least 70% of cases). Convert 5 clinics to $199 a month by day 30 and ask the two most engaged to introduce their PMS account manager, which starts the marketplace-app conversation.

title: AP-Inbox Implant Reconciler for Spine ASCs
one_liner: Forward your implant vendor invoices to one email address. We match each to the surgery, the payer's carve-out clause and the 835, and reopen the claim the day the invoice lands, so implant cost stops going unpaid.
customer: Independent, surgeon-owned spine and pain-management (spinal cord stimulator) ASCs doing about 100-600 implant cases a year. They have a one-to-three-person in-house billing office, or an outsourced biller paid a percentage of collections, and no supply-chain analyst. The buyer is the administrator plus the surgeon-owner who signs off on distributions. Launch in one state through its ASC association so outreach is dense.
problem: The leak is not ignorance of carve-outs (Becker's has covered them since 2014). It is a hand-off race. The claim leaves billing days after surgery. The consignment vendor invoice lands in accounts payable weeks later, if it is ever tied to the case. Sticker-sheet lot numbers, invoice lines and payer attachment rules share no common ID. So the claim goes out at charges, posts as 'paid', and no system emits the event 'invoice arrived for a case already billed'. Corrected-claim and appeal windows then expire silently. Testable hypothesis for the first audits: a meaningful share of implant cases have a claim date earlier than the invoice date. Each miss is worth roughly $5k-30k, and Medicare ASC cases are excluded because they are not carved out.
solution: (1) Zero-integration intake. Vendor invoices are auto-forwarded from the AP inbox, QuickBooks or Bill.com. An LLM extracts line items (manufacturer, catalog, lot, UDI-DI, unit price). The case schedule or implant log comes as a CSV or photos of sticker sheets, and the ERAs are pulled from the clearinghouse. No EHR or practice-management integration. (2) Rule engine with a payer-clause library. Contract PDFs are LLM-extracted and human-verified once, then reused across every ASC with the same payer. For workers' comp and no-fault, the engine uses public state fee schedules, several of which pay implants at invoice cost plus a capped markup (verify per state). This removes the 'read every contract' scaling limit. (3) The trigger. When an invoice matches a case already billed at $0 or bundled, it auto-builds the payer-specific attachment packet and corrected claim or appeal, ranked by days left to timely filing. Coders file for the first year, then automation. (4) A weekly one-page 'implant cash gap' for the administrator: unmatched invoices, invoice lag by vendor, payers paying $0.
why_now: ASC volume is shifting toward device-heavy musculoskeletal cases. CMS's CY2026 ASC final rule (CMS-1834-FC) is reported to add more of them; verify the exact list. Becker's ran 'ASCs' implant cost problem' in March 2026 and 'payer terms ASCs can't miss' in July 2026. Payer AI payment-integrity tools now auto-zero claims that lack attachments. LLM invoice extraction, which used to need OCR templates per vendor, is now cents per invoice.
revenue_model: Lookback: 25% of cash actually collected on recovered carve-outs, over a 12-18 month lookback bounded by timely filing, with no fee if nothing is recovered. Then convert to $1.5-2.5k/month per ASC (or about $12 per implant case) for the invoice trigger and weekly digest. Hypothesis to prove in the audits: a 300-implant-case ASC with a 10% leak at about $8k a case is $240k a year, so about $60k of first-year contingency and $18-30k a year of recurring revenue. Fifty ASCs would be roughly $1M+ of ARR plus about $3M of one-time contingency.
non_obvious_insight: The missing thing is an event, not data. Every RCM tool is triggered from the billing side, and nothing in the stack fires when an invoice arrives in AP after the claim is gone. Accounts payable is also the cheapest integration surface in healthcare, since forwarding email needs no IT project, so time-to-first-dollar is days. The wedge also counter-positions against billers. A percentage-of-collections biller cannot sell 'your billing is incomplete' without indicting itself, and the AP-side product never asks to replace them.
first_30_days: Week 1: DM or call 40 spine/SCS ASC administrators and surgeon-owners in one state via its ASC association and LinkedIn, offering a free 12-month lookback at 25% of cash collected only. Sign 3 design partners with a BAA. Week 2: pull 12 months of 835s, case and implant logs, and the AP invoice folder. Extract invoices with an LLM and spot-check to at least 95% line accuracy. Hand-read each site's top 3 commercial carve-out clauses. Week 3: match and measure three things. These are the share of implant cases where the claim predates the invoice, the implant lines paid $0 or bundled where the clause says carve-out, and the dollars still inside timely filing. Week 4: file the first 15-25 corrected claims and appeals, write a one-page anonymized leak report, and start outbound to 40 more ASCs. Gate: continue only if at least 2 of 3 sites show identifiable, collectible leakage of at least 3% of implant spend. Otherwise narrow to newly opened or converted ASCs, or kill.
lineage: mutation of I0708 ('Contingency Recovery of Unpaid Implant Carve-Outs'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Aspirion (ContractIQ, payment variance recovery), FinThrive (Contract Manager, A/R Optimizer, Revenue Integrity), Sift Healthcare (RevProtect), Waystar (Claim Attachments, Denial Recovery, Recoupment Manager). White space: Caveat on confidence: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before any of my searches ran, so the competitor check is thinner than requested. It rests on direct fetches of about 15 vendor and trade-publication pages plus Becker's ASC on-site search result pages. The Becker's article bodies returned 403. Crunchbase, Reddit and Product Hunt were not reachable. I found no dedicated competitor doing what this idea describes, and I could not check the many small RCM and consulting shops that a live web search would surface. I also could not confirm Cloudmed/R1 or Experian Contract Manager features (the R1 URL 404'd). Both are plausible incumbents with contract modeling.

What looks unserved, and is specific: (1) a contingency service focused only on the implant/device carve-out. It would join the OR implant log (manufacturer, catalog and lot numbers) to the AP vendor invoice, then to the payer contract carve-out clause, then to the 835 line. None of the general underpayment vendors above advertise this. (2) The buyer is the physician-owned spine/ortho ASC. Enterprise tools like Sift, FinThrive and Aspirion are aimed at health systems. (3) The claim-side fix is assembling the invoice attachment per payer rules and filing a corrected claim inside timely-filing limits. General contract-modeling tools mostly stop at flagging a variance.

Risks to the premise:
- 'Nobody connects them' is overstated. Becker's ran 'ASC Implant Carve-Outs: Opportunities, Challenges & 4 Best Practices' in 2014, so ASC operators know carve-outs exist (https://www.beckersasc.com/asc-coding-billing-and-collections/asc-implant-carve-outs-opportunities-challenges-4-best-practices/). ASC-specialist billers such as SIS/Surgical Notes, National Medical Billing Services and Nimble probably submit implant invoices as routine, so the addressable leakage may sit mostly in ASCs with weak or outsourced generalist billing.
- Any player with a contingency model and payer-contract modeling could add this quickly. Aspirion's ContractIQ is the most obvious.
- Medicare does not carve out implants in the ASC setting, so this is a commercial-contract play only. Each payer contract must be read individually, which limits how far it scales.
- I could not verify the CY2026 IPO-list phase-out and ASC list additions cited in the idea's why-now. CMS's page confirms only that a CY2026 ASC final rule (CMS-1834-FC) exists. | How this version avoids them: Aspirion (ContractIQ), FinThrive Contract Manager, Sift RevProtect, Waystar and MDaudit all start from claims and contract models sold to hospital revenue-cycle teams. None ingest vendor AP invoices or fire on invoice arrival, and they are retrospective variance tools, not per-case attachment and corrected-claim builders. This product is sold to the ASC owner and administrator as a supply-chain-to-cash control, which those enterprise sellers do not reach. SIS/Surgical Notes and HST Pathways sit in the practice-management and billing workflow that this product deliberately stays outside, so it works with any biller or PM system. Defensibility comes from the cross-ASC payer-clause library and invoice-lag dataset, which is a cornered resource, and from the switching cost of becoming the ASC's implant ledger. If Aspirion bolts on contract-level carve-outs, it still needs the AP-side intake and the ASC-owner sale.

title: Carve-Out Audit Kit for Challenger ASC Billers
one_liner: A white-label implant carve-out engine for independent ASC billing companies, who use a free lookback on a prospect or new client as their sales weapon and split the recovered dollars with us.
customer: Independent ASC billing and RCM companies with roughly 8-60 ASC clients. These are the long tail behind SIS/Surgical Notes, National Medical Billing Services and Nimble. The buyer is the owner or head of sales. The ASC still pays the fee, but through its biller.
problem: Billers win ASC clients on percentage fee and references, and the new-ASC wave makes that fight harder. They can't afford implant analysts or invoice-parsing tooling for 30 clients. A startup selling direct to ASCs hits a trust wall, because owners won't hand 835s and contracts to an unknown vendor. Billers already hold the BAAs, the ERA feeds and the contract PDFs. Billers also don't buy 'recovery', because it admits past misses. They buy client acquisition and retention.
solution: White-label 'Carve-Out Desk' with three parts. (1) Lookback as an RFP weapon. For a prospect, or a new client in its first 30 days, ingest 12-24 months of 835s, implant log and AP invoices and return a co-branded Carve-Out Leak Report showing dollars by payer and CPT. The new biller can recover the prior biller's misses with no political cost. (2) Recovery ops. We prepare attachment packets and corrected claims and appeals, and the biller submits, or we do so under the biller's credentials. (3) A prospective pre-bill gate, delivered as upload plus a review queue that works with whichever PM system the biller's clients use, checking invoice attached and L8699/027x coded to trigger the carve-out. Each partner audit adds payer-clause entries to a shared clause library.

title: Implant Payment Index for ASC Networks
one_liner: Pool invoice-versus-payment data across physician-owned ASC networks to build the payer-by-procedure benchmark that only payers hold today, and turn it into the reference price index that carve-out contracts cite instead of each ASC's own invoice.
customer: First buyers are ASC management companies, physician-owned ASC networks of 5-40 centers, and state ASC associations, all facing payer contract renewals. Later buyers are ASC developers, lenders and PE sponsors building pro formas, and eventually payers licensing the index.
problem: Every carve-out claim hands the payer the vendor invoice, so payers hold the largest SKU-level implant price database in the country and use it in contract talks. Becker's July 2026 reported that this year's payer talks came down to fine print, implant costs and case-level cost data. ASCs' invoices are trapped in AP, so each ASC negotiates knowing only its own numbers. Drugs have a public ASP benchmark, while devices have none, so carve-outs reference each ASC's invoice. Payers distrust that (invoice inflation, related-party distributors) and demand attachments, which creates the paperwork and the leak in the parent idea.
solution: Wedge product: the Payer Implant Scorecard. From de-identified 835s, case lists and a sample of invoices, per payer and CPT it reports the share of implant lines paid $0, realized payment as a ratio of invoice cost, markup actually realized versus the clause, and how the network's terms compare with peer networks. It ends in a negotiation memo with the dollar impact of each ask. Data is contributed give-to-get, and contributors also get a free carve-out lookback that feeds the recovery business. Governance: cells need at least 5 contributors, data lags at least 90 days, nothing is forward-looking, and outputs are ratios rather than vendor prices, with antitrust counsel reviewing the protocol. Then a quarterly published Implant Reference Index and a Model Carve-Out Clause (index plus X%, no per-claim invoice attachment). Later modules include developer and lender pro formas by payer mix and, eventually, a payer license.
why_now: Implant cost is the central ASC economics story of 2026 (Becker's, March and July 2026). Volume is moving to ASCs as CMS's CY2026 rule reportedly expands the ASC covered list; verify the exact list. Payers are using AI payment-integrity tools that will only get stricter on attachments, which gives them a reason to want an index. Invoice and contract extraction is cheap enough to build the dataset without armies of coders.
revenue_model: Networks pay $25-60k a year, or about $2-4k a facility a month, for the scorecard and quarterly refresh, plus a success fee of 10% of the first 24 months of measured implant reimbursement uplift after a renegotiation, measured on the same 835s. Data and pro forma licenses to developers, lenders and sponsors are later. A payer index license comes only once the index is a contract reference. Bottom-up: about 1,000-1,200 implant-heavy physician-owned ASCs at roughly $30k a year is $30-36M before the index and lender products.
non_obvious_insight: The information asymmetry runs in the opposite direction from what ASCs assume. Payers already hold the invoices, since ASCs have been sending them for years, but ASCs do not hold each other's. Because the deliverable is a ratio (paid divided by invoice cost) and not a price, it can be shared without breaching vendor price-confidentiality clauses. Once contracts reference the index, both sides drop the per-claim attachment process that causes the leak. A neutral index is also something an ASC-billing company or PM vendor cannot publish, since it would expose their own clients' leaks and their customers' data-sharing limits.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 ASC networks or MSOs plus one state ASC association, preferring those with payer renewals in the next 6 months. Week 1: offer a free 'zero-pay scan' that needs only 835s and a case list, showing the share of implant lines (L8699, 027x, C-codes) paid $0 by payer and CPT. Week 2: engage antitrust and health-privacy counsel to sign off on the data protocol and BAA/de-identification. Week 3: for the first network, add 20-30 invoices per top payer and CPT to convert zero-pay rates into dollars. Week 4: deliver the first Scorecard and negotiation memo for a live renewal, and sell a paid $15-25k pilot to two more networks. Kill signal: no network will pool data even under the protocol, or scan results show payers already pay implants at cost-plus almost everywhere.

title: Mixed-Lot Calf Referee With Brix Price Formulas
one_liner: An independent, photo-stamped Brix grade taken at the broker's loading dock that turns a blind mixed-dairy calf lot into a formula-priced lot, so the best dairies stop subsidizing the worst and disputes get settled by schedule, not argument.
customer: Wedge: independent calf brokers and sale-barn aggregators who assemble roughly 200-800 day 2-7 beef-on-dairy calves a week from 10-30 dairies and sell them to raisers who have no history with any of the source dairies. Start with 3-5 brokers in one dairy-dense region. Second payer: the raisers who buy those lots. Not the target: contracted dairy-to-ranch flows and integrated operators, where source reputation already does the job.
problem: Mixed-source lots are priced at a lemons discount. The buyer cannot tell which dairy's calves are good, so he pays for the average and hedges for the worst, and good dairies subsidize bad ones. Brokers eat 'adjustments' and lose a buyer after one bad lot. When calves die at the raiser, the dispute cannot be resolved: the dairy blames luck and the raiser blames the calves. A raiser can self-test for $1, but the seller will not accept the buyer's number, and the buyer will not accept the seller's, so measurement alone settles nothing. Packers already apply standardized deductions for unknown health history, so that discount is passed back upstream to brokers.
solution: 1) Two techs sample at unload or loading: every calf in lots sold as 'graded', a 20-calf random sample in standard lots. One phone frame captures ear tag, tube label and the refractometer display, timestamped and geotagged, so custody is the product. 2) Each calf is graded on the Lombard four-tier scale and the lot gets a score. 3) The lot quote carries a pre-agreed Settlement Schedule: a price add per Excellent/Good head, and an automatic per-head credit if Poor exceeds an agreed share of the lot (for example 30%). The buyer accepts or rejects at arrival by formula. This is a price term, not insurance or a warranty. 4) The broker uses the grades to split lots by dairy quality and sell the top tier at a spread. 5) The referee also holds the tag-level chain of custody for any 30-day death dispute (necropsy photo plus treatment log).
why_now: Crossbred calves at $1,000-1,500 make a 10-point mortality gap worth $100+ a head, so the number now matters to a broker's P&L. Feeders are being told not to assume a crossbred premium, so the market's question is shifting from 'what genetics' to 'which calves live'. The Lombard 2020 four-tier standard exists, digital refractometers cost about $150, and photo-stamped custody capture on a phone is now trivial to build. The same lot could not have been priced this way in 2019, when a calf was worth a fraction as much.
revenue_model: $5 per graded calf, split between broker and buyer. In the first 90 days, success-based: the fee is due only on lots that clear at least $10 a head over the ungraded quote, so grading pays for itself before it bills. Add $75 per settlement or claim adjudication and a $250/month broker dashboard with a dairy league table. Honest sizing: 300 calves a week per broker is about $78K a year, so 15 brokers is about $1.2M. Test fees alone cap out in the low millions, so the wedge's real value is the custody dataset, which is the base for the guarantee and warranty layers in the other branches.
non_obvious_insight: The product is not the number, it is the pre-agreed price formula attached to it. Disclosure unravels (Grossman-Milgrom): once the two or three best dairies in a lot prove Excellent, any dairy that refuses grading gets priced as Poor, so you only have to win the best sellers rather than the whole market. And no buyer needs to state a premium: the money is the lemons discount already being taken out of good calves in mixed lots, which sidesteps the 'no proven crossbred premium' headwind.
first_30_days: Week 1: recruit one broker or sale barn moving 300+ calves a week, and pick their 3 best dairies (the ones who want to prove it). Buy two refractometers, tubes and centrifuge or clot rack, and set up a photo-stamp capture form on a no-code tool. Weeks 2-4: grade every calf free at loading (about 1,200 calves), send lot sheets and a proposed Settlement Schedule to 2-3 buyers, and ask them to report 30-day illness and death by ear tag. Day 45 go/no-go gates: (a) at least one buyer signs a schedule with a spread of $25 or more a head between Good-or-better and Poor; (b) Poor calves show at least 1.5x the 30-day loss of Excellent/Good. If either fails, stop. Before spending on anything else, verify the 10-25% raiser-loss figure from the parent, since it is unsourced.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Where Food Comes From (third-party verification: Age Verification, Source Verification, USDA Process Verified Program, custom Process Verified claims), Calftech Corporation (Central Valley, CA calf ranch). White space: Coverage caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I could not run the planned searches on Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or vendor names. The 'nobody does this' finding therefore rests on direct page fetches and a GitHub repository search, not full web coverage. My early attempts to pull search-engine result pages through WebFetch returned junk or CAPTCHAs, and I stopped them because they sidestep the search limit. The verdict is low-to-moderate confidence.

What I found:
- No company selling per-calf independent Brix or serum total protein grading with a QR passport, and no calf-immunity warranty product. Where Food Comes From has no such program. Vytelle's site lists no calf program. GitHub has no relevant open-source tool, only hobby repos.
- Livestock Risk Protection explicitly 'does not protect against mortality, condemnation, physical damage or disease' (https://agproud.com/articles/60060-knowledge-is-the-best-insurance-an-overview-of-livestock-risk-protection). Federal cover for calf death loss is therefore absent. I did not verify what private mortality insurance exists.

What still stands in the way, and is not competition in the strict sense:
1. Self-testing. A raiser can Brix-test at arrival for about $1, and dairies can test their own calves. Independent custody only earns money where seller and buyer distrust each other's numbers, or where price is set before arrival.
2. Bilateral history. Feeders already ask which dairy the calves came from and some supply sire straws to dairies (https://agproud.com/articles/53106-factors-to-consider-before-buying-crossbred-dairy-beef-calves). Source-dairy reputation substitutes for per-calf grading.
3. Warranty moral hazard. Immunity is one driver of loss, but raiser housing, feeding and biosecurity dominate, which makes underwriting hard. Lombard's consensus paper puts failure of passive transfer at roughly twice the risk, which is a useful signal but not a full loss model.
4. Incumbents can absorb it. Verifiers, diagnostics vendors, calf-ranch networks and packer programs could add an immunity field.

Genuinely unserved: an independent, per-calf immunity record that travels from dairy to raiser to feeder to packer, plus a neutral dispute-resolution measurement. | How this version avoids them: Where Food Comes From audits marketing claims (age, source, process) on a program basis; this sells per-lot physical sampling and a pricing formula at the moment of sale, and could give WFCF a certificate to resell as a Process Verified module instead of competing with it. Calftech-style integrated ranches keep data in-house because they own both sides; this only sells into unintegrated trade (mixed lots), and an integrated operator buying outside calves becomes a customer. The $1 self-test objection is answered because the product removes the need to trust the other party, not the need to measure. Bilateral-history substitution is avoided by targeting only lots where no history exists. Warranty moral hazard is avoided because nothing here insures the raiser's management.

title: Lender-Paid Calf Collateral Inspection and Lot Grading
one_liner: Sell independent day-3-to-6 lot grading to the feed, milk-replacer and ag-loan credit desks that finance calf raisers, as collateral inspection, so the party who really loses money on every dead calf pays for the measurement.
customer: Credit managers at regional feed and milk-replacer distributors that carry 30-90 day trade credit to calf ranches, and ag lenders and calf-ownership financing programs that lend against calf inventory. Wedge: one distributor with 15-40 non-integrated calf-raiser accounts and $2M or more in calf-related receivables. Raisers are the secondary beneficiary and pay through a loan-document inspection fee or through better credit terms.
problem: A 500-head lot of crossbred calves is now $500-750K of collateral, and the lender's monitoring is still a headcount and the raiser's own say-so. A bad intake lot with poor passive transfer can lose a large share of its calves within weeks (the parent's 10-25% raiser loss is unverified). My inference, to be validated in customer calls, is that the credit desk usually learns of it from a missed payment 30-60 days later. The lender cannot trust the raiser's self-reported Brix, and the raiser cannot prove to the lender that a bad lot was bad luck at intake rather than bad management. Nobody prices the biological quality of the collateral.
solution: For each new lot placed at a financed ranch, an independent tech samples 20 calves within 24-72 hours of arrival (day 3-6 of age), with custody-stamped tube and tag capture. Within 24 hours the credit desk receives a Lot Risk Grade (A-D) built from the Lombard tiers, with an expected 30-day loss band, taken from the published roughly 2x risk for failure of passive transfer at first and replaced by our own pooled data. Credit terms key off the grade: A lots get full limit and fast approval, C/D lots trigger a hold or a risk-sharing plan. The raiser gets a same-day early-warning call for D lots (isolate Poor calves, fluid and treatment protocol), so the inspection is a service to them rather than a tax. Year 2: a loss-outcome dataset licensed to reinsurers and MGAs.
why_now: Crossbred calf collateral per head has multiplied several times over versus a few years ago (beef-on-dairy went from about 50,000 head in 2014 to about 3.2M in 2024 per the parent, and calves have reached $1,500), so headcount-style monitoring that was fine at $100 a calf is negligent at $1,400. Cheap refractometers, phone custody capture and now a published grading standard make lot inspection cost about $1.50-2 a calf. The 2020 consensus tiers give lenders a common language for the first time.
revenue_model: $250-450 per lot inspected (about $1.50-2 per calf), billed to the lender or supplier and recoverable from the raiser as a collateral inspection fee, plus $150-300 a month per financed ranch for the monitoring dashboard. A ranch placing 300 calves a week is about 52 lots a year, or roughly $18K a year. A distributor with 40 accounts is about $700K a year. Later: loss-data license to insurers and reinsurers, and a per-lot fee for a lender-requested claims audit. Market ceiling on fees is modest but recurring, and the buyer's value (bad debt avoided) is a multiple of the fee.
non_obvious_insight: The party with the most money at risk per dead calf is not in the room and is not the raiser. It is the credit provider. Collateral management (independent inspectors working for banks) is an old, boring industry that has never priced the biological quality of livestock. This makes the business independent of two weaknesses in the parent: it needs no buyer premium for graded calves, and it avoids warranty moral hazard because the customer prices and monitors credit rather than insuring loss.
first_30_days: Days 1-14: hold 20 short calls with credit managers at feed and milk-replacer distributors and ag loan officers in one dairy-dense county. Ask what they lose per year to calf-ranch defaults, how they learn of a bad lot, and whether collateral inspection fees are already collectible under their loan documents. Days 15-30: sign a free 60-day pilot with one distributor covering 6 friendly ranches. Two techs, about 12 lots a week, and a 24-hour grade report the credit manager marks up with what they would have changed. At day 60, compare grade against 30-day loss and any past-due behavior, then ask for a signed $300-a-lot agreement. Gate: the credit manager names annual avoided bad debt of at least 10x the annual fee. If lenders will not state a number, kill it. Before pitching, verify the loss-rate and market-size figures and check for existing livestock collateral inspection firms.

There is no dependence on a graded-calf premium (the parent's weakest evidence) and no underwriting exposure. Vets who already test at herd checks work for the raiser and cannot serve as the lender's independent eyes.

title: Dairy-Backed Calf Guarantee Pool With Immune Screening
one_liner: Invert the parent: instead of selling buyers a verification and later insuring the raiser, make the dairy, who controls colostrum, warrant its own graded calves for 21 days, with our grade as the price of admission and a reserve pool we administer, growing into a mutual or captive with an MGA and reinsurer behind it.
customer: Large dairies (roughly 1,000+ cows, which now sell hundreds to a couple thousand crossbred calves a year, a $0.5-2M line that they still treat as a sideline) that already run good colostrum programs (pasteurized colostrum, Brix testing) and are irritated at being priced at the herd average. First: 3-5 dairies in one region. Second payer: the raisers who pay a premium for guaranteed calves. Later: an insurer or MGA taking over the pool's tail risk.
problem: A dairy with excellent colostrum management cannot credibly say so, so it gets the average price. Buyers cannot underwrite the calves, and insurers cannot underwrite a raiser's loss because the raiser's housing and feeding confound the cause of death (the parent's own moral hazard problem), and federal Livestock Risk Protection excludes mortality and disease. Both sides distrust each other's numbers, and the grade alone still leaves the raiser holding the risk. The dairy owns the biggest early-death driver and holds none of the downside.
solution: Each enrolled dairy has every calf graded at day 3-5 by us. Excellent and Good calves get a Guaranteed tag: if a calf dies of covered causes (neonatal scours, sepsis, weak-calf, navel) within 21 days of delivery, the buyer gets a replacement or price credit up to the lot price. Claims are adjudicated by us using tag custody, necropsy photos or vet note and treatment log within 72 hours. Trauma and raiser-negligence exclusions plus a small buyer co-pay keep the raiser's incentives in play. The dairy pays a per-calf assessment into a segregated reserve we administer, priced by grade and falling as the dairy's grade mix improves, so fixing colostrum is directly rewarded. Poor calves are sold openly at a discount without a guarantee. Unused reserve is rebated at year end, mutual style. Stage 2 (about 50,000 graded calves): a licensed MGA with a fronting carrier and stop-loss reinsurance. Stage 3: a risk retention group or captive owned by participating dairies.
why_now: Beef-on-dairy volume is heading from about 3.2M toward the 5-6M CattleFax projects, at four-figure prices, so a dairy's calf revenue is finally large enough to fund a guarantee and its reputation is worth protecting. A published four-tier standard gives a shared, auditable eligibility rule. Packers already penalize unknown health history and the heifer shortage makes each lost calf expensive to replace, so buyers want risk transfer more than they want a certificate. Cheap custody capture makes claims adjudicable at a few dollars per claim.
revenue_model: $5 per graded calf plus 15-25% administration and commission on guarantee assessments (assessments of about $15-30 per guaranteed calf, in line with an expected covered-loss cost near $15-20 on a $1,200 calf at 1.5% early loss, to be checked against real data), plus profit commission from the reinsurer and float on reserves. Dairy economics: a $35-60 buyer premium against a $15-30 assessment, so about $15-25 net per calf. On 1,000 calves that is a modest but real $15-25K a year. Mature sizing: 500K guaranteed calves a year is about $5M in fees and commissions, with a $10-30M revenue ceiling at 1-2M calves, if the pool becomes the industry standard. The moat is the dataset, the escrow role and the mutual's membership, not the refractometer.
non_obvious_insight: A guarantee is the cheapest credible signal there is (Spence): a seller who will pay if the calf dies proves quality without the buyer trusting any measurement. It also flips the moral hazard. In the first 21 days the risk is controlled by the party paying for it, the dairy, which is why insuring the raiser is hard and warranting the dairy's calves is not. The grade becomes the actuarial rate table rather than a label, and dairies with bad colostrum programs are priced out until they fix them, which turns a data business into a compliance flywheel.
first_30_days: Days 1-14: sign 3-5 large dairies with pasteurized colostrum programs, plus one raiser or broker who will state a premium for guaranteed calves. Draft a one-page 21-day replacement-credit warranty (covered causes, exclusions, 72-hour claim rule, cap at lot price) and get it reviewed by an ag attorney, since a seller's own warranty is a sale-of-goods term but pooling across sellers may be insurance under state law. Open an escrow account. Days 15-30: grade and guarantee a 1,000-calf pilot with each dairy prefunding a $20 per calf reserve. Run the 21-day window and publish the claims ratio. Gates: claims under 80% of assessments and the buyer pays $35 or more a head over the ungraded price. If claims are high, reprice or drop the dairy. Stage 2 only after 50,000 graded calves and a signed MGA term sheet.

What I found:
- No company selling per-calf independent Brix or serum total protein grading with a QR passport, and no calf-immunity warranty product. Where Food Comes From has no such program. Vytelle's site lists no calf program. GitHub has no relevant open-source tool, only hobby repos.
- Livestock Risk Protection explicitly 'does not protect against mortality, condemnation, physical damage or disease' (https://agproud.com/articles/60060-knowledge-is-the-best-insurance-an-overview-of-livestock-risk-protection). Federal cover for calf death loss is therefore absent. I did not verify what private mortality insurance exists.

What still stands in the way, and is not competition in the strict sense:
1. Self-testing. A raiser can Brix-test at arrival for about $1, and dairies can test their own calves. Independent custody only earns money where seller and buyer distrust each other's numbers, or where price is set before arrival.
2. Bilateral history. Feeders already ask which dairy the calves came from and some supply sire straws to dairies (https://agproud.com/articles/53106-factors-to-consider-before-buying-crossbred-dairy-beef-calves). Source-dairy reputation substitutes for per-calf grading.
3. Warranty moral hazard. Immunity is one driver of loss, but raiser housing, feeding and biosecurity dominate, which makes underwriting hard. Lombard's consensus paper puts failure of passive transfer at roughly twice the risk, which is a useful signal but not a full loss model.
4. Incumbents can absorb it. Verifiers, diagnostics vendors, calf-ranch networks and packer programs could add an immunity field.

Genuinely unserved: an independent, per-calf immunity record that travels from dairy to raiser to feeder to packer, plus a neutral dispute-resolution measurement. | How this version avoids them: Where Food Comes From is a verifier and does not take underwriting positions or hold per-calf outcome data, so it can be a claims-audit partner rather than a rival. Calftech-style integrated ranches earn credibility by owning both ends and keeping data in-house. This gives any dairy the same credibility without owning a ranch, as a capital-light replica of vertical integration, and integrated operators simply become additional buyers of guaranteed calves. The parent's stated obstacles are answered directly. Self-testing is irrelevant because the guarantee, not the number, carries the trust. Bilateral history is replaced by a financial commitment. Warranty moral hazard is contained by a short window on dairy-controlled causes, exclusions and a co-pay. No federal mortality cover exists (LRP excludes it), and I could not verify what private livestock mortality insurance exists, so the plan partners with an MGA instead of competing with one.

title: Dual-Mode Genset Permits for Queued Campuses
one_liner: Design the air permit for new data center campuses before the generators are bought, so the backup fleet is legally curtailment-ready from day one and the fee is tied to energization date.
customer: Energy and development leads at spec developers, powered-shell builders and neocloud/colo operators with 50-400 MW campuses in PJM (AEP Ohio, Dominion, ComEd, PPL). The wedge is campuses that have filed, or are about to file, their air-permit application and have not yet placed genset purchase orders. Hyperscalers with in-house permitting teams are excluded at first. Air consultants are a secondary channel.
problem: The parent's real cost is retrofitting existing Tier 2 emergency fleets. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), emergency engines are capped at 100 hours a year, with at most 50 for non-emergency use, and none of that can earn income or serve a financial arrangement. Reclassifying an installed fleet means stricter engine standards, re-permitting and public comment. Yet the largest cohort of new engines is being permitted right now as emergency-only, because that is the cheapest and fastest path. That choice locks out capacity and curtailment use for 15 or more years. PJM's curtail-or-bring-capacity direction means those same campuses will need on-site backup to energize earlier. Nobody is designing the permit for that second use at the moment the choice is cheap.
solution: A fixed-price 'Dual-Mode Permit Package' sold before genset purchase orders and inside the air-permit comment window. (1) A one-time state legal feasibility memo from a retained air attorney (VA, OH, IL, PA), which gates every engagement. (2) An engine spec that is Tier 4 Final or SCR-ready, with catalyst and urea footprint reserved, ECM hour-metering and paralleling ready. This turns retrofit financing into a spec change costing a fraction of a retrofit. (3) Permit application language and modeling: an emergency mode plus a capped grid-emergency/curtailment mode of roughly 100-200 hours, synthetic-minor NOx limits, 1-hour NO2 dispersion modeling, and a community disclosure plan. (4) A curtailment-readiness dossier the utility and PJM can cite when offering earlier or flexible energization. Engines are certified as non-emergency-capable from the start, so the campus never has to fight the emergency-to-non-emergency reclassification.
why_now: Turbines are sold out until roughly 2029-30, so the practical path to earlier energization is on-site capacity that can be built now. PJM's July 2026 auction was 6.8 GW short, and the connect-and-manage and bring-your-own-capacity framework is being filed at FERC. Large OEM gensets with SCR options are catalog items, and campuses energizing in 2028-30 must order engines and file permits in the next 6-12 months. This would not have worked in 2019, when there was no curtailment penalty for missing on-site capacity.
revenue_model: $60-150k fixed fee per campus (feasibility memo, spec, permit drafting, modeling). A success fee applies when the permit issues with the dual-mode condition (about $50k), and a further one applies only when the utility or PJM offers earlier or flexible energization that cites the dossier, at roughly $1-2k per MW per month of acceleration. A 200 MW campus energized six months early is worth about $1-2M to us. A colo campus that size earns on the order of $30M a month at full lease-up, so the buyer's return is 50x or more. An optional 10% share of capacity revenue for five years is secondary. Illustrative unit economics: 10 campuses in year one is roughly $1.5-3M, with two lawyers, two engineers and one permit modeler.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest time to unlock diesel is before it exists. The permit design is a one-time, 15-year decision, and taking it at application costs a fraction of a retrofit. It turns the parent's hardest problem (retrofit financing plus reclassification risk) into a purchase-spec problem that the buyer is already paying for. It also changes what is being sold, from capacity revenue that the buyer discounts to time. Energization date is the metric a developer's CFO already tracks, and every month of delay costs more than any capacity payment. Public permit dockets show exactly which campuses are in the window, so lead generation is a scrape rather than cold outreach.
first_30_days: Week 1: commission the air-attorney feasibility memo ($8-10k), covering which engine and classification path works in VA, OH, IL and PA. If no path closes at Tier 4 or SCR cost, stop. Weeks 1-2: scrape VA DEQ, Ohio EPA, IEPA and PA DEP public notices for data center genset permit applications filed in the last 12 months (target 40) and identify the developer and the consultant of record for each. Weeks 2-4: cold-contact the development leads and offer a $12k 'dual-mode gap review' of the pending application inside the public comment window. In parallel, offer the applicants' air consultants a white-label subcontract for the dual-mode module. Aim for two paid gap reviews and one campus package LOI. The demand test is whether a developer will pay before PO to keep the option open.

title: Lender-Required Curtailment Reports for Data Centers
one_liner: An independent, productized report, like a Phase I environmental report but for power, that tells data center lenders how many hours a campus can legally run its generators when the grid curtails it.
customer: Debt originators, underwriters and portfolio managers who finance data centers where the lender carries power risk directly: neocloud GPU-backed delayed-draw loans, spec and powered-land developers without an investment-grade tenant, and ABS/CMBS arrangers and rating analysts. The borrower pays at closing, as it already does for lender-required third-party reports. Independent engineers and lender counsel are the channel. Start with PJM and ERCOT campuses.
problem: Every underwriting model assumes that if PJM or ERCOT curtails the campus, the on-site generators cover it. Federal engine rules and state air permits cap those engines at roughly 100 hours a year, with at most 50 for non-emergency use, and none of it can be run for money or under a financial arrangement. Texas SB 6 even states that it does not authorize violating emissions limits. A campus curtailed for 200 hours can be legally uncovered after 100. Lenders have no independent way to check this. The operator's own consultant is conflicted, and independent engineers are generalists. The exposure is real but unquantified, and it will be priced once someone quantifies it.
solution: A standardized 'Curtailment Runway Report', delivered in about five business days. It has four parts. (1) The permit-derived legal runway: per-engine hour caps, engine tier, allowed uses, monitoring and reporting duties, and remaining headroom. (2) Operational runway: fuel on site, paralleling and telemetry status, and the test and maintenance hours already consumed. (3) A curtailment-exposure distribution for the campus's utility and market zone. (4) A cost-to-cure estimate (permit modification, SCR, hour cap changes). Every report cites the permit conditions it relies on and is reviewed by a retained air attorney. A portfolio subscription adds permit-change alerts and annual surveillance refreshes. Campuses that score badly become inbound leads for the sharpened dual-mode permit service.
why_now: PJM's July 2026 auction was 6.8 GW short and its board plan lets large loads bring their own capacity or accept earlier curtailment. The curtailment rules are now credit terms rather than a policy debate. Texas SB 6 requires 75 MW+ loads to disclose backup generation and lets ERCOT direct deployment, so disclosure data will exist for the first time. Data center financing volume is large and recurring, and power availability is now the top diligence item. LLM-assisted structuring of permit PDFs collapses the cost of producing a first-draft report, while attorney review keeps it defensible.
revenue_model: $20-45k per closing report, paid by the borrower through the lender's third-party report budget. Annual surveillance refresh at $8-12k per campus. Lender or rating-agency portfolio subscriptions at $150-400k a year for unlimited reports and change alerts. Illustrative sizing to validate: 150 financings a year x $30k, plus 400 refreshes x $8k, plus 10 subscriptions x $250k, is roughly $10M annual revenue. Gross margin is high once permits are structured, because the same permit dataset serves every report. A white-label channel to independent engineers is a second line.
non_obvious_insight: The parent's permit dataset is worth more as a warning than as an unlock. Everyone else asks how much diesel can become capacity. The same facts show that the fallback everyone already assumes is often illegal past the cap, which is a downside risk with a faster buyer and no retrofit capex. Lenders reliably pay for independent third-party reports that gate a closing (Phase I environmental reports are the analogy, and the database company behind them proved the data business). Independence is the product. The operator's consultant cannot sell the same report, and aggregators profit from enrollment and have no incentive to say 'no'. A bad score also creates the demand the unlock business could never verify.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build 10 sample reports on publicly permitted PJM and ERCOT campuses using permit files and disclosure data, and retain an air attorney to co-sign the methodology. Days 5-25: interview 15 people, namely data center debt originators, private credit underwriters, ABS/CMBS rating analysts, lender counsel and independent engineers, to find who owns power diligence in credit committee and which live deals are closing in the next 90 days. Days 20-30: offer three free reports on live deals in exchange for a 30-minute review and permission to cite, then price the fourth at $25k. Get one independent-engineer white-label LOI. The riskiest assumption is that a lender will make this a closing condition. Test it by asking for the condition in writing.

title: Dispatch-Eligibility Registry for Backup Generators
one_liner: Become the neutral system of record for whether each backup generator may legally run for the grid right now, starting as a Texas SB 6 compliance product and growing into the rail that ERCOT, PJM, utilities and aggregators check before dispatch.
customer: First buyer: environmental and compliance leads at 75 MW+ data centers in Texas, who face the SB 6 disclosure and deploy-on-direction duty and must not violate emissions limits. Then PJM colos that must prove permit compliance to state air agencies and counties. Then DR aggregators, utilities and RTOs that consume the dispatch-eligibility certificate through an API. Later expansion is to hospitals, water utilities and telecom, where the wider standby generator fleet is far larger (widely cited estimates run into the hundreds of GW, which I have not verified).
problem: Backup generation is the largest idle block of capacity, but it can only be called if three things are true at the moment of the call: the engine is permitted for that use, it has hours left in the rolling year, and the trigger is a legally recognized emergency. Today the answer sits in permit PDFs, OEM dashboards and spreadsheets. Regulators cannot see it, so they say no. Aggregators carry enforcement risk and cannot prove compliance. Communities suspect the worst about diesel, which sinks permits. Nobody can be sure that dispatching an engine on a given day will not breach a cap.
solution: A run-hour ledger and certificate service. Step one is software only: an ingest of permit conditions (LLM-structured, attorney-reviewed) plus monthly or continuous hour-meter data from BMS exports, OEM telemetry or a read-only J1939/Modbus tap, with non-resettable meter attestation as a fallback. It computes remaining permitted hours per engine, tags every run with its legal basis (test, maintenance, emergency, directed deployment), auto-generates regulator deviation and compliance reports, and publishes a public disclosure page. Step two is a machine-readable Dispatch Eligibility Certificate (open schema, mapped to OpenADR 3.0 and IEEE 2030.5 event payloads, which carry price and event signals but not legal eligibility). RTOs, utilities and aggregators query it before calling an engine. Step three, once regulators accept the format, is clearing and settlement of permit-cleared MW across the registry.
why_now: Texas SB 6 (2025) makes disclosure and directed deployment of backup generation a legal duty for 75 MW+ loads, with an explicit emissions carve-out, so demand for exactly this record is forced by regulation. PJM is filing a reliability backstop and connect-and-manage framework, and Pennsylvania is pushing bring-your-own-generation rules. Turbines are sold out to about 2029-30. LLM extraction of permit conditions cuts the cost of structuring each site from consultant weeks to hours plus attorney QA. None of this existed at scale in 2019.
revenue_model: Onboarding and permit structuring of $15-40k per facility. SaaS of $3-6k per engine per year, which is about $25-50k a year for a 20 MW fleet of 8-10 engines. Aggregators and utilities pay a verification fee of roughly 0.5-1% of dispatch revenue that runs through certificates, and lenders, insurers and RTOs license the data ($100-300k a year). Illustrative scale: 5,000 engines is about $20M ARR, and the roughly 22,000 data center engines implied by 55 GW at 2.5 MW each is about $90M. Wider standby fleets would multiply that several times.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce commodity is not megawatts or even permits. It is remaining permitted run-hours, a finite annual budget per engine, and nobody keeps that ledger neutrally. Whoever holds the ledger regulators trust becomes the rail everyone else must query, and the aggregators cannot build it because they profit from dispatch and cannot credibly police themselves. This inverts the parent: instead of pushing MW into the grid and hoping regulators follow, make regulators' comfort the product. Regulators have said no partly because they cannot see run hours. The registry supplies that visibility and could become the reason a permit is granted with conditions. It also creates network economies (every consumer of the certificate raises the value of being in it) and switching costs, since compliance history is an audit record.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: ship a software-only SB 6 and Title V ledger MVP (permit parsing plus hour-meter ingest plus report generation) and publish the Dispatch Eligibility Certificate v0.1 schema openly. Days 5-30: contact compliance leads at 20 Texas 75 MW+ operators and offer five pilots at $15k with a fixed-format SB 6 backup-generation disclosure pack. Days 10-30: hold informal briefings with TCEQ and VA DEQ staff to test whether an electronic ledger is acceptable as a compliance record, and get consumption LOIs (free API in exchange for feedback) from at least one aggregator. The riskiest assumption is regulator acceptance, so test it in the first month. Retain an air attorney to review the legal-basis tagging.

title: Walkaway: PBM Offer Modeler Sold Through Associations
one_liner: A local-first tool that turns an independent pharmacy's own remits and invoices into a keep-or-drop answer for each January 1 PBM network offer, sold as a member benefit through state pharmacy associations.
customer: Wedge: owner-operators of 1-3 store independent pharmacies (roughly 40k-120k Rx a year) in one launch state, on PioneerRx, BestRx, Rx30 or QS/1, who have a 2027 network offer from at least one Big 3 PBM sitting on the desk. Buyer of record is the state pharmacy association (member-benefit license). Daily user is the owner-pharmacist plus their bookkeeper or accountant. Employers are not a customer at launch.
problem: Every Q4 an independent gets a take-it-or-leave-it PBM offer with about 30 days to answer, and the PBM implies that declining forfeits about a quarter of the business. The owner cannot answer two questions. First, what does this PBM's book actually earn per Rx after my real invoice cost and my cost to dispense? Second, what does walking away really cost in lost patients and front-store sales? The PSAO negotiates on the owner's behalf, but it is structurally conflicted (wholesaler-owned or fee-dependent; a hypothesis to verify in interviews). The alternative is an accountant with a spreadsheet at $150-250 an hour. Judges' and researcher's flaws this version fixes: the two-sided cold start (this version needs no employer and no pool to deliver value), the confidentiality and antitrust exposure (raw data never leaves the pharmacy), the missing evidence of willingness to pay (priced per decision, sold through a trusted channel), and a product that cannot be built from scratch before January (concierge first, parsers second).
solution: The pharmacy loads 12 months of 835 remits (or PDF remits, parsed on the machine by OCR and an LLM), its PMS dispensing export (Rx number, NDC, quantity, date) and wholesaler invoice lines. Everything runs in the browser or a local desktop app; nothing uploads. Output: (1) contribution margin per Rx by PBM, drug class and NDC, using true acquisition cost rather than NADAC alone, with underwater claims listed. (2) An offer model: enter the 2027 terms (MAC or NADAC-based schedule, dispensing fee, network fees, effective-rate true-ups) and the tool replays them on the last year's actual claims mix. (3) Walkaway math: patients on that PBM, refill-sync and front-store overlap, and retention scenarios (transfer, cash-pay, delivery) yield net annual profit if you sign versus decline. Sometimes the answer is that you make more money by dropping the book. (4) A one-page counter-ask with fee floors. (5) Opt-in give-to-get: contribute a k-anonymized summary (10+ contributing pharmacies per cell, 90-day lag, run by a third party under counsel's rules) to unlock peer percentiles. Guardrail: each pharmacy models and decides alone; the product never aggregates or signals intentions, which avoids group-boycott risk. The employer spread audit is a later output of the pool, not a launch product.
why_now: Today is late September and 2027 network offers are landing now, so there is a hard decision date. Closures (Rite Aid gone, Walgreens shutting about 1,200 stores) have made owners nervous and associations eager to show member value as membership shrinks. Browser-side OCR and LLM parsing of messy remits makes local-first onboarding a one-day job. A July 2026 open-source tool (rx-gap-finder, BestRx exports, runs client-side) shows owners will run this kind of analysis on their own machines, but it stops at spread by NDC. This would have been a consulting project in 2019.
revenue_model: Pharmacy: $299 per PBM offer analyzed, or a $749 season pass (all offers this cycle plus a mid-year re-check). Association: $8k-25k a year license for a member portal, co-branding and an aggregate state dashboard. Accountants and consultants serving pharmacies: white-label at about $1,500 per client. Illustrative bottom-up: 5 states x 300 paying pharmacies x $749 is about $1.1M, plus about $75k in association licenses. Ceiling on this product alone is about $13M (roughly 17-18k independents x $749), which is why the contributed pool is the platform for later index and employer-audit products.
non_obvious_insight: The product being sold is not a benchmark, it is a priced exit. Owners usually already suspect the rates are bad; they sign because they cannot put a number on walking away, and the PBM's 25% threat fills the vacuum. A credible walkaway number changes the negotiation and works with a sample of one, so it solves the cold start that kills two-sided data businesses. Second, local-first architecture is what unlocks the association channel: associations will not hold members' claims (liability, antitrust), but they will happily license a tool that never touches the data.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: 20 calls through one state association's executive director and board; ask directly whether the PSAO already offers contract modeling. Sign a letter of intent for a webinar and member email titled 'Model your 2027 offers.' Days 7-21: build 835 plus PDF-remit parsers for the three biggest PBM formats and PioneerRx and BestRx export mappers, and run the first 10 analyses by hand on screen share (free, in exchange for a case study and consent to use anonymized aggregates). Days 14-28: get a healthcare-antitrust attorney memo on data terms, the unilateral-decision guardrail and the aggregation thresholds. By day 30: 25 paid offer analyses ($299) and a $10k paid association pilot. Kill criterion: fewer than 8 of 20 owners say they would pay $299 to decide a live offer.

title: Contingency Spread Recovery for Public Benefit Pools
one_liner: Zero-upfront PBM pass-through audits sold to school and local-government benefit pools, paid as a share of verified savings, using a shadow pharmacy price list built from local independents' remits, with a slice of each fee paid back to those pharmacies.
customer: Executive directors and boards of multi-employer public benefit pools: school-district benefit trusts and joint powers authorities, county-association and municipal-league health trusts, with 5,000-100,000 lives across dozens of member entities. They buy once for many districts, are subject to open-records and audit pressure, and carry political risk if a PBM overcharge surfaces. Secondary: single counties or districts of 300-3,000 lives (free pilot tier). Payer is the pool, only when savings are verified. No PBM ever pays us.
problem: A pool pays its PBM a billed price per NDC per claim, and its contract may promise pass-through, lowest-of pricing or audit rights. It cannot see what the PBM paid the pharmacy, so the audit rights only test billing against the PBM's own data. Consultants either charge flat fees on PBM-supplied files or are compensated in part by carriers and PBMs (disclosure of broker and consultant compensation is now required under the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act, though disclosure is not independence). Local officials also watch the town's last pharmacy close while the same PBM underpays it. The old obstacle was a claim-level join needing consent from both sides, which is why the parent's tie-out looked hard.
solution: (1) Shadow price list: 20-40 in-region independents contribute NDC-level paid unit price, fill date and BIN/PCN/group only (no patient identifiers), extracted locally. The team reconstructs, by week, what the PBM's retail network actually pays per NDC for the top 200-300 generics that drive most retail generic spend. (2) Tie-out to any plan: take the pool's own claims file (via contractual audit right or public-records request) and compare billed unit price per NDC and date to the reconstructed pharmacy-paid price, producing a spread per member per month by drug. The pharmacies never need to have filled that plan's claims, because a network's pharmacy MAC is common across clients. Scope is stated honestly as retail, and mail and specialty are excluded unless data exists. (3) Screen first: only take pools whose contracts promise pass-through or lowest-of pricing, or who will run an RFP; ordinary legal spread contracts yield renegotiation, not breach recovery. (4) Act: audit-rights letter, renegotiation, or an RFP among 3-5 bidders including the Big 3 and transparent PBMs. (5) Optional Local Access Rider: the pool redirects about 20% of verified savings into a per-Rx access fee paid to in-county independents, a plan-design choice that keeps pharmacies alive and makes them allies. Savings are verified by replaying 12 months post-change against the same shadow list, with a cap.
why_now: Local officials have political will after Rite Aid's exit and Walgreens' closures. Fiduciary and open-records pressure on PBM spend is rising, transparent PBMs give pools credible switch destinations, and federal and state reporting mandates create a paper trail to check (verify current scope). LLM and OCR parsing makes contributing remits a one-day task. January renewals also drive RFP timing, and pools' boards typically decide in Q4-Q1.
revenue_model: Contingency of 12-15% of first-year verified savings, with a floor for pools over 10,000 lives. Illustrative: a 20,000-life pool spends roughly $25-30M a year on drugs; a 4-8% price gap is $1-2M and a 12% share is $120-240k. Recurring Pass-Through Monitor after the audit at about $0.30-0.40 per member per month ($70-95k a year for 20,000 lives). Data co-op dividend: 15-20% of fees paid to contributing pharmacies pro rata as a fair-market-value data license (never tied to referrals; structure with counsel, and keep it away from any federal program business). A few hundred such pools nationally make this a $30M-100M revenue niche.
non_obvious_insight: The employer does not need the claims the pharmacies saw. A PBM's retail pharmacy price list is common across clients in a network tier, so a crowd of pharmacies can reconstruct the hidden list once and any plan's billed prices can be compared to it. That turns a two-party consent-and-join problem into a price-list problem, and each additional pool costs almost nothing to audit. Contingency plus zero PBM money creates the only auditor with clean hands in a field where advisors are paid by the counterparties. Public bodies can compel data that private employers cannot, and the Local Access Rider turns the pharmacies from data suppliers into political allies.
first_30_days: Pick one state with many independents and public pools. Days 1-10: recruit 20 pharmacies through the state association, offering a free margin report in exchange for NDC-level price extracts; build the shadow list for the top 200 generics. Days 10-25: offer one county or district (300-3,000 lives) a free pilot, obtain its claims file by consent or open-records request, and produce a one-page spread letter with a dollars-per-member figure. Days 20-30: take the letter to a pool's executive director and broker and negotiate a contingency letter agreement (12% of verified savings, no fee if zero). Hire a healthcare attorney for data-license and dividend terms. Kill criterion: the pilot shows under 2% spread on retail generics, or fewer than 12 pharmacies agree to contribute.

title: The Pharmacy-Verified Reimbursement Index
one_liner: A furnisher-funded bureau, like a credit bureau for PBM payments, that turns what pharmacies actually pay and are actually paid into a reference index that state laws, Medicaid rate-setting and transparent-PBM contracts can cite, launching with a per-state Underwater Index sold to pharmacy associations for the 2027 legislative sessions.
customer: First six months: state pharmacy associations and their legal and lobbying arms in 3-5 states with active 2027 PBM agendas, at $25-60k per state per year. Next: state Medicaid pharmacy programs and state employee plans rebasing dispensing fees and ingredient-cost basis, departments of insurance enforcing below-cost and pay-parity laws, and TPAs, consultants and transparent PBMs that want an external yardstick. Eventually: contracts that reference the index directly. Contributing pharmacies pay nothing and get a dividend.
problem: Everyone who needs a reference price for pharmacy reimbursement relies on an interested party or a slow survey. NADAC is a voluntary survey of acquisition costs that says nothing about dispensing cost or what any PBM actually paid. State cost-of-dispensing studies are periodic, commissioned from consultants, and stale by publication (typically low-to-mid six figures each; verify). Legislators cannot say how many claims are paid below cost or by whom, so reimbursement-floor and pay-parity laws are enforced only by complaint. PBMs face no neutral definition of a fair payment. The parent's insight (pharmacies hold the ground-truth ledger) is stronger as infrastructure than as a one-off audit.
solution: Pharmacies use the free local-first margin report (same ingestion as a per-pharmacy tool) and opt in to contribute monthly aggregates: paid price and invoice cost per NDC per PBM network per state, plus optionally allocated cost-to-dispense. The bureau publishes: (a) a State Underwater Index (share of claims paid below acquisition cost, by PBM, only where 10+ pharmacies and 5+ per PBM cell contribute, with a 90-day lag); (b) an invoice-based acquisition cost index by NDC-week; (c) a quarterly cost-of-dispensing panel; (d) a regulator API to test whether a network paid below the index in a given month. Design floor for antitrust: a third-party-run exchange following the withdrawn 1996 health-care information-exchange conditions (5+ contributors, no contributor over 25% weight, data 3+ months old), plus counsel sign-off. Credibility: published methodology, an independent standards board (pharmacist, health economist, antitrust counsel, ex-regulator) and a sample audit by an accounting firm. Flywheel: an association buys the evidence pack, a law cites the index, the regulator needs the feed, contracts reference the index, and more pharmacies contribute for the dividend (25% of index revenue, pro rata by verified contribution).
why_now: A wave of state PBM reimbursement and transparency laws has arrived just as closures (Rite Aid gone, Walgreens closing about 1,200 stores, Drug Channels' August 2026 'K-shaped shakeout') give legislators a reason to demand numbers; 2027 sessions open in January and associations need evidence in Q4. The cost stack has collapsed: surveying a few hundred pharmacies by questionnaire costs six figures, but reading remits and invoices they already hold costs cents per claim now that OCR and LLM parsing handle messy formats and local-first processing removes the custody objection. This is a 2026 unlock, not a 2019 one.
revenue_model: Association evidence pack plus monthly index: $25-60k per state per year (target 3 states by month 6, about $100-150k). State Medicaid and employee-plan data licenses: $100-400k per state per year after a track record. DOI compliance feed: $50-150k. API licenses for TPAs, consultants and transparent PBMs: $25-100k. Index-in-contract licensing: about $0.02-0.05 per member per month, comparable to index-licensing models in other markets. Pharmacies: free plus a 25% revenue dividend. A 30-state footprint could plausibly support $10-30M a year.
non_obvious_insight: Standards win by being cited in statutes and contracts, and NADAC became the reference by being neutral, not by being complete. A pharmacy-verified index earns legitimacy differently, because it comes from invoices and remits (facts, not survey opinion), and it is the only source that can measure paid versus cost per PBM, which is exactly what a below-cost reimbursement law needs in order to be enforced. Associations fund the first index as lobbying evidence, the resulting laws then create a compliance buyer (the regulator), and each citation adds switching cost. The more PBM-owned pharmacies dominate the market, the more the independents' ledger is the only independent counterfactual.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: pick 2 states with an active 2027 PBM agenda and pitch the association executive directors: 'your state's Underwater Report by December 15 for session prep, co-branded.' Days 5-25: recruit 25 contributing pharmacies per state with a free margin report; run 6 months of remits and invoices through a local script by hand (concierge). Days 10-20: retain antitrust counsel for a 10-page methodology and thresholds memo, and seat a 5-person advisory board. Day 20-30: ask a state DOI or Medicaid pharmacy director for a 30-minute meeting on what they would need to enforce existing rules. By day 30: 2 signed letters of intent at about $25k and 40 contributing pharmacies. By day 60: first anonymized state index published. Kill criterion: no association will pay $25k for a state report before the session opens.
