title: Stack-Pooled 24/7 Article 14 Desk for Non-EU Brands
one_liner: A guaranteed-SLA Assigned Representative that files CRA Article 14 reports for 50-250 person non-EU connected-device brands, doing the triage once per shared component stack (Tuya, ESP-IDF, OpenWrt/Realtek) and fanning it out to every client on that stack.
customer: Medium-sized (50-250 staff, above the small-enterprise fine exemption) non-EU smart-home, e-mobility and networking brands based in Shenzhen, Taiwan, Korea and the US that sell into the EU via Amazon EU and retail. Their firmware comes from an ODM on one of 3 shared stacks: Tuya/Matter modules, ESP-IDF/ESP32, or OpenWrt/Realtek SDKs. The buyer is the head of product or compliance; the introduction comes through the EU Responsible Person/EPR (WEEE and packaging) service providers who already serve these sellers.
problem: These brands do not know what is inside their own firmware because the ODM built it, so they cannot tell whether a KEV/EUVD entry hits them. They have no one awake in Europe at 3am Sunday to decide 'actively exploited, affects us, file'. The 72h and 14-day clocks carry fines even if the 24h clock does not, and their EU retail partners will start asking for proof of process. Existing options each miss part of this. Software (CVD Portal, CRACI, Regulus) stops at timers and drafts, with filing left to the customer. Finite State and H-X draft notices but leave filing to the customer. TridentSec sells operations with no stated 24/7 or price. EcoComply is an AR mandate with no triage.
solution: Three things in one contract. (1) Named-analyst AR mandate plus a written SLA: triage decision within 4h and early warning filed inside 24h, weekends included, under a client-approved decision tree and pre-authorised actions. (2) Stack-pooled triage: a stack owner analyses each exploited entry once against the stack's component graph and issues per-firmware-version pre-approved VEX and notice drafts to every enrolled brand on that stack, so a client-named analyst only checks the version delta and files. (3) Firmware-fingerprint onboarding: the brand uploads a firmware image or OTA URL and the desk builds the component list itself, removing the missing-SBOM problem. Every KEV/EUVD entry also gets a timestamped per-product 'affected / not affected' decision, delivered monthly as a signed monitoring evidence log. That log is the recurring deliverable when nothing was exploited, and it is what retailers and market surveillance authorities will ask for. The 24h and 72h drills run on the client's own stack.
why_now: Article 14 reporting went live on 11 Sep 2026 (about 18 days ago) and the ENISA SRP opened the same day. Patchstack shows managed filing is now legal and being productised, so the window before it becomes a checkbox is roughly 6-12 months. Retail supplier manuals are being rewritten for the Dec 2027 full application, and GPSR (since Dec 2024) already trained these sellers to buy EU-representative services.
revenue_model: Base fee of about EUR 3.6-4.8k per year per product family (AR mandate, stack monitoring, monthly evidence log, one drill), well above EcoComply's EUR 1.5k AR-only anchor but below a monthly PSIRT retainer. Filing events cost EUR 1.5-3k each. Tabletop drills and 'clock audit' are EUR 1.5-5k. Wholesale white-label 24/7 back-end capacity is sold to TUV, DEKRA, Bureau Veritas, TridentSec and SBOM platforms. Target is 100 product families by month 12 (about EUR 400k ARR). One stack analyst covering 30-100 clients keeps gross margin above 65%.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not filing, it is the stack-to-firmware truth table. Brands do not know what is inside, but the desk sees which SDK forks and versions actually ship across dozens of brands. That is a cornered resource that a one-off consultancy cannot copy: each new client on a stack has near-zero marginal analyst cost and improves the fingerprint coverage. Also, 95% of what the desk produces is 'not affected'. Selling signed negative evidence as the monthly deliverable fixes the judges' 'insurance nobody buys until audited' flaw. Targeting 50-250 person firms sidesteps the Art 64(10) small-enterprise exemption on the 24h fine.
first_30_days: Week 1: get a professional-indemnity quote, and get written confirmation from ENISA or a national CSIRT that an external firm can serve as AR using personal EU Login accounts. Get counsel to settle how the 24h clock starts when the desk detects first, and draft the AR mandate and decision tree. Weeks 1-2: build component graphs for 3 stacks (ESP-IDF, OpenWrt/Realtek, Tuya) covering the top 25 exploited component families of the last 24 months, using open-source firmware unpacking such as EMBA. Weeks 2-4: sell a EUR 1.5k '24h drill + firmware fingerprint' to 20 brands sourced from 3 EPR/GPSR representative providers and Amazon-EU seller communities. The drill simulates an exploited entry hitting their stack and measures their real time-to-decision. Convert 5 into annual AR+desk contracts. Contract 3 part-time named analysts across time zones and confirm the SRP login rules apply to them.
lineage: mutation of I0374 ('Outsourced 24-Hour Vulnerability Reporting Desk (CRA)'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: TridentSec (PSIRT-as-a-Service), Finite State (managed CRA service), Cybellum (managed PSIRT / incident response service), Patchstack (managed CRA Article 14 reporting for open source). White space: The genuinely unserved piece is a contractually guaranteed 24/7 desk that files as the client's named Assigned Representative on the SRP, priced for 20-500 person device makers.
- Nobody found sells this in that form. TridentSec sells operations with no stated 24/7 and no published price. Finite State and H-X draft the notice but leave filing to the customer. Cybellum's service targets enterprises. CVD Portal, CRA Evidence and other tools stop at timers and packages, and their final filing is a human step by the customer. Patchstack files as AR but only for open source, and free.
- The intake step is also unserved: nobody takes weekend and night hits on 'is this KEV/EUVD entry in our firmware' and makes the call inside the 24h window.

What is not white space:
- The SBOM-to-CVE matching layer is commoditised. CVD Portal's Reporting tier is EUR 99/mo, and CRACI, Zealience, Regulus and ONEKEY sell the same thing.
- Boutiques and large consultancies can add 'PSIRT retainer' as a line item in weeks.
- The idea's claim that there is 'almost no visible tooling' is wrong. The service layer is thin, but the tooling layer is crowded.

Structural problems to plan around:
- The CRA fine exemption for micro and small enterprises on the 24h deadline (Art 64(10), https://cra-facts.com/penalties) removes the sharpest fear driver for the smallest customers. The 72h and 14-day deadlines still carry fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover.
- The SRP requires each AR to use a personal EU Login with MFA (https://www.enisa.europa.eu/topics/product-security/single-reporting-platform-srp/frequently-asked-questions), so named analysts must sit in the loop.
- Liability stays with the manufacturer, and the desk needs professional indemnity cover.
- The 24h clock starts when the manufacturer becomes aware, so a desk that spots an exploit may start the client's clock.
- An actively exploited vulnerability in one specific product's components is a low-frequency event. The retainer therefore risks being seen as insurance that customers only buy under audit pressure. | How this version avoids them: It refuses the generic 'PSIRT retainer' frame owned by TridentSec, Finite State and Cybellum. It sells the one thing they call customer-owned, which is a contractually guaranteed filing as the named AR. Incumbent MSSPs and certification bodies (Kudelski, TUV SUD, DEKRA, Bureau Veritas) become white-label distributors rather than rivals, since the desk offers them the back end they lack.

title: Retailer-Mandated Vulnerability Desk, Paid by Suppliers
one_liner: EU retailers and distributors put the desk on their approved-provider list for connected private-label and marketplace products, and their non-EU suppliers pay per SKU family, the way suppliers already pay retailer-nominated test labs, while the retailer gets a live exposure dashboard for its whole connected catalogue.
customer: Mandating party: product-compliance heads at mid-size EU consumer-electronics, DIY, sports (e-bikes), toy and discount retailers and distributors with 50-2,000 connected SKUs, including own-brand ranges. Payers: the 20-200 non-EU suppliers and ODMs behind those SKUs, each paying for the product families it sells to that retailer.
problem: A retailer that sells connected products under its own name is treated as the CRA manufacturer (to confirm with counsel), and an importer or distributor must chase unreachable non-EU suppliers when a vulnerability appears. Retailers have no view of which of their 1,800 connected SKUs contain the component in this morning's exploited-vulnerability headline. Their suppliers will not share firmware willingly and cannot show a 24h capability. The parent's problem is that small makers will not buy a desk they see as insurance. Here the party with the pain is not the party with the budget, and the retailer holds the leverage over the supplier.
solution: Product 1 is a retailer-paid 'Connected Range Exposure Baseline'. The desk collects firmware for 25-50 SKUs, which the retailer can compel from suppliers. It unpacks them, builds the component lists, checks current exposure to KEV/EUVD, tests each supplier's vulnerability-contact deliverability, and delivers a supplier-requirement clause for the next supplier manual. Product 2 is the ongoing service. The retailer's supplier manual names the desk (and any equivalent that passes its audit) as an approved provider. Each supplier enrols product families and the desk becomes its AR and 24/7 filing service, with stack-pooled triage. The retailer sees a live dashboard: for each SKU, affected, not affected or unknown, with supplier response time, supporting delist or recall decisions and its own regulatory file. The desk's fan-out model is reused, but the sales motion is one retailer mandate that brings in many suppliers.
why_now: CRA reporting has been live since 11 Sep 2026 and retailer supplier manuals are being rewritten ahead of Dec 2027. RED delegated-act cybersecurity rules (in force since Aug 2025) and GPSR (since Dec 2024) have already taught retail compliance teams to demand supplier documents and chase non-EU suppliers, so the workflow and budget owner exist. Retail groups have not yet named a vulnerability-reporting provider, so early mandates set the approved list.
revenue_model: Retailer-paid baseline of EUR 10-25k per range as the first sale. Dashboard licence of EUR 15-40k/yr per retailer. Supplier-paid subscription of EUR 600-1,200 per product family per year (falling with volume), plus EUR 1.5-3k per filing event, contractually paid by the supplier. One mid-size retailer with about 150 connected SKU families across 60 suppliers yields roughly EUR 100-130k/yr. Ten retailers gives roughly EUR 1M+ ARR with sales cost amortised across 60 or more payers per mandate.
non_obvious_insight: Change the buyer chain, not the product. Retail supply chains already run on the 'nominated lab' pattern, where the buyer mandates a provider and the supplier pays, and testing spend per product (EN 18031 or similar) dwarfs a EUR 600-1,200 annual desk fee, so suppliers barely resist. The dashboard turns a rare-event insurance product into something a compliance head opens every morning. And retail is the only place where a 24/7 filer has real leverage, because the retailer can delist a supplier that does not respond.
first_30_days: Identify 15 EU retail and distribution product-compliance heads via GPSR, RED and product-safety forums and trade-association events. Pitch each a EUR 12k baseline on 25-50 own-brand SKUs, with the deliverable being an exposure table plus supplier scorecard plus draft supplier-manual clause. Publish the clause as a free template through retail associations to seed demand. Sign 2 paying baselines by day 30-45. Use the baselines to build the first supplier cohorts (20-40 suppliers) and open partnership talks with SGS, Intertek, Bureau Veritas and TUV, who hold the current nominated-lab relationships, about white-labelling the 24/7 back end.

title: Outside-In Product Security Ratings for Insurers and Buyers
one_liner: Invert the desk: instead of helping one maker meet the 24-hour clock, independently measure from the outside whether thousands of connected-product makers can, and how exposed their shipped firmware is, and sell the scores and accumulation data to insurers, fleet buyers and lenders.
customer: First buyers: cyber and product-liability insurers and MGAs writing hardware and IoT makers, who need product-level exposure and accumulation data. Second: B2B fleet and infrastructure buyers (EV-charging operators, micromobility fleets, smart-building integrators, telcos buying CPE) that run supplier due diligence. Third: lenders and PE firms doing diligence on hardware brands. Manufacturers do not buy scores. They pay only for evidence review and remediation (a funnel to the desk).
problem: Every maker will soon say 'we comply' with the CRA, but the declarations are self-assessed and unverified until a market surveillance authority acts, which is slow and under-resourced. Insurers have no product-level model of accumulation, even though one exploited component hits every device on that stack. That is a catastrophe-modelling problem with no model. Procurement teams rely on questionnaires. The 24-hour clock is uniquely measurable: it is a dated, binary behaviour, unlike vague 'security posture', but nobody measures it from outside.
solution: A rating built outside-in from three layers. (a) Clock-readiness signals: security.txt, a published CVD policy, a working vulnerability contact, advisory history, stated support period, update cadence, and time-to-acknowledge on a clearly labelled contact-verification probe. (b) Firmware exposure: public firmware and OTA images, plus purchased units for top SKUs, unpacked and matched against exploited-vulnerability feeds to give a component list, exposure count and stack cluster. (c) Portfolio accumulation: for an insurer's book of insureds or a fleet buyer's supplier list, how many share a stack with a newly exploited component (the correlation number). Makers get a right of reply and can submit evidence, but cannot pay to change a score. Method: month 0-3 process-signal ratings for about 500 brands across e-mobility, smart home, routers, chargers, cameras and wearables; month 3-6 firmware exposure on the top 200 SKUs and the first accumulation reports. A separate analyst team runs the desk as the remediation upsell, behind a conflict-of-interest firewall.
why_now: The reporting duty went live on 11 Sep 2026, so 'time to report' just became a legal, checkable behaviour. Insurers are pricing CRA-driven product liability for the first time. Outside-in ratings are a proven category for company networks, and firmware unpacking is now cheap through open-source tooling and LLM-assisted triage. No dominant product-level rating exists.
revenue_model: Data licences of EUR 25-80k/yr per insurer or MGA; EUR 6-15k/yr per fleet operator or integrator per category; EUR 3-8k per diligence report for lenders and PE; EUR 2-5k per maker for evidence review; desk upsell as a funnel. Long term the rating is written into insurance pricing and procurement clauses ('supplier must hold a score of B or better'), giving standard-setter economics with a data moat.
non_obvious_insight: Insurers care about accumulation more than any single score, and the desk's pooled stack graph is exactly an accumulation model, so the same data serves the desk and the rating. Real filings and drills, with consent and anonymised, give a calibration set showing which outside-in signals predict actual time-to-report, and that validation is what makes a rating credible. Every desk client both funds and calibrates the rating. Flaw of the inversion: legal risk (defamation, unauthorised access), which is why probes are labelled, analysis uses lawfully obtained units and public images, scores are aggregated and methodology is public.
first_30_days: Weeks 1-2: build a crawler over 500 brands in 6 categories to score security.txt, CVD page, contact deliverability, advisory history and support-period statements. Week 2: send a benign, clearly labelled contact-verification probe and record response times. Week 3: publish a free report, 'State of vulnerability-reporting readiness among 500 connected-product brands' (for example, what share have no working vulnerability contact weeks after the duty began), to earn press and insurer attention. Weeks 3-4: hold 20 discovery calls with cyber/product-liability underwriters, MGAs and fleet operators, and offer paid pilots of EUR 8-15k to score their insureds or suppliers. Aim for one signed pilot by day 45 and confirm that no insurer-grade product rating already exists before scaling.

title: Section-Level Hydrogen and Helium Leads for Landmen
one_liner: Sell 90-day exclusive, page-linked lists of Nemaha-corridor sections with hydrogen or helium evidence buried in old mud logs, DST reports and driller notes, to the landmen and lease shops who spend the first dollars of every junior's program.
customer: Independent landmen and lease-brokerage shops (2-50 people) in Kansas, Nebraska and Oklahoma who assemble acreage for natural hydrogen and helium juniors, plus the roughly 40-120 junior explorers themselves (Rystad counts 40, AKAP counts 123 companies). Wedge buyer: the lease shop, because it is paid per acre leased, has a hard deadline (leases are taken in a rush after each well announcement), and has no geoscientist on staff.
problem: The free datasets (USGS/BLM 16,000 gas analyses, KGS OFR 2025-59, SMU/GDR temperatures) already give away the structured layers, so an atlas built on them is worthless. What they omit is the unstructured evidence in page images at KCC/KGS-type archives: mud-log gas shows, drill-stem-test and production-test gas notes, driller remarks such as 'gas would not burn', 'non-flammable' or 'heavy N2 odor', and water-well gas notes. Landmen today pick where to lease by copying the footprint of the last press release, which means they arrive after the price of a lease has already moved. Juniors that do this in-house (HyTerra, MAX Power, Koloma) are not customers, so the sellable market is the long tail and the lease shops serving it.
solution: A curated evidence-card product for one live fairway (Nemaha Uplift and Midcontinent Rift, KS/NE/OK). A VLM pipeline reads page images for a defined set of document types, a geologist verifies every card that reaches a customer, and each card carries the page image, the quoted text, and a confidence grade for sampling method, air-contamination signs (N2/O2 ratio) and analytical era. Cards roll up to a ranked list of 30-60 sections per block, plus a short 'do not lease' list of sections with clean hydrocarbon gas and no signal, which saves buyers money. Free layers (USGS, KGS, BLM/state mineral ownership) are ingested as baseline and shown for context but never sold. Delivered as a GeoPackage/KMZ and a PDF, with a courtroom-simple audit trail so a landman can defend the pick to a junior's board. Geothermal is dropped from v1 because SMU/GDR and GeoMap give it away.
why_now: Natural hydrogen went from about 10 to 40+ searching companies since 2020 (Rystad) and 123 by AKAP's count; HyTerra's Kansas McCoy 1 result (up to 83-96% H2) turned the Nemaha corridor into an active lease play in 2025-26, so lease shops need defensible picks right now. VLMs now read typed and handwritten well forms at cents per page, which broke the cost barrier that made a section-level re-read uneconomic before 2024. State surveys (KGS/KCC) are releasing more scans, and the academic OCR/LLM methods are public, which lowers the technical risk for a two-person team while making curation and speed the real product.
revenue_model: Entry pack: $5k non-exclusive, 3-township block. Exclusive block: $12-20k for a 90-day first-look on a 6-10 township block, renewable. Success fee: a capped per-net-acre finder fee (for example $2-5) or 0.5% ORRI on leases taken from exclusive-block sections. Year-1 bottom-up: 25 entry packs ($125k) + 6 exclusive blocks ($90k) + fees (~$50k) is about $265k with a two-person team; the business scales by adding fairways (Michigan/Ohio Rift extension, Colorado, Texas Panhandle helium) rather than by raising price per corridor. The buyer's ROI check: a 20,000-acre lease program at even $20-50/acre bonus is $0.4-1M, so a $5-15k pack is single-digit percent of spend.
non_obvious_insight: The product is not data, it is time-boxed scarcity. Lease information is perishable: once one buyer signs, the price of that section moves, so the value of a lead decays over weeks, and the right pricing unit is a 90-day exclusive option on a block, exactly how prospect generators sell in oil and gas. Second, the 0.5% hit rate seen in the Paris Basin OCR study (26 wells of about 5,000) is a weakness for a broad atlas but a strength for a precision shortlist: sell 40 sections, not 40,000, and let the 'do not lease' list carry the rest of the value. Third, buyers who drill a lead and share the result get a discount, and those results become a private ground-truth set that calibrates the confidence score, which no free dataset can copy.
first_30_days: Week 1: pick the Nemaha corridor counties in Kansas, download KGS/KCC scanned ACO-1 forms, driller logs, DST reports and mud logs for about 5,000 wells, and run VLM extraction on the four document types. Week 2: have a geologist verify the top 150 candidate cards and produce a 60-section block map with page-image links. Week 3: contact 10 lease shops and 10 juniors (LinkedIn plus the AAPL and Kansas Independent Oil and Gas Association member lists) with one free sample card and a demo map. Week 4: ask for a $5k prepay for the block pack. Kill test from the parent: if fewer than 3 of 10 prepay, stop and go to the state-survey channel instead. Also offer an exclusive 90-day option on the sections buyers like best.

competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. White space: The wedge that remains is narrow but real. Nobody found sells page-level, provenance-linked hydrogen, helium and heat evidence extracted from the unstructured parts of old well files. That means mud-log gas shows, drill-stem-test and production-test reports, driller notes such as non-flammable gas, and water-well gas, all at lease-block or section level. Koloma, HyTerra, MAX Power, Zanskar: they hold their own in-house archives and are not customers, and our buyers are the lease shops and the long tail they cannot serve. title: Plug-or-Pitch: Turning Idle Wells Into Assets
one_liner: Screen idle and orphan oil wells for hydrogen, helium and heat evidence, and get paid a share of the plugging liability that disappears when a well is transferred to an explorer who wants a ready-made hole to the basement.
customer: The payer is the liability holder, not the explorer. Wedge: independent operators in Kansas and Oklahoma holding 50-500 idle, shut-in or temporarily abandoned wells under rising plugging and bonding pressure. Phase 2: state orphan-well programs (funded by the $4.7B IIJA orphan-well money) and state land offices. The other side of the transaction, who takes the well and pays a placement fee, is a hydrogen, helium or geothermal junior that today drills new holes at seven-figure cost.
problem: An idle well is a negative asset: plugging often costs tens of thousands of dollars per well (an estimate to confirm state by state), and operators or states carry that liability for years. Meanwhile the parent idea's buyers spend roughly seven figures to drill a test hole to basement, and a wellbore that already penetrates basement, with a file that shows non-flammable gas or elevated temperature, is worth many multiples of its plugging cost to them. The two sides never find each other because the evidence sits in scanned well files, and juniors in the parent's research 'do not budget $15-50k a year for data' but do budget hard money for holes. Price anchored to a known plugging cost is a much easier sale than price anchored to speculative exploration value.
solution: A per-well 'Reuse Dossier' built from each idle well's own file and its offsets: hydrogen/helium/N2-rich gas shows from mud logs, DSTs and driller notes, depth to basement, casing/cement/plugging status, bottom-hole temperature and gradient, and produced-water chemistry, each with page-image provenance and a confidence grade. A Reuse Score estimates re-entry cost against new-drill cost and states the single test that would confirm the lead. Wells are bundled into small re-entry lots and placed with repurposers under a recorded assignment of plugging liability (with state transfer approval and financial assurance), often keeping a retained royalty or carry for the seller. The operator pays nothing upfront: screening is free and the startup is paid from the avoided liability and from the placement. Geothermal scoring can be sourced from partners such as WellScout AI rather than built.
why_now: State and federal pressure on idle wells is at its peak: IIJA orphan-well plugging money is flowing through the late 2020s, and states have built lists that did not exist five years ago. Hydrogen and helium juniors raised $20M-$245M rounds (Koloma, Terra AI, Mantle8) and HyTerra proved that twinning historic wells works, so demand for cheap access to basement-penetrating holes is real. VLM extraction cost per well file has collapsed to a few dollars, which makes free screening for an operator affordable on a contingency basis; that would have been uneconomic in 2022.
revenue_model: Contingent success fee of about 15% of the avoided plugging cost (from the operator or state) when a well transfers, plus a $10-25k placement fee (or 5% of any bonus or sale price) from the repurposer, plus $500-1,500 for a premium dossier and a $10-25k/year 'reuse lot' feed for juniors. Illustrative unit economics: an operator with 200 idle wells costs about $16k to screen (about $80/well compute plus geologist review); if 1-2% clear the bar (1-2 wells above the 0.5% Paris Basin rate is plausible for a targeted fairway) and each saves about $40k of plugging cost, revenue is $6-12k in liability fees plus placement fees per portfolio, and a state program is 10-50x that. The wedge is deliberately contingent so the customer has no downside.
non_obvious_insight: The bid-ask spread has the wrong sign: the holder sees a negative asset (minus the plugging cost) and the explorer sees a hole worth a multiple of its plugging cost, and the only missing ingredient is verified evidence about which wells sit on the positive side. Low hit rate (about 0.5% in the Paris Basin study) kills a subscription atlas but not a contingency screen, because the operator's cost is zero and one hit pays for the portfolio. The startup's true asset is not the data but the transferable, state-approved playbook for liability assignment plus a book of buyers, which creates a two-sided market that data vendors and free datasets cannot replicate.
first_30_days: Week 1: pull the public inactive/TA well lists from the Kansas KCC and Oklahoma OCC and pick 300 wells that reach basement in the Nemaha corridor. Week 2: extract their files and offsets and produce 30 Reuse Dossiers with a scored top 10. Week 3: call 25 independent operators and the plugging-fund manager at one state agency with the offer 'give us your 100 worst idle wells, screening is free, we take 15% of the avoided plugging cost if we place a well'. In parallel get 2-3 juniors to sign non-binding LOIs to consider re-entry lots. Week 4: sign 3 contingency agreements and confirm with the state regulator what transfer-with-assumption of liability requires. Before building further, run 15 calls to check the two unverified assumptions: state transfer rules and re-entry cost versus a new drill.

title: Pumper-Sampled Hydrogen and Helium Ground-Truth Registry
one_liner: Stop digging through what the industry failed to measure and start measuring it: pay lease pumpers to grab wellhead gas samples, assay them for hydrogen and helium, and build the depth-tagged registry that becomes the standard for what is under the ground.
customer: Wedge: hydrogen, helium and geothermal explorers and their modelers (Koloma-type juniors outside their own acreage, HyTerra/MAX Power-type juniors, Terra AI, HyReveal) who commission sampling campaigns across a fairway. Contributors: small independent operators and the pumpers (lease operators) who visit each well weekly, starting with the Kansas and Oklahoma independents. Later payers: lenders, insurers and resource certifiers who need a standard, auditable measurement before they finance a discovery.
problem: Old well files are noisy for a structural reason: the industry never measured hydrogen or helium. Standard mud-logging and production gas analysis use flame-ionization detectors that cannot see H2 or He, so a 1935 'gas contains 40% hydrogen' note is an accident, contamination and sampling method are unknown, and the parent's archive is capped at about 16,000 free analyses and a 0.5% hit rate. Explorers who need to know where hydrogen and helium are today either drill blind, run private one-off campaigns, or use soil-gas anomalies. Nobody keeps a standardized, depth-tagged, contamination-corrected, fresh measurement for the roughly one million producing US wells or the tens of thousands of new holes drilled each year.
solution: A three-layer business. Layer 1 (first product, sellable in 6 months): buyer-commissioned sampling campaigns. A buyer specifies a transect or 200-well fairway; operators allow their pumpers to fill a $12 sample container at the casinghead or separator vent following a safety protocol; a bounty of about $25 goes to the pumper; samples go to a partner lab or an in-house GC-TCD unit, and the buyer gets H2/He/N2/CO2/Ar/O2/C1-C6 with GPS, photo, chain of custody and an air-contamination correction. Layer 2: a registry with an open measurement spec (sampling method, contamination QC, lab certification) and a contribution scheme: operators get a free full gas assay (which many already pay $50-150 for to support BTU, sales or flaring reports, a hypothesis to test), exclusive rights to their own well results for 90-180 days, and a revenue share. Layer 3: a certified add-on H2/He TCD channel for mud-logging contractors and geothermal drillers so every new hole feeds the registry, and a scoring layer that uses fresh samples to calibrate the archive-based confidence grades from the parent idea.
why_now: Hydrogen and helium explorers are funded (Koloma about $245M, Mantle8 EUR31M, Terra AI $20M with BHP and Khosla, 123 companies per AKAP) but starved of trustworthy labels, and the modelers (Terra AI, HyReveal) explicitly need fresh ground-truth data. Portable micro-GC/TCD analyzers and smartphone chain-of-custody have made distributed sampling cheap, and VLM tools make the old archive a cheap starting prior rather than the product. Geothermal and helium buyers want auditable data for financing, and no standard exists yet, which is the moment a standard can be set.
revenue_model: Sampling campaigns at about $250 per well (cost roughly $60-120 with in-house GC and $130-170 with outside labs); a 200-well campaign is about $50k. Registry subscriptions of $10-50k per basin per year for explorers and modelers. Data licenses to modelers and financiers. Lab certification and channel fees from mud-logging contractors. Optional later: small overriding royalties on leases taken over registry-flagged sections. Year-1 target: 1,500-3,000 wells sampled, 5-8 campaign customers (about $300-400k), 10 registry subscribers.
non_obvious_insight: The right inversion is that data quality, not data availability, is the bottleneck: every archive layer the parent proposed is limited by a measurement nobody made. Because operators pay for gas analysis anyway, the marginal cost of adding H2 and He to a routine sample is almost zero, so the contributor network can be built with a bounty rather than a salesforce. The registry's moat is network economics plus a standard: contributors are also the sources, the modelers need the labels, and lenders will trust the one dataset with certified provenance. Fresh samples also calibrate the archive-derived confidence scores, so the parent idea becomes a cheap prior on top of a proprietary ground-truth set.
first_30_days: Week 1: contract a commercial gas lab that runs GC-TCD (or buy a used micro-GC with TCD for about $15-25k) and design the sample kit and safety protocol with an experienced pumper. Week 2: sign 2 independent operators (about 100 wells each, via the Kansas Independent Oil and Gas Association and personal referrals) on the free-assay, 90-day-exclusive deal. Week 3: sample 100 wells across a transect crossing the Nemaha uplift and publish a one-page ground-truth map. Week 4: pitch 15 juniors and modelers a 200-well campaign at $250 per well with half prepaid, and ask HyReveal and Terra AI for a data-partner letter. Kill test: if no buyer prepays by week 6, sell the same samples as a section-level pack to landmen (see the sharpened offspring).

title: Line-Keyed Cross-Examination Kits for LOP Defense
one_liner: A $395, 48-hour kit for defense counsel that turns a letter-of-protection bill into line-by-line cross-examination questions and a signed rebuttal, with the testifying coder as the real profit center.
customer: Wedge: 3-20 lawyer defense boutiques in Houston-area and Atlanta-metro courts that take carrier-assigned auto and commercial-vehicle bodily-injury files worth $25k-$250k. On those files a $3-5k billing expert usually needs carrier pre-approval or gets skipped. Buyer is the associate or partner running the file. Florida is a second-phase rebuttal product, not the entry market.
problem: Defense lawyers do not lose LOP cases for lack of a reasonable-value number. They lose because they cannot make the treating doctor's price, referral source and billing habits look bad on the stand. The billing expert is a $3-5k bespoke item, so on mid-size files it goes unordered and inflated bills get tried at face value. Claims examiners forward demand packages, often polished by plaintiff AI tools, without anyone able to read the coding. The parent idea sold a benchmark report. Florida's 768.0427 already gives a free Medicare-multiple benchmark, and hospital price files barely touch the chiropractors, pain clinics and physician-owned ASCs that do most LOP care.
solution: Order flow: firm uploads the LOP disclosure packet (letter, itemized CMS-1500/UB-04, records, factoring purchase price and referral facts where disclosed). Within 48 hours the kit returns (1) a line-item coded audit flagging unbundling, modifier-25 patterns, E/M level outliers and stacked facility fees; (2) a benchmark table with three anchors that are not hospital files: Medicare multiple, the same billing TIN's own negotiated rates from payer Transparency-in-Coverage files where it is in-network, and the factor's purchase price when disclosed; (3) a provider-bias sheet listing referral and ownership facts to ask about; (4) a two-page cross-examination outline keyed to specific bill lines for the treating-provider deposition; (5) a rebuttal outline against the plaintiff's billing expert, who will cite FAIR Health charge percentiles (the kit shows charges are what providers bill, not what anyone pays); (6) optional signed declaration; (7) optional testimony by a named coder-expert. LLM pre-codes the bill and a CPC/CCS reviews and signs in about 25 minutes, so marginal cost is roughly $40-90 per kit. Intake parsers are built for the structured demand packages plaintiff AI tools produce, so the plaintiff's arms race becomes feedstock.
why_now: Florida (2023) and Georgia (2025) reforms made LOP arrangements and amounts actually paid discoverable, and other states, including Texas, are fighting the same paid-versus-incurred battles. Plaintiff-side AI (EvenUp at a $2B+ valuation) is making bills and demands more polished, which raises defense spend on rebuttal. Payer Transparency-in-Coverage files give rates by billing TIN and NPI for free, and LLM bill extraction cuts coder time per file by more than half. None of this was workable in 2019. (Verify the current statutory status of each state before launch; I could not re-check because the search budget was exhausted.)
revenue_model: Kit $395 per file, deliberately set below the amount at which carrier litigation guidelines typically require expert pre-approval (verify the threshold in the first 10 calls). First kit free for each new firm. Signed declaration $1,900. Deposition prep $250/hr. Trial or deposition testimony $3,500/day. Panel-counsel program for firms or carrier panels at $3-6k/month for a kit quota. Target mix after 6 months: 12 firms at about 5 kits/month is about $24k/month, plus 10-15% of kits converting to declarations or testimony at 60-70% gross margin. Kits are the funnel, testimony is the margin.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is a testifying coder with a public track record in that state, not coder hours or a benchmark. Judges and juries reward a credentialed ex-hospital revenue-integrity director who has survived Daubert and cross before. Every deposition transcript, Daubert or Robinson ruling, judge and outcome the company accumulates becomes a compounding cornered resource (process power plus brand) that a carrier workflow vendor cannot copy by hiring nurses. Pricing below the pre-approval threshold is also a distribution hack. Counsel can order without asking the carrier, and the carrier sees the value afterward.
first_30_days: Days 1-3: spend one day on the searches the parent's check could not run ('letter of protection billing expert flat fee', 'reasonable value LOP Texas Georgia') to confirm no flat-fee incumbent exists, then run 15 calls with defense lawyers to confirm the pre-approval threshold and how often the billing expert is skipped. Days 4-14: recruit two testifying coders (one Texas, one Georgia, ex-hospital or health-system revenue integrity, CPC/CCS/CPMA) plus 2 contractor coders, and one ex-panel-counsel partner as methodology advisor. Build the kit template from Medicare fee schedules and Transparency-in-Coverage files for the top payers in Houston and Atlanta, filtered to the roughly 60 CPT codes that dominate LOP bills (99203-99215, 97110-97140, 98940-98942, 72148, 73721, 62323, 64483, 64493-64495). Days 15-30: give 10 free kits on live files in exchange for a 30-minute review and a quote, then convert 3-5 firms to $395 kits and price the first declaration.

title: Independent Post-Reform Valuation for Medical Lien Funders
one_liner: A neutral, coder-signed valuation agent that tells LOP factoring companies and the lenders behind them what their medical receivables are worth after tort reform.
customer: Regional medical-lien funders and LOP factoring companies in Florida, Texas and Georgia that buy receivables from ortho, pain, chiropractic and ASC providers, plus the warehouse lenders and private-credit funds financing them. Buyer is the funder's CFO or head of underwriting, with the lender's credit analyst as the forcing party. First target list is 30-40 funders.
problem: Funders buy receivables at a fraction of billed charges, priced on attorney reputation and past collections. Reform changes the collateral. In Florida, 768.0427 makes the LOP, coded billing, the factoring purchase price and referral relationship disclosable and admissible, and amounts actually paid become the reference point. Cases accruing after March 2023 are only now reaching settlement, so the first post-reform collection cohort is landing on funders' books. Their lenders want borrowing-base reporting and independent collateral valuation, and no neutral standard exists. Carrier vendors, plaintiff platforms and data utilities serve everyone but the person holding the risk.
solution: Phase 1, fixed-fee 'Book Audit' in 10 business days. The funder sends a de-identified export (purchase price, coded bill lines, provider NPI, attorney, venue, dates, outcomes on closed files). Output: cohort-level expected collection and time-to-cash curves under current state rules; the top-decile at-risk receivables; a signed independent valuation letter the funder can hand to its lender or investors; and a 'bid sheet' of maximum purchase price by CPT bundle, provider type, venue and attorney tier. Phase 2: per-receivable scoring at purchase and monthly re-marking through a portal or API. Phase 3: lender-appointed valuation agent, where the warehouse lender designates and co-signs the engagement and receives monthly portfolio monitoring, like a collateral field exam. The coder bench and methodology from the parent are reused, but the output is a valuation, not a courtroom opinion.
why_now: First post-reform (Florida 2023) case cohort is resolving in 2026, so books are repricing now and lenders are asking questions. Private credit has moved into esoteric legal and medical receivables, and lenders in that class expect third-party collateral valuation. Florida's mandatory disclosure of factoring purchase price means every funder now knows its own buy price is evidence against the receivable, which forces a rethink of pricing and structure. LLM bill extraction makes coding a 2,000-line portfolio in days instead of months, with coder sampling for sign-off.
revenue_model: Book Audit $15-40k per portfolio, repeated semiannually. Subscription $3-6k/month plus $12-25 per receivable scored. Lender-facing monitoring $2-4k/month per credit facility, mandated by covenant. Illustration: 30 funders at $60k/year is about $1.8M, with upside from expanding to hospital-lien, workers' comp lien and pre-settlement receivables, and eventually independent collateral valuation for rated securitizations of medical receivables, where third-party valuation is mandatory.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody has looked at LOP bills as collateral. The same benchmark that is a weapon in a deposition is a valuation input in a credit agreement, and the buyer has the best data. Funders hold the only ground-truth set of what LOP bills actually settle for, by code, provider, attorney and venue, which carriers, defense lawyers and every vendor lack. Serving funders buys that dataset and tightens every later model. The issuer-pays conflict that damaged rating agencies is solved by making the lender the appointing party and by fixed fees, like an ABL field examiner.
first_30_days: Pull UCC-1 filings (for example the Florida Secured Transaction Registry) that name medical receivables or accounts as collateral, to identify funders and the banks and credit funds financing them. Recruit two coders, one ex-ABL field examiner or credit analyst who has run a borrowing-base review, and one part-time attorney to build a rules matrix by state. Run a blind backtest pilot with 2-3 funders. They send 200-500 closed receivables with outcomes hidden, we predict the realized collection, they compare. Offer it free in exchange for permission to use the calibration. Convert the best pilot to an $18-25k Book Audit and use the result to approach that funder's lender.

title: Subpoena-Ready Rate Cards for Lien-Based Clinics
one_liner: Invert the parent by selling the coder bench to the clinics being attacked, using their own ledgers to defend their prices and build the industry's only record of what LOP care actually collects.
customer: Owner-operators of multi-location chiropractic groups, pain-management practices, ortho groups and physician-owned ASCs in Florida, Texas and Georgia that treat on letters of protection, especially those who have just received a subpoena or whose plaintiff-firm partners ask for 'defensible bills'. Wedge is 3-15 location groups in Houston, Atlanta, Orlando, Tampa and Miami. Plaintiff-firm referral managers act as influencers and channel.
problem: Reform made a clinic's pricing method, LOP arrangements, factoring and referral relationships discoverable. Owners are now deposed on how they priced a CPT code, and 'it is our standard rate' loses against a chart showing 8-15x Medicare. The honest answer is that LOP care is a credit product. The clinic waits 12-24 months, bears loss risk and often writes off 30-60% blindly at settlement. That premium is legitimate but undocumented, and nobody derives it from the clinic's own ledger. Plaintiff lawyers are not billing experts, and today's billing experts are hired after the attack.
solution: Product: LOP rate-card defense. (1) Ledger study: ingest 24-36 months of the clinic's LOP AR ledger from its practice-management export, computing realized collection per billed dollar, time-to-cash and non-recovery by code, attorney and venue. (2) Cost-of-carry model: derive a documented deferred-payment and collection-risk premium from that data. (3) Rate-card rebuild: restructure the fee schedule to a stated formula (local commercial median from payer Transparency-in-Coverage files times the documented premium) with coding hygiene fixes, written up in a dated, contemporaneous methodology memo signed by a certified coder and a health economist or CPA. (4) Deposition-defense packet for the owner and a ready declaration. (5) Annual attestation, quarterly drift check, and a per-bill 'rate-card attestation' clinics can attach. Scope excludes anything that hides referral or funding relationships. Disclosure remains counsel's job, and a healthcare regulatory lawyer reviews the offer for anti-kickback and fee-splitting risk.
why_now: Florida cases post-2023 and Georgia cases post-2025 are producing the first wave of provider subpoenas and depositions about rate-setting and referral relationships. Messy practice-management exports can now be normalized cheaply with LLMs, and payer Transparency-in-Coverage files make a local commercial median computable for free. Neither existed at usable cost in 2019.
revenue_model: Ledger X-ray free. Rate-card study $6.5k one-time. Monitoring and attestation $750-1,500/month per practice. Deposition prep $250/hr. Illustration: 100 clinics at $6.5k plus $900/month is about $1.7M in year one. The 10x layer is data and standard. After 150+ clinics and 30 months of ledgers, publish a quarterly 'LOP Realized Value Index' (free summary, paid detail) sold to carriers, funders, reinsurers and legislators, plus a registry that carriers pay to query. Carriers that agree to a fast lane for attested bills within the index band create a private fee schedule for the schedule-less LOP world, the way workers' comp fee schedules replaced price fights. Balance-sheet optionality later is a fund that buys attested receivables at index-based prices.
non_obvious_insight: The best defense of an LOP bill is explaining why it is what it is, not proving it is cheap, and the party holding the most valuable data on real LOP value is the clinic, not the carrier or the lawyer. Selling to the attacked party is the cheapest way to acquire that data, since a subpoena is a fear purchase with budget behind it. Providers will hand ledgers to a neutral appraiser but never to a carrier vendor, which is counter-positioning that Enlyte and CLARA cannot copy without alienating carriers. The credibility risk is issuer-pays conflict, mitigated by algorithmic pass/fail thresholds, a published methodology, a visible fail rate, a carrier-side advisory seat and a firewall from any case-specific testimony.
first_30_days: Pick Houston and Orlando/Tampa. Build a list of 60 lien-based groups from provider directories and plaintiff-firm referral networks, and approach through state chiropractic and pain-medicine associations and referral managers at plaintiff firms. Offer the free 'ledger X-ray': send an AR export and in 5 days get a one-page showing billed versus collected, time-to-cash and the five lines an expert would attack first. Sign 5 paid studies at $6.5k within 60 days. In parallel, hold 3 carrier claims-executive calls to test whether an attested schedule would be accepted in pre-suit, and one call with a healthcare regulatory attorney on structure and disclaimers.

Stat. 768.0427 (https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0768/Sections/0768.0427.html) already makes evidence of what was actually paid, or 120% of Medicare (170% of Medicaid where there is no Medicare rate), the benchmark for uninsured claimants. The fetched summary does not settle whether that applies to LOP treatment, so check the statute text. A large part of the Florida 'report' is therefore a Medicare-multiple calculation from free CMS files, which a claims shop or existing vendor could copy quickly. (b) The hospital price-transparency 'why now' is weaker than the idea claims. CMS says enforcement of the new rules starts April 1, 2026 (https://www.cms.gov/priorities/key-initiatives/hospital-price-transparency). But LOP care is mostly delivered by chiropractors, pain clinics, orthopedic groups and physician-owned ASCs, not hospitals. I inferred that from how LOP cases usually work and did not verify it. The defensible professional-fee benchmarks would come from Medicare multiples, payer transparency-in-coverage files or licensed data, not hospital files. | How this version avoids them: Enlyte and CLARA serve carriers and cannot sell to providers without channel conflict, and providers will not share ledgers with them. FAIR Health measures charges and allowed amounts, while we measure realized LOP collections and carry cost, so the index complements it and rebuts the plaintiff's usual-and-customary anchor. EvenUp is plaintiff-side treatment and demand software with no rate-card defense and is a possible channel partner for its firms' referral networks. Turquoise does payer-contracting analytics, not lien care, and is a data supplier with some entrant risk to watch. The closest direct substitute is per-case billing experts (including plaintiff-side JurisPro-type experts). They are hired after the attack and sell single-case declarations, while this is contemporaneous, subscription-based, data-backed documentation that carries more weight than a declaration created after the fact.

title: Consent Ledger for Land-Scheme Family Cohorts
one_liner: A cohort-priced heir-consent ledger sold to the family 'treasurer' of heirs from ONE 1960s-80s land-buying company or settlement scheme, with a partner law firm as the legal entity of record and a recurring Title Watch on top.
customer: The 'family treasurer': the salaried eldest or most solvent sibling (30-55, in Nairobi, Nakuru, Dallas or Dubai) of a family whose parent or grandparent was an allottee or member of one named land-buying company or settlement scheme in one county (pick one scheme in Murang'a, Kiambu, Nakuru or Trans Nzoia through the founder's own church/alumni/clan network). Distribution partners are the scheme's officials and welfare committee. One partner law firm is the entity of record for all legal work.
problem: Judges flagged three flaws in the parent: thin unit economics (field trips per single estate eat the KES 15-25k fee), the Advocates Act risk of a non-lawyer company selling a 'court-ready bundle' (from memory, unverified), and unproven diaspora willingness to pay. The underlying pain is real but narrower than 'succession': the blocker is proving that all 8-20 heirs were found, asked and agreed, and getting them to sign at all. There is also a sharper trigger than paperwork guilt: land in a dead man's name is an easy target for forged transfers and brokers, and absent children fear waking up to find it sold. A generic 'succession kit' has neither the density to be profitable nor a legal shape that survives scrutiny.
solution: Three steps, each cheap to buy. (0) 'Title Check', KES 1,500 over WhatsApp: photo of the title or parcel number, official search (about KES 500 fee, verify), LLM read of the result, one-page plain-language answer: registered owner, is that person dead, who must be involved. (1) 'Consent Ledger', KES 18k (KES 14k cohort price when 8+ estates from the same chief's location are booked): Kenyan name-variant-reconciled heir map, list of required consents, and a live status board the treasurer shares in the family WhatsApp group ('9 of 14 heirs signed, 3 outstanding, reasons'). A home-area agent runs one scheduled 'signing day' per chief's location per month for chief's-letter requests, ID copies, thumbprints and video consent; heirs elsewhere sign by ID-video on WhatsApp witnessed by the nearest agent. Output is a non-legal 'Consent and Kinship Evidence Pack' with a dispute flag (silent heir, second household, contested claim). The partner law firm receives the pack through a case-management seat, drafts, files and shepherds the case, and bills its own scale fee directly; the company never drafts affidavits or quotes legal fees. (2) 'Title Watch', KES 4k per parcel per year: alerts on registry changes plus a caution/restriction workflow run through the advocate. Asset discovery (SACCO, coop, UFAA letters) is a flat add-on sold only after grant, since UFAA beneficiary claims need the confirmed grant first.
why_now: LLMs now read scanned titles, IDs and share certificates and reconcile Kenyan name variants for cents a page, and drafting copilots (Wakili-Intel appeared July 2026 as a hobby project) are commoditising the paperwork, so the scarce, defensible piece moves to field evidence and multi-heir consent, which is still custom work. The settlement-scheme allottee generation is dying now. WhatsApp Business plus M-Pesa/card make small cross-border payments routine, and digitised searches (Ardhisasa; coverage to be verified) cut registry running. None of this worked in 2019: reading messy scans and chatting in Swahili and English at this cost did not exist.
revenue_model: Ladder per estate: KES 1.5k Title Check, then KES 18k ledger (14k at cohort density), then KES 3k flat advocate seat fee per file (software and case management charge, explicitly not a fee split; verify with counsel), then KES 4k/yr Title Watch, then KES 5k asset-discovery add-on after grant. Assumption to test: at cohort density, field plus search plus ops cost is about KES 7-8k per ledger versus KES 12-15k for one-off estates, giving roughly 45-55% gross margin and about KES 26-30k first-year revenue per estate. A county team (coordinator, 2 agents, share of ops, about KES 3M a year) breaks even near 200 estates a year, which one large scheme can supply. Title Watch gives recurring revenue that the parent lacked.
non_obvious_insight: The unit of production is not the estate but the chief's location. Neighbouring estates in one scheme share the same registry, chief, original allottee list, surnames and often the same feuds, so every ledger makes the next one cheaper and better (name-variant dictionary, known-disputer flags, chief relationships). That density economy is invisible to per-estate advocates and to national software. Second, the treasurer is buying a status board, not paperwork: it turns family guilt and pressure into visible progress that nudges holdout siblings. Third, fear of land-grabbing is the purchase trigger, so sell 'protect it' first and 'sort the succession' second.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: pick one scheme and one county through your own family, church or alumni network; sign one partner law firm as entity of record on a one-page engagement letter (advocate bills the client directly; company charges a flat seat fee). Days 7-20: launch the WhatsApp 'Is your family land still in a dead man's name?' Title Check at KES 1,500 in the scheme's clan and welfare WhatsApp groups and in diaspora groups for that county; run 40 checks. Days 20-30: convert to 10 pre-sold Consent Ledgers at pilot price, of which at least 8 in one chief's location; schedule the first group signing day. Core metrics: days from intake to all heirs signed, percent of heirs signed on the first visit, and check-to-ledger conversion. Kill test: fewer than 3 of 40 checkers buy a ledger.

title: SACCO-Financed Succession Desk, Paid on Milestones
one_liner: A white-label succession desk that payroll SACCOs offer their members: a check-off-repaid 'estate clearing loan' goes into a milestone escrow, and the company earns only as each case step is proven.
customer: The payer and channel is the mid-size payroll or sector SACCO (5k-100k members: teachers, health workers, county staff, police and prison staff) in central and western Kenya, sold to the CEO and credit committee. End users are two groups: salaried members (30-55) whose deceased parent's land is still in a dead name, and heirs of deceased members whose deposits and shares are stuck without a grant. The diaspora child is no longer the only payer.
problem: SACCOs hold two stuck pools. First, deposits and shares of deceased members that cannot be paid out cleanly until heirs produce a grant or agree among themselves (many SACCOs allow small nominee payouts; larger balances and family disputes stall; exact limits to verify): a governance headache, audit query and source of angry families. Second, living members who would borrow large development or mortgage loans against family land, but the land is in a dead person's name so the SACCO cannot take security. Members themselves cannot find a KES 100-250k lump sum for advocate, fees and travel, and distrust strangers who take money for land paperwork, yet they have salaries that can be deducted at source.
solution: The SACCO brands a 'Succession Desk'; the company runs it. Wedge (sellable in 30 days, no SACCO cash outlay): 'Deceased-Member Deposit Clearing'. The SACCO gives a letter of introduction and the list of stuck estates; the company does WhatsApp intake, heir map, consents and field work with a fixed-fee advocate panel; heirs consent in writing to a flat fee deducted from the released deposits. Stage 2, after three or more cases close: 'Estate Clearing Loan' for living members, sized KES 60-250k and repaid by payroll check-off. Proceeds sit in a SACCO-held milestone escrow released at proven steps: heir map and consent pack complete, petition filed and gazetted, confirmation of grant, transmission registered. Advocate fees (from a pre-agreed schedule) and the company's fee are paid from escrow to each party directly against milestones, so the member never hands cash to a stranger and the company never holds client money. At the end the SACCO has a pledgeable title (with heirs' consents to charge) and can pre-approve a development or mortgage loan.
why_now: Payroll SACCOs now run digital member ledgers, USSD and M-Pesa collections, and face competition from banks and digital lenders for their best salaried members, so they want secured, sticky products. Regulator attention on SACCO governance and deceased or dormant member balances (SASRA; verify current rules) makes stuck estates a board-level problem. LLM intake and heir mapping cut the cost of a case enough that a flat KES 12-18k fee works inside a loan. The succession backlog from 1960s-80s allottees is at its peak. Without cheap AI intake the desk would have needed paralegal armies, so this business model did not pencil out in 2019.
revenue_model: Contingent milestone fees of KES 12-18k per estate case, split over the four milestones (for example 40% at consents plus filing, 60% at grant and transmission), funded either from released deposits (deceased-member cases) or from estate clearing loan proceeds via escrow. The company takes no interest and no percentage of estate value. Flat per-loan bounty of KES 3-5k when a cleared title later secures a SACCO loan. After a successful pilot, a white-label desk fee of about KES 150-250k a year per SACCO. Illustration: 10 SACCOs at 100 cases a year each is roughly KES 15M in case fees plus about KES 2M in platform fees (about US$130k), with the SACCOs, not the company, carrying credit risk. The SACCO earns loan interest and clears a liability.
non_obvious_insight: Affordability and trust, not awareness, are the barriers, and the SACCO uniquely owns what neither an advocate nor a startup can: payroll check-off (repayment that costs almost nothing to collect), a welfare touchpoint at the exact moment of a death, and a balance-sheet motive (release stuck deposits, make land pledgeable). The estate clearing loan turns a scary lump sum into a monthly deduction, and the milestone escrow turns a scary stranger into a vendor who is only paid for proven progress. The SACCO's deceased-member float is an embarrassing liability nobody currently sells a fix for.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: list 40 SACCOs whose managers you can reach through personal, church, alumni and county networks (teachers', hospital, county-staff SACCOs first). Ask one question: how many deceased-member accounts are pending succession and how many shillings are stuck? Days 10-20: sign two advocates to a fixed-fee panel schedule and draft a one-page pilot contract: SACCO letter of introduction, member-consented flat fee deducted from released deposits, no SACCO cash outlay, so it fits within a CEO's delegated authority and does not need a board vote. Days 20-30: sign one SACCO for 15-20 stuck estates, start intake on the first 5 by WhatsApp, and publish an anonymised 'stuck member deposits' figure to open the next SACCOs. In parallel, draft the estate clearing loan term sheet with that SACCO's credit committee. Metric: days from intake to consents complete, and shillings released per case.

title: Mzee's Testament: Family Land Councils Before Death
one_liner: Invert the parent: instead of untangling the dead man's land after the funeral, hold a video-witnessed Family Land Council this December while the parent is alive and every heir is home, lock it into a will, family agreement, capacity certificate and time-locked vault, and grow the format into a registry of family land intent.
customer: Diaspora and urban children (30-55) with living rural parents aged 65-90 who hold unsubdivided family land. The child pays in September-November for a December council, but the parent is the legal client of the partner advocate. Later payers are SACCOs, lenders and insurers who buy verified family land plans (with family consent), and churches and clan associations as channels.
problem: After death, succession takes 1-3 years, is contested and costs heirs dearly (parent's figures). Every year of delay means heirs die, feuds harden, and evidence disappears. Children abroad only get all siblings into one compound at Christmas. Parents avoid 'death talk' and fear that gifting land makes them dependants. Where informal wills exist they are often unwitnessed or challenged for lack of capacity or undue influence, and daughters and second households are frequently excluded by custom, which produces litigation later. No one sells a cheap, provable record of what the parent actually wanted, agreed by all children while the parent can still speak.
solution: 'Family Land Council': a one-day facilitated event at the family home in the 20 Dec to 5 Jan window, prepared in October-November by WhatsApp intake, an official title search, a heir list including second households and a parcel sketch. On the day a team of three attends: a facilitator, a partner advocate who acts for the parent and first meets the parent alone, and a videographer, plus a clinician's capacity assessment on site or the same week. Outputs: (1) the parent's recorded, parent-alone statement of wishes; (2) a Family Land Agreement signed by all adult children in person or by video (allocation, parent's lifetime use and residence, burial ground, provision for daughters and widows); (3) a properly witnessed will drafted by the advocate; (4) an encrypted Family Land Vault holding video, documents and a machine-readable Family Land Plan, released to named heirs only when a death certificate is uploaded and two heirs confirm. Optional track: transfer by gift or subdivision with the parent's use protected, through surveyor, Land Control Board consent and registry, which skips the court queue entirely. The exact legal structure (gift versus will, consent requirements, stamp duty treatment) must be confirmed with Kenyan counsel.
why_now: December 2026 is about ten weeks away and diaspora flights are booked in October-November, so the product's launch window is literal. The allottee generation is 65-90 now: each year removes some of the people whose testimony is the whole point. LLMs, phone video and e-signature make an evidence pack cheap, and drafting is commoditising (Wakili-Intel, July 2026) while witnessing, capacity evidence and convening a family are not. Remittances of roughly US$5bn a year (parent's figure, verify) show families already pay to 'sort out the land' from abroad. This would have worked in 2019 only as a boutique law-firm service; the cost of running councils at scale with intake, video and vault software is new.
revenue_model: Council package: KES 40k service fee (about US$310) for pre-work, facilitation, video and capacity evidence and vault setup, pilot price KES 25k. The advocate's will and agreement drafting (KES 15-25k, assumption) is billed directly by the advocate to the parent as client, and the clinician's fee is passed through at cost. Vault subscription KES 3k a year per family (annual refresh video on the parent's birthday, updates for births, marriages and deaths), target 60% attach. Gift or subdivision track: KES 20k service fee on top of surveyor, Land Control Board and registry costs at cost. Later B2B: per-verified-plan fees from SACCOs, lenders and insurers, with consent. Year one aim: 50-60 councils, about KES 2M revenue at roughly 55% gross margin (cost about KES 14-18k per council), validating the model rather than making money. Scale-up: church and clan chapters delivering 500+ councils per December.
non_obvious_insight: The paying child is the likeliest future litigant, so the product only works if the parent is the client: parent alone on tape, an independent advocate, a capacity certificate and a cooling-off period. That evidence can only be produced while the parent is alive, which is why no post-death service, however good, can replace it. December is the one moment all 8-20 heirs are physically together and emotionally invested, so the coordination problem that costs a year after death costs a day before it. The inversion also turns a one-off dead-paperwork job into a living, recurring relationship (vault refresh, births and deaths) whose data compounds into a standard-setting registry of family land intent.
first_30_days: October: recruit two advocates who do wills and agree a parent-as-client engagement letter, and one clinician for capacity assessments. Run a dry-run council for a friendly family (Murang'a or Kakamega) to time the day and script the parent-alone interview. Launch a landing page and WhatsApp booking with 30 December slots at the KES 25k pilot price and a 30% M-Pesa deposit, sold through diaspora Facebook and WhatsApp groups, church and alumni networks, with a free 'Family Land Map' quiz as lead magnet. Recruit and train four facilitators (paralegals, community mobilisers, retired chief's assistants). Targets: 15 paid slots by 30 October and 30 by end of November. The riskiest assumption is that parents agree, so measure the parent-consent rate among families whose child pays (target above 60%).

title: Hall-Ready Gate for Liquid-Cooled GPU Tranches
one_liner: A fixed-price, 10-business-day release/hold decision, made 60-90 days before GPU delivery, on whether a liquid-cooled data hall will be energized and flowing when the racks arrive.
customer: Credit-desk principals and VPs at mid-market private credit funds, BDCs and specialty lenders on their first to fifth delayed-draw GPU facility to a sub-investment-grade neocloud, with no in-house commissioning bench. Secondary: mid-size AI labs signing take-or-pay capacity in a non-hyperscale hall. Excluded on purpose: hyperscalers and mega-funds that have their own engineers.
problem: In a delayed-draw GPU facility, the lender funds a GPU purchase order on the sponsor's word that the hall will be ready. That is roughly $3M+ per NVL72-class rack and hundreds of racks per hall. If the hall slips, the GPUs idle. My estimate is about $0.75M per day per $1B stranded (8% interest plus 5-year straight-line depreciation). Nobody on the lender's side is retained to say 'hold' at that moment. IEs certify construction draws. The technical advisors seen in GPU deals check fleet files, telemetry and power documents (per Peony). The RFS date is a sponsor sales number. NVL72-class racks have no air-cooled fallback, so the loop must be proven flushed, filled and leak-tested before any tray draws power. That work is done last, by scarce people. The parent's weakness was a broad 'better IE' pitch, sold through trust-gated relationships, with no software moat and an unproven right of site access. All of these are addressed below.
solution: One product for one decision, the 'Gate Memo'. It is $30K fixed, delivered in 10 business days. It has 12 binary hold-point tests, all in the failure zone: (1) written utility authorization to energize; (2) MV gear energized, with serials matched to bills of lading; (3) Cx Level 4 closed, with Level 5 IST script pass/fail counts; (4) CDU flush and pressure-test logs signed by the mechanical contractor; (5) punch-list burn-down slope over the last three weekly snapshots; (6) OEM startup technicians booked for named dates; (7) fiber acceptance; and five others. It also includes one site day by an ex-Cx lead and a probability of RFS by the sponsor's date. The memo ends in one of three recommendations: release, release with staged delivery, or hold N weeks. It is expressly not a certification. It does no draw certification, no cost-to-complete and no liability-bearing sign-off, and it leaves those to the IE. That keeps liability small and stops us from being an IE substitute. Access is solved with a free 'Readiness Rider', a two-page information-covenant and hold-point rider that finance counsel can paste into GPU facility documents. It gives the lender the evidence pack and one site visit as a condition precedent to each GPU tranche. The rider is both the access mechanism and the lead generator. After the gate, a $6K/month watch runs until RFS.
why_now: GPU-backed delayed-draw loans became standardized and large in 2026 (for example CoreWeave's $8.5B A3-rated DDTL closed 2026-03-31). That is pulling in mid-market credit funds that copy the structure without an infrastructure bench. Liquid-cooled racks removed the air-cooled fallback. Liquid-cooling engineers top a Q2 2026 US bottleneck index (Spencer Ogden, scarcity 80/100), and one missing controls technician can hold a finished hall out of service. Lenders are capping neocloud exposure and neocloud deals are stalling on credit risk. Satellite vendors have commoditized the exterior view, so the interior last 90 days is the scarce truth.
revenue_model: $30K per Gate Memo and $6K/month per hall for the watch. A retainer of $75K per fund buys 3 gates. Delivery cost is a 1099 Cx lead for about 4 desk days plus 1 site day, roughly $8-10K, so gross margin is about 65-70%. Year-1 target is 25 gates ($750K) plus watch fees ($250-300K), with about 6 principals doing the work. Year 2 adds a licensed benchmark dataset.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not purchasing a forecast. The buyer is purchasing an option trigger. The gate is timed to a decision with a cheap 'hold' branch (staged delivery or a 2-4 week deferral) and an expensive 'release' branch (idle carry). A false alarm costs weeks and a miss costs months of carry, so a forecast that is only about 65% accurate still has large positive value. This is why the lender does not need certainty and why the fee is trivially small next to the decision. Second, every gate produces structured data that IEs, who bill hourly and file Word reports, never accumulate: punch-list burn-down slope by hall, OEM startup lead times, and utility energization durations. After roughly 30 gates that becomes a reference-class dataset that sharpens each forecast, which is a process and data moat built from work you were being paid to do anyway.
first_30_days: Week 1: sign 4 retired or between-jobs Cx leads on 1099 contracts, prioritizing anyone who has commissioned liquid-cooled GB-class halls. Draft the 12-test Gate Memo template. Run it retroactively on 2 publicly delayed projects and publish the teardowns. Week 2: give 2 boutique finance law firms that do GPU facilities a co-branded Readiness Rider. List 40 mid-market credit funds with GPU or data center facilities, sourced from DDTL closing press releases and BDC filings. Weeks 3-4: hold 25 conversations with principals and VPs. Offer a design-partner Gate Memo at $15K on a live deal in exchange for an anonymized case study and permission to keep anonymized metrics. Target 2 signed by day 30. Riskiest assumption to test first: a credit desk will pay $30K for a hold/release memo that is not a certification. Test it with a pre-sale at day 14.

title: Delay-Risk Underwriting Desk for Data Center Insurers
one_liner: Sell Delay-in-Start-Up underwriters a 5-day hall-level readiness review and a portfolio 'collision calendar' so scarce DSU capacity can be written on more projects with fewer surprises, funded by the insured through a policy subjectivity, and later share in the premium.
customer: Delay-in-Start-Up underwriters and engineering leads at construction and specialty carriers and Lloyd's syndicates, plus the construction-broker teams that place data center DSU, and reinsurers. The insured (sponsor or lender-as-loss-payee) funds the work through a policy subjectivity. Later: backstop providers whose payout depends on delay thresholds, for example a backstop that only triggers if construction is under about 180 days late.
problem: DSU is the most contentious and expensive element of data center construction cover. Zurich commentary says adding it cuts available capacity, and underwriters call it disproportionate to premium. A flood of AI data center submissions is hampering underwriters' ability to process them, and DSU capacity is being reserved for projects judged best risk-managed. Delay exposure can exceed $1B on a single campus. Carriers now require phased handovers and detailed commissioning protocols, and they ask who is building, what equipment is specified and how commissioning sequences, but they can only check documents. DSU claims later need programme evidence, commissioning records and contemporaneous project records that are rarely captured cleanly. Worst, DSU losses are correlated through shared scarce pools (OEM startup crews, CDU and coolant-chemistry lots, utility energization windows) that per-risk underwriting cannot see.
solution: Four layers, sold in order. (1) Pre-bind 'DSU Readiness Review' in 5 business days per submission: desk review of the commissioning plan and sequence, capacity check of the contractor and OEM startup technicians, the utility energization path, a stage-appropriate Readiness Ladder score, and an underwriter-facing recommendation on deductible, waiting period and warranty wording. The underwriter commissions it and makes it a bind subjectivity, so the insured pays. (2) In-policy monthly Ladder monitoring, framed as compliance with the commissioning-protocol warranty, with early warnings to the underwriter. It also builds the contemporaneous evidence file for any delay notice, which cuts adjusting cost and disputes. (3) Portfolio 'Collision Calendar' for carriers and reinsurers: how many insured halls need the same OEM startup crew or utility window in the same month, so accumulation is priced rather than discovered. (4) Year 2: delegated authority. We become an MGA or coverholder on DSU excess layers, or offer a readiness-triggered parametric top-up where a verified Ladder milestone missed by a date is the trigger, earning a profit commission.
why_now: Insurers began rationing DSU exactly as data center project sizes jumped, with average project value rising from roughly $150M to roughly $3M+ per the coverage above. Aon expanded its Data Center Lifecycle Insurance Program to $2.5B in January 2026, covering construction all risks, DSU and operational damage/BI. Brokers publicly call DSU the pressure point. GPU-backed lenders and offtakers increasingly want delay cover as a condition of their deals, which pulls more submissions into an already constrained market. Document AI now turns commissioning scripts, test reports and punch lists into structured evidence for cents per page, so a small bench can serve many risks.
revenue_model: $12-25K per pre-bind review, paid by the insured through the subjectivity. $4-8K per month per policy for monitoring. $75-200K per year for carrier and reinsurer portfolio analytics. From year 2, a 10-20% profit commission on DSU premium written under delegated authority, which creates outcome-linked economics: we earn more when our screening keeps loss ratios low. Bottom-up: 40 reviewed risks and 25 monitored halls in year 1 is about $0.8-1.2M, before any delegated-authority income.
non_obvious_insight: Underwriters do not buy diligence, they buy capacity. A credible hall-level score lets a carrier say yes to more DSU premium at the same loss ratio, so the buyer has a revenue reason to pay rather than a cost to minimize. Second, the pre-bind, in-policy and claims evidence needs are the same ledger, so one dataset serves three insurer budgets (underwriting, risk engineering, claims). Third, and most non-obvious, DSU is a systemic-correlation business disguised as a per-project one. Ten independently insured halls that all need the same OEM's startup crew in the same month are one risk, not ten. Nobody has the hall-level calendar to see it, and reinsurers will pay to.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 Cx leads plus one former DSU underwriter or claims adjuster as a paid adviser. Build a loss-cause taxonomy of about 6 delay causes from public litigation, insurer and broker commentary on delayed data center projects. Map about 20 DSU underwriters and construction-broker teams. Offer 8 of them a free shadow review, delivered in 5 days on a live submission with details blinded. Aim for 2 shadow reviews completed and 1 paid pilot by day 45. Insurance cycles are slow, so accept that. Riskiest assumption to test first: carriers will make an outside readiness review a subjectivity instead of relying on in-house or outsourced risk-engineering surveys. Ask each underwriter directly how surveys are commissioned today and who pays.
