title: Commissioning Passport: The Data Center Readiness Standard
one_liner: Invert the model: the sponsor pays a neutral party to verify hall readiness once, in a machine-readable ledger every lender, insurer, landlord and offtaker can read, which grows into the standard definition of ready-for-service and the trigger written into loan, lease and backstop documents.
customer: Payers: sub-investment-grade neocloud sponsors and colocation developers, who face 4-6 counterparties each re-diligencing the same hall (issuer-pays). Readers who license access: lenders, DSU insurers, offtakers and backstop providers. Supply side, seeded free: commissioning agents, general contractors and IEs, who become named attestors.
problem: One liquid-cooled hall is diligenced repeatedly. The GPU-loan lender, the landlord's lender, the DSU insurer, the offtaker and any GPU-vendor backstop provider each hire their own advisor or IE, and evidence moves as emailed PDFs. Sponsors lose days on every draw and every counterparty re-asks the same questions. There is no shared definition of 'ready for service'. Lease commencement, financial close and backstop triggers can each key off a different milestone, and a backstop can lapse if construction runs more than about 180 days late. Because credibility is scarce, sponsors post letters of credit or parent guarantees, which is expensive capital to lock up.
solution: Two things. First, an open 'Readiness Ladder' spec, about 40 evidence-backed binary milestones for the last 90 days, published free so it can be adopted like a template. Second, the Passport ledger. Evidence is captured at source (Cx platform exports, utility letters, OEM startup bookings, CDU flush certificates, gear serial and bill-of-lading matches), timestamped and hashed, and tied to a named attestor (Cx agent, IE, OEM technician, utility). We add independent spot audits and a per-party permissioned view. Outputs are a Passport Score, a probability of RFS by date using reference-class priors, and a covenant schedule template (for example 'Ladder milestone L-7 certified in Passport') that counsel can drop into loan, lease and backstop documents so RFS is defined once. First product, sellable within 6 months, is the 'Draw Pack': within 5 business days of a draw or tranche request, we convert the sponsor's own commissioning evidence into a verified Passport snapshot that the lender has agreed to accept. It costs the sponsor $15K per pack or $8K/month per hall. Pilots go to sponsors that lenders cap, for whom verified readiness is a currency. The capture workspace is free for Cx agents and GCs, which seeds the supply side.
why_now: Lenders are capping neocloud exposure, deals are stalling on credit and some operators demand letters of credit or parent backing. Multi-party GPU structures with vendor backstops mean the same hall gets underwritten by many parties at once. The first-principles cost stack changed: turning IST results, punch lists and flush logs into structured pass/fail facts used to take a 3-person review team, and document AI now makes one reviewer per hall economically feasible. That makes portable verify-once evidence cheap enough to sell to the party that would otherwise pay for every counterparty's separate review. It would not have worked in 2019, when there was no GPU-debt market and no extraction tooling.
revenue_model: Issuer-pays verification at $15K per pack or $8-12K/month per hall. Read-side seats for lenders, insurers and offtakers at $40-150K per year, free for the first year to any lender that writes the Ladder into its documents. Licensed Passport Score and delivery-time benchmark indices for funds and reinsurers. Later, lenders offer margin step-downs or lower letter-of-credit haircuts for Passport-verified halls, and we take a fee from the sponsor's saving. Scale illustration: 150 halls under continuous verification at about $100K per year blended is about $15M revenue, with data licensing on top.
non_obvious_insight: Verification is a public good with a payer problem, and the answer is the one project-finance already uses. IEs are borrower-paid but lender-selected, and rating agencies are issuer-paid. The independence safeguards are a lender-vetoable attestor panel, published methodology and an audit trail. For the sponsor the product sells speed and a cheaper substitute for letters of credit and parent guarantees, not virtue. The moat is a cornered dataset: durations by OEM, utility, GC and hall type across every verified hall, which makes forecasts better as more halls join, so the network effect is in the prior. Counter-positioning also works: incumbents bill by the hour for each counterparty, and a portable verify-once artifact cannibalizes that repeat billing. The standard is won by whoever gets its definition of RFS into the legal templates first.
first_30_days: Publish Ladder spec v0.1 and teardowns of 2 publicly delayed projects, built from public documents. Recruit 4 Cx leads and one finance lawyer to draft the covenant schedule. Interview 15 sponsors and 10 lenders to measure which draw-package friction costs the most days and dollars. Sign 2 design partners: one sub-IG neocloud sponsor with a live delayed-draw facility, and its lender, who agrees in writing to accept the pack. Run the service by hand ('Wizard of Oz'): shared drive, spreadsheet and document-AI extraction, with no product build yet. Success by day 45: one lender accepts a Passport pack in place of a second-round advisor visit. Riskiest assumption to test first: sponsors will pay for verification that lenders accept, and lenders will accept sponsor-paid attestation. If not, fall back to Offspring 1 (lender-paid) and keep the ledger as a by-product.

title: Cure Desk: Cash-Worker Packets for Health Centers
one_liner: A Spanish-first text-message case tool for health-center enrollment staff that turns a Medicaid noncompliance notice (or a pre-emptive look-back audit) into a state-formatted evidence packet for cash-paid workers, built on batch attestations from the crew leaders, landlords and households who pay them, billed per accepted packet.
customer: Enrollment and patient-navigation managers (certified application counselors, community health worker leads) at FQHCs and community health centers whose panels are heavy with day laborers, house cleaners, landscapers, roofers, temp-agency and informal restaurant workers, and street vendors. Narrow wedge: one Nebraska health center with a large Spanish-speaking panel (plus one refugee language), then a second state that verifies early. The end user is the patient in a 15-minute session with a CHW. The patient installs nothing and pays nothing.
problem: The parent idea was a self-serve wallet sold to MCOs. Judges flagged slow MCO procurement, weak enrollee adoption, and the IFR limiting plans to a support role. The competitor check found SteadyIQ and Emmy giving states free or bundled bank, payroll and gig linking, and Pointcare and Findhelp already holding the FQHC and MCO relationships. What none of them can serve is the worker with no digital trail. The IFR counts self-employment, gig work and in-kind work and lets people combine activities, so someone who cleans three homes for cash and helps on a landscaping crew is legally compliant but has no payroll record, no bank deposits to link, and a 30-day cure clock the day a notice arrives. Timing nuance: an HFMA summary of the IFR says self-attestation is allowed through 2027 (and once per beneficiary in 2028), so the documentation wall arrives in waves. Early-verifying states and audit-driven renewals come first, the general wall later. The first-year job is therefore both cure packets and building an audit-proof evidence file in advance.
solution: Six pieces. (1) Notice intake: the CHW photographs the notice, or the patient forwards it on WhatsApp or SMS. OCR extracts state, case ID, look-back months and deadline, and a 30-day countdown lands in the CHW queue. (2) State evidence rule pack: a maintained library of what each state and program accepts (in-kind work, combined activities, third-party statements, receipts), calibrated by logging every accept and reject reason. (3) Attester rail: the patient names who paid them, and that person gets a text in their own language ('Did Ana Ruiz work for you in August? About how many hours or how much did you pay? Tap to confirm'), creating a timestamped third-party statement in the state's format. Crew leaders, labor contractors, property managers, day-labor centers and church job boards get a batch screen that confirms 5 to 30 workers in one pass, with a reusable profile. (4) Packet: a PDF or portal-ready bundle with the hours or $580 computation, attachments and the patient's e-signature. The CHW submits as authorized representative, and the tool never decides compliance. (5) Outcome capture: accepted or rejected plus the caseworker's reason feeds the rule pack and billing. (6) Routing: patients who do have a digital trail are handed to the state's own Emmy or SteadyIQ consent flow, and exemption flags such as medical frailty are asked as a triage question only.
why_now: The June 3, 2026 IFR sets a Jan 1, 2027 start and a 30-day cure window, and six-month renewals for expansion adults begin around the same time (verify exact start), so notices and renewal checks multiply from Q1 2027. Nebraska is already live and is expected to move from self-attestation to verification. WhatsApp Business API, cheap OCR and LLM translation make a bilingual, photo-based intake cost cents per case, where a bilingual caseworker hour costs roughly $30. That is what makes a 15-minute assisted cure economical for a health center. In 2019 this would have needed a call center.
revenue_model: Per-case fee to the health center: $40 when a packet is opened plus $110 when the state accepts it (max $150, inside the parent's $50-150 range), with a $750 per month per-site minimum. Flat per-case fees rather than percent of Medicaid revenue keep it clean under inducement and billing-agent concerns (healthcare counsel to confirm). Channel revenue: white-label the packet builder as an API or module inside Pointcare, Findhelp or other health-center platforms at a 20-30% revenue share. Illustrative year-1 math (assumptions): 20 health centers x 40 packets a month x $120 average x 12 = about $1.15M. Later: a state-accepted-evidence data license to navigators and legal aid.
non_obvious_insight: Informal work is clustered behind intermediaries. One crew leader, property manager or household employer can attest for many workers at once, so each new attester makes the next patient's evidence nearly free, and the same attester serves patients at other health centers. The hardest segment for bank-linking vendors, where every cash worker is a costly manual exception, becomes the one segment with a network effect. The scarce asset is not the ledger but knowing what each state's caseworkers actually accept, which can only be learned by filing packets and logging outcomes. That data compounds with every case and cannot be bought or scraped.
first_30_days: Week 1: sign one Nebraska FQHC (or health center with a large Spanish-speaking panel) for a free concierge pilot, and call the state Medicaid policy office and two caseworker offices to ask which third-party statements are accepted as evidence. Weeks 2-3: build the flow from a Twilio or WhatsApp number, a Google Form, and a PDF template, with a bilingual attester text. Have the CHW enroll 25 real cash-paid patients and collect at least 40 attestations. Week 4: file the packets, or run the pre-audit in a state that is not yet verifying, and record acceptance rate and CHW minutes per case. Target: 60%+ acceptance and under 30 minutes a case versus 2+ hours today. Then take the numbers to a second health center and to Pointcare and Findhelp as a module partner.
lineage: mutation of I0573 ('Medicaid Hours Wallet for Gig Workers'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CMS Emmy (Eligibility Made Easy) app and Emmy API, SteadyIQ (Income Passport / Verification Hub), Digital Public Works, Maximus, Optum, Acentra, Deloitte, Gainwell, Conduent, Curam/Merative (state-side community engagement modules). White space: Nobody I found sells an enrollee-side monthly ledger to MCOs or FQHCs that ingests bank, gig and pay-stub data, computes $580 or 80 hours against a state's look-back rules, and produces a state-specific 30-day cure packet. Nothing turned up in searches, CMS vendor pledges or CBPP/KFF/Georgetown landscape coverage. Vendors sit on either side of that gap. State-side vendors (SteadyIQ, Emmy, Maximus, Optum, Deloitte) sell to state agencies. Provider and plan-side vendors (Pointcare, Findhelp, mPulse) sell eligibility monitoring and outreach without gig-income packet building. The clearest unserved segment is workers with no digital trail: cash, informal and 1099-below-threshold workers such as day labor, cleaning and landscaping. Consent-based verification (CBV) via payroll, bank or gig platforms cannot reach them. The 30-day cure step, meaning a compiled packet after a noncompliance notice, is also not addressed by any product I found. The wedge is narrow and could close quickly. States with CBV (SteadyIQ, Emmy) let the enrollee connect accounts directly, which makes a separate packet redundant there. MCOs may be poor buyers because the IFR bars plans from determining compliance and gives them only a supporting role. Pointcare and Findhelp already own the FQHC and MCO relationships and could add a module. Research limits: my web search budget ran out after four searches, so I relied on page fetches. I could not load the CBPP vendor landscape, the Health Affairs piece or the Federal Register text (all blocked), and I could not confirm what Propel for Plans does or any vendor's funding. | How this version avoids them: SteadyIQ and CMS Emmy: they win wherever a bank, payroll or gig account can be linked, so Cure Desk does not compete there and routes those patients to their consent flows. It serves only the cash and informal residue, where their cost per case is highest. Free state-side tools and the vendor pledges (Maximus, Optum, Acentra, Deloitte, Gainwell, Conduent, Curam) are sold to states and track hours. Cure Desk is a staff workflow sold to health centers. Pointcare and Findhelp: they do lapse detection and dashboards without informal-income packet building, so they are channel partners, not rivals. Propel and mPulse do notices and outreach, and CareRoute is informational. None builds attester-backed evidence. Digital Public Works is a nonprofit focused on mobile income verification. It is adjacent, and could become a partner or a free-riding substitute in some states (risk to monitor). Buyer choice removes the parent's MCO procurement and IFR-role problems.

title: Bedside Coverage Recovery for Safety-Net Hospitals
one_liner: A pay-on-success desk that helps safety-net hospital financial counselors convert lapsed or presumptively covered patients into full Medicaid within the shrinking retroactive window, with informal-income evidence built over text message, paid a flat fee per approved case by the hospital's revenue cycle budget.
customer: Patient financial services and revenue-cycle leaders, plus hospital presumptive eligibility (HPE) and Medicaid enrollment managers, at safety-net, critical-access and county-owned hospitals in expansion states. Start in Nebraska and adjoining expansion states, where the state hospital association has already campaigned against retroactive-coverage cuts. The enrollee pays nothing. The hospital pays only when a case is approved.
problem: Two hospital-side facts changed. First, starting January 1, 2027, retroactive Medicaid coverage for expansion adults shrinks to one month before the application month (per Justice in Aging and other H.R. 1 explainers), so every day a lapsed patient waits to reapply can turn a billable encounter into charity care. Second, HPE screens for the work requirement by attestation and gives up to 60 days of temporary coverage, after which the patient needs a full determination, and hospitals are being urged to build conversion assistance. Projections cited by Applied Policy put FY2027 coverage losses at 2.3M, with about 43% procedural. The hospital sees the loss first: an inactive eligibility response at registration or the ED desk. But the counselor's usual application flow stalls on cash, gig and informal workers, who cannot produce payroll or wage records. The hospital eats the bill. (Assumption to verify: existing hospital Medicaid-eligibility outsourcers handle standard applications but not informal-income compliance evidence.)
solution: A Coverage Recovery Desk delivered as a light workflow, not an EHR integration. (1) Daily feed: a CSV or SFTP list of registrations with inactive or self-pay coverage and prior Medicaid, plus HPE patients at day 20 of 60. (2) Outreach in hours: hospital-branded SMS or WhatsApp in the patient's language. (3) Evidence build: the attestation and receipt engine from the sibling Cure Desk, with third-party attestations for cash workers. Patients who have a bank or payroll trail are routed to the state's own Emmy or SteadyIQ flow. Exemption triage and any state-optional excused months for inpatient stays are documented. (4) Retro-clock calculator: maps each open encounter to the one retroactive month and tells the counselor which filing date protects which claims. This is the hospital-specific feature, and the first thing they will use daily. (5) Counselor submits with a complete packet; we never decide eligibility. (6) Dashboard: dollars of self-pay converted to Medicaid-billable, by lapse reason. Digital-trail patients cost us almost nothing, so margin comes from doing the cash residual efficiently.
why_now: Jan 1, 2027 combines the work requirement, six-month renewals for expansion adults, and the retroactive-coverage cut, all landing on the hospital revenue cycle at once. Uncompensated care is already implicated in rural hospital closures. Hospitals are being told to strengthen HPE-to-full-Medicaid conversion assistance now. Cheap messaging, OCR and translation mean a counselor can handle several times more cases per day than with paper and phone tag.
revenue_model: Pay-on-success, no software fee to start: a flat $150-300 per approved reinstatement or HPE-to-full conversion, tiered by encounter dollars at stake. A flat fee per approval, not a percentage of Medicaid collections, because Medicaid billing-agent payment rules generally restrict percentage-of-collections arrangements (counsel to confirm). Optional $2-4k per month CFO analytics tier (self-pay at risk by lapse reason, retro-window leakage). Illustrative unit economics (assumptions to validate in the audit): a 150-bed hospital sees 120 lapse-related self-pay encounters a month, 25% are reinstated at $200, giving $6k a month or $72k a year per hospital, versus a Medicaid-paid stay worth thousands. 30 hospitals is about $2.2M ARR. Later: subcontract informal-income packets to incumbent eligibility outsourcers.
non_obvious_insight: The hospital registration desk is the earliest reliable detector of work-requirement and procedural terminations, because an eligibility check runs at every visit. Plans learn from monthly files, and states rely on notices that cash workers miss. It is also the moment of maximum patient motivation, with the bill in hand. Plans are limited to a supporting role under the IFR and MCO procurement is slow, but hospitals are neither plans nor determiners, and their counselors already file Medicaid applications every day. The cash-flow logic is lopsided: a $200 fee against a stay Medicaid may pay thousands for, and the one-month retro window makes speed a priced variable for the first time.
first_30_days: Send 15 Nebraska and regional revenue-cycle leaders a free 'lapse leakage audit': they share a de-identified 90-day list of self-pay encounters with prior Medicaid, and we estimate dollars at risk and how many are informal-income cases (procedural lapses today stand in for work-requirement lapses). Sign a BAA and a pay-on-success pilot with the first one or two. Run 20-25 live cases by hand: the counselor works from our SMS templates and packet PDF, and we track time to filing, approvals and the encounters saved by the retro-clock calculator. In parallel, ask the state Medicaid agency and a hospital association contact how reinstatement, reapplication and HPE conversion work for noncompliance terminations, and get counsel's sign-off on the fee structure.

title: Hours Exchange: Supply Side of the Work Requirement
one_liner: Invert the wallet: instead of helping people prove hours they already work, build the network of pre-certified nonprofit and public hosts that supply verifiable, flexible community-service and training hours, with insured hosts and signed hour records, paid per active member-month by health systems and plans.
customer: First buyer: population-health, community-benefit and Medicaid-strategy leads at nonprofit and county-owned safety-net health systems. Second buyer: plans. Supply side: 20-50 hosts per county, such as food banks and church pantries, school after-care, libraries, senior centers, community gardens, and clinics' own non-clinical roles. Members: the residual slice of expansion adults who are not exempt, not already working and need hours.
problem: Every product in the parent's competitor set assumes the hours exist and only tracks or verifies them (SteadyIQ, Emmy, the state tracking portals from Maximus, Optum and Acentra, Pointcare, Findhelp). For a member who lost a job or has no hours, no amount of documentation fixes anything. The IFR does count community service, work programs and combined activities toward the 80 hours a month, but there is no supply chain: hosts do not know the state verification standard, cannot supervise flexible 4-hour shifts, lack liability cover, and have no time to produce signed logs. A member 30 days from termination cannot find, book and verify 40 missing hours on their own.
solution: An activity marketplace with a verification rail. (1) Host certification: each host signs a one-page state-format verification protocol (who may sign, what is recorded, non-displacement pledge) and joins a registry that we pre-clear with the state Medicaid agency wherever possible. (2) Micro-shift board: hosts post 3-6 hour shifts (pantry Saturday 8-12), and members claim them by SMS in their language. (3) Verification: check-in and out by phone geofence or supervisor QR or SMS confirmation, producing tamper-evident hour records. (4) Monthly hours letter in the state's format, delivered to the member, the case file and the plan. (5) Master volunteer accident and liability policy plus background checks carried by us, which is the small balance-sheet element and a reason hosts join. (6) Guardrails: the flow starts with an exemption and already-compliant screen, so nobody who qualifies is routed to slots. Participation is voluntary. Later: the same hours count toward SNAP's parallel 80-hour rule (widened by the 2025 law; verify scope), TANF work participation, and court-ordered or scholarship service hours.
why_now: The requirement starts Jan 1, 2027, but the documentation phase is later (an HFMA summary of the IFR says self-attestation is allowed through 2027 and once per beneficiary in 2028). That makes 2027 the year to build the host registry and get states to accept it, before the paperwork wall. The first wave of notices will expose the supply gap, and first movers will hold the hosts and the state relationships. Health systems and plans need a measurable coverage-retention lever for community-benefit and health-related-social-needs spending. Cheap SMS, geofencing and LLM-drafted state-format letters make per-shift verification nearly free.
revenue_model: Health systems or plans pay $20-30 per active member-month (active means at least one verified shift that month). Pilot: about $40k for 150 members over 6 months at roughly $45 per member-month, including host onboarding. Illustrative unit economics: coordinator time $8-10, insurance about $1, SMS and verification about $1, for roughly 50% gross margin. Possible additional flows: SNAP E&T third-party reimbursement (50% federal match on eligible non-federal spending) for host costs where the state plan allows (verify eligibility of this activity), state workforce-board contracts, and later fees from courts and scholarship programs. Bottom-up ceiling, illustrative only: if 1 in 10 of the 2.3M projected FY27 coverage losers (per the HFMA/Applied Policy figure) needs slots, that is 230k people x $240 a year, about $55M a year before SNAP, TANF and court hours.
non_obvious_insight: For the residual slice, the constraint is not proof but the absence of qualifying, supervisable, flexible hours near the member's home. Hosts are short on labor and long on facilities, so this market clears cheaply for whoever supplies the insurance, verification and coordination. Second, a registry-verified, insured host is cheaper for a caseworker to trust than an individual's self-report. Once one state lists registry-verified hosts as accepted evidence, verification cost falls for everyone and the registry becomes the standard, with network economies (hosts and members) and a cornered resource (the state-acceptance record). That is the difference between a tool and infrastructure.
first_30_days: Pick one county in a state that verifies hours early. Ask the state Medicaid agency in writing what a community-service host must sign and record, and whether members can cure by showing current-month hours (the IFR summary says 30 days to demonstrate compliance; test whether that includes hours earned during the window). Get an LOI from one food-bank network covering 10 to 15 pantries as hosts, and quotes for a master volunteer accident policy. Run a manual pilot with 25 members from a clinic's at-risk list using a shared sheet and a Twilio number, and produce real hours letters. Have five conversations with health-system community-benefit leads and price a $40k, 6-month pilot. The 2027 honesty test: do hours letters raise state acceptance versus self-attestation alone?

title: Herd Roll-Forward: Lender-Paid Cattle Collateral Reconciliation
one_liner: Sell ag lenders a loan covenant that rebuilds the borrower's herd from paper that third parties generated (vet records, sale-barn settlements, brand certificates, tag and vaccine purchases) and flags loans where expected head and claimed head do not reconcile.
customer: Wedge: the chief credit officer and senior ag lender at one Farm Credit association or one $500M-$3B community bank in a brand-inspection state (Nebraska, South Dakota, Montana, Wyoming or the Texas Panhandle). It should carry $50M+ in cow-calf, bred-heifer and heifer-development loans of $500K-$5M. The bank pays, and the cost passes through to the borrower as a collateral inspection fee that lenders already charge. The vet is a paid data source, not the customer.
problem: The parent's own flaws are the problem to fix. A borrower-initiated count means fraudulent borrowers never opt in. A chute-side count proves only what was at the chute that day, not cattle on other leases, cattle sold since, or cattle double-pledged. It says nothing about ownership or lien priority. Vets may refuse to sign anything that reads as a collateral audit. And $2-3/head split with the vet is thin. Meanwhile lenders still rely on drive-by counts and borrower spreadsheets on loans where a 500-cow herd is $1.5M+ of collateral nobody independent has counted.
solution: An annual 'Herd Roll-Forward' per loan that closes an inventory equation: last year's verified head + expected calf crop (from preg-check records) + purchases (sale-barn buyer settlements, health certificates) - sales (consignor settlements, brand and feedyard closeouts) - deaths = expected ending head. That figure is compared with the borrower's claimed head and any chute-side scan. A second check triangulates consumables: EID tags bought, vaccine doses and dewormer from the vet, mineral and hay purchases, and grazing-lease animal-unit-months, all versus claimed head. The borrower signs one information-rights rider at loan closing, which lets the vet, sale barns, brand agency and feed suppliers release records to us. That rider is what removes adverse selection: the loan agreement opts the borrower in, not the borrower. LLM extraction reads the messy PDFs and photos. The vet is one attestor, contracted narrowly ('I handled N head with these IDs on this date', no collateral opinion) and paid a flat $150-300 per session for exporting the sheet they already made and one-tap signing. The lender gets a variance flag, a lien and ownership panel (UCC or state central-filing search plus brand records) and a portfolio dashboard.
why_now: (1) Reading hundreds of differently formatted settlement statements, invoices and health papers used to take an analyst hours per loan, and LLM document extraction has cut that to cents. That is the cost-stack collapse that makes reconciliation cheaper than a drive-by. (2) Federal EID tag rules for many interstate cattle movements (Nov 2024) mean more animals carry digital IDs and more vets and barns hold exportable records. (3) Record cattle prices are pushing herd rebuilding onto debt, with bred cows around $3,000+, so each loan carries big collateral. Lenders are also carrying delinquencies, and a fresh cattle-collateral fraud case (claimed in the parent, unverified) is prompting loan-committee questions. (4) It is fall, when preg-checks, weaning and calf sales generate the documents, and December-February annual renewals are when banks decide on inspections.
revenue_model: The bank pays per loan per year: about $600 under $1M, $1,500 for $1-3M and $3,000 above $3M, roughly 5-10 bps of balance. A portfolio dashboard is $1,000-2,000/month at 100+ loans. A bank with 120 cattle loans is worth about $130K-180K/yr. Vets get a flat per-session data fee, so their cost does not scale with head count. Target gross margin is 70%+ once extraction is automated, with human review only on flagged loans. Later add anonymized county and herd-size variance benchmarks for credit committees and examiners.
non_obvious_insight: Do not count the cattle, count the paper. Every animal movement leaves a record in a third party's hands (barn, brand inspector, vet, feed store, feedyard), and fraud shows up as arithmetic that does not close. Counting heads is the least informative check, so the chute day is a calibration anchor rather than the product. This also makes the vet's reluctance irrelevant, since any attestor or document set works, and it turns the borrower's own suppliers into the fraud detectors.
first_30_days: Weeks 1-2: run 12 interviews (5 loan officers or credit officers, 3 vets, 2 barn clerks, 2 brand inspectors). Ask each bank who does its inspections now and what it costs, and search for existing third-party collateral inspectors. Weeks 2-3: get one bank to pick 15 existing borrowers up for renewal and get consent. Manually reconcile each from documents the borrower already holds (sale settlements, preg-check sheets, vet invoices, tag orders) and from one vet's exports. Charge $500 per loan, or waive the fee for the first five if the bank agrees to write down what it learned. Week 4: present the variance results to the bank's ag loan committee, especially any loan that did not close. Convert the result into a one-page 'inventory information rights' rider for new bred-heifer and operating-line loans, priced at $750-1,500 per loan.
lineage: mutation of I0338 ('Chute-Side Cow Counts for Ag Lenders'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global / Where Food Comes From (Beef Passport), Merck Animal Health (Allflex tags/readers, Vence). White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I ran zero searches. I did direct fetches of about 15 vendor and agency pages, plus GitHub repo searches. Nothing here rules out a direct competitor. The biggest gap is that I could not identify the third-party collateral-inspection firms that lenders already pay for cattle counts, or any startup selling vet-verified herd inventory to lenders. Do not treat 'gap' as 'open'.

What the direct fetches showed: none of the herd-software, EID, tracking or verification vendors I checked advertise a lender-facing 'independent count' product. The vendors were CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global/WFCF, Ceres Tag, Halter, HerdDogg and Gallagher. Merck/Vence returned 403, so I could not check it. The unserved wedge is a lender-mandated, third-party-attested herd inventory built as a covenant workflow. It would cover the vet-signed chute-side count, a portfolio dashboard, and year-over-year anomaly flags such as head count down, pregnancy rate down, or tags missing versus last year.

Structural weaknesses to be skeptical of:
- Adverse selection: 'borrower-initiated' verification means fraudulent borrowers never opt in. The product only works if lenders make it a loan condition.
- Coverage: a preg-check only counts animals brought to the chute that day, not cattle on other leases or sold or double-pledged since. It does not prove ownership or lien priority.
- Vet liability and willingness: vets may refuse to sign anything that reads as a collateral audit.
- Economics: $2-3/head split 50/50 leaves the vet about $1-1.50/head on top of a preg-check fee that is already several dollars.
- Entry by an existing vendor: IMI Global (WFCF) or Merck/Allflex could add this as a feature. | How this version avoids them: CattleMax, AgriWebb, Gallagher, Merck/Allflex and Vence, HerdDogg, Halter and Ceres Tag are all producer-paid management or hardware tools. A borrower-paid tool sees only what the borrower records, and those vendors cannot audit the customers who pay them. IMI Global's Beef Passport verifies supply-chain claims for a producer-paid program, not cross-counterparty reconciliation or a covenant workflow. We are lender-paid and source-agnostic, and we ingest their CSV exports as just one input, so they become feeders rather than rivals. Their incumbent asymmetry is real: adding lender variance reports means telling their own paying customers they are now audited. The remaining risk is unknown third-party inspection firms, which the interviews must surface, and a possible white-label deal with IMI or an EID vendor.

title: Independent Herd Audits for Loan Participation Buyers
one_liner: Charge the correspondent banks, credit unions and credit funds that buy pieces of cattle loans they cannot see, using sampling audits and a verified collateral tape sold through bankers' banks.
customer: The participation desk or chief credit officer at correspondent ag banks, credit unions and ag-focused credit funds that buy participations in cattle loans from community banks. Community banks hit legal lending limits and sell off big pieces of $2M+ herd loans. Channel partners are the bankers' banks that broker those participations. Later buyers are pool purchasers such as Farmer Mac-style secondary-market programs.
problem: A participant that owns 80-90% of a cattle loan has never seen the cattle. It relies on the lead bank's annual inspection, and the lead bank has already sold most of the risk, keeps servicing fees and has reason to want the loan to look clean. Participation agreements normally give buyers information and inspection rights, but the rights go unused because sending an inspector to a ranch two states away costs $1,500+ and buyers do not know how to audit a herd. The parent's fraud case (about $2.8M against 850 head, claimed and unverified) sits in the loan size that small banks typically participate out. That is a hypothesis to confirm.
solution: A 'Participation Audit' program sold to the buyer of risk, not the originator. Tier 1 desk audit ($300-500): a document reconciliation (sale-barn and brand records, tag and vet purchases) plus a lien search, compared against the lead bank's inspection report. Tier 2 ($1,200-2,000): adds a vet-attested chute-side scan or a credentialed field inspector, with geotagged photos and an EID or visual tag scan, timed to preg-check, weaning or a scheduled sale. Tier 3: surprise audit triggered by a lead-bank downgrade, a delinquency or a cattle-price drop. Buyers audit a random 15-25% of each pool every year, so every borrower knows the draw could land on them, which deters fraud. Buyers also get a verified collateral tape with loan-level fields (head, class, pregnancy rate, variance, lien position, date). That tape lets them price participations and lets funds bid for them. Bankers' banks embed the service in their participation platform for a 20-25% revenue share.
why_now: Herd rebuilding is debt-financed, so more cattle loans are being participated, and delinquencies are rising. A cattle-fraud headline (claimed in the parent, unverified) makes participants ask why they trust the lead bank's word. Examiner guidance generally expects participants to do their own credit analysis rather than lean on the lead, which is worth confirming with counsel. Non-bank capital has been moving into ag credit and needs diligence infrastructure. Remote document reconciliation makes a $400 Tier 1 audit profitable, where a field-only inspector could never be. Farm-loan stress typically creates an appetite for independent verification.
revenue_model: Per-audit fees: Tier 1 at about $400 and Tier 2 at about $1,500. Add $250/loan/year of monitoring, plus a 20-25% share to the bankers' bank. Data subscription for the verified collateral tape at $2-5K/month per buyer. Later, a 5-10 bps diligence fee on pool trades. Example: a correspondent buyer holding $150M across 150 cattle loans pays 150 x $400 + 38 Tier 2 audits x $1,500 + 150 x $250 = about $155K/yr. Ten such buyers is roughly $1.5M in recurring revenue. Field inspection labor is variable, using vet and tech partners paid per visit.
non_obvious_insight: In a participation, the party with the most money at risk has the least information and holds a contractual right that nobody uses because exercising it is operationally impossible. The buyer's question is not 'is the borrower honest' but 'is my lead bank's report honest'. Independence from the lead bank is therefore the product, and adverse selection disappears because the buyer picks the sample after buying, and randomness is the deterrent. Vets are optional at Tier 2, so vet reluctance no longer blocks the business.
first_30_days: Call 15 people: 5 bankers' banks and correspondent participation desks, 5 community-bank lead lenders that sell cattle participations, and 5 credit unions that buy them. Ask for the inspection clause in an actual participation agreement, whether anyone has ever inspected a participated cattle loan, who did it and what it cost. Find one buyer willing to pay $1,000 each for 5 participated cattle loans and invoke its inspection rights with the lead bank. Time the visits to fall preg-check or weaning days with two partner vets or field inspectors. Deliver five Tier 2 reports and a one-page comparison of what we found against the lead bank's file. Use that comparison to pitch a bankers' bank on adding the program to its participation platform.

title: Cattle Lien Registry and Sale-Barn Exit Alerts
one_liner: Invert the problem: instead of counting cattle in the pasture, watch the few gates cattle must leave through. Start with consignment alerts to lenders and lien matching for auction markets, then grow into the neutral title registry for cattle.
customer: Two-sided. Lenders with cattle collateral pay first. Livestock auction markets, which carry conversion liability when they sell pledged cattle without paying the lienholder, supply the data and pay later. Wedge: one region where 8-12 markets and 10-20 lenders overlap (for example the Nebraska Sandhills, Flint Hills or northern plains), so alerts are dense enough to matter. Eventual customers are feedyards, packers, brand agencies, participation buyers and secondary-market programs.
problem: Cattle have no VIN or title. A lender's lien follows the animals to sale, but the barn's lien check is a paper or fax list of seller names plus state central-filing lists. Borrowers consign under a relative's name, a shell entity or a barn 150 miles away, and the lender finds out months later at the next inspection, or never. Markets are exposed to conversion suits and often end up paying twice, once to the seller's account and once to the lender. Counting cattle on inspection day cannot catch cattle sold the day after, or the same cattle pledged twice (the parent's fraud case, claimed and unverified, involved a $2.8M loan against 850 head).
solution: Phase 1 (sellable in 6 months), 'Consignment Alert'. The lender uploads a pledged-collateral profile per loan: legal entities, DBAs, family names, brands, counties and any tag or EID lists from chute scans or borrower spreadsheets. Markets email or upload their consignment list before sale day, as they already assemble it for clerks. Fuzzy matching on name, brand, county and tag produces an alert to the lender ('Borrower X consigned 143 steers at Y Thursday') and a prompt to the market to issue a joint-payee check. Phase 2: EID matching. Chute-side scans (the parent's product) and barn intake scans feed the registry, so alerts match animals, not just names. Phase 3: the registry becomes a title layer where pledges and releases are recorded per animal or lot and queried by feedyards, packers, brand agencies and participation buyers. Verified movement history plus pledge status then supports collateral-managed advances on bred heifers (through a licensed lending or warehouse-funded partner) as the balance-sheet extension. The registry is tag-vendor-neutral and works on visual tags and brands where EID coverage is thin.
why_now: October-November is the peak fall calf run, so a pilot sees dense consignments right now, and lender annual renewals arrive in December-February. Digital EID tags are more common after the Nov 2024 federal rule. Cheap fuzzy entity matching and LLM parsing of messy consignment sheets make a small-team registry feasible where it was not in 2019. Record cattle prices and debt-financed herd rebuilding raise the dollars at risk per lien. A fresh fraud case (claimed in the parent, unverified) is making lenders ask what happens after the inspection. The neutral registry position is open until a tag vendor or state agency takes it.
revenue_model: Lenders pay $25-50/month per monitored loan ($300-600/yr). A bank with 150 loans is $45-90K/yr, and 40 banks is roughly $2-3M recurring. Markets get free lien checks at first because they are the data supply, then a $200-500/month tier for clearance workflow (joint-check prompts, an audit trail for their liability insurer). Later a per-lot clearance fee of $0.10-0.25/head consigned, on the well over 10M head a year that pass through auctions. Phase 3 adds registry-lookup fees from packers, feedyards and participation buyers, and net interest or fee share from collateral-managed advances through a licensed partner.
non_obvious_insight: Fraud needs an exit. Herds can be hidden, borrowed for inspection day or double-counted, but cattle converted to cash pass through a handful of chokepoints: auction markets, feedyards, packers and brand-inspected private sales. Watching the exits is cheaper and harder to game than counting the pasture. The barn has legal exposure and is a willing data supplier, whereas the borrower is not. Lender pledge data is a cornered resource: once enough lenders load it, no producer-side software vendor can replicate the registry without the lenders.

The barn emails the consignment list Monday or Tuesday, we match it against lender profiles (20-50 loans to start) and send text or email alerts within hours. Log every hit, the head at stake and whether the lender already knew, for four weeks. Aim for one or two consignments a lender did not know about, and turn them into an anonymized case. In week 4 ask each lender for $300/loan/yr on a minimum of 20 loans, and ask the barn for two more barns in its trade area. Confirm with counsel how Food Security Act lien-notice rules and state central-filing systems interact with the alerts.

The biggest gap is that I could not identify the third-party collateral-inspection firms that lenders already pay for cattle counts, or any startup selling vet-verified herd inventory to lenders. Do not treat 'gap' as 'open'.

What the direct fetches showed: none of the herd-software, EID, tracking or verification vendors I checked advertise a lender-facing 'independent count' product. The vendors were CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global/WFCF, Ceres Tag, Halter, HerdDogg and Gallagher. Merck/Vence returned 403, so I could not check it. - Adverse selection: 'borrower-initiated' verification means fraudulent borrowers never opt in. The product only works if lenders make it a loan condition.
- Coverage: a preg-check only counts animals brought to the chute that day, not cattle on other leases or sold or double-pledged since. It does not prove ownership or lien priority.
- Vet liability and willingness: vets may refuse to sign anything that reads as a collateral audit.
- Economics: $2-3/head split 50/50 leaves the vet about $1-1.50/head on top of a preg-check fee that is already several dollars.
- Entry by an existing vendor: IMI Global (WFCF) or Merck/Allflex could add this as a feature. | How this version avoids them: CattleMax, AgriWebb, Gallagher, HerdDogg, Halter and Ceres Tag are producer-side herd management or tracking tools, and none holds lender pledge data. They cannot collect it without alienating the producers who pay them. Merck/Allflex and Vence own tags but a vendor-run registry would be distrusted by rival tag vendors and lenders. IMI Global's Beef Passport ties EIDs to verification records for the supply chain, not to liens or exits. State central-filing systems and brand agencies are passive, annual or paper-based lists, so we sit on top of them and can partner. The real risks are sale-barn clerking-software vendors and state agencies adding matching. Being lender-funded and neutral, with lender pledge data as the cornered resource, is the counter.

title: Deficiency-Suit Add-On Credit Audits for Consumer Defense Firms
one_liner: A flat-fee, 24-hour audit that rebuilds a repossession deficiency from the retail installment contract and shows the unearned add-on credits, notice defects and fee errors the lender or debt buyer left out, sold to the consumer-defense lawyers who already have the client and the deadline.
customer: Consumer-defense and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid offices that defend post-repossession deficiency suits. Start in two or three states chosen from docket data in week 1 (candidates: Maryland, Pennsylvania, Ohio, where notice rules and fee-shifting tend to favor borrowers; confirm before committing). Wedge buyer: small consumer-law firms of 1 to 10 lawyers that take flat-fee or fee-shifting cases, plus 3 to 5 legal aid units.
problem: A repossessed borrower is typically sued 6 to 18 months later, often by a debt buyer, on a one-line balance backed by a thin affidavit. The defense lawyer has about 30 days to answer, no numbers person, and a flat fee or grant-funded hours. The deficiency figure usually does not credit the unearned GAP, service-contract and other add-ons that were rolled into the loan, and may carry defective post-sale notices or inflated fees. Rebuilding it by hand takes a paralegal hours, so most defendants default or settle blind. The parent's borrower-side value is real but lacked a buyer with standing, a deadline and a fee-shifting statute. This buyer has all three.
solution: The attorney uploads the complaint, contract image, pre- and post-sale notices and auction bill. Within 24 hours the tool returns a Deficiency Autopsy PDF: (1) a rebuilt ledger from the retail installment contract (amount financed, itemized add-ons, finance charge, payments, fees); (2) unearned add-on credits owed under the contract and state rule, with the administrator's cancellation requirement and a computed pro-rata figure; (3) a notice checklist against UCC Article 9 and the state motor-vehicle finance act (timing, required content, explanation of the deficiency calculation, commercial-reasonableness red flags such as sale price versus wholesale value, and whether a defective notice bars the deficiency in that state); (4) an exposure sheet covering offsets, defenses and potential statutory damages under UCC 9-625(c)(2) as adopted by the state; (5) draft answer paragraphs, counterclaim language and targeted discovery requests aimed at cancellation records. A human analyst reviews every output at first, later only exceptions. Flat fee only, never a share of a fee award, which avoids fee-sharing problems with non-lawyers (Rule 5.4) and keeps this an attorney work tool rather than advice to consumers.
why_now: Subprime 60+ day delinquency hit a 32-year high in January 2026 and roughly 3M repossessions a year feed a deficiency pipeline that debt buyers monetize through suits. 84-month loans and underwater trade-ins make deficiencies large, so a $99 audit is small next to the dollars at stake per case. LLMs now read messy contract scans, auction bills and notices for cents per case, which was not economic in 2022. Federal consumer-finance enforcement has retrenched since 2025 (verify), so what enforcement remains is private and state-level, and it runs through exactly these lawyers.
revenue_model: $99 per audit; $499 per month for up to 8 audits plus template library for small firms; about $2,400 per year site licenses for legal aid; $750 for attorney-directed analyst declarations. Second, higher-value stream: anonymized pattern reports on defect prevalence by lender, debt buyer and collection law firm (for example, the share of one plaintiff's notices that omit add-on credits), sold to class-action firms and state AG staff at $25K to $100K per report. Audit revenue alone is a small wedge (likely single-digit millions a year), so the dataset and pattern reports are the scale path.
non_obvious_insight: Each audit is a product and a labeled data point. Deficiency defects are systematic because one plaintiff's template produces the same omission in every case, and UCC 9-625 statutory damages attach per consumer, so the pattern is worth far more to class counsel than a single case is to a defendant. The parent's flaw, that lender incentives run against the borrower, becomes the moat: lenders and their in-house recovery teams can never sell this because they are the party being audited. The borrower's claim also needs a number and a deadline, not the dealer's or administrator's cooperation.
first_30_days: Week 1: pull about 300 recent deficiency complaints from public dockets in the candidate states (plaintiff, amount, whether the defendant had counsel) to pick two states and list the 10 heaviest filers; have a consumer-law ethics lawyer review the template for unauthorized-practice and fee-sharing risk. Weeks 2 to 3: ask 15 consumer-defense firms and 3 legal aid units (through NACA, NCLC and state consumer-law listservs) for their next 3 deficiency cases free in return for a written outcome; deliver each audit manually in 24 hours using LLM extraction plus an analyst. Week 4: switch to $99, publish an anonymized 'five places deficiency numbers lie' guide, and log the dollar swing on every case. Target: 30 audits delivered, 10 paid, 5 documented cases where the balance moved by more than $1,000.

title: Insurer-Paid Total-Loss Add-On Refund Concierge
one_liner: When a financed car is totaled, the auto insurer's settlement packet is exactly what GAP and service-contract administrators demand, so the insurer pays a flat fee to have every unearned add-on refund and GAP claim filed and tracked for the claimant, who keeps 100 percent of the money.
customer: Personal-auto insurers' total-loss claims and claims-experience leaders, starting with regional and mutual carriers (roughly 50K to 1M policies; dozens to low hundreds of them, estimate) and independent-agency channels, reached through total-loss valuation and claims-platform vendors and claims TPAs as channel partners. The claimant is the beneficiary; the insurer is the payer.
problem: About one in five collision claims ends in a total loss (2M+ vehicles a year, estimate; verify with CCC-type data). Many of those cars are financed and carry rolled-in GAP, service contracts, tire-and-wheel, paint and key products that are worthless the day the car is totaled. Unearned pro-rata refunds are owed and GAP may pay a deficiency, but each has deadlines and document demands (valuation report, settlement letter, proof of loss date, payoff letter). The dealer that sold the products is long gone, the lender only sees a payoff, and the insurer never touches the retail installment contract. The claimant, already at peak frustration with the insurer, leaves money on the table, then shops for the next car and the next policy.
solution: A link in the total-loss settlement email or adjuster portal. The claimant photographs the retail installment contract (or uploads the payoff letter and dealer bill of sale). LLM extraction lists the financed add-ons and administrators; the engine computes refunds owed as of the date of loss under the contract and state rules and flags any possible GAP claim; it then auto-assembles the packet using the insurer's own valuation report, settlement letter and loss date, submits to each administrator, chases to payment, and escalates stalled cases to the state insurance department. The claimant sees a live tracker and receives 100% of recovered money (or it reduces the payoff if the loan is open, per contract). The insurer gets a dashboard of dollars recovered, days to pay and complaints avoided.
why_now: Total-loss frequency is at record levels as repair costs outpace vehicle values. Insurers just lived through 2023 to 2025 record rate increases and policyholder shopping, so retention after a claim is now a board-level metric. Claims workflows are digital end to end (e-settlement letters, text-based claims), so a link fits where a call center never did. LLMs read contract scans and administrator forms for cents, and 84-month loans with stacked add-ons mean more claimants carry unearned products than in 2019.
revenue_model: Insurer pays only for completed value: about $45 per claim where a refund or GAP payment is recovered, plus a $60K to $150K annual platform fee for integration and dashboards at a mid-size carrier (estimates to test). Channel partners take 20 to 30 percent of revenue. Illustration: a regional insurer with 8,000 total losses a year, 20% eligible with financed add-ons, is 1,600 cases at $45, about $72K a year plus platform fee. The claimant is never charged. Later modules: replacement-vehicle loan referral and title chase, and sold benchmarks of administrator refund and GAP payment speed to insurer vendor-management teams and regulators.
non_obvious_insight: The parent assumed the lender's payoff desk is the one place that sees the loan end. Total loss is a second such moment, and there the insurer, not the lender, holds the documents administrators need and has the motive to make the claimant whole. Because the insurer's paper carries a valuation report and loss date, administrators cannot stall on it the way they stall on a consumer's cancellation request. The insurer's motive is retention and complaint ratio, not the refund itself, so the fee-optics problem disappears (nobody skims the claimant's money), and the purchase comes from a claims-experience budget that already exists rather than a compliance budget that must be fought for.
first_30_days: Weeks 1 to 2: build the refund and GAP-claim rules engine for the 15 largest administrators, the claimant flow and the insurer letter template. Weeks 1 to 4: pitch 10 independent insurance agencies (who feel post-loss churn directly), 3 regional or mutual insurer claims VPs and 2 claims-technology partners. Offer a free 60-day pilot on 100 total-loss claimants with a signed LOI at $45 per recovered case if average recovery exceeds $500. Run the first 30 to 50 claimants as a concierge (analyst plus LLM), tracking opt-in rate, share with financed add-ons, average dollars and days to pay. Publish a one-page 'what a total loss leaves on the table' note from those numbers to open insurer doors.

title: Auto Loan-End Event Exchange for Add-On Refunds
one_liner: Start by recovering unearned add-on refunds on repossessed and charged-off loans for small lenders on pure contingency (cash the lender itself keeps), then turn those lender-attested loan-end events into a neutral exchange that administrators, carriers and regulators plug into, so refunds become a statutory event pushed to the administrator instead of a claim the borrower must pull.
customer: Stage 1: collections and recovery managers at credit unions and community banks with $200M to $3B in auto loans (too small for in-house recovery teams), plus the collection agencies and recovery BPOs that serve them. Stage 2 payers: GAP and service-contract administrators and their fronting or contractual-liability carriers and reinsurers; regulators get free access. Governance: founding lenders receive equity or rebates through a cooperative structure such as a CUSO.
problem: At repossession or charge-off, the unearned refund on financed GAP, service contracts and other add-ons is collectible cash for the lender and shrinks the deficiency billed to the member. Small lenders rarely chase it because each administrator has its own paper process and the dealer chargeback fight breeds stalling. The deeper failure is informational: where a state requires automatic refunds on payoff (the parent cites New Jersey; verify), the administrator cannot comply because nobody tells it the loan ended. No one sits between the lender who knows and the administrator who owes, so every refund is a bilateral fight with no shared standard, no SLA and no scoreboard.
solution: Stage 1, sellable within 6 months, is a Repo Refund Desk. The lender drops a monthly file of repossessions and charge-offs plus contract images (secure upload, no core integration). The system reads the add-ons, matches administrators, computes refunds by state rule, files cancellations under the lender's assignment of unearned premiums, and tracks to payment. Refunds post to the lender's loan account, cutting both the write-off and the member's deficiency. Fee: 20 to 25% of cash actually recovered, nothing upfront. Stage 2: every processed case becomes a signed loan-end event (VIN, contract ID, event type, date, products, computed refund). Publish an open Loan-End Event schema and API; administrators get structured, lender-attested cancellation requests in their own intake format, cheaper than manual intake and a defensible statutory trigger. Payoff and total-loss events join (the parent's payoff-desk plug-in becomes a free module). Stage 3: carriers and reinsurers get true early-termination curves and refund-SLA dashboards; regulators get a free supervisory view; later a settlement layer and a refund-advance facility.
why_now: Record subprime delinquency and roughly 3M repossessions a year create a large event flow today. 84-month loans mean add-ons are unearned at almost every repossession. LLM contract reading cuts per-case processing from tens of dollars to cents, which is what makes contingency pricing work. State regulators and private plaintiffs are filling a federal enforcement retreat (verify), raising the value of an audit trail. Core-processor API marketplaces and CUSOs make plug-in distribution to credit unions cheaper than a direct sales force (verify).
revenue_model: Stage 1: 20 to 25% contingency on recovered cash. Illustration to validate in the free retrospective audit: a lender with $1B in auto loans, about 1,000 repossessions a year, 45% with financed add-ons, about $700 average unearned, 60% currently unclaimed is roughly $190K of new cash a year and a $40K to $47K annual fee. Stage 2: administrators pay $2 to $5 per attested event plus a compliance subscription; carriers and reinsurers pay $50K to $250K a year for termination and SLA data; regulators free. Stage 3: a 0.5 to 1% network fee on refunds settled through the exchange, and a refund-advance facility funded with outside capital. Stage 1 alone is a viable small business; the exchange is the venture-scale option.
non_obvious_insight: The stalling problem is less about willingness than information: nobody tells the administrator the loan ended, and the one party that knows, the lender, has never had a reason to say so. Refund-on-repossession, unlike refund-on-payoff, is the lender's own cash, so the lender pays willingly, and the same act produces the signed events that convert each administrator's private float into a scoreboarded, regulator-visible liability. The exchange's real asset is the true early-termination rate for financed add-ons, which no administrator, reinsurer or regulator can observe today because they see only claimed cancellations, not loans that actually ended. That number prices and reserves every GAP and service-contract program.
first_30_days: Weeks 1 to 2: build administrator playbooks for the 20 largest administrators and 10 states (as in the parent) and the pro-rata engine. Weeks 1 to 3: offer 5 credit unions or community banks a free retrospective audit of their last 12 months of repossessions and charge-offs and report the cash left on the table. Weeks 3 to 4: sign 2 on 25% contingency and process live cases weekly; recruit one collection agency or recovery BPO as a reseller. In parallel, publish Loan-End Event schema v0.1 openly, and send an SLA-scoreboard mockup built from the first 100 cases to compliance heads at 10 administrators and consumer-services staff at 2 state insurance departments. Target: $25K of recovered cash logged, 3 lender LOIs, 1 administrator willing to receive structured requests.

title: ERCOT Large-Load Energization Files, Fixed Fee
one_liner: A two-engineer Texas specialist that sells neocloud and colo developers a fixed-fee, six-week package of ISO-acceptable PSS/E and EMT models, a ride-through study and a compliance file, with a fee kicker paid when ERCOT accepts it.
customer: Wedge: VPs of power and interconnection leads at 30-60 mid-size neocloud, colo and AI-campus developers with 25-300 MW sites in ERCOT's large-load study queue, plus the EPCs that own their energization schedule. They have no in-house power-electronics staff. Hyperscalers with in-house power simulators are excluded on purpose.
problem: Since PGRR115 and NPRR1234 (effective late 2025), ERCOT wants studies and dynamic models for loads of 25 MW or more before energization. NOGRR282 (effective Aug 1, 2026) adds frequency and voltage ride-through requirements for large computational loads. A developer holds only OEM spec sheets. UPS and power-shelf control details sit behind OEM NDAs, and bespoke PSCAD consultants are slow and have never modeled a GPU power shelf. Every rejected model or resubmittal loop delays energization. At 100 MW of leased AI capacity, a month of slip defers roughly eight figures of rent or GPU revenue (rough estimate: about $100+/kW-month of critical IT), so a $150k package is a rounding error next to the delay it prevents.
solution:
Sell acceptance, not artifacts, in four steps.
1) A $15-25k gap analysis against the NOGRR282, PGRR115 and NPRR1234 texts, using the site's one-line diagram and UPS/PSU bill of materials.
2) A fixed-fee package of $90-180k: an ISO-submittable PSS/E dynamic model and EMT model, a ride-through and oscillation study, and a compliance file. It is built from reusable platform-level models of specific UPS, power-shelf and facility archetypes. Those models are HIL-validated at a partner lab (Typhoon HIL or OPAL-RT time, or a university lab) under OEM NDAs.
3) Submission handling and resubmittal support through ERCOT's large-load process.
4) A 25% success kicker paid on ERCOT acceptance, plus an annual re-issue subscription when GPU generation, UPS firmware or 800V DC changes the load.
why_now: NOGRR282 was approved July 9, 2026 and took effect Aug 1, 2026. PGRR115 (Nov and Dec 2025) and NPRR1234 (Dec 15, 2025) already gate energization on studies and models. The first wave of 25 MW and larger neocloud sites is hitting the queue now, before any consultancy has a large-load specialty. Rubin-generation hardware and 800V DC change the load behavior again within 12-18 months, which creates re-issue demand.
revenue_model: $15-25k gap analysis, $90-180k fixed-fee package, and a 25% success kicker on acceptance (about $25-45k). Add $20-40k per year model maintenance and re-issue per site, and later OEM test-and-listing fees for platform models. A year-1 target of about 12 packages at about $150k is roughly $1.8M with 2-3 engineers. Reuse of platform models across sites is what lifts gross margin past a consultancy's 30-40%.
non_obvious_insight: The developer does not want a model. It wants ERCOT's planners to sign off without a resubmittal loop. The durable business in inverter modeling after Blue Cut was not the model libraries, because vendors and ISOs published those. It was the shops that knew what the ISO's planners would accept. A single-regulator focus (ERCOT only) lets a two-person shop become the known acceptance expert in six months, and each accepted submission is precedent no generalist consultant has. Free generic EPRI or NERC models help us: they are conservative, and a developer who submits them risks being told to add buffer capacity or accept curtailment, while a product-specific validated model avoids that.

title: Grid-Readiness Model Audit for Data Center Lenders
one_liner: An independent checker for private-credit funds, banks and delay-in-start-up insurers that audits a borrower's large-load models and ride-through evidence and gives an energization-risk opinion, the same way financial-model auditors already serve project-finance lenders.
customer: Data center and GPU-cloud finance teams at credit funds, banks and ABS arrangers, plus the lender's independent engineers, technical advisors and project-finance law firms that act as the channel. Delay-in-start-up (DSU) insurers and MGAs are the second payer. The borrower's fee is paid at lender direction, which is the market norm for lender advisors.
problem: Lenders finance billions of dollars of campuses and GPU fleets. Interest accrues and hardware depreciates while the site waits for energization. Their diligence covers construction cost, schedule, MEP and offtake, but grid dynamic behavior is a black box authored by an interested party: the borrower's own consultant says interconnection is on track. After the 2024 Northern Virginia load-loss event and ERCOT's new rules, lenders have no independent way to judge whether the load model will pass, whether ride-through settings will trip the site, or how far energization could slip. Developer-side consultants such as Electranix and Danovo are conflicted, and the lender's independent engineer typically lacks EMT skills.
solution:
Sell a check, not a build.
1) A pre-close Grid-Readiness Opinion of $30-75k per site. It is an independent review of the borrower's PSS/E and EMT models, study reports, interconnection-agreement conditions and UPS, PSU and firmware settings against the ISO's rules and generic reference models. It ends with a red/amber/green rating and a P50/P90 energization-slip range.
2) A conditions-precedent and covenant kit for law firms: draw conditions such as ISO-accepted model, passed ride-through test and firmware freeze.
3) Re-attestation of $10-20k whenever GPU generation or UPS firmware changes, triggered by covenant.
4) A portfolio dashboard for lenders by ISO and site, and an anonymized risk dataset for DSU underwriters.
Analysts run rule-based checklists and scripted checks through the PSS/E Python API, so each review takes about 40-80 hours. Our own modeling is never required.
why_now: Neocloud and data center debt (delayed-draw term loans, GPU-backed facilities, ABS) grew explosively in 2025-26, and energization delay has become a visible schedule risk in publicly reported neocloud results. Regulatory rules that make models and ride-through a gating item are now in force in Texas, with PJM and NERC large-load work following. Lenders and insurers are looking for a diligence item to price, and nobody offers it yet.
revenue_model: Borrower-paid, lender-directed fees of $30-75k per site per financing and $10-20k per refresh re-attestation. DSU insurers pay $10-25k per underwriting review, or a data license, and later take a share of premium through an MGA program. Rough bottom-up: 200 qualifying US financings a year (assumption to verify) at $50k is about $10M, and 400 sites refreshed at $15k is about $6M, so this is a $15-25M niche. It is a thin, high-margin analyst business that later becomes a rating or registry.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer of a grid model is whoever bears the cost of delay, not the grid. Project finance already has an independent-checker culture, with financial-model audits and independent engineers, because lenders will not trust numbers authored by the borrower. A dynamic load model is the same kind of black-box spreadsheet driving a billion-dollar decision. The parent's three structural threats become tailwinds here. Free EPRI or NERC generic models become the benchmark we audit against. OEM secrecy is irrelevant because we test the borrower's model against acceptance criteria and measured behavior and need no OEM IP. In-house hyperscaler tools do not matter because hyperscalers are not project-financed on this basis. Independence is the moat, which the developer-side consultants cannot claim.
first_30_days: Run 15 interviews: 5 data center finance leads at credit funds and banks, 5 lender independent engineers or technical advisors, 3 DSU underwriters or brokers, and 2 project-finance law firms. Offer a $25k pilot Grid-Readiness Opinion on one live financing. Sign one independent-engineer firm as a white-label channel, since it can bill our add-on and lacks EMT capability. Recruit one ex-ISO planner and one project-finance analyst. Publish a 20-question Grid-Readiness Diligence Checklist for lenders and a redacted sample opinion built from public queue and rule data, and pass it through law firms as collateral.

title: Ride-Through Witness: Measure-First Large-Load Network
one_liner: Invert the parent's model-before-energization: ingest the UPS logs and power-quality waveforms sites already record, join them with grid-side PMU data, and auto-produce ISO-format ride-through and oscillation reports, growing into the reference data network that ISOs, OEMs and insurers rely on.
customer: Wedge: reliability and compliance managers and facility engineering leads at operators of 25-200 MW neocloud and colo sites in ERCOT and PJM, already energized or energizing. Second-side payers later are ISOs and TOs (aggregate feeds and model-validation reports), UPS and power-shelf OEMs (fleet analytics), and insurers.
problem: When a grid fault drops hundreds of MW of data center load, the ISO asks every site whether it tripped and why. The evidence sits inside the facility: UPS event logs, PQ-meter waveforms, power-shelf telemetry and transfer-to-backup thresholds. ISO PMUs only see the outside. As I read the reported 2024 Northern Virginia loss of about 1.5 GW, its cause was facility-side protection and backup-transfer behavior that grid operators could not see (verify against the NERC incident review). Pre-energization models are never validated against reality, and they decay as GPU firmware and UPS settings change monthly. Operators face blame, curtailment and NOGRR282 exposure with no forensic evidence and no ride-through margin figure.
solution: Software-first, with no hardware in the first release. 'Witness' ingests existing data (UPS event logs, PQDIF and COMTRADE files from existing PQ meters and relays, generator and BESS logs) and time-aligns it with public ISO and PMU frequency data. Within 24 hours of any event it generates an ISO-format disturbance report: what tripped, at what threshold and delay, how fast load recovered, and the oscillation signature. It also runs a continuous dashboard against NOGRR282 thresholds and detects GPU-cluster synchronized swings. Phase 2 adds a white-label certified point-on-wave recorder for sites without one. Phase 3 turns fleet data into measurement-validated models, a model-versus-reality score, OEM firmware benchmarks and an insurance risk score. We offer the report schema to ISOs and NERC as a standard, the equivalent of the IBR event-analysis and monitoring standards (PRC-028/029/030).
why_now: NOGRR282 has been in force since Aug 1, 2026, so the industry moves from modeling to operations, and the first real ride-through events at AI sites are being recorded now. NERC's IBR standards (PRC-028/029/030) show the regulatory template of monitoring plus event analysis for inverter-based resources, and it is plausible to extend it to large loads (unverified). GPU-load oscillation is now a public concern. Every operator already logs the data, and cheap cloud compute plus LLM-assisted log parsing make ingesting heterogeneous vendor formats cheap for the first time.
revenue_model: Operators: $30-70k per site per year for the subscription, or $10-15k per retro-analysis or event report. ISOs and TOs: $100-500k per year each for aggregated feeds and model-validation reports once 30 or more sites are connected. OEMs: $50-200k per year for cross-brand fleet analytics. Insurers: risk-score licensing. Data network effects and standard-setting are what make this a 10x outcome, with 300 sites at $50k as $15M in operator revenue alone, plus roughly the same again from the other sides.
non_obvious_insight: The 2024 event was an inside-the-facility information problem, and only the join of facility recorders and grid PMUs establishes causation. No single site sees aggregate risk, and only a neutral third party can pool data across UPS brands and operators, which OEMs and hyperscalers will not. That gives network economies and a cornered resource, proprietary as-measured behavior of real AI facilities in real faults. The parent sells the exam and this sells the proof you keep passing it. Free generic models cannot substitute for a fleet-wide, as-measured dataset. A retro-analysis of an operator's own past voltage dips is a sellable product with no OEM or pre-energization model required.
first_30_days: Sell a $10-15k Ride-Through Margin Audit built from an operator's own historical voltage-dip and UPS-transfer events, delivered by hand as a concierge service. Recruit one power-quality or protection engineer and one data engineer. Build parsers for PQDIF, COMTRADE and two or three UPS log formats. Contact reliability and compliance leads at 20 operators (ERCOT and PJM) and 3 TO or ISO planners, and offer a free report on one public event to each. Publish the draft report schema and an open primer on GPU oscillation signatures. Confirm what NOGRR282 requires in terms of operations-phase reporting.
