title: AI Exclusion Diff for Pro-Liability Renewals
one_liner: Forward a renewal quote or binder PDF and get, within 24 hours, a diff against the expiring policy, a breadth score for any new AI exclusion, and a client-ready gap letter. It is built for the professional-liability desk of independent agencies, and it also ranks competing quotes by exclusion breadth.
customer: The professional-services desk at independent agencies of 8-60 staff. That means the producer or account manager who handles 60-120 E&O, tech E&O, D&O, cyber and pro-services CGL renewals a year for architects and engineers, accountants, law firms, marketing and design agencies, and IT and software services firms. Much of their paper is surplus lines placed through wholesalers, which SERFF-based tools cannot see.
problem: AI exclusions on professional-liability paper are the broadest and most bespoke (Berkley's 'absolute' PC 51380, 'any AI' versus gen-AI only, vendor-supplied AI, BI/PD versus advertising injury, manuscript wording). They arrive buried in a stack of quote and binder PDFs, and the premium barely moves. The producer has about 10 minutes per renewal and no way to tell whether the exclusion is new, how wide it is, or whether it hits what the client actually does. Quandri and Zywave compare premium and limits. Patra checks 900+ points but is not AI-specific and does not diff against the expiring form. Filing trackers show what a carrier filed in a state, not what is attached to this client's policy.
solution: Intake is an email-in address with no AMS integration. The producer forwards the quote, binder or policy PDF plus the expiring policy. The output is a one-page report with five parts. (1) Diff: is an AI exclusion new, widened or unchanged versus expiring. (2) Breadth score of 0-5 across six dimensions: gen-AI only versus any AI, BI/PD versus advertising or personal injury, vendor-supplied AI, professional-services carve-outs, defence-cost treatment, and prior-acts effect. (3) A short 8-question client AI-use intake, which shows which of the client's real AI uses are now stranded. (4) A client-ready gap letter with a signed-acknowledgment page. (5) Quote-stage ranking: when the producer holds 2-4 competing quotes, it ranks them by exclusion breadth and drafts the exact carve-back request to send back, for example 'replace any-AI with gen-AI-only and carve out vendor-supplied AI'. Public filings (Trades Coverage, Certian, Gridex) are used only as a free auto-labeller for known forms. Delivery in the first months is LLM extraction plus a retired E&O underwriter reviewing every report. The output is a PDF plus JSON that files into Epic or Zywave as an attachment, so the product is a partner add-on and not a rival dashboard.
why_now: Renewals dated 1 Jan 2027 are the first big cycle after the ISO CG 40 47/40 48 forms and Berkley's absolute exclusion, and those quotes reach producers in Nov-Dec 2026, which is now. Trade press and associations (IA Magazine on 9 Sep 2026, Big I, Agents United) are telling agencies to review renewals for AI exclusions, but they give no tooling. Zywave's Advisor Agent, in early access since June 2026, is teaching agencies to expect renewal triage, and it does not read endorsements. Long-context PDF extraction on scanned binders is now cheap and reliable enough to do the classification at a cost of about $1 per document.
revenue_model: Pay per renewal at $150 for a standard quote diff and $450 for a multi-policy or manuscript diff. A $600/month plan includes 20 diffs. A $500 concierge audit on an agency's five largest accounts is the entry offer. Unit economics: about $1 of inference plus 15 minutes of reviewer time at about $60/hour gives roughly 85% gross margin on a $150 diff. This is my estimate: 1,000-2,000 US agencies run a real professional-liability desk, at 80 renewals a year that is $12-24k per agency, so 100 agencies is about $1.2-2.4M ARR. Referral revenue from affirmative markets is optional upside, and nothing depends on it, which answers the judges' doubt about the 10-15% commission.
non_obvious_insight: The thing a producer pays for is the ask, not the detection. Manuscript AI exclusions are negotiable, and a diff that says 'this wording is broader than the same carrier's competitor quote, ask for this replacement' turns a defensive letter into a shopping and negotiation tool that wins the account. The E&O-fear trigger also does not depend on the duty-to-advise law, which is weak in most states. Agencies that sell 'annual coverage reviews' assume a duty, and the signed acknowledgment turns that exposure into a documented file. The moat is not the public filings database. It is a labelled corpus of issued forms as attached to real quotes, including surplus lines, with outcome labels showing which carve-backs carriers actually granted. That corpus grows with every diff, and nobody can scrape it.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: recruit 10 pro-services-heavy agencies through LinkedIn and state agent-association contacts, and hire a retired professional-liability underwriter at 10 hours a week to write the 6-dimension rubric. Days 8-20: collect each agency's last 3 renewals for its 5 biggest pro-liability accounts (about 150 documents) and run the manual-plus-LLM diff. Measure the hit rate, meaning the share of renewals containing an AI exclusion the producer had not flagged. Proceed if it is 30% or more, and treat under 15% as the kill signal. Days 15-30: sell the $500 concierge audit and convert each agency to per-diff pricing for its live Nov-Dec 1/1 renewals. Publish the breadth scale v0.1 with 20 anonymised specimen forms as free content, and open a developer-partner conversation with Zywave and the Epic marketplace.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Patra (AI Policy Checking), Quandri, Zywave Apex / Advisor Agent, Testudo. White space: A real gap remains, but it is much narrower than the pitch. Nobody found sells a commercial-lines, broker-facing workflow that (1) takes a book's actual renewal forms schedules, quotes and binders (not just carrier-level filings), (2) detects and normalises AI exclusion breadth for each client, including bespoke wording such as Berkley PC 51380 and unnamed 'AI' language, (3) ties it to a 90-day renewal calendar, and (4) hands the producer a client-ready gap letter and a matched affirmative placement. Pieces exist separately. Patra reads commercial policies for hidden exclusions but is not AI-specific. Quandri and Zywave own the 90-day renewal trigger but show no exclusion-level AI flagging. Three parts of the plan are weak. (a) The SERFF scraper and exclusion database are not a moat. Trades Coverage already compiled 4,078 records for free. Gridex, Certian, Vorp Labs and ShadowLock publish free trackers, and Certian even ships CC BY 4.0 CSV and JSON. (b) A filing shows a carrier adopted a form in a state. It does not show the form is attached to client X's policy, so the real signal is the policy document, not the filing. (c) SERFF filing access covers admitted markets only. Surplus lines is where most E&O, D&O and tech-E&O AI exclusions sit, and it is largely invisible to SERFF.

Wedge that looks unserved: commercial professional-liability and tech-E&O accounts (design firms, law, accounting, software, agencies) where exclusions are broadest and most bespoke, for independent agencies without an in-house risk-advisory team, priced as a renewal-review add-on rather than a filings database. | How this version avoids them: Patra is outsourced whole-policy checking across 12 lines, with no AI-specific taxonomy and no expiring-versus-renewal diff. This is a specialist quote-stage tool with a per-renewal price, and it could later be a partner or a buyer. Quandri is AMS-embedded and mostly personal lines, and its renewal review focuses on premium and coverage shifts. This is email-in and reads endorsements. Zywave Advisor Agent owns the 90-day trigger, and this product is the classifier it could plug in, not a competing dashboard. Testudo, Armilla, AIUC, Mount and Munich Re/Mosaic are carriers or coverholders with placement conflicts. This is neutral and earns nothing from placement. The free trackers (Gridex, Certian, Vorp Labs, ShadowLock) and Trades Coverage's 4,078-record dataset are carrier-level, so they cannot answer 'what does my client's quote say', and they become free inputs, not competitors. Rosella and FurtherAI do generic policy comparison with no AI breadth score, no gap letter and no negotiation ask. SERFF vendors (InsuranceFiling, Filing360, FilingRamp) sell to compliance teams, and their data misses surplus lines.

title: Agency E&O Insurers Fund AI-Exclusion File Reviews
one_liner: The insurers and endorsed programs that cover insurance agencies pay to put an AI-exclusion review and a client-acknowledgment file behind every commercial renewal their insured agencies handle. It is funded as loss control, in the way cyber insurers fund security scans, and the agency pays little or nothing.
customer: Payer: underwriting and program managers at insurance-agency E&O carriers and MGAs, and the state independent-agent associations that endorse an E&O program to their members. Users: the insured agencies with 5-100 staff. Buyer chain: the party who bears the cost of failure-to-warn claims pays, and the party who does the work receives the tool.
problem: Agency E&O carriers will pay defence costs and settlements when a client discovers, after an AI-caused loss, that the renewal quietly excluded AI and nobody told them. The exclusions are silent (the premium barely changes), they arrive in mass on 1/1/2027 renewals, and the claims will surface in 2027-2029. Even where the duty to advise is weak, defence costs are incurred anyway. Today these carriers have only PDF advisories and webinars, no data on whether any insured agency did anything, and no view of aggregate exposure across their book.
solution: A white-labelled program, called the 'Exclusion File' in the carrier's brand, with three parts. (1) Agency workflow: the agency forwards the renewal quote or policy PDF and receives the diff, the breadth score and a gap letter. The client e-signs an acknowledgment, either accepting the exclusion or asking for affirmative cover or a negotiated carve-back. Everything is stored in an audit-ready vault, which is the classic E&O defence of documented advice. (2) Carrier dashboard: the share of insured agencies enrolled, the share of commercial renewals reviewed, unresolved acknowledgments, and anonymised aggregate exclusion prevalence and breadth by line and by carrier form. It shows the carrier's own exposure. (3) Underwriting hook: a supplemental question on the E&O application, 'Do you review renewals for AI exclusions and retain client acknowledgments?', and an optional rate credit or deductible break for agencies that complete the program on 90% or more of their commercial renewals. The diff engine underneath is the same as in the sharpened offspring, so the marginal build cost is the vault, the e-sign flow and the dashboard.
why_now: The first large exclusion cycle is 1 Jan 2027, so an E&O carrier that acts in Q4 2026 has a defensible risk-control story before any claims exist. Trade and association content already urges agencies to review renewals (Big I on the Verisk rollout, Agents United, IA Magazine on 9 Sep 2026), so the carriers' insureds are being asked to act with no help. Cyber insurers that fund scans and security tooling for insureds have made the loss-control-for-premium-credit model familiar to underwriters. Agency E&O is a concentrated market with few carriers and programs, so a small number of decisions covers a lot of insured agencies.
revenue_model: The carrier or program pays $600-1,500 per enrolled agency per year, plus $25-60k per year for a quarterly AI-exclusion exposure report for its underwriters and reinsurers. The agency pays a $49-99 copay per diff, or nothing where the carrier sponsors it fully. An association that endorses the program takes an endorsed-vendor fee of 10-15% of agency revenue, which is how associations already monetise vendor programs. As an illustration: a carrier insuring 1,500 agencies, 20% enrolled at $900 each, is about $270k a year, plus the data subscription. These figures are estimates to be tested in pilot.
non_obvious_insight: The E&O insurer is the only party in the chain that pays whether or not a court finds a duty to advise, so it does not care about the legal debate that weakens the broker-side pitch. The distribution lever is also the E&O application. Once the supplemental question is on the form, agencies need a compliant answer every year, and this program becomes the standard way to give one. The same carrier-funded logic scales to the next silent-exclusion wave, whether PFAS, cyber war, biometric or another, so the customer can renew and expand on the same integration.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: write a 2-page memo for underwriters with three concrete failure-to-warn fact patterns on 1/1/2027 renewals and a list of the largest agency E&O carriers, MGAs and association-endorsed programs. Book calls through LinkedIn and state association staff, and aim for 5 calls. Days 10-25: offer 3 state associations a free 45-minute webinar, 'AI exclusions on your Jan 1 renewals', which is a cheap way to capture 100+ agencies. Sign 10-25 of them as a pilot cohort using the concierge diff. Days 20-30: take the pilot cohort's hit-rate numbers (how many renewals had a new AI exclusion the agency had not flagged) back to the carriers and associations as a pilot pitch. title: Verified AI Coverage Levels for Vendor Contracts
one_liner: Invert the parent by checking the vendor's insurance from the counterparty's side. AI-enabled vendors upload their policies and get an independent, shareable 'AI Coverage Level' (L0-L3) with monitoring, so enterprise procurement teams can write 'L2 or higher' into contracts. Over time that makes it the insurance-sufficiency standard for AI vendors.
customer: Payer: AI-enabled software and services vendors of 10-300 staff (SaaS with AI features, dev and marketing agencies, MSPs, fintech and health-tech vendors) who sell to banks, health systems and other regulated enterprises with insurance clauses in their MSAs. Free users: enterprise general counsel, TPRM and procurement teams. Later payers: those enterprises' portfolio-monitoring subscriptions, and vendor-compliance and trust-center platforms embedding the check by API.
problem: Enterprise MSAs require vendors to carry, for example, $5M tech E&O and $5M cyber. Proof is a certificate of insurance, which shows limits, carrier and expiry but not exclusions. An absolute AI exclusion in the E&O policy makes the certificate hollow for exactly the failures the buyer worries about (a hallucinated output that costs money, model-vendor data leakage, generated-content IP claims, an autonomous action). The vendor rarely knows, because the broker did not flag the endorsement. The buyer relies on coverage nobody has read, and the indemnity is only as good as the vendor's balance sheet. The insured is the party least motivated to find out its coverage is hollow, so it never gets found. (I could not run web checks in this session to confirm that no COI tracker already reads endorsement wording, so treat that as an assumption to verify first.)
solution: First product, sellable within 6 months: the 'AI Coverage Attestation'. The vendor or its broker uploads the policies and endorsements, and the same diff and classification engine runs. An independent reviewer signs a one-page output. It shows the level and, for four AI failure modes (erroneous output, IP infringement from generated content, data leakage through a model provider, autonomous action), whether each is covered, excluded or silent, plus retro date and whether defence costs sit inside limits. The vendor gets a shareable live link for procurement teams and trust centers. Monitoring re-verifies at every renewal or cancellation and alerts the vendor and anyone who holds the link. The published levels run from L0 (absolute or any-AI exclusion), L1 (gen-AI exclusion with carve-backs), L2 (silent, with no AI exclusion) to L3 (affirmative AI cover). The buyer gets a free portal and an 'AI insurance rider' clause library, so a GC can write 'vendor must hold L2 or higher' into an MSA. Vendors at L0 or L1 are given a neutral list of affirmative markets, but nothing in the model depends on placement.
why_now: Enterprise AI procurement is now standard, and AI addenda in MSAs and security questionnaires are spreading. Vendors renewing on 1 Jan 2027 will be the first large cohort to lose AI coverage silently, just as customers' contracts assume it. Trades Coverage counted 2,369 AI exclusions in force by 31 July 2026, so the exposure exists at scale. Trust-center tools have made 'share evidence by link' the normal way to close security reviews, and AIUC-1 shows that buyers accept an AI assurance standard when it is credible. Long-context extraction over policy PDFs is what makes independent attestation affordable.
revenue_model: Vendor pays $900-2,400 per year per attestation including monitoring, or $250 for a rush one-off when a deal is waiting. Enterprise portfolio monitoring for 200+ vendors is $12-30k per year. Platform API checks are $20-60 each. Affirmative-market referral fees are a later, secondary line. These are estimates to test. The payer is the vendor, because a tick-box that blocks a six-figure deal is worth far more than the fee.
non_obvious_insight: This flips the buyer chain. The party that relies on the coverage, and holds contractual leverage, is the one who can force a hundred vendors to verify, so the value of the credential rises with each buyer that references it. That is a network effect broker software does not have. It also sidesteps the duty-to-advise weakness, because the obligation is contractual, not tort-based. And the level scheme lets an independent attestor become the standard, while carriers cannot credibly grade their own wording and the AI-liability carriers have a conflict.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: interview 20 vendor CFOs and founders and 10 GC or TPRM leads, and collect 5 real security questionnaires or MSAs that contain an AI-insurance question. Days 8-20: run 10 free attestations on real policies from vendors who agree, and publish Levels v0.1 with one redline rider clause. Days 15-30: pre-sell 5 attestations at $500 to vendors with a live deal blocked on the question, and pitch 2 trust-center or COI platforms for a pilot integration. Kill signal: if fewer than 3 of the 20 buyers can name a deal or contract review where the insurance question mattered, the counterparty pull is not there.

title: Same-Week MFP Refunds for Senior-Care Pharmacies
one_liner: A refund-purchase facility for independent long-term-care pharmacies that becomes the payee of record on Medicare's negotiated-price refunds and pays out within two business days, underwritten claim by claim.
customer: Owners and CFOs of independent closed-door long-term-care (LTC) and senior-living pharmacies, and groups of 3-30 of them. First reached through the Senior Care Pharmacy Coalition, whose members warned that 60% may close in 2026 without a fix. Our estimate, to be checked against real claims exports, is a float of $150k to $1M+ per LTC pharmacy (Eliquis, Xarelto, Jardiance, Januvia, Farxiga and Entresto dominate senior volume). That is 5-30x the $27k a month NCPA cites for an average community pharmacy, so each logo is worth far more.
problem: LTC pharmacies pay wholesalers full price on a 7-14 day cycle and then wait about 21 days (CMS/MTF average; 67% of NCPA respondents wait 22+ days) for the difference between price and Maximum Fair Price. They already carry slow nursing-home and PBM receivables. Their bank has a blanket lien and almost certainly treats a non-trade manufacturer refund as ineligible collateral, so the refund float is funded from owner savings or by cutting stock of the drugs seniors need. Merchant cash advances cost far too much for a stream that is statutory.
solution: 1) Onboard with 8-12 weeks of PMS claims exports and MTF remittance files. The free 'refund aging and dilution audit' is our underwriting diligence, not the product. 2) Make the refund land where we control it. Preferred route is being the pharmacy's designated payee, either as a registered third-party support entity if CMS and the facilitator allow it, or through a deposit account under a control agreement. That puts cash upstream of the wholesaler's weekly debit. Fallback is use-of-proceeds control, where the advance pays the MFP-drug invoice lines straight to the wholesaler. 3) Each week, score every MFP claim for dilution and buy the scored-eligible refunds at about 85% within two business days. The 15% reserve, net of our fee, is released when the actual MTF payment arrives. Recourse is limited to dilution through the reserve. There is no blanket credit recourse, and no 'non-recourse' promise we cannot keep. 4) Get the existing senior lender's consent or carve-out at onboarding, pitched as relief for their borrower's cash squeeze. Capital starts at $500k-$2M from a family office or regional bank, then a warehouse line from a specialty credit fund once 6 months of loss data exist.
why_now: The program has run since January 1, 2026 and the pain is measured and public (NCPA survey of 500+ owners, SCPC closure warnings). NCPA was still lobbying CMS on faster payment in September 2026 comments on the 2028 guidance, so no fix is in sight. On January 1, 2027 fifteen more drugs, including semaglutide, join and the float grows. The window is roughly the next three to four quarters, before a wholesaler or a bigger lender standardizes an answer.
revenue_model: Discount of about 0.9-1.25% per roughly 3-week cycle on purchased refunds (roughly 15-22% annualized), plus a $250 a month servicing fee per pharmacy. Illustrative unit economics for a pharmacy averaging $400k outstanding: $60-85k gross a year, about $36k cost of funds at 9%, under $6k expected dilution loss, leaving $20-35k contribution. Forty LTC pharmacies is about $16M outstanding and roughly $1M of annual contribution. An association endorsement, not Facebook groups, is affordable CAC at that revenue per account. Later, syndicate or sell seasoned receivables to a credit fund and keep servicing.
non_obvious_insight: LTC is the one segment where the parent's economics and its main risk both improve. Float per logo is 5-30x larger, so one association relationship replaces thousands of low-value retail leads. The dilution mode that worries everyone in retail, 340B lesser-of rejections, should be structurally small because nursing-home residents are rarely patients of 340B covered entities (verify pharmacy by pharmacy). The remaining dilution modes, discharge or death reversals and partial-cycle credits, are predictable from census and cycle-fill data that we ingest and a bank never sees. The lasting asset is a labeled dataset that maps each claim to its refund outcome. Interest is only how it is monetized.
first_30_days: Ask the Senior Care Pharmacy Coalition for introductions to 20 LTC owners and run willingness-to-pay interviews, pricing against 8-12% bank A/R lines and 30%+ MCAs. Sign 5 pharmacies to a free 60-day dilution audit in exchange for claims and remittance files. Build the dilution model in a notebook from those files. Ask the MTF help desk and a healthcare payments attorney what payee-designation options exist. Have a fintech attorney set the true-sale purchase structure, UCC filings and state commercial-financing disclosures. Line up a $500k credit line from a family office or regional bank. Fund the first three advances at $25-50k each with a 25% holdback.
lineage: mutation of I0499 ('Bridge Loans for Medicare Drug-Price Refunds'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SpendMend (MFP Rebate Reconciliation), Plenful (MFP Intelligence / MFP Command Center), ScriptPro Financial Advantage, Liberty Software (and other PMS vendors, e.g. PioneerRx, PrimeRx, Redsail). White space: Verdict: gap, and a narrow one. In roughly 27 searches across varied terms (MFP refund advance, bridge loan, factoring, fintech, PSAO program, wholesaler program) I found NO product that specifically underwrites and advances against MTF-remitted MFP refunds. Pharmacy lenders sell generic A/R and MCA lines, and the MFP players only sell reconciliation. The unserved space is a claim-level underwriting and servicing capability for refund dilution risk: 340B lesser-of rejections (RARC N907 inappropriate rejections), reversals, Good Faith Inquiry disputes, and authorized-generic refund amounts. It is most valuable for borrowers whose float is large: LTC/senior-care pharmacies, 5-50 store groups, and possibly 340B covered entities in the HRSA rebate pilot, where the float is $8.9M-$208M a year for hospitals (Health Affairs). It also applies to the January 2027 step-up when semaglutide joins.

The wedge is weak in five ways.
1. The 'free missing-refund report' is already crowded: SpendMend, Plenful ($76M raised), ScriptPro, Liberty, and free Beacon MFP dashboards.
2. A typical independent's float is small, about $11k a week or $27k a month per NCPA. At 15-25% APR that is roughly $4-7k a year of gross revenue per pharmacy, before losses and a cost of funds of 8-10%. Customer acquisition through state associations and Facebook groups will be costly relative to that.
3. Wholesalers control the payment path. Cardinal routes MFP refunds through Central Pay and wholesalers auto-debit weekly, so a lender's sweep sits behind the wholesaler in practice. Cardinal customers cannot easily direct refunds to a lender-controlled account.
4. 'Non-recourse' is hard to deliver. Manufacturers can reverse refunds and CMS's own materials describe reversals when claims prove ineligible, so a lender will need pharmacy recourse or holdbacks. That undermines the 'prime paper' insight.
5. Policy is a moving target. CMS made manufacturers include cash-flow mitigation plans in their MFP effectuation plans (accelerated refunds, self-identification). NCPA is still pushing CMS and manufacturers for faster payment, including in Sept 2026 comments on the 2028 guidance.

Adjacent generic lenders can also just add MFP refunds to a borrowing base.

Caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) ran out, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and open-source sweeps were not fully run. 'No direct competitor found' means not found, not proven absent. | How this version avoids them: We do not sell reconciliation. SpendMend, Plenful, ScriptPro, Liberty and the free Beacon dashboards all compete on the report. Here the report is an internal underwriting input given away inside the advance, so there is no head-to-head feature race. Plenful targets health systems. Generic pharmacy lenders and Corporate Capital Direct advance against PBM A/R or MCA-style revenue and do not underwrite MFP refunds claim by claim. Live Oak's cheap SBA-style paper funds acquisitions, not a weekly refund float. We complement the senior lender through an intercreditor consent. The wholesaler's payment path, which the parent's research flagged as make-or-break, is handled by payee routing or direct invoice-line payment. That protects the wholesaler's payment, so it has no reason to object. Narrowing to LTC also sidesteps the small-float, high-CAC retail independent.

title: Refund-Netted Dating: Wholesalers Fund the Float
one_liner: Sell regional wholesalers and buying groups a claim-underwritten '28-day MFP dating' program that defers payment on MFP-drug invoice lines and nets them against the refund, so the pharmacy never borrows and the wholesaler is paid a dilution-risk fee to us.
customer: The independent-pharmacy channel head or CFO at regional full-line wholesalers, independent buying groups and non-wholesaler-owned PSAOs. These are the first wave because they can decide in weeks and cannot out-finance the Big 3 on other terms. The franchise programs of the Big 3 (Good Neighbor Pharmacy, Health Mart, Leader) come second. The pharmacy is the beneficiary, not the payer of record.
problem: The wholesaler owns the weekly auto-debit, the invoice detail and, as a possible third-party support entity, a view into refund flows. It is the cheapest and best-placed capital in the system. But the float squeezes its customers. NCPA-cited behavior includes 70% of pharmacies limiting stock of high-cost drugs and 60% using personal or business savings. That means lost brand volume, rising credit exposure to weakened accounts, and closures (SCPC warns 60% of its members may close). Wholesalers have not extended MFP dating at scale because they see invoices, not claims. They cannot tell which MFP refunds are safe or price the dilution risk of reversals, disputes and 340B rejections. Outside lenders sit behind the wholesaler's debit and cannot fix this.
solution: 'MFP Dating Desk' is software plus a capped dilution guarantee. 1) Connect the wholesaler's invoice and EDI feed with each participating pharmacy's PMS claims export and MTF remittance files, with the pharmacy's consent given inside the wholesaler's normal account flow. 2) Each week, match MFP-drug invoice lines to eligible claims and score dilution risk. 3) The wholesaler moves those lines into a 28-day bucket, or nets them against the refund where it already handles payment routing. 4) We cover dilution losses above the pharmacy's holdback, up to a cap, funded by our reserve and excess capacity from a credit fund or licensed carrier. The guarantee is structured as contractual recourse or through a licensed carrier so it is not unlicensed insurance. 5) The pharmacy sees one dashboard showing what is deferred and when the refund clears. Extended trade terms are commercial credit, not a loan, which avoids most of the lending-license and disclosure work in offspring one.
why_now: In January 2026 the refund lag became a recurring weekly mismatch between 14-day wholesaler terms and a 21-day refund average. On January 1, 2027 semaglutide and 14 other drugs join and the mismatch grows. Independents are choosing wholesalers and buying groups for 2027 terms, so a cash-flow feature is a retention weapon. CMS now expects manufacturers to include cash-flow mitigation in their refund plans, which shows the problem is recognized but unsolved on the distribution side.
revenue_model: The wholesaler pays a platform fee of about $5k a month plus about $10 per active pharmacy, and a risk-and-data fee of about 0.25-0.5% of the deferred refund amount per cycle, calibrated to measured dilution. The wholesaler recovers this through a small service fee. The pharmacy's all-in cost lands near 8-12% annualized, in line with bank A/R lines and well below an MCA. Illustrative: a regional wholesaler with 300 senior-heavy accounts averaging $50k of float has $15M deferred at any time. That is roughly $0.4-0.9M a year of risk fee before losses. Add more wholesalers and buying groups without adding a lending license.
non_obvious_insight: The parent treated the wholesaler as an obstacle. It is actually the best-collateralized lender in the chain, because it holds the debit right, the invoice line item and the relationship. It does not lack capital. It lacks a price for statutory-refund dilution, and that price lives in claim-level data it does not own. Selling underwriting to the party that owns the rails turns a capital-intensive 15-25% lending business into a small fee on a much larger base. It also removes the CAC problem, because the wholesaler's sales reps are the distribution.
first_30_days: List 15 regional wholesalers, buying groups and independent PSAOs and reach the CFO or independent-channel head through association conventions and cold outreach. The pitch is a free 'MFP exposure map' built from their own invoices. Aim for one 60-day shadow pilot with no cash at risk, covering 20-30 senior-heavy accounts. Compare what the deferral would have cost against measured dilution, and use it to set the fee. In parallel, get indicative excess-of-loss terms from one credit fund or specialty carrier and check with counsel whether the guarantee needs a license.

title: Credit Bureau for Federal Drug-Refund Receivables
one_liner: Invert lend-and-learn into learn-and-license. A consortium data utility and certified servicer that makes Medicare price-negotiation refunds, later 340B rebates and Part B refunds, a standard scorable collateral class for any lender, wholesaler or credit fund.
customer: First wave is 8-15 specialty lenders, regional banks with pharmacy desks, and family offices or credit funds that already lend to pharmacies or want to. Corporate Capital Direct, ARF, Fora and similar firms, and regional banks, are the named types. Later customers are wholesalers, insurers and note buyers. Pharmacies and hospitals are data suppliers, not customers. They consent because their lender then advances more, faster and cheaper.
problem: Every lender that could fund the refund float meets the same gaps. They cannot verify which claims are MFP-eligible, aged or disputed. They have no dilution history, no controlled payment route and no standard documents. Collateral is invisible to them, so they treat it as ineligible or advance blind at 50-75%. Each lender sees only its own few borrowers, too small a sample to price dilution, so capital does not flow to a float of $500M+ a month. The same gap will repeat in 340B rebate floats (Health Affairs estimates $8.9M-$208M a year per hospital) and in Part B refunds when the 2028 drug cohort arrives.
solution: Product ladder. 1) Within 6 months, the MFP Borrowing-Base Certificate, a portal and API. A lender invites a borrower, the borrower connects a read-only PMS export and the MTF remittance files, and we return a weekly certificate listing eligible refund receivables by claim, age, dilution score, dispute status, recommended reserve and exceptions, with alerts when refunds miss 14- and 21-day marks. 2) The consortium. Anonymized claim-to-refund outcomes from all lenders' borrowers feed a Refund Dilution Index by manufacturer, drug and pharmacy type (median days to pay, reversal and rejection rates), published quarterly. Contributing outcomes is a condition of use, as with credit-bureau furnishing. 3) Standard paper. A master receivables purchase agreement, control-agreement templates and a certified-servicer mark. 4) Later, servicer-of-record and small risk retention on pooled notes sold to insurers and credit funds, and extension to 340B rebate refunds and Part B refunds. Claim data can contain PHI, so we use minimum-necessary fields and business associate agreements from day one.
why_now: The refund class is nine months old and has no standard, no data owner and no legal template. Two expansions are scheduled (semaglutide and 14 more drugs in January 2027, another cohort in 2028). Private credit is hungry for short-duration paper whose obligors are large manufacturers. CMS and HRSA policy keeps shifting, which favors a utility that spans programs over a single-program lender. The MTF remittance and 835 files are standardized, so ingestion is buildable by a small team in months.
revenue_model: Subscription of about $150-$300 a month per monitored borrower, plus about 15-25 bps annualized on certified balances. Index licensing to funds at about $25-100k a year. Later, 30-50 bps servicing on pooled receivables and a 5% retained slice of notes. Illustrative first year: 10 lenders, 600 monitored borrowers and $36M certified is roughly $1.1-1.9M of recurring revenue. The upside is in scale, since each additional program (340B, Part B) reuses the same engine and consortium.
non_obvious_insight: Credit bureaus and ABL field examiners exist because collateral quality is unobservable to lenders. Here it is observable, but only in files that sit in the pharmacy. Whoever collects the first 20 lenders' claim-to-refund outcomes owns the only labeled dataset of statutory-refund dilution, and it compounds, since each new lender lowers every other lender's losses. It also hedges policy risk. If CMS speeds refunds, the index shows it and lenders shift to cheaper advance rates. If not, the float grows and demand rises. The standard travels to other federal refund flows. A single-program lender cannot make that claim.
first_30_days: Build ingestion for the three most common pharmacy management system exports and the MTF remittance files, using files from about 10 pharmacies. Approach 15 lenders and family offices with a free 60-day shadow certificate on three of their existing pharmacy borrowers, in exchange for outcome data and a design-partner letter of intent. Sign 2-3 letters of intent. Put together the borrower consent template and business associate agreement with a healthcare privacy attorney. Sound out one credit fund on eventually buying certified pools.
lineage: mutation of I0499 ('Bridge Loans for Medicare Drug-Price Refunds'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SpendMend (MFP Rebate Reconciliation), Plenful (MFP Intelligence / MFP Command Center), ScriptPro Financial Advantage, Liberty Software (and other PMS vendors, e.g. PioneerRx, PrimeRx, Redsail). White space: Verdict: gap, and a narrow one. In roughly 27 searches across varied terms (MFP refund advance, bridge loan, factoring, fintech, PSAO program, wholesaler program) I found NO product that specifically underwrites and advances against MTF-remitted MFP refunds. Pharmacy lenders sell generic A/R and MCA lines, and the MFP players only sell reconciliation. The unserved space is a claim-level underwriting and servicing capability for refund dilution risk: 340B lesser-of rejections (RARC N907 inappropriate rejections), reversals, Good Faith Inquiry disputes, and authorized-generic refund amounts. It is most valuable for borrowers whose float is large: LTC/senior-care pharmacies, 5-50 store groups, and possibly 340B covered entities in the HRSA rebate pilot, where the float is $8.9M-$208M a year for hospitals (Health Affairs). It also applies to the January 2027 step-up when semaglutide joins.

The wedge is weak in five ways.
1. The 'free missing-refund report' is already crowded: SpendMend, Plenful ($76M raised), ScriptPro, Liberty, and free Beacon MFP dashboards.
2. A typical independent's float is small, about $11k a week or $27k a month per NCPA. At 15-25% APR that is roughly $4-7k a year of gross revenue per pharmacy, before losses and a cost of funds of 8-10%. Customer acquisition through state associations and Facebook groups will be costly relative to that.
3. Wholesalers control the payment path. Cardinal routes MFP refunds through Central Pay and wholesalers auto-debit weekly, so a lender's sweep sits behind the wholesaler in practice. Cardinal customers cannot easily direct refunds to a lender-controlled account.
4. 'Non-recourse' is hard to deliver. Manufacturers can reverse refunds and CMS's own materials describe reversals when claims prove ineligible, so a lender will need pharmacy recourse or holdbacks. That undermines the 'prime paper' insight.
5. Policy is a moving target. CMS made manufacturers include cash-flow mitigation plans in their MFP effectuation plans (accelerated refunds, self-identification). NCPA is still pushing CMS and manufacturers for faster payment, including in Sept 2026 comments on the 2028 guidance.

Adjacent generic lenders can also just add MFP refunds to a borrowing base.

Caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) ran out, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and open-source sweeps were not fully run. 'No direct competitor found' means not found, not proven absent. | How this version avoids them: SpendMend, Plenful and ScriptPro sell workflow to the pharmacy or health system, and their data is siloed per customer. They are not lender-grade certificates and not a consortium. Beacon and CMS give free dashboards to dispensing entities, not to lenders. Corporate Capital Direct, Live Oak, ARF, Fora and wholesalers become customers instead of competitors, and we never fight for the pharmacy relationship. We can even ingest SpendMend and Plenful outputs as data sources. The main threat is Plenful adding a lender module. The defenses are lender-neutral consortium data that a single vendor cannot replicate, and a certified-servicer standard that lenders can rely on and a wholesaler such as Cardinal cannot credibly be neutral about.

title: Satellite Witness for Neighbor Construction Claims
one_liner: A fixed-price, court-ready satellite-radar history of a condo tower's movement before and during the neighbor's pile-driving, sold through the plaintiff-side attorneys who represent Miami-Dade condo associations.
customer: Plaintiff-side construction and property-damage attorneys (start with about 25 Miami-Dade firms) who represent condo associations. The wedge buildings are barrier-island and downtown towers of 15+ stories in Sunny Isles Beach, Bal Harbour, Surfside, Edgewater, Brickell and Miami Beach that sit within roughly 200-300 m of permitted deep-foundation, dewatering or excavation work. The association's engineer and manager are co-users. Direct sales to boards come later.
problem: When a developer starts driving piles or dewatering next door, unit owners report cracks and vibration. The only pre-condition evidence is usually the developer's own visual crack survey, which is commissioned, held and dated by the party who may be liable. A sensor installed after work starts (SmartCore, about $20K at Marenas) has no baseline. A bespoke InSAR expert report from TRE or Fugro costs tens of thousands and takes months. The 2024 UM study found subsidence in 35 towers and tied some of it to nearby construction, so the fight is about causation: was the tower already sinking on fill, or did the neighbor's work do it? Without an independent baseline, associations either lose that argument or never file. This is a problem with a live trigger, a live adversary and a budget. It is not diligence the board has to be talked into.
solution: A permit-triggered evidence engine. (1) Monitor building, dewatering and foundation permits across Miami-Dade jurisdictions and auto-draw a 200-300 m influence zone around each site. (2) Process free Sentinel-1, OPERA DISP-S1 and ESA archive data into a retroactive per-building time series, so the baseline can be built after work has started. (3) Sell a $3,500 Causation Baseline Report: pre-construction trend, differential tilt across the footprint, and a difference-in-differences comparison against control towers on similar fill outside the zone. It ships with a hashed data package and a reproducible method note. (4) Sell $1,500/quarter Construction Watch, with a change memo each quarter. NISAR L-band corroborates it from June 2026 onward. (5) Provide a declaration and testimony through a contracted independent PE or geodesist, billed as pass-through. Everything is worded as a measurement of motion, never as a structural safety opinion. Work is structured as attorney-retained consulting.
why_now: The Dec 2024 UM/UH/GFZ study put construction-linked subsidence in Miami towers on the public record. Estructura's June 2026 Surfside-anniversary push has normalized InSAR for condos. Post-Surfside associations are hyper-vigilant and litigious. Florida courts apply the Daubert standard (since 2019), so a peer-reviewable, reproducible method matters. OPERA DISP-S1 (free since May 2025) and NISAR (public July 20, 2026) cut processing cost to near zero, while the expert-report incumbents still price as quote-based consulting. The Dec 31, 2026 milestone deadlines have boards hiring engineers who now ask about neighbors.
revenue_model: Per engaged association: $3,500 baseline, plus $1,500/quarter Construction Watch averaging 8 quarters, plus expert pass-through at cost plus 20%. That is roughly $16K in the first 24 months at about 80% gross margin before expert time. A $299/month Permit Radar alert feed for firms and property managers covers their client lists. Attorneys often advance evidence costs on contingency or hybrid matters and recover them in settlement, so the law firm is often the effective payer. Target is about 40 engaged associations in year one, or about $600K revenue, then repeat cases per firm (3-5 a year). Later, the same engine feeds the wholesale-to-engineers layer from the parent idea.
non_obvious_insight: The satellite is a disinterested witness that logged the building before anyone had a dispute. That means the baseline is built retroactively, at the moment of peak willingness to pay, which sensors physically cannot do. The parent's 'no moat, open-source' weakness becomes a strength here: in a Daubert setting the opposing expert can re-run the method, so credibility comes from reproducibility, chain of custody, the control-tower design and a growing record of accepted declarations. The buyer is not buying monitoring, which boards avoid. They are buying leverage: a $3.5K report that turns a multi-million-dollar claim from unprovable to provable. Attorney-retained work also blunts the parent's 'discoverable bad report' problem, since the client chooses whether to disclose (confirm with counsel).
first_30_days: Week 1: pull the roughly 50 active or pending foundation, pile and dewatering permits in Sunny Isles, Edgewater, Brickell, Miami Beach, Surfside and Bal Harbour. Compute influence zones (about 700 towers) and run the free Sentinel-1/OPERA stack. Week 2: contract one university-affiliated geodesist or PE as expert of record. Cold-contact 25 plaintiff-side construction and condo firms and 10 property managers with a named sample: 'the six towers next to [site] have moved X mm/yr since 2016, and here is the control comparison.' Weeks 3-4: sell 3 design-partner baselines at $1,500, convert 2 to Construction Watch, and get one attorney to write a methodology-review letter. Kill test: if fewer than 3 of 25 firms take a paid pilot, or the expert will not put a name to the method, stop.

competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. White space: No one found sells a productized, fixed-price, board-readable per-building InSAR settlement history for Florida condo towers, wholesaled to the engineers who already write milestone and SIRS reports. The InSAR firms (TRE Altamira, Sixense, Fugro, SkyGeo, Detektia) sell quote-based enterprise projects. SatSense does per-property InSAR but for the UK. Any incumbent or Estructura could productize this quickly, so the wedge is distribution through engineers, engineer sign-off, and price. | How this version avoids them: Estructura and SmartCore sell forward-looking monitoring subscriptions to boards, built on sensors that cannot go back in time. This sells backward-looking, litigation-grade evidence through attorneys, triggered by a public permit event. TRE Altamira, Fugro, SkyGeo and NHAZCA sell bespoke quote-based expert projects at tens of thousands of dollars. This is a fixed $3,500 package with a pre-built method and a testifying expert on call. Sixense sells to contractors, who are the defendant side, so it is structurally conflicted here. OPERA is free but coarse and carries no chain of custody or expert. Domexa, CondoScan and CleanCondo have no physical-movement data. SatSense and Detektia are not in Florida litigation workflows. The defensible pieces are the permit-lead engine, attorney relationships, an accepted-expert track record and the control-tower dataset.

title: Neutral Ground Baseline for Foundation Projects
one_liner: A developer-paid, two-sided satellite baseline of every neighboring tower, delivered at the same time to neighbors and insurers, and sold as a line item by the geotech and vibration-monitoring firms already on the job.
customer: Payer: mid-size South Florida condo developers and general contractors (and their deep-foundation subcontractors) on projects with pile-driving, dewatering or deep excavation within about 300 m of occupied towers. Co-buyers: builders-risk and CGL underwriters, MGAs and wholesale brokers who insure those projects. Channel: geotech and vibration-monitoring engineering firms who already write the monitoring plan and can resell.
problem: Neighbor claims are the tail risk of urban high-rise foundation work. Vibration and settlement claims, injunction threats and stop-work fights can add months of construction-loan carry on a $150M-$400M tower. The developer's own crack survey is discounted as self-serving. Underwriters have no independent evidence of pre-existing condition, so they price the whole neighborhood as worst case, or add sublimits, higher deductibles or exclusions for adjacent-property damage. The UM study showed many towers were already sinking at mm/yr for reasons unrelated to any neighbor. Developers cannot prove that, and neither can anyone else.
solution: Neighbor Ledger. At permit or early foundation stage, process the archive for every building in the influence zone (typically 15-40 towers) and issue a neutral baseline package. It goes the same day to (a) the developer and its insurer and (b) each neighboring association through a read-only portal. Neighbors get a free 3-page report on their own tower, which gives them evidence and a reason to stop fighting the permit. Timestamps and data hashes are anchored, so neither side can dispute the record. During construction, a monthly delta report flags any tower whose motion departs from its own trend or from control towers. When a claim is filed, a dispute packet is generated within days. A rule is written into every contract: the company gives identical data to both sides and never testifies for either. Expert work goes to an independent geodesist panel. Priced fixed per project and sold as an add-on line item on the geotech firm's monitoring contract.
why_now: Miami's high-rise foundation boom is running against an unusually alert neighbor base: the 2024 UM study was widely covered, Marenas spent about $20K on sensors after a neighbor started work, and the Estructura June 2026 campaign has associations asking developers for data. Post-Surfside underwriters demand structural documentation, and softening reinsurance capacity makes MGAs hungry for differentiated loss-control tools. Processing cost has collapsed with free OPERA DISP-S1, Sentinel-1 and NISAR data.
revenue_model: $18K baseline per project at permit, plus $2.5K/month during foundation and superstructure phases (about 18 months), so about $60-65K per project against a $150M+ build. Reseller share of 20-25% to the geotech or vibration firm. Insurers and MGAs get a portfolio loss-control dashboard as a $25-50K/year program license, in exchange for a premium credit or a warranty requiring the ledger. Assumed 30-40 new high-rise foundation starts per year across Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach (verify from permit data), so about 12 projects in year one at roughly $700K. Expansion to Tampa, Orlando and Houston follows once insurers accept it.
non_obvious_insight: The parent's flaw was that boards may not want to know. Here the party with the strongest need to know is the developer, whose worst nightmare is a false or mistaken damage claim. A baseline showing the neighbor was already sinking is worth more to the developer than to the neighbor. Neutrality is the product: one record both sides accepted is worth more than two competing reports, the way an escrow agent is worth more than two lawyers. Because every competitor is on one side, refusing to take a side is a position none of them can copy without losing their existing clients. Once about 10 projects and two insurers rely on ledgers, a city or county can make a settlement baseline a permit condition, as some European cities require for deep excavation next to older buildings. That would turn a product into infrastructure (hedge: verify local precedent).
first_30_days: Week 1: list the 6-8 geotech and vibration-monitoring firms with active Miami-Dade or Broward jobs, using their public monitoring plans and permit files. Build unsolicited Neighbor Ledgers for 5 currently active sites from free data. Week 2: pitch each firm 'add this as a line item, you keep 25%, we do all the work.' Meet 4 builders-risk and CGL wholesale brokers and MGAs with a one-page loss-control pitch and one question: would you give a premium credit or require it? Weeks 3-4: close one developer pilot at half price ($9K) on a site in early foundation stage, in exchange for an underwriter introduction, and sign one geotech reseller. Kill test: if no geotech firm will bundle it and no underwriter will credit it, drop the model.

title: Stability Mark: Verified-Stable Tower Registry
one_liner: Invert the idea: instead of screening buildings for sinking, certify the many towers that have been stable for 10-30 years with a satellite-verified public mark and lookup registry that agents, lenders and insurers can trust, later backed by a scoping guarantee.
customer: Wedge: boards and building-specialist listing agents at older concrete towers (1970s-2000s) in Aventura, Sunny Isles, Bal Harbour, Brickell and Miami Beach whose owners are stuck with post-Surfside price discounts and need to prove soundness. Second wave: lenders, title companies, master-policy underwriters and MLS platforms as registry API subscribers. Engineers act as co-signers and reviewers.
problem: After Surfside, buyers, lenders and insurers treat every older tower as suspect until proven otherwise. Milestone and SIRS reports are long, alarming to non-engineers and describe conditions, not movement. Florida condo scores like Domexa's or CondoScan's rest on paperwork (did the board file on time?), not on how the ground and structure have behaved. Fine buildings cannot prove they are fine, and unit owners eat a discount. The parent idea also has a demand flaw: boards do not buy reports that might create a discoverable bad document. Selling fear to a reluctant buyer is hard.
solution: The Stability Mark: a 1-page certificate with a QR code to a live registry page, issued only to towers that pass published, pre-registered criteria. Example criteria: at least 10 years of persistent-scatterer coverage (Sentinel-1 alone gives 2016-2026; ERS/Envisat extend it if Miami coverage is usable), no differential settlement above a stated threshold, no accelerating trend, and a matched-control comparison. Participation is opt-in. Passing towers are published. Ambiguous or failing towers get a private result and a monitoring plan, with no public listing. The certificate covers the measurement, not structural safety, and a PE co-signs the method. The method is open and reproducible. There is annual re-verification with automatic revocation triggers, MLS-compatible listing fields, and a lender and insurer API. In year two, add a Scoping Guarantee: a reinsured parametric cover that pays for the Phase 1 engineering evaluation ($15-40K) if a certified tower later trips the threshold, priced at about $150/building/year. The certifier's own capital then stands behind the mark.
why_now: Post-Surfside stigma on older Florida towers is still discounting resale values, and inventory has been elevated since 2024-25 (verify current data). The Dec 31, 2026 milestone deadlines are about to push a wave of alarming paperwork at buyers who cannot interpret it. Reserves can no longer be waived from 2026, so buyers ask about condition. Only satellite archives hold a 1990s-to-present record of how a tower behaved: FIU found Champlain Towers South's 1990s subsidence in ERS data, and no sensor bought today can create that history. Free Sentinel-1 and OPERA data plus NISAR (L-band, from June 2026) make re-verification cheap. Estructura's fear-first marketing leaves the good-news position empty.
revenue_model: Initial certificate $1,800 per building ($995 founding price for the first 50), then $500/year re-verification. PE review fee of about $250 per certificate, and about $60-100 of compute per building. Year two: registry API for lenders, title and insurers at $20K/year flat or $1-3 per lookup, and Scoping Guarantee premium of about $150 per building per year. Year one: about 150 marks at about $1,400 average is roughly $210K, plus $75K recurring. The 10x case: several thousand concrete towers in Florida and tens of thousands nationwide (assumed, verify), with Gulf, Houston, Tampa, Jersey City and Honolulu next. A registry adopted by MLS platforms and lenders, plus a warranty book, is a platform business that a report shop cannot become.
non_obvious_insight: Mandatory-inspection regimes create fear purchases. A voluntary mark creates status purchases, and it has an unraveling dynamic: once 20-30% of comparable towers in a submarket carry the mark, silence becomes a signal that a building is sinking or hiding something, so competitors' badges drive demand rather than the board's fear. Demand rises non-linearly with adoption, which no report business gets. The 10-30 year archive is a cornered resource: nobody can retroactively install a 1996 sensor. Every engineer-reviewed pass or fail adds to a proprietary labeled dataset of which radar signatures precede real findings, which tightens the thresholds and beats sensor bundles that only see the future. The warranty forces honest calibration, since the certifier pays if it is wrong.
first_30_days: Take the parent's roughly 400-tower Sentinel-1 stack and process the 150 oldest concrete towers against the full available archive. Publish the pass criteria before running the results. Confirm persistent-scatterer density and ERS/Envisat usability on Miami; if pre-2015 coverage is poor, use the Sentinel-1 decade. Contract one PE or geodesist to co-sign a methodology memo with measurement-only wording. Approach 10 building-specialist listing agents and 10 presidents of towers that passed, at the $995 founding price. Aim for 8 marks sold, 3 live on agent sites or MLS remarks with the QR code, and 2 lenders or title underwriters willing to read the registry page. Kill test: if fewer than 5 of 20 boards buy at $995, or no PE will co-sign the wording, stop.

title: Contributor-Only Delay Outcome Ledger for Immigration Solos
one_liner: A give-to-get ledger that joins public dockets with the USCIS action dates only the filing lawyer sees, sold as a triage score plus a consent-order-first filing pack for a solo's existing stuck files in the four highest-moot districts.
customer: Solo and 2-5 attorney immigration firms whose book is mostly naturalization, family-based, I-751 and I-765 work, already admitted in E.D.N.Y., D.N.J., D. Conn. or E.D. Mich. (the districts where Mandamus.com's own tally shows 83-85% voluntary dismissal after agency action). Narrowest wedge: a firm holding 10+ files already past posted times or more than 120 days past a naturalization interview. Those are existing paying clients, so each filing is a $2.5-5k upsell with zero acquisition cost. Secondary buyers later: boutique mandamus firms and litigation funders, as data licensees.
problem: Solos sit on stuck files and do not file, for reasons the judges and the competitor research surfaced. (1) They cannot tell which suits will be quietly mooted and which will draw a motion to dismiss: nationality-hold suits went 0-13 in D.D.C. this summer, and the Fifth Circuit bars I-485 delay claims (Cheejati). (2) They cannot price a flat fee without knowing the tail if the government fights. (3) A free pro se guide plus a $5,000 boutique make a $400 drafting tool look redundant, and general AI drafting is eroding the 6-10 hour learning curve. Public stats are hand-tallied for about 7 districts, and a docket shows when a case ended, not why or when USCIS actually acted.
solution: Three pieces, all attorney-of-record signed (the company is software). (1) Stuck-Case Book: paste or CSV-import pending cases from any case-management export (no partnership needed). It ranks each file by ripeness and expected days from service to USCIS action. Ripeness is tiered: N-400s more than 120 days after interview under 8 U.S.C. 1447(b), where the statute supplies the clock and in most circuits USCIS cannot adjudicate until the court remands, come first; then I-751, I-765 and long-idle I-130/I-140 under the APA. It refuses to generate filings for nationality-hold and Fifth Circuit I-485 cases and says why. (2) Filing pack: complaint, exhibits, service checklist, 60-day answer calendar, a documented pre-suit exhaustion checklist (e-request, Ombudsman, congressional inquiry) that also builds the 'not substantially justified' record, and a consent-order-first settlement template with an express EAJA reservation and a 30-day fee-petition reminder. (3) The ledger: after each case the attorney logs service date, USCIS action date and how it ended (consent order, quiet adjudication, MTD granted or denied). Judge- and AUSA-level detail unlocks only for contributors; everyone else gets a free coarse district scorecard.
why_now: The Oct 2025 end of the 540-day EAD auto-extension made I-765 delay suits a primary remedy, and holds keep files idle, but D.D.C.'s June-Aug 2026 record (government 13-0) means undifferentiated 'just file' now loses, so triage suddenly has value it lacked two years ago. LLM drafting has turned complaint templates into a commodity, pushing value to judgment and data. Honest caveat: RECAP counts look flat (385, 352, 477 filings a year in 2023-25), so the pitch is a higher win rate per filing, not a volume surge.
revenue_model: Free: coarse district scorecard (lead magnet and SEO). Paid: $299/month Ledger Pro (unlimited Stuck-Case Book, 2 filing packs a month, judge/AUSA-level data for contributors), extra packs $250 each. Flat fees only, never a share of the lawyer's fee. Year 2: data licenses ($1-3k/month) to boutique firms, litigation funders and case-management vendors. Bottom-up (assumptions to validate): about 1,500 target solos in the four districts x 20% penetration x about $3.6k/year is roughly $1.1M ARR before adding districts.
non_obvious_insight: A docket records when a suit ended, not when or why USCIS acted; stipulations and the 60-day answer clock add weeks of noise. The real key is service date, then USCIS action date, then dismissal type, and only the filing lawyer holds the approval notice. Every competing stat (Mandamus.com's hand tally, Lex Machina/Trellis-style docket analytics, raw CourtListener) is blind to it, so the moat is a cornered resource that accrues only through contributors and cannot be scraped. Second, the solo's blocking question is not 'can I draft this' but 'what does it cost me if the government fights'; tail probability by district is what lets them quote a confident flat fee.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: run the 8 real web searches the prior research could not (mandamus AI, delay-suit software, Crunchbase, AILA toolkits). title: Work-Permit Gap Desk for Frontline Employers
one_liner: Employer-paid, pre-cliff delay suits for workers whose EAD renewals are pending, sold to home-care, nursing and staffing employers as a per-worker maintenance plan instead of a one-off legal purchase.
customer: HR and compliance directors or owners of 150-1,500 employee home-care agencies, skilled-nursing operators and staffing firms in the NYC-metro and New Jersey area (workers resident in E.D.N.Y., S.D.N.Y. and D.N.J., where delay suits most often end in agency action), each with hundreds of workers on time-limited work authorization (asylum-pending, adjustment-pending, parole and DACA categories). The worker is the lawyer's client; the employer is the payer and the buyer of the platform. Later channel: I-9/E-Verify vendors, PEOs and state home-care and staffing associations.
problem: Employers eat the cliff. Since the 540-day automatic EAD extension ended for renewals filed from late Oct 2025, a worker whose I-765 renewal is still pending on the expiry date must come off the schedule. A care agency watches a predictable slice of its workforce disappear for months, pays replacement and onboarding costs, and has no lever to pull. Its HR team already tracks every expiry date for I-9 compliance, but that process ends at 'alert' with no remedy step. Immigration counsel are hired by individuals or for petitions like H-1B and PERM, never as an operations service for frontline workforces, so this problem has no owner.
solution: Gap Desk in three parts. (1) Free EAD Gap Calculator: HR uploads employee ID, EAD category code and expiry date (no names), and gets the projected number of workers who will hit expiry before a decision, priced in lost margin and replacement cost. (2) Enrolled program: the employer offers a voluntary benefit to every employee with time-limited work authorization regardless of nationality (to limit anti-discrimination exposure). The platform watches filing date against expiry; when a ledger-set trigger fires (case beyond posted time and expiry approaching), it obtains the worker's consent and files through a panel of federal-admitted attorneys at a flat fee. Structure: the worker is the client, the employer pays as a third-party payer with informed consent (independent judgment and confidentiality preserved), and the employer sees only a status date. (3) Bridge kit: job-hold and leave templates and a reinstatement re-verification checklist so the employer keeps the seat during the gap. Out of scope by design: TPS terminations, revoked parole and denials, which are not delay problems.
why_now: The auto-extension ended in Oct 2025, and Mandamus.com's case-law tracker calls I-765 mandamus a 'primary remedy' since then, so the cliff is new and the remedy is proven. Expiry dates are known 6-12 months ahead, so the risk is forecastable. Care-sector labor is scarce, making each lost seat expensive. LLM drafting plus a per-district ledger lets a panel attorney turn a routine I-765 suit in about an hour, making a $1,750 flat fee profitable. The USAO's 45-90 day resolution pattern matches the length of a typical gap.
revenue_model: Employer pays $5 per covered worker per month (monitoring, calculator, case management) plus $2,000 per triggered case: $1,750 paid directly to the panel attorney and $250 to the platform as a flat administrative fee. Never a percentage of the legal fee. Illustration for a 400-worker agency: $24k/year subscription plus about 20 triggered cases (about $5k platform, $35k to attorneys). Assumption to validate in pilots: a 90-day gap costs an agency roughly $5-10k in lost margin and replacement, so 20 avoided gaps clearly exceed the roughly $59k program cost. Year 2: I-9 vendors and PEOs resell for a cut of the subscription only.
non_obvious_insight: The party with the most to lose from a stuck case is the employer, yet employers have never been the buyer because immigration law treats the individual as the client; third-party payer rules allow the employer to pay while the worker stays the client. Once the employer pays, the product changes character: expiry dates are known a year ahead, so demand is a forecastable renewal calendar and recurring subscription instead of lumpy, panicked legal purchases. And the employer's I-9 tickler is already the distribution asset, since it holds exactly the dates that trigger the suit.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: build the calculator as a spreadsheet plus web form and run it on anonymized expiry lists from 3 friendly employers. Days 1-10: sign 2-3 panel attorneys admitted in E.D.N.Y., S.D.N.Y. and D.N.J. at $1,750 flat and get an employment-law read on third-party-payer, anti-discrimination and prepaid-legal-plan rules. Days 7-30: contact about 60 NYC-metro and NJ home-care agencies and staffing firms through state association events and LinkedIn, lead with their own calculator output, and close 3 paid pilots at about $2,500/month concierge plus per-case fees. Go/no-go: at least one employer with a real expiring cohort authorizes a filing within 30 days, and outcomes are logged to seed the ledger.

title: Solos Refer, We File: National Delay-Suit Bench
one_liner: Invert the tool model: a lawyer-owned litigation bench that takes stuck cases referred by immigration solos, files at industrial speed for about 60% of the boutique price, and pays the referring lawyer a fee share, building a national referral network and the full-cycle dataset as a by-product.
customer: Payer: stuck applicants (post-interview N-400, I-751, I-765, long-idle I-130/I-140) referred by their own immigration lawyer, paying a $2,995 flat fee plus about $455 in costs. Channel: 1-10 attorney immigration firms in NY, NJ and CT that hold stuck clients but will not be counsel of record on a federal suit. Expansion: solos in any state, then boutique firms as overflow customers.
problem: The parent's model needs solos to pay $400 to do something they fear, and the research found no evidence that solos pay for tooling. What solos do have is client trust and a pile of stuck files. Their current choices are to do nothing or to refer the client to a boutique for no reward and the risk of losing the client. Meanwhile the one visible provider (Mandamus.com) is a small boutique with about 30 litigated petitions in 15 years, prices at $5,000 plus $500, and runs no co-counsel program for other lawyers. That leaves a large pool of unserved clients who cannot pay $5,000.
solution: A lawyer-owned litigation bench with the software company as management-services provider under a flat per-case fee (not a percentage of legal fees). The referral flow: a solo submits a stuck case through a 4-minute referral link or a case-management export; the ledger triages it (declining nationality-hold suits and Fifth Circuit I-485 claims); the client e-signs a fee-division consent that names each lawyer's share and the joint responsibility; the bench files within 72 hours, runs the 60-day clock, negotiates consent-order-first, and files the EAJA petition when a consent order supports it. The referring lawyer stays counsel on the underlying application, receives status in their own system, and earns 30% ($900) of the fee. The flat fee covers all litigation including an MTD opposition, matching the boutique's promise. Key legal gate: joint-responsibility fee division rules vary by state (NY 1.5(g) and ABA Model Rule 1.5(e) style), so launch only where ethics counsel clears it.
why_now: AI drafting and docket automation cut attorney time per routine filing from 6-10 hours to about 3 with paralegal support, which lets price fall to roughly 60% of the boutique at a healthy margin. The USAO's 45-90 day resolution pattern means one litigator can carry 60-100 live files, so the constraint on a litigation shop is intake, not lawyer time. Solos are overloaded and fear being first to file. The research found no co-counsel or referral program for other lawyers, so the economics of referral are unexploited.
revenue_model: Client pays $2,995 flat (court costs about $455 passed through). Referral share $900. Illustrative unit economics (assumptions): about $300 paralegal and attorney time, $40 service, about $225 expected tail (15% of cases x roughly $1,500 of MTD opposition work), $60 support, leaving about $1,450 contribution per case. 3,000 cases a year (a year-3 target that requires expanding the market, since the RECAP sample shows only 350-480 filings a year) would produce about $4.3M contribution. Upside: license the ledger, sell overflow capacity to boutiques, and reuse the same referral rails for other agency-delay claims (consular administrative processing, FOIA, passports).
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not tooling but willingness to be counsel of record. Solos already own client trust and stuck files but earn nothing from referring out and fear the suit; a fee share for zero litigation risk turns them from prospects who must be persuaded to pay into an eager, unpaid-acquisition channel, at 30% of fee versus the boutique's SEO and ad spend. Because most cases moot in weeks, the bench recycles capacity fast, and it is the bench, not a tool, that naturally accumulates the full-cycle data (service date, USCIS action date, fee outcome) that makes the ledger better than anyone's public docket analytics. Scale economies and a referral network are both reachable within 24 months.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: get an ethics-counsel memo for NY, NJ and CT on joint-responsibility fee division and a flat-fee MSO; secure a lawyer cofounder or contract litigator admitted in E.D.N.Y., S.D.N.Y., D.N.J. and D. Conn. (the Mandamus.com boutique, admitted in D. Conn., D.D.C. and S.D. Tex., is a possible bench partner rather than only a rival); draft the referral agreement and client consent. Days 10-30: recruit 15 NY/NJ/CT solos through AILA chapters and direct outreach to attorneys of record on RECAP naturalization suits, pre-load 30 stuck cases from their own books, file the first 10 within 72 hours of consent, log every outcome, and pay the first referral share when the client pays. Go/no-go: 10 cases filed, more than half of referrers sending a second case, and modeled contribution of at least $1,000 per case.
