title: Serial Match: AP-Only Recovery for Exchange Buyers
one_liner: A success-fee audit that takes one accounts-payable export from an independent rotable pool or Part 145 station, finds money its repair vendors already owe, and collects it. It starts with credits the vendor has already conceded, then moves to repeat-failure claims.
customer: Independent rotable exchange pools, parts resellers and Part 145 stations that buy a few hundred outsourced repairs and exchange units a year from 10 or more shops, roughly $5-40M of repair spend (my assumption, unverified). The buyer is the Controller or VP Materials at a firm with a 2-4 person back office. These firms sit outside power-by-the-hour contracts, so the warranty exposure is theirs. They multi-source on price, so they have little vendor-relationship fear. They also see the same serial number pass through many hands. Regionals, EMS operators and lessors are phase 2.
problem: The parent idea had four named weaknesses: PBH and maintenance-plan contracts remove warranty exposure for many small fleets, integrating with each operator's maintenance system is hard, fear of annoying the shop, and no proof anyone pays. A pool has none of these. Its serialized units cycle through repair invoices, exchange credits and core returns. The same P/N and S/N can appear on two invoices from one shop within the warranty window, and nobody joins invoice lines by serial number. Beside that sit credit memos issued but never applied, core credits not netted, no-fault-found evaluation fees on in-warranty units, and turnaround guarantees never credited. Pool gross margins are thin, so recovering 1-3% of repair spend moves EBITDA. The warranty windows are short and full of exclusions, so recovery has to be systematic, with a claim filed for every eligible unit.
solution: Input is one vendor-ledger export plus the invoice PDFs, with no maintenance-system integration. An LLM extractor builds a serial-level table: P/N (including interchangeable P/Ns), S/N, repair date, charges and the warranty text printed on the invoice or PO. Recovery runs in three passes, ordered from least to most disputed. Pass 1 is zero-dispute money: open and unapplied credit memos, duplicate payments, and core credits not applied. Pass 2 is the repeat-serial detector: the same S/N back to the same shop inside its window, plus the same S/N failing after different shops' repairs. Pass 3 is contested items: NFF fees on in-warranty units and turnaround-guarantee credits. Claims go out on each vendor's own form. A vendor playbook library covers the top 60 shops: warranty terms, exclusions, contacts, average days to credit and past acceptance rate. We chase every claim to a posted credit or cash. Phase 2 adds read-only receiving and removal data from the customer's ERP to confirm failures the invoices alone can't show.
why_now: Reliable, cheap LLM extraction from messy repair-invoice PDFs and warranty fine print is what makes an AP-only audit viable. Before 2025 it needed offshore data-entry teams, which killed contingency margins. Aftermarket parts prices and repair turn times have also climbed since the 2022-23 supply squeeze (my assumption, unverified). That makes each exchange unit worth more, so pools tie up more capital in them and each unclaimed failure costs more.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 20% of cash and credits recovered, or 25% on contested pass-3 items, with a 12-month tail after the audit. The fee is due only when cash arrives or the credit is applied, not when the memo is issued. That solves the objection to paying cash on a credit the customer can only spend at that shop. There is no upfront cost and no minimum. Year 2 adds a $2-4k/month continuous-monitoring tier for pools with over $15M of spend. Anonymized vendor-acceptance and turn-time data is a later product.
non_obvious_insight: Sequence matters more than segment. Leading with credits the vendor has already conceded gives first cash in 3-4 weeks, with no dispute and no relationship risk. That builds the trust to file contested claims later. Every contested claim, won or lost, adds to the playbook library: per-shop acceptance rates, exclusion language and time to credit. That library is the cornered resource and process power a generalist cannot copy. The pool is also the freight-audit shipper of aviation: high invoice volume, many vendors, serial-tracked goods and no reason to protect any single vendor.
first_30_days: Build a target list of about 60 pools and Part 145 stations from public repair-station and trade-association directories. Send 40 direct outreach messages offering a free scan: they send 12 months of vendor ledger and invoices, and we return the dollars found within 10 business days. The only thing we ask for is permission to file. Hire a retired warranty or materials coordinator as a paid advisor for vendor quirks. Close 3 audits and deliver ranked claim lists. File pass-1 claims first and aim for the first credit memo by day 30. Set an explicit kill test: if the median first-pass yield is under 1% of repair spend across the first 5 files, stop or narrow the segment. Publish the aggregate finding, such as the share of eligible repeat repairs never claimed, as the lead magnet.
lineage: mutation of I0195 ('Contingency Recovery of Missed Rotable Repair Warranties'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ramco Aviation (MRO/ERP software, warranty management module). White space: Caveat: this verdict rests on thin evidence. The WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200) after the first two lookups. Every further search was refused, and I did not work around that limit. I could only fetch vendor homepages directly. I found no dedicated contingency-fee warranty auditor for rotable repair claims. I also could not rule one out, because I could not run Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or 'startup + key terms' searches. Vendor pages I checked (Trax eMRO, Veryon/Rusada, Pentagon 2000, CAMP) showed no warranty-claims features on their homepages, but homepage silence is weak evidence. I could not check IFS Maintenix (HTTP 429). Gaps that look unserved: (1) an outsourced, success-fee service that reads unstructured repair-invoice PDFs and joins them to removal records. This is the cross-system join the idea describes. (2) Small and mid-size operators such as regionals, Part 135 fleets and air-ambulance operators, which sit below the large ERP buyers Ramco targets. (3) The adjacent leaks, meaning no-fault-found fees within warranty, unreturned core penalties and turnaround-time guarantee credits. None of the vendor pages I read mention these. Unverified risks from my own domain knowledge, not from research: power-by-the-hour and maintenance-service-plan contracts remove warranty exposure for many small fleets. Shop warranty terms are often short and carry exclusions. Getting AP and maintenance-system exports from a small operator is hard. The addressable market may be small. Someone should check all of these before building. | How this version avoids them: Ramco's warranty module is software that large operators run themselves, and I could not verify its claims. This is an outsourced, success-fee claims service for smaller buyers, which Ramco does not offer. The Trax, Veryon/Rusada, Pentagon 2000 and CAMP homepages showed no claims features, though that is weak evidence. Generalist AP recovery-audit firms exist (an unresearched risk to check). They run duplicate-payment and vendor-statement logic and cannot read repair invoices, match serial numbers or judge warranty eligibility. Targeting pools and stations sidesteps PBH shielding, sidesteps the maintenance-system integration problem, and reduces relationship fear.

title: Warranty Desk Embedded in Maintenance Software
one_liner: A white-label, success-fee warranty desk sold through mid-tier maintenance-tracking and MRO software vendors. The removal event, the PO and the repair invoice meet inside a system the operator already uses, and the software vendor earns a revenue share.
customer: The channel buyer is the partnerships or customer-success head at a mid-tier maintenance-tracking or MRO software vendor with 50-400 operator customers. The payer is the operator on that software: a regional airline, Part 135 or cargo-feeder fleet, or helicopter operator. The vendor pays nothing. It receives 30% of our fee and gets a renewal and differentiation story.
problem: Operators on these systems already hold structured removal, install, hours and cycles data, plus POs and receiving records. That is the data-access problem the parent idea could not solve. Still, warranty stays unclaimed, because the missing pieces are things software does not do. Someone has to read negotiated PDF terms, file on each shop's own template, and chase the shop for 60-90 days. Vendors cannot staff claims specialists. Operators' thin materials teams cannot absorb the work. The claim is decided at the removal moment, when a technician pulls a unit at 3 AM and nobody sees the terms. Only the maintenance software sees that event.
solution: The vendor gives a read-only export or API for removals, installs, POs and receiving. We load each shop's warranty terms from the operator's contracts and invoice PDFs. When a technician posts a removal against a serialized component, we return a lookup card in seconds, inside the vendor's UI or by email or Slack in the first version. The card shows who repaired the unit and when, the remaining window in days, hours or cycles, the evidence checklist, and a pre-drafted claim. Our claims specialists then file, chase and post the credit memo back into the system as a warranty record. A monthly sweep catches misses, late turn times, no-fault-found fees and open cores. Operators sign a contingency agreement. The vendor contract is non-exclusive and revenue-share only.
why_now: LLM extraction of warranty fine print and invoice PDFs means one specialist can now run claims for dozens of operators. Software vendors are also under pressure to prove value in the renewals of small and mid-size operators. Ramco advertises warranty-recovery savings, which shows the outcome is being marketed. Nobody sells the outcome as a service to the other vendors.
revenue_model: Operators pay 20% of cash and credits recovered, with a 12-month tail. The vendor gets 30% of our fee, about 6 points of recoveries, and owns the relationship. From year 2, vendors can bundle a Warranty Desk line item at $1-2k/month per operator, with us as wholesale fulfillment at about $600/month plus the success fee. Aggregated vendor-level claim data is a later product.
non_obvious_insight: Maintenance software has an adoption problem, not a feature problem. Warranty fields and modules sit empty because filling them takes human work: reading PDFs and chasing vendors. A managed service that makes the module produce cash is worth more to a vendor than building the feature. The vendor also supplies what our own sales cycle lacks: structured removal data, a warm introduction, and a trigger at the exact moment the claim is won or lost. Vendors will not build claim-chasing themselves. Terms are negotiated PDFs, and staffing claims desks is not a software margin.
first_30_days: Approach 8 mid-tier software vendors' partnership heads with a one-page offer: we make a slice of your customers' warranty tracking pay, with no cost to you and 30% of our fee. Ask each for 2-3 design-partner operators. Work as a concierge service, with no integration yet. The operator exports removals, POs and receiving from the software's standard CSV export, we match against invoice PDFs, and we deliver a ranked claim list with the vendor's customer-success manager on the call. Build the removal lookup as a simple web form or email responder. Sign a revenue-share MOU with the first vendor and aim for the first credit memo by day 30-45. Hire a retired materials coordinator for shop quirks. Success is 2 operators with live removal-time lookups by month 3.

title: Chargeback Network for Aircraft Component Warranties
one_liner: A neutral claims network that moves a failed-repair claim up the chain from operator to pool to shop to piece-part supplier, inside each link's warranty window, with standard reason codes, response clocks and netted settlement. It starts as a back-to-back claim desk for rotable pools.
customer: The first customers are independent rotable pools and Part 145 stations that sell exchange units with warranty downstream and buy repairs with warranty upstream. They are the only parties who are both claimant and respondent. Shops and piece-part suppliers join as respondents, at no cost at first. Operators and lessors join as claimants. Airline procurement teams, lessors and insurers later buy shop-performance data.
problem: One rotable failure triggers a chain of warranties: operator to pool or lessor, pool to shop, shop to piece-part supplier. Each link has its own window, evidence rules, template and email address. The clocks are mismatched. A pool may give the operator a longer window than the shop gives the pool (a typical gap I have not verified). A claim arriving late in the downstream window is already dead upstream, and the pool absorbs the gap. Claims are rejected on paperwork, sent back and forth by email, and never passed up the chain in time. Nobody sees the whole chain. Every party recovers, or fails to recover, alone.
solution: Version 1 is a back-to-back desk for pools. It has an intake address and portal for customer claims. An LLM and rules engine check serial history, the warranty terms and the evidence. Valid claims are auto-converted into a standard upstream packet and sent to the pool's shop inside that shop's window. Invalid claims get a reason-coded response. The desk tracks each claim to a credit and sends a monthly netting statement of credits and debits with each counterparty, settling only the net. Shops receive a complete, pre-checked packet with one-click accept, deny or counter, response timers and a bounded dispute path. In parallel we publish open Rotable Claim Rules v1: reason codes (repeat failure, NFF in warranty, core, turn-time, piece-part defect), an evidence checklist, response clocks such as 10 days to acknowledge and 30 to decide, and a neutral technical panel for disputes. Later layers are shop scorecards for procurement, and advances on approved claims, an early cash payment against approved claims from a small credit facility.
why_now: Cheap LLM reading of repair paperwork, terms and evidence packs makes standard packets and pre-checks possible at low cost per claim. Higher unit values and longer repair turn times since the 2022-23 supply squeeze (my assumption, unverified) make each missed claim costlier and make pools hold more capital in exchange units.
revenue_model: Pools pay about $45 per claim processed plus 3% of upstream recoveries. Shops with more than 20 claims a month can pay $500-1,500/month for an adjudication assistant. Disputes cost about $250 per panel case. Year 2-3 adds shop-performance data subscriptions: repeat rate by P/N, days to credit, acceptance rate. Later, advances on approved claims at a small monthly discount, a balance-sheet layer priced from our own claim-outcome data.
non_obvious_insight: The warranty chain is a chain of mismatched clocks and formats, and the intermediary pays for the gap. That intermediary is also the one participant who is both claimant and respondent, which is why a pool is the natural seed for a two-sided network, as issuers and acquirers are in card chargebacks. Standard reason codes and evidence rules make a claim cheaper to settle than to fight. Shops gain a filter for invalid claims. At scale the network holds the only serial-level record of repair durability across owners: lemon units, repeat-failure shops and days to credit. No single-company ERP can see that. Defensibility comes from network economies, switching costs in claim histories and netting, and the data.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 pools as design partners, using the free scan from the pool wedge as the way in. Point their customer-claim email address at a shared inbox we monitor. Process claims manually with LLM assistance for 30 days, and send upstream claims in the standard packet to 5 shops. Measure acceptance and days-to-credit against the pool's own baseline. Draft Rotable Claim Rules v0.1 with two retired shop warranty managers as advisors and circulate it to trade groups. Set the target as one upstream credit on a claim that would otherwise have missed its window. Then convert to paid pilots at $2-4k/month across 3-5 pools by month 6.

title: Phantom-Load Registry: Land Records Meet Utility Queues
one_liner: A utility-funded vetting desk that joins courthouse land-assembly signals with co-op and municipal large-load inquiry logs, so it can say which 100-1,000 MW projects are real and which LLC families are shopping the same megawatts to five utilities.
customer: Electric co-ops, G&Ts, municipal utilities and PUDs with 5-person engineering staffs. They pay per memo or on retainer. Secondary buyers are developers' land teams and site-selection consultants, infrastructure and energy funds buying alt-data, and county economic-development offices.
problem: Every party sees half the picture. A small utility sees the inquiry (an LLC, a MW ask, a PowerPoint) but not the land trail. The land-assembly watcher sees option memoranda and easements but cannot tell a real hyperscale campus from a speculator flipping dirt. Nobody sees the same MW shopped across states. Texas SB 6's collateral rule (final expected by end of 2026) will push phantom load onto softer neighbors.
solution: First product is the fixed-price vetting memo ($7.5-25k) with a red/amber/green result and a recommended security amount. The site-control and LLC-principal items in the 12-point physical-reality test are powered by an image-level read of recorded options, leases and easements, clustered by return-to law firm, notary, signatory and mailing address. Air-permit and equipment-slot checks come from the vetting desk. Utilities that share their inquiry logs (LLC, MW, node, date, outcome) get discounted memos. Those logs become a multi-utility duplicate-request registry that flags land-assembled-but-no-equipment-slot projects and the same LLC family filing at several utilities. Later products are a county-level real-versus-phantom alert feed and alt-data licenses for funds.
why_now: Texas SB 6 (PUCT rule final due by 12/31/2026, $50,000/MW security) is exporting speculators to neighboring states. About half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or cancelled, so utilities are burned and skeptical. FinCEN's 2025 exemption for domestic companies means LLC unmasking has to come from primary records. LLM vision now reads messy scanned instruments accurately.
revenue_model: $7.5-25k per vetting memo. $60-150k per year G&T retainers. $2-8k per month regional developer seats. $750-2,000 per tract title packet. $50-150k per year alt-data licenses for funds. Utilities often pass memo cost to applicants as a study-deposit line item. Later, registry subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Land records show intent, and an option memo is cheap to buy. The equipment and permit trail shows capability. The utility queue shows the ask. No single dataset separates real from speculative, but the join does. Land assembled with no transformer slot, by an LLC family filing at five utilities, is a land flip. Each utility's eventual outcome (built, cancelled, withdrawn) is also a free labeled training set for the tape's classifier, which no scraper competitor can get. Utilities will only share inquiry logs with someone they already trust to vet, and that is a trust position a pure data vendor lacks.
first_30_days: Through state electric cooperative associations, get 3 co-ops to hand over their last 10 inquiries each. Pull 24 months of recorded instruments in those territories, plus state air-permit and LLC filings. Run a free back-test showing which past inquiries were real. Publish a '12 signs your data center inquiry is real' one-pager and send a sample 'who is assembling where' memo to 10 site-selection consultants. Convert 2-3 co-ops to paid $7.5k memos on live inquiries and pitch one G&T retainer.
lineage: hybrid of I0773 + I0079 (Courthouse Tape: Land-Assembly Radar for Infrastructure + Phantom Load Vetting Desk for Rural Utilities). Why stronger: The vetting desk alone is a services business with a thin data moat, and the tape alone fights for alt-data budgets with no ground-truth labels. Together, memo revenue funds data collection, utility outcomes label the data, and the pooled duplicate registry gets more valuable with each utility that joins. ACV rises, and utilities can be reached through co-op associations instead of cold outreach.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ATTOM Data, Reonomy, Regrid, Enverus. White space: The specific product in the idea, a feed that reads recorded option memoranda, leases and easements from county recorders, classifies them from the image rather than the clerk's label, clusters LLC families by notary, return-to firm and address, and alerts on assembly patterns, was not found at any vendor I could read. Everything I could read is adjacent. Parcel and ownership vendors (Regrid, ATTOM, Reonomy) sell deeds, mortgages and LLC piercing but not options or easements. Siting and diligence vendors (Paces, Enverus, GridCARE) help a client find its own site. Project trackers (Cleanview, DC Byte, Heatmap Pro, Data Center Watch) start at permit or public news. Land-management vendors (Pandell, Enverus LandScape) manage a client's own documents. What remains open is cross-county, image-level reading of recorded non-deed instruments to detect other parties' assembly, sold as alerts. It is plausibly protected by the hard part, which is getting recorder access county by county, not the ML. The main structural doubts I could not test are whether developers actually record option memoranda before announcement, and how many counties allow bulk commercial pulls of document images. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: GridUnity, Clean Power Research (PowerClerk), Enverus, LandGate. White space: I found no direct competitor. No startup, consultancy or association was selling a utility-side, per-inquiry 'is this developer physically real' memo with a recommended collateral amount and milestone-gated study structure. The gap is real but narrow.

What is unserved: (1) External physical-trail verification for small utilities, meaning air-permit generator counts vs claimed MW, recorded deeds and options, LLC principal cross-checks, and OEM or EPC evidence. GridUnity and PowerClerk track applicant-supplied data but do not verify it. Enverus, LandGate and GridCARE serve the developer side. (2) A cross-utility duplicate-request registry. Texas SB 6 mandates duplicate-request disclosure only inside ERCOT. Outside ERCOT there is no pooled registry. Developers do file the same project with several utilities (Latitude Media, Utility Dive). (3) Packaging for 5-person co-op engineering staffs: I found no NRECA vetting checklist or tool, and no small-utility-specific vendor.

Serious weaknesses the founder must address:
- Regulation and tariffs are substituting for vetting. Collateral, study fees and site-control mandates make the applicant self-prove. Exelon cut its estimates about 40% after stricter collateral. AEP Ohio's pipeline fell by more than half after study fees of up to $100K (https://techstartups.com/2026/09/01/ai-data-centers-request-700-gw-of-u-s-power-but-much-of-the-demand-may-be-an-illusion/). Once a co-op requires a deposit, site control and a signed LOI, much of the 12-point test becomes documents the applicant hands over.
- Texas SB 6 / 16 TAC 25.194 applies only in ERCOT (https://www.dlapiper.com/en-us/insights/publications/2026/03/texas-proposes-new-interconnection-standards-for-large-electric-loads). The 'small utilities in neighboring states get the displaced phantoms' claim is plausible but I found no evidence for it.
- Several tests may not be observable by an outsider. OEM order acknowledgments and financing letters are confidential, and real developers often approach the utility before ordering equipment.
- Regulators are absorbing the LLC-transparency piece. Texas ordered an audit requiring true-ownership disclosure, and Pennsylvania issued an August 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW.
- Big engineering consultancies could add this as a service line. I could not verify whether they already do. My web-search budget ran out before I could check.

title: Neutral Monitoring That Unlocks Backup Diesel Dispatch
one_liner: A permit-to-dispatch package for data center backup generators that bundles neutral fence-line and neighbor-home monitoring with an automatic neighbor payout guarantee, so regulators and neighbors can say yes to more run-hours.
customer: Colo and hyperscale operators in PJM (Northern Virginia, Ohio, Illinois) with 20-500 MW of backup gensets who want to count them as capacity. Secondary buyers are county and state regulators who can make the monitoring a permit condition, and utilities and capacity buyers who need fast MW.
problem: Backup fleets sit idle because air permits cap non-emergency run-hours, and any permit change invites a public fight. Neighbors and regulators distrust operator-supplied modeling. Moratoria are spreading: New York paused permits in July 2026, Texas halted TCEQ data center permits in September 2026, and local pauses exist in at least 14 states. The permit-lawyer playbook alone doesn't win the social license, and neutral monitoring alone doesn't monetize.
solution: Fixed-price 'Dispatch Readiness + Neighbor Guarantee'. (1) Permit headroom audit and modification strategy (run-hour caps, synthetic-minor limits). (2) A 60-day ambient baseline of PM2.5, NO2/NOx and night noise at the fence line and at 5-15 volunteer neighbor homes, with hash-anchored timestamps and a public read-only dashboard reviewed by an outside expert. (3) The monitoring plan written into the permit application as the verification method. (4) A developer-funded escrow that pays households automatically when a verified exceedance coincides with a dispatch or test run. (5) The same telemetry doubles as the third-party measurement and verification for PJM programs.
why_now: PJM cleared 6.8 GW short and wants large loads to bring capacity or be curtailed. Turbines are sold out until 2029-30, so backup gensets are the only large block of capacity that exists today. Simultaneously, permit fights have gone from town boards to governors' offices, and regulators are drafting what evidence counts.
revenue_model: $15k fixed-fee dispatch-readiness audit as the wedge. $40-150k per site for permit and engineering work. $75-150k per site for baseline setup plus $4-10k per month for monitoring. An 8-10% administration fee on the guarantee escrow. 10-20% of the first five years of capacity revenue. At the roughly $325/MW-day cap, a 20 MW fleet is worth about $1.5-2M a year after derating, so the fees are easy to justify.
non_obvious_insight: Emergency-only runtime means expected neighbor payouts are tiny compared with the capacity revenue, so the parametric guarantee is nearly free to fund. Its real job is to turn permission from an adversarial fight into a priced product. The monthly 10-30 minute test runs are a free experiment. Sensors can measure the actual ambient impact of routine test runs before any expansion, giving regulators real measurements instead of dispersion models. The baseline also protects the operator against blame for pollution that came from traffic or other sources.
first_30_days: Pull public Title V and minor-source permits for about 30 colo sites in VA, OH and IL and build the permit headroom map. Retain one air-permitting consultant. Build 10 sensor nodes from off-the-shelf parts (about $1.5-3k each) and co-locate them against a reference monitor. Offer 25 facility and sustainability leads a $15k dispatch-readiness audit that includes a 30-day pilot on one site, and aim to close two. Bring the live dashboard to the first public hearing.
lineage: hybrid of I1172 + I0836 (Neutral Baselines and Neighbor Guarantees for Data Centers + Air-Permit Unlock for Idle Data Center Diesel). Why stronger: The permit playbook alone has long enterprise cycles and depends on regulators trusting the operator. The monitoring business alone competes with KETOS-style sensor vendors and is a cost center for developers. Combined, the monitoring is the missing permission-to-operate evidence, and the permit unlock gives the monitoring a clear ROI, a percentage-of-capacity-revenue upside, and a repeatable per-state playbook that is hard to copy.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: KETOS (SHIELD / KELP data-center water monitoring), Aethair (Aethair PRO, Environet, Thiamis), Envirosuite (ASX:EVS), Kunak. White space: Nobody found sells the bundle, so the status is 'gap' and not 'open'. The sensor and baseline layer is not open: KETOS (about $45M raised) pitches an independent baseline for data centers, Aethair pitches pre-construction baselines, Envirosuite has community dashboards, and consultancies bundle baselines into permitting. The unserved wedge is what sits on top of the sensors. (1) A neutral administrator holding escrowed, tamper-evident data whose governance the county and community accept, unlike developer-hired consultants and unlike opposition-side groups such as CEDS. (2) The Neighbor Guarantee: an automatic, no-litigation payout to households from a developer-funded escrow when a pre-agreed trigger is hit. No vendor, insurer, county ordinance or developer program found does this. The nearest things are Franklin County, Indiana's draft rule (escrow for 24-hour emergency potable water to impacted neighbors, plus developer-funded monitoring wells), one-off buyouts and lump-sum checks. (3) A 10-year, multi-parameter (wells, noise, PM2.5, voltage) record packaged as a permit-condition template that regulators can adopt. Weak points: the sensor baseline will commoditize; attribution is hard, because well drawdown from drought or other pumping is indistinguishable from data-center drawdown unless the design uses upgradient control wells and pumping records; automatic payouts may look like insurance under state law; and developer counsel may resist a pre-committed payout as an admission of liability. Note: the web-search budget ran out before I could check Crunchbase/YC directly for a startup doing exactly the escrow-plus-parametric bundle, so 'nobody found' means no evidence in about 25 searches, not proof of absence. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Voltus, CPower, Enchanted Rock (ERock), Trinity Consultants (data center and power team). White space: Verification caveat: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted, so no search-engine, Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or TechCrunch queries could be run. I did about 30 direct page fetches and 2 GitHub searches instead. The GitHub searches found no open-source tool for this. I found no company selling a fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' package for existing data center diesel fleets (permit modification, emissions retrofit financing, telemetry, PJM enrollment and M&V). That is absence of evidence from a constrained search, not proof that none exists.

What appears unserved:
(1) A productized, per-state permit playbook tied to capacity outcomes. Trinity-type consultants sell hourly, per-project permitting. DR aggregators (Voltus, CPower) sell enrollment and revenue share. Generator OEMs and ERock sell hardware. Nobody I found owns the seam between them.
(2) Retrofit financing on the subset of engines that need it.
(3) A permit-headroom dataset across Title V and minor-source files.

The binding constraint is legal, not competitive. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), as summarized from Cornell LII, emergency engines are limited to 100 hours a year for maintenance, testing and emergencies, with at most 50 of those for non-emergency use. The 50 hours cannot be used for peak shaving or non-emergency demand response, and cannot generate income or serve a financial arrangement with another entity. Only narrow exceptions exist, dispatched by local authorities for transmission and distribution limits. Selling emergency-designated diesel as PJM capacity therefore likely requires reclassifying engines as non-emergency, which triggers stricter engine standards (Tier 4 or SCR-type controls), plus state NOx limits and possible major-source permitting. That is why the founder's 'retrofit the subset' step is likely the real cost and risk. It is also why incumbents have stayed away. The wedge exists only where the permit and retrofit math actually closes.

Other risks: PJM DR accreditation rules and limited-duration derating, which I could not verify because the PJM manual fetch returned only a table of contents. Local opposition to diesel. Hyperscalers and utilities choosing gas or battery capacity instead.

title: Plumber Parts Ledger: Margin Recovery Plus Failure Evidence
one_liner: Give plumbing shops a free contingency audit of unbilled parts, and pay them a bounty to bag failed pipes and fittings. The invoices become the installed-base denominator that makes the failure evidence valuable to insurers and manufacturers.
customer: Plumbing, HVAC and electrical shops ($1.5-15M revenue, 5-40 techs) as the supply side. Paying buyers are regional and mutual homeowners insurers' subrogation units and subro vendors, plumbing manufacturers and private-label buyers, and later distributors.
problem: Shops leak margin on parts bought but never billed. Plumbers also throw away the failed supply line or fitting that would have made a $9k water loss recoverable, because nobody pays them the four minutes it takes to bag it. Failure counts alone are weak, since manufacturers' lawyers can dismiss them without knowing how many units were sold, installed and stayed fine.
solution: Shops forward supply-house invoices and give a field-service export. An LLM parser ties invoice lines to jobs and returns a weekly leak list, paid at 25% of recovered revenue, with no fee if nothing is found. The same app hands out tamper-evident QR bags. A 90-second phone flow captures photo in place, date code, homeowner e-signature and claim number, and a weekly courier pickup delivers chain-of-custody parts. Each bag is auto-linked to the job's SKU, install date and installer from the invoice ledger. Outputs are subrogation evidence packs, per-SKU failure-rate reports (failures per 10,000 units sold), and at-risk-address lists for proactive replacement.
why_now: Water damage is one of the top two homeowner claim categories, and insurers are squeezed enough that routine $8-15k losses are never pursued. LLM invoice parsing now works on messy supply-house PDFs and photos, which made both products cheap enough for a two-person team.
revenue_model: 25% of recovered and newly captured revenue for 12 months, converting to $199-499 per month monitoring. $75-150 per bagged part from insurers or subro vendors (of which $40-60 goes to the shop and tech), plus a 3-8% success share on recoveries. $15-60k per year failure-data licenses to manufacturers and distributors. Later, per-address replacement programs sold to insurers as loss prevention.
non_obvious_insight: The denominator only exists in the shop's invoices, and it arrives as a byproduct of margin recovery. It converts anecdotes into rates manufacturers can't wave away. It also identifies who installed which SKU at which address and when, which decides warranty windows and statute of repose. The installed-base list is the real prize: when a lot goes bad, the insurer can pay $15 to replace a braided line at every address that received it, instead of paying $9k after it bursts.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 shops through a local PHCC chapter and owner peer groups with a free 90-day audit and a free evidence kit. Turn each audit around in 48 hours with a single 'found money' number. Pay a flat $50 per bag and collect the first 50 parts with photos. Link each part to its invoice line. Take 20 case files to two regional mutual insurers and a subro vendor and sell a 100-part paid pilot.
lineage: hybrid of I0689 + I0068 (Failed-Part Bounty for Insurance Subrogation + Contingency Audit of Unbilled Plumbing Materials). Why stronger: The audit alone is a crowded, ServiceTitan-adjacent feature with thin defensibility. The bounty alone has a cold-start problem: shops have no reason to stay engaged and the data has no denominator. Together, the free audit is the near-zero-CAC hook into the same shops, the bounty gives them a second paycheck, and the joined install-and-failure ledger is a dataset neither ServiceTitan nor a forensic firm can assemble.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Donan Engineering - Loss Logistics, Envista Forensics and Rimkus (forensic engineering / property loss consulting), LeakBot, ServiceTitan and CompanyCam (plumber field software). White space: Caveat: the session's WebSearch budget ran out (200 of 200) before any search ran. This verdict rests on direct page fetches of about a dozen vendor, industry and government sites, plus two empty GitHub searches. I did not check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or trade press, so I could not rule out a small funded startup doing exactly this. Run 4-6 searches before committing money. Suggested queries: 'subrogation evidence preservation plumber', 'failed part bounty', 'water loss evidence kit', and the same on Crunchbase.

What I found is a real gap in what I could reach. Evidence logistics and forensic engineering exist for engineer-assigned losses (Donan, Envista, Rimkus). Insurer-funded plumber networks exist (LeakBot). Plumber field software exists (ServiceTitan, CompanyCam). No page I read describes any of these paying or equipping the plumber to retain the failed part on routine sub-$15k water losses. The public failure data I found is weak (SaferProducts.gov). Nothing I found is a date-code and brand-level failure-rate dataset.

Unserved specifically: (1) plumber-side capture at the moment of removal, including a per-part payment. (2) A neutral custodian and evidence package for the $8-15k tier, which is below the point where a $2k engineer is dispatched. (3) A structured brand, model and date-code failure dataset from real removed parts.

The main risks are structural, not competitive. (a) The plumber often arrives before a claim exists, so the claim number and the bounty payer are unknown at bagging. (b) Mitigation contractors and insurer-dispatched vendors may reach the site first on many losses. (c) The recovery economics of small product-defect claims are unproven, so insurers may not pay $75-150 for parts they would not pursue anyway. (d) A public brand-level failure report invites manufacturer legal pushback. (e) A 'cause-of-loss statement' from a tech risks unlicensed-engineering objections. (f) I could not fetch HomeServe (403), so I cannot say whether that plumber-network incumbent already does something like this. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ServiceTitan Accounts Payable (bill inbox, 3-way matching, Manage Statements, Manage Credits, discrepancy flags), Kojo, BuildOps (Procurement and Payables), Fergus. White space: Nobody I found offers a contingency-fee, done-for-you recovery audit for trade shops. What remains unserved is the customer-side leak: parts on a supply-house ticket with a job name, or pulled from truck stock, that never reached the customer invoice, plus supplier price drift and quoted-price violations tied back to the shop's own pricebook and markup targets. Existing tools (ServiceTitan AP, Kojo, BuildOps, Ramp) are software the shop must adopt and operate, and they focus on paying suppliers correctly. Three parts are open: (1) shops on Housecall Pro, Jobber, FieldEdge or Simpro, or ServiceTitan shops not using Procurement/AP, who have no PO-to-job workflow; (2) the done-for-you, no-recovery-no-fee commercial model, which no software vendor offers; (3) a cross-shop SKU price benchmark from pooled supply-house invoices. I found no evidence anyone has assembled that for residential and light-commercial trade shops. ServiceTitan's Manage Statements and Manage Credits are the closest overlap with the returns-credit and price-error pieces.

title: Vet-Verified Herd Exposure and Outbreak Index
one_liner: Rural large-animal vets sell two things from one app: borrower-approved, chute-side verified herd counts for ag lenders, and anonymized weekly syndrome tallies whose denominators come from those counts, giving lenders, insurers and traders a true disease-rate signal.
customer: Community banks and Farm Credit lenders (verified herd reports), livestock insurers and reinsurers, cattle analytics desks, packers and feedlot risk managers, animal-health company territory teams, and state animal health boards. Supply side is 25-50 large-animal practices.
problem: Lenders can't verify how many cows exist or where they are, and vets sit on that data unused. Vets can see outbreaks weeks before the state does but their tallies have no denominator, so a count of abortions means nothing without knowing how many bred cows are in that ZIP3. Vets also refuse to police clients, so neither product works if it feels like surveillance.
solution: One vet app and one relationship. At preg-check and weaning, the vet logs every head by EID or tag scan, age class, pregnancy status and location. The borrower approves sharing with a single tap, and the lender gets a timestamped Verified Herd Report. Every week the same vet sends a 30-second SMS tally by syndrome (abortion clusters, maggot wounds, sudden deaths, respiratory, milk drops), aggregated with k-anonymity. Outputs are a per-1,000-head regional index for subscribers, a lender portfolio dashboard with a regional disease overlay, and later an exposure-plus-hazard dataset for livestock insurers.
why_now: Fall preg-check season is live now, so the first verified counts can be collected this quarter. Screwworm and other disease anxiety has traders, insurers and state boards asking for leading indicators. The vet-as-verifier trust position is the same in both products, so one sales conversation with each practice covers both.
revenue_model: $2-3 per head per verification, split about 50/50 with the vet, charged to borrower or lender. $500-2,000 per month lender portfolio dashboards. $2-10k per month institutional subscribers for the outbreak index. $100-300 per month revenue share to each contributing practice on top of the per-head fee. Later, data licensing and pricing support for livestock disease cover.
non_obvious_insight: Verified herd inventory is an exposure layer, and vet syndrome tallies are a hazard layer, which is exactly what an insurer needs to price livestock disease cover. Neither layer alone can be underwritten. The denominator also lets the index read the 'absence of calls' signal properly, since call volume per 10,000 head falling during a quarantine looks different from a quiet region. Two revenue streams turn vets from reluctant borrowers' auditors into advocates: verification is borrower-initiated and tallies are anonymized, so the conflict-of-interest objection goes away.
first_30_days: Sign 3-5 rural practices in TX, OK, KS or NE that each do thousands of head of fall preg-checks, and pitch 3-4 community-bank ag lenders via the state bankers' association ag committee. Run about 10 borrower pilots at $2/head with a form-based app and a PDF report. In parallel, start the plain SMS weekly tally with 25 practices and a free regional newsletter as the give-to-get hook. Backtest screwworm lead time against official confirmation dates and pitch 3 analytics shops for a $1-2k per month paid pilot.
lineage: hybrid of I0338 + I0199 (Chute-Side Cow Counts for Ag Lenders + Rural Vet Call Logs as Outbreak Early Warning). Why stronger: Cow counts alone are a small per-head fee and the outbreak signal alone is a free-data-for-nothing pitch to vets. Combined, vets earn twice from one workflow, the outbreak index gets denominators nobody else has, and the herd data gains a hazard overlay, which opens the much larger livestock insurance and reinsurance buyer that neither product reaches alone.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global / Where Food Comes From (Beef Passport), Merck Animal Health (Allflex tags/readers, Vence). White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I ran zero searches. I did direct fetches of about 15 vendor and agency pages, plus GitHub repo searches. Nothing here rules out a direct competitor. The biggest gap is that I could not identify the third-party collateral-inspection firms that lenders already pay for cattle counts, or any startup selling vet-verified herd inventory to lenders. Do not treat 'gap' as 'open'.\n\nWhat the direct fetches showed: none of the herd-software, EID, tracking or verification vendors I checked advertise a lender-facing 'independent count' product. The vendors were CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global/WFCF, Ceres Tag, Halter, HerdDogg and Gallagher. Merck/Vence returned 403, so I could not check it. Every one of them is a producer-side management or supply-chain tool. GitHub searches turned up no open-source lender-verification tool, only hobby herd apps.\n\nThe unserved wedge is a lender-mandated, third-party-attested herd inventory built as a covenant workflow. It would cover the vet-signed chute-side count, a portfolio dashboard, and year-over-year anomaly flags such as head count down, pregnancy rate down, or tags missing versus last year.\n\nStructural weaknesses to be skeptical of:\n- Adverse selection: 'borrower-initiated' verification means fraudulent borrowers never opt in. The product only works if lenders make it a loan condition.\n- Coverage: a preg-check only counts animals brought to the chute that day, not cattle on other leases or sold or double-pledged since. It does not prove ownership or lien priority.\n- Vet liability and willingness: vets may refuse to sign anything that reads as a collateral audit.\n- Economics: $2-3/head split 50/50 leaves the vet about $1-1.50/head on top of a preg-check fee that is already several dollars.\n- Entry by an existing vendor: IMI Global (WFCF) or Merck/Allflex could add this as a feature. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SAVSNET / FAVSNET (University of Liverpool), Morrison Swine Health Monitoring Project (Univ. of Minnesota) and Swine Health Information Center (SHIC), Equine Disease Communication Center (US Equestrian), USDA APHIS / NAHLN and Texas Animal Health Commission (mandatory reporting). White space: Verdict basis: I found no commercial or non-commercial system that turns weekly counts from US large-animal (cattle) vet practices into a regional syndromic index sold to institutional buyers. I could not test that claim against Crunchbase, YC, TechCrunch or Product Hunt, so treat it as unconfirmed on the startup side.

What exists today:
- Academic systems, mostly in Europe (SAVSNET/FAVSNET in the UK).
- A 2025 scoping review of 126 animal syndromic systems: 67 percent were still proof-of-concept, only 20 percent were fully operational, and it noted that even established systems are vulnerable to loss of funding. Operational ones were mostly government run. This is a nearby-review finding, not proof that nobody is building this in the US. Source: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&retmode=xml&id=40327964
- Free industry models such as MSHMP (swine) and the equine EDCC.
- Companion-animal practice data businesses (Animalytix, Vetsource).
- Government mandatory reporting, which now covers confirmed and suspected screwworm within 24 hours in Texas.

Unserved, specifically:
1. Pre-confirmation, syndromic, cattle-specific signals: abortion clusters, maggot wounds, sudden deaths and milk drops, at ZIP3 or county level, weekly. Government reporting only covers confirmed or suspected reportable disease.
2. A denominator and absence-of-calls signal that no current system produces.
3. A decision-grade product for private actors who face NWS movement restrictions and have no ground-level feed: sale barns, order buyers, feedlots, packers, insurers and animal health territory teams.

Structural risks that keep this a gap rather than open:
- Government and free alternatives (TAHC and USDA public case counts, EDCC-style free alerts) satisfy much of the need.
- Vets are legally obligated to report suspects to TAHC, so a private feed adds little for confirmed cases.
- Privacy and trade-implication concerns were the top barrier in an Australian stakeholder study (https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&retmode=xml&id=40037116).
- Selling vet-sourced early disease signals to commodity funds carries legal and ethics exposure (material non-public information, duty-to-report conflicts).

title: Graduate Pay Ledger for CDL Schools and Carriers
one_liner: CDL schools get the verified placement and earnings evidence Workforce Pell requires by having graduates upload settlement stubs to a pay-verification app. Carriers pay to reach those graduates with verified pay pages, and lenders pay for stub-based income packets.
customer: Small and mid-size CDL schools and other short-program providers (paying per completer verified) as the beachhead. Carriers with 50-1,000 trucks that pay $6-15k to hire a driver (verified-pay badge and graduate funnel), mortgage and auto lenders serving drivers, and state workforce boards.
problem: Workforce Pell requires verified placement (about 70%) with a clock that starts before the governor application, and CDL schools typically track completion, not employment. State wage records lag by quarters and miss owner-operators and per-diem pay. Meanwhile the pay-verification app has a cold-start problem: recruiting drivers one Facebook group at a time is slow and noisy.
solution: At completion, schools enroll graduates in the pay app. In exchange for a verified profile and a small incentive, graduates upload their first settlement stubs at 30, 90 and 180 days. The AI extracts employer, paid miles, deadhead, detention and pay per hour away from home. The school gets an audit-ready placement and earnings ledger, the governor application packet, and an earnings-premium exposure score. Carriers that look good buy a Verified Pay page and a graduate applicant funnel, and lenders buy income packets built from stubs.
why_now: Workforce Pell went live for provider approvals in 2026 and the placement and completion evidence rules make this a compliance purchase with a deadline. The stub-parsing AI is cheap now. Carriers are paying up to $15k per driver hired and are locked out of trust because drivers only believe stubs.
revenue_model: $150-300 per completer verified or $4-12k per year per program. $3-5k for a governor application packet. $1.5-3k earnings-premium exposure report. $500-3,000 per month carrier subscriptions for verified pay pages and graduate funnel. $300-1,000 lender referral fees per funded loan. Free for graduates.
non_obvious_insight: A settlement stub proves placement, employer, and earnings in a single document that drivers, carriers and lenders already trust, which employer-email verification and state wage matching can't do for small carriers or per-diem pay. The school-by-carrier pay matrix is a data product in its own right. It tells each school which carriers to steer graduates toward, which raises next year's placement rate and protects Pell eligibility, so verification pays for itself in outcomes.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 CDL schools in two states that have opened Workforce Pell approval, at a $1.5k pilot price. Backfill the last 12 months of completers by text, asking for stubs, to produce a baseline verified placement rate and a sample governor packet. Publish a 'State of Real Pay for New CDL Graduates' report naming carriers. Sell Verified Pay badges to the 3-5 mid-size fleets that hire the most graduates and sign one bank-statement mortgage broker for lender leads.
lineage: hybrid of I0916 + I0227 (Placement Proof for Workforce Pell Providers + Verified Pay Receipts for Truck Driver Hiring). Why stronger: Placement Proof alone has to chase completers by text and email, and the pay app alone has a slow consumer cold start. Combined, schools deliver a captive, motivated cohort of new drivers every month, the pay data comes from the exact graduates schools need to verify, and carriers and lenders subsidize a verification service that schools would otherwise pay for entirely themselves.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ellucian (incl. former Anthology CampusNexus SIS, Occupation Insight), Populi, Gradelink, Lightcast. White space: Confidence is LOW. My WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200) before any searches ran. Only 9 direct page fetches went through, and they returned homepage-level content. I also tried a Google URL through WebFetch and then stopped, because that was an attempt to get around the search limit. I found no direct competitor, but I did not search for one, so this is not evidence that none exists. Homepage checks of Populi, Ellucian/Anthology, Gradelink and Lightcast showed no Workforce Pell or placement-verification features. Orbund's site was bot-blocked, and the Federal Register and ed.gov pages redirected or returned 403, so I could not check the rule text. Likely unserved wedge: a Workforce Pell-specific product that (1) backfills the 12-month look-back by contacting completers and employers, (2) reconciles evidence to the rule's placement definition, and (3) produces the governor application packet for small CDL, CNA, barbering and cosmetology schools. Not searched, so still unknown: startups or Product Hunt and YC entries; existing placement-verification services already sold to accredited career schools (ACCSC, NACCAS, COE reporting); consultancies selling this as a service; state-built portals; and SIS vendor Workforce Pell roadmaps. Structural risks visible without further research: (a) if the final rule lets states verify placement from UI wage records, a self-collected pay-stub product loses much of its value; (b) SIS vendors can bolt this on as a feature; (c) the number of approved programs, and so the buyer count, may be small at first. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: TruckersReport (carrier reviews and salary survey), Best Fleets to Drive For (CarriersEdge), Tenstreet (Driver Pulse, IntelliApp, Hiring Center), Drive My Way. White space: Web search was unavailable (the session's 200-search budget was used up), so this rests on about 25 direct page fetches plus prior knowledge. Confidence is moderate to low. A reviewer should re-run searches for 'verified driver pay', 'settlement stub scanner' and 'trucker mortgage per diem' before committing.

I found no product that does all of this: (1) collect settlement stubs, (2) verify them with fraud checks, and (3) publish per-carrier, receipts-backed effective pay, including dollars per hour away from home. The closest, TruckersReport, has an unverified self-reported salary survey run by a site paid by carriers' recruiting budgets. Best Fleets to Drive For is survey-based. Tenstreet and Drive My Way own recruiting flow but show no pay-verification product.

Specific unserved gaps:
- A trust-backed pay number that uses stubs as proof, computed as dollars per hour on the road rather than per mile.
- Lease-purchase and owner-operator drivers, whose settlements are itemized and who are the most exposed to deceptive ads.
- A stub-based income packet that handles per-diem structures for non-QM and bank-statement lenders. Truv and Argyle verify through payroll connections and are not built for per-diem trucker income.

Weak points that could still sink it:
1. Cold start and selection bias. Unhappy drivers upload more, and carriers with a bad median will not buy a badge. A pay-for-badge model also has a credibility conflict.
2. Stubs do not show time away from home. Hours-away metrics need driver-entered dates or ELD integration, which is hard.
3. The truth-in-leasing itemized-settlement rule (49 CFR 376.12) applies to owner-operator leases, not W-2 company drivers. The idea's 'raw material already exists' claim is only partly true. I could not fetch the regulation this session.
4. Publishing rankings of named carriers invites legal threats. Self-published analytics are not covered by Section 230 the way user reviews are.
5. Per-funded-loan referral fees to a non-lender may run into RESPA Section 8, so this needs counsel. Lenders will also likely re-verify borrower-supplied stubs, which limits the lender product's value. This is from prior knowledge and not verified.

title: Replication Bench: Poll-Triaged Experiments With Signed Records
one_liner: A poll-first replication service: anonymous postdoc consensus tells biotech investors and AI-bio builders which claim to test, and a pool of laid-off bench scientists runs the decisive experiment and returns a signed, machine-readable execution record.
customer: Seed and Series A biotech VCs, corporate venture arms and pharma BD teams evaluating spinouts (poll memos and replications). AI-first biotechs and AI-for-science startups with agent swarms and no wet lab (ticketed experiments). Later, licensees of the replication registry.
problem: Investors can buy candid consensus but can't cheaply convert it into a test. Agent-driven startups can buy experiments, but cannot tell which literature claims their designs are built on. A bench network alone has speculative, nascent demand from agents. A poll shop alone has no way to run the decisive experiment.
solution: Bench Pulse: within 5 business days, 8-15 vetted, paid, anonymous subfield postdocs and senior techs give a structured memo on the named claim (consensus, red flags, fragile reagents, what to test first). Where the poll narrows the question, the same team runs 'Key-Figure Replication' at rented bench space with pre-registered success criteria. Each job returns a signed record separating protocol, human edits and physical execution (deviations, photos, instrument logs, raw data). AI-agent customers order the same protocols through an API and can request 'claim-verified' runs before building on a paper.
why_now: There is a large pool of laid-off molecular biologists and postdocs available at near-market rates, seed funds are scrutinizing academic-spinout claims harder, and AI-for-science startups are producing agent-designed experiments faster than anyone can run them.
revenue_model: $4-6k per poll memo, $15-40k per key-experiment replication, $30-60k per year fund retainers for pipeline-wide bench pulse, $1.5-8k per agent experiment at roughly 35-45% gross margin, and later licenses of the labeled replication registry to AI-bio firms.
non_obvious_insight: Poll consensus is the cheap triage that decides where a $15-40k replication is most informative, so the bench network needs less capacity to make more money per experiment. Each replication then scores the poll: 'polls predicted X of Y outcomes' becomes proof that lets the company sell poll-only memos at scale. Every job adds to a labeled dataset of what replicated, what didn't and why, in a machine-readable format, which is precisely what AI-for-science companies lack and can't obtain from papers.
first_30_days: Pick one subfield where you personally know about 20 contacts (for example CAR-T, organoids or targeted protein degradation) and draft the NDA and anonymity protocol (about $3k in legal). Recruit 10 laid-off molecular biologists, sublet 2-3 surplus benches, and define a fixed-price ticket type for replication. Offer 3 seed funds a free poll on an asset they are already reviewing, convert one to a paid $5k poll, and upsell a replication. Pitch 10 AI protein-design startups on the same bench.
lineage: hybrid of I0400 + I0868 (Bench-Truth Diligence for Biotech Investors + Human Bench Network for AI Agents). Why stronger: Each parent has a missing half: bench-truth diligence lacks capacity to run the decisive experiment, and the human bench network lacks a buyer with an urgent budget and a filtered question. Together, a $5k poll funds triage, a $15-40k replication uses the bench, and the labeled replication registry becomes a moat that neither Hoeford-style polls nor cloud labs can build.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hoeford Research, Alacrita, Fios Genomics, GLG. White space: Caveat on coverage: the WebSearch quota was exhausted (200 of 200) before this task started. I substituted direct WebFetch of competitor pages, Google News RSS, and some Brave and Bing queries. Brave rate-limited me (429) and Bing returned junk. Hoeford and Fios pages were blocked or truncated. So 'nothing found' is weaker than a full sweep, and the founder should confirm with Crunchbase and LinkedIn plus 10 calls to seed VCs.

What I found. Both halves of the idea have adjacent players, but I found no one selling the specific product as described.

Poll half. Expert networks (GLG, Guidepoint, Third Bridge) and scientific-diligence boutiques (Alacrita, Fios) all sell expert input to investors. They interview senior experts and KOLs, sell bespoke projects, and market to finance clients. I found no fixed-price, 5-day, named-claim consensus poll of 8-15 anonymous junior bench scientists. That is a real wedge, and it fits the founder's critique that the incumbents rely on conflicted seniors.

Replication half. 'Wet diligence' at CROs or independent labs is an accepted practice (LifeSciVC says it should be 'gating before investing'). Hoeford appears to sell it. Science Exchange has the marketplace and the history (Reproducibility Initiative, RP:CB). The bundle, where the poll narrows the question and then a pre-registered, blinded replication follows, looks unserved. Owning a bench pool of laid-off scientists is the least defensible and most operationally risky part.

Segment. AI-bio founders building on published wet-lab claims are the least served, but Adaptyv Bio (raised $40M, 3-week assays from $149 per protein) is already serving protein-design validation.

Structural threats.
- GLG or Guidepoint can copy the poll cheaply once it is proven, since they already sell surveys.
- Anonymity is leaky in subfields of 20-50 people.
- Postdocs risk their careers and may breach university confidentiality or employment terms.
- A negative poll about a named PI's paper carries defamation and tortious-interference exposure.
- A replication that fails in a new lab does not prove the claim is false, which is the ambiguity buyers hate. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Adaptyv Bio (Adaptyv Biosystems), Ginkgo Bioworks (Cloud Lab and Datapoints), Emerald Cloud Lab, Science Exchange and Scientist.com (CRO marketplaces). White space: Things I did not find. I could not run WebSearch (the session budget of 200 was used up), so this comes from Google News RSS queries and direct page fetches. I did not check Crunchbase, YC's directory, Product Hunt or GitHub in depth; a GitHub repository search returned nothing.

1. No funded company sells human-executed, ad hoc, arbitrary-protocol wet-lab work through an agent-native ticket API with a fixed price and a signed record separating AI proposal, human edit and physical execution. The nearest pieces are split across companies. Adaptyv has the agent API but runs standardized automated assays. CRO marketplaces have custom human work but run on quotes and SOWs. Transfyr has the execution-record capture but no labor. Emerald and Ginkgo have flexible automation but were not found to offer human-run ad hoc work to agents.
2. The long tail beyond fixed assays is the actual gap. That means multi-step, protocol-specific molecular biology that a robot cannot be programmed for in time: novel enzyme or nuclease activity validation, cloning plus cell-free expression plus a custom activity readout, and unusual cell-culture assays. Anthropic's post confirms this is where a frontier lab keeps human scientists.
3. Nobody I found sells biosafety-screened human execution of AI-proposed protocols as a service, even though oversight of AI-directed experiments is in the news (Lab Manager, 'Biosafety Oversight for AI-Directed Lab Experiments', Sept 28, 2026; Frontiers paper on automated-lab security tiers).

The window is narrow and closing.
- Adaptyv has $40M, agent-native positioning, a stated plan to add 'more complex biological workflows', and Chai and Boltz as customers. It can move toward the ad hoc tail with automation.
- Scientist.com and Science Exchange could add an agent API or MCP layer around their existing providers with modest effort.
- Transfyr could bundle records with any CRO.
- Anthropic and other frontier labs are insourcing bench capacity.

Risks to the idea's own claims:
- BioSpace headlines show layoffs are easing: August 2026 biopharma layoffs were about 500, down 90% year over year, and the Q2 job report says postings are rising. Skilled hands are still available, but the 'layoff wave' supply story is weakening (via https://news.google.com/rss/search?q=biotech+layoffs+2026+BioSpace+job+cuts+tracker).
- Sublet-bench operations carry insurance, contamination, quality-control and IP-chain-of-custody risk that a software-style API hides.
- The 35-45% gross margin at $1.5-8k per experiment is unproven against commodity CROs and against Adaptyv's automation, which starts at $149 per protein for screening-level binding.

title: Supplier Watch: Customs Trails Plus Tool Census
one_liner: A supplier-monitoring subscription that reads US customs records for what your factory really ships and to whom, and upgrades to laser-tagged tool census and cavity-fingerprint forensics when the trail looks wrong or a divorce is coming.
customer: US OEMs and PE-owned manufacturers ($50-500M revenue) with $200k-$5M of tooling in China (COO/VP supply chain, with general counsel). Secondary: small and mid-size importers re-sourcing to Vietnam, India, Mexico and Turkey, customs brokers, and factories buying verified credentials.
problem: Brands leaving a Chinese contract manufacturer rarely know which molds and dies they own, or whether the ex-supplier is still running them off the books. Importers of new suppliers can't tell a real factory from a shell. Customs rows tell you who ships what to whom but not what machines exist. A physical audit tells you what tools exist but is expensive and one-time.
solution: Tier 1 is a $2,500 remote 'Supplier Trail + Marketplace Overrun Audit': pull three years of import records for the supplier and its affiliates, find shipments matching the client's product descriptions and codes to consignees other than the client, compare volumes against the client's purchases and plausible capacity, and buy about 10 look-alike units from 1688, Alibaba and Temu to match against the golden sample and lot codes. Tier 2 is Tool Census ($6-15k per site) with a local partner, laser-tagging and cavity fingerprinting. Tier 3 is the forensic evidence pack and tool extraction. Tier 4 is a $149-499 per month watch subscription and a supplier-owned credential for smaller importers and factories.
why_now: Tariff pressure in 2025-26 is pushing brands to move production out of China within the last 24 months, and divorces put tooling at stake exactly when leverage is lowest. LLM parsing of shipping records and computer-vision matching of cavity marks are now cheap enough for a small team.
revenue_model: $2.5k remote audit, $6-15k per Tool Census site, $2-5k per month Overrun Watch per product family, $3-8k per evidence pack, 8-12% of appraised tool value on extraction, $149-499 per month and $150-400 per dossier for smaller importers, and $600-1,200 per year factory credentials. Expected first-year ACV for a manufacturer is $40-120k.
non_obvious_insight: The customs trail lets you run forensics remotely before anyone flies to China, since an ex-supplier shipping your part number to a third consignee shows up in the record as a shipper-consignee pair with volume. Conversely, every confirmed overrun case is a rare labeled positive for the anomaly model, which is otherwise unlabeled and generic like ImportGenius, and the census provides ground-truth capacity to sanity-check shipping volumes. The cheap watch subscription also identifies which suppliers are about to become the high-ticket cases.
first_30_days: Buy 12 months of import records for two categories and auto-build about 1,000 factory profiles, hand-auditing 20. Sell the $2,500 remote audit to 3 design partners through Ohio plant-manager and Reshoring Initiative networks. Line up a Dongguan or Ningbo audit contractor by referral and book an hour with an IP litigator who will white-label the evidence-pack format. Send 200 emails to sourcing managers and customs brokers for the watch subscription.
lineage: hybrid of I0552 + I1209 (Supplier Divorce Protection: Tool Census and Overrun Forensics + Real-Factory Credentials From Customs Shipping Records). Why stronger: Tool Census alone is a high-ticket, low-frequency service with a long sales cycle, and customs credentials alone compete directly with ImportGenius, Panjiva and ImportYeti. Together, the cheap subscription is the funnel to the expensive census, the census and forensics supply ground truth that makes the credential defensible, and forensic cases keep improving the anomaly model.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Harris Sliwoski (China Law Blog), Alitheon (FeaturePrint), Red Points, Corsearch (Zeal 2.0, Investigations 360, Distribution Control). White space: Coverage caveat: the WebSearch quota (200 per session) was already used up when I started, so I could not run the planned 6-12 searches. I also could not check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or open-source repos. The findings below come from about 25 direct page fetches, so treat 'nobody does this' as unproven. The vendors most likely missed are the many small China-based QC and sourcing agents that sell 'mold audits' and 'mold relocation', plus PI and investigation firms (Kroll-type). Do a manual pass on those before committing.

What I found: I found no productized, US-facing service that bundles (a) a serialized tool census, (b) cavity-level physical fingerprints, and (c) marketplace test-buy attribution of overruns to a specific tool. The problem is documented and treated as an unproductized legal-advice problem: Harris Sliwoski tells clients to keep an inventory form and audit quarterly, and never mentions a third-party vendor for it. Marketplace monitoring and takedown (Red Points, Corsearch, Alibaba's free IP platform) is commoditized and crowded. Object fingerprinting exists (Alitheon) but is aimed at electronics, aerospace and gray-market diversion, not tool-mark attribution.

Genuinely unserved: (1) cavity-level 'which tool made this part' attribution that holds up as evidence; (2) a tooling census standard for mid-market OEMs, timed to the exit window; (3) an evidence pack designed for counsel that a brand-protection vendor's screenshot-and-takedown workflow does not produce.

Weak points: Extraction (tool 3) is freight, customs and re-qualification work that sourcing agents and forwarders already do at low margin. Monitoring (tool 2, first half) is a commodity. Attribution is legally useful only when the overrun carries the client's IP (trademark, design patent, trade dress) and the client can enforce it. If the part is generic or unbranded, a match proves little. Chinese-court enforceability is unproven here. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ImportGenius, Panjiva (S&P Global Market Intelligence), Descartes Datamyne, ImportYeti. White space: The narrow wedge that appears unserved is a fixed-price, human-reviewed 'reasonable-care file' for a small US importer, sold through customs brokers. The SMB importer (Amazon or Shopify brand, or a $2-50M distributor) needs one factory checked before one PO. Enterprise tools (Sayari, Altana, Tradeverifyd, Trademo, Exiger) are sold by demo and are priced and scoped for large compliance teams. Data tools (ImportGenius, Panjiva, Datamyne, ImportYeti) sell rows and leave interpretation to the analyst. Inspectors (QIMA) and sourcing agents (Sourcify) sell physical checks, not a documentary file that maps to CBP's reasonable-care standard. The part I found nobody offering is a factory-claimed profile with consent-based buyer references, which is a two-sided credential. No visible player runs a supplier-owned reputation credential built on customs ledgers. However, the wedge is thin. (1) ImportGenius already markets 'supplier verification via shipping history' at the same $229-449/mo price band. (2) The raw-data floor is free or near-free. (3) Any one of Altana, Trademo or ImportGenius could add a 'transshipment risk report' feature quickly. (4) The factory-pays credential side has no demonstrated demand and needs a two-sided marketplace. Risks I could not check with the exhausted search budget: whether resale of licensed bill-of-lading data is allowed, that US import records often name the forwarder or trading company as shipper instead of the factory, that importers can request confidentiality under 19 CFR 103.31, and that no CBP safe-harbor exists for third-party dossiers.

title: Rural County Night Desk for Hospitals and Jails
one_liner: One pool of licensed remote night nurses and NPs sold as a county bundle: the recorded independent second RN for the critical access hospital, and the video screening that lets a deputy clear an arrestee for booking without a four-hour ER trip.
customer: Chief nursing officers and pharmacy directors at critical access hospitals, county sheriffs and commissioners, state hospital associations, county risk pools, and malpractice and captive insurers, all reached through the same rural-county channels.
problem: At 3am a rural county has three nurses on at the hospital and one or two deputies on the road. The nurse who is supposed to witness a narcotic waste or double-check a high-alert drug is mid-code, and the deputy with an arrestee is stuck in that same ER for hours, leaving the county unpatrolled. Each problem alone is too small to support a dedicated clinical team.
solution: Start with the $150 tablet-and-camera cart at the dispensing cabinet: a remote RN appears within 60 seconds, watches the waste on video, and attests, with a time-stamped clip and an audit log matched to the cabinet record. Add a booking-desk kit (vitals, pulse oximeter, glucometer, breathalyzer) with a physician-signed, ACEP-based clearance protocol and 24/7 RN and NP video screening ('fit for booking with monitoring plan', 'needs ER now', 're-check in 2 hours'). Both run on one recording platform, one compact-licensed clinician pool, one supervising physician and one malpractice policy. The county gets a single dashboard showing diversion-audit coverage, ER visits avoided and 'deputy hours returned to patrol'.
why_now: Rural hospitals are staffed thinly at night and rural jail deaths and diversion are in the news, so both insurers and risk pools are actively looking for evidence-grade controls. Compact licensure and cheap video hardware let a small team run a multi-state night pool for the first time.
revenue_model: $1,500-2,500 per hospital per month plus per-event fees above volume, and $2,000-3,500 per county per month for about 40 jail screens plus $85 per extra screen, so roughly $4-6k per month for a county bundle. Discounts through malpractice insurers and county risk pools convert to distribution. Gross margin of 40-50% at a pool of about 8-12 hospitals per RN per night.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing is the same: a credentialed, recorded, independent clinician on camera at 3am, with a defensible protocol. The evidence infrastructure (timestamped video, audit log, physician-signed protocol) that proves a diversion witness also proves a jail clearance, so one product convinces both insurers. Waste events cluster around medication passes while booking clusters around bar close and weekends, so the two workloads plausibly smooth each other out, and a pilot can confirm that before hiring. The hospital is a natural co-payer, since every cleared arrestee is an ER visit it no longer has to staff for free.
first_30_days: The founder, a rural ER nurse, recruits 6 per-diem or retired RNs with compact licenses plus 1-2 NPs on remote night hours. Write the clearance protocol with a supervising rural-ER physician and have one county attorney review it. Pick one county with both a critical access hospital and a jail the founder knows. Offer the hospital a free 30-day cabinet pilot and the sheriff a $1,500, 60-day booking-desk pilot. Bring the combined numbers (waste attestations logged, ER trips avoided, deputy hours saved) to the state hospital association and the county risk pool.
lineage: hybrid of I0016 + I1025 (Remote Second-RN for Rural Night Shifts + Tele-Clearance for Sheriffs' Booking Desks). Why stronger: Each parent has the same expensive fixed costs (clinician recruiting, compact licenses, recording platform, physician oversight, malpractice) and a small revenue per site. Pooling spreads those costs over two products sold to overlapping counties, lets one relationship close a larger $4-6k per month deal, and lets two insurers see one shared evidence trail, which raises ACV and lowers cost per sale versus either service alone.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: MIDAS Healthcare Solutions (MidasVIEW / Anytime Witness, aka V.I.E.W.), BD Pyxis Med Link Queue & Waste, Avel eCare, VirtuAlly (with Teledigm Health). White space: Nobody I found sells a shared, pooled, live remote-RN witness subscription to critical access hospitals. The specific gaps are:
(1) Live human supply. MidasVIEW replaces the second person with recorded video reviewed later. Pyxis remote witness still needs a colleague on shift. Virtual-nursing vendors cover admissions, discharges, sitters and documentation. Remote pharmacy vendors cover order verification. Nobody provides a licensed second person on demand at 3am.
(2) Transfusion, high-alert and pediatric double-checks. Asynchronous video cannot substitute for a live independent check before administration. Remote IDC is documented as feasible but under-evidenced, and only a few institutions do it (ONS 2024).
(3) Small-hospital fit. MidasVIEW pilots are at tertiary and children's hospitals. Small facilities lag on diversion controls: only 57% of single facilities actively monitor camera footage, and CAHs lack pharmacy staff to review video the next day.
(4) Insurer-linked audit trail. No diversion vendor sells to liability or captive insurers.
The wedge is narrow and time-limited. Avel eCare, VirtuAlly and the telepharmacy vendors could add a witness line quickly, and MidasVIEW could add live witness routing. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: NaphCare (STATCare 24/7 telehealth), Wellpath, Southern Health Partners, Turn Key Health. White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before I could run any searches, so this verdict rests on about 14 direct page fetches. That is far short of the 6-12 searches the task called for, and I found no startup-specific evidence either way.
