I found no vendor whose page shows a tele-clearance product for booking desks, meaning a remote RN/NP screening arrestees before booking with a time-stamped disposition (fit for booking, needs ER now, re-check in 2 hours). Incumbent jail-health vendors (Wellpath, NaphCare, Southern Health Partners) sell on-site staffing or in-custody care. Avel eCare sells 24/7 virtual clinicians to rural ERs and to law enforcement, but only for behavioral crisis. The unserved wedge is a pre-booking, per-county-per-month subscription for jails too small to justify a contracted health vendor, priced against deputy-hours and ER bills. Hospital-run or jail-staff-run tele-clearance programs may already exist locally and I could not check.\n\nTwo structural risks weaken the wedge and need validating early. First, the pitch says the Nurse Licensure Compact makes cross-state night staffing workable, but the NLC covers RNs, not NPs. As far as I know the APRN Compact was not yet operational, so NP staffing likely needs per-state licenses. Second, a remote clinician clearing an intoxicated or injured person on vitals and video alone shifts head-injury and withdrawal liability onto the vendor. That is a malpractice-insurance and clinical-governance problem, and a risk pool may or may not accept it. Revenue is also thin: 12 counties at $2-3.5k a month is roughly $290k-500k a year, with slow county sales cycles.

title: Rotor Rescue as Scrapyard Deal-Sourcing Engine
one_liner: Use the pay-per-rotor magnet program as the free-to-yard front door that surfaces retiring scrapyard owners and gives search-fund buyers a day-one margin lever and guaranteed magnet supply.
customer: Laid-off mid-career managers with $100-300K who pay cohort tuition to buy and run a yard. Scrapyard, motor-shop and appliance-recycler owners, both as rotor sellers and as retiring owners. Rare-earth magnet recyclers that need domestic feed. SBA lenders as a channel.
problem: The accelerator's scarce input is proprietary, fairly priced deal flow (brokered scrap-yard listings are thin) and a differentiated value-creation story for lenders and sellers. Rotor Rescue's scarce inputs are trust with thousands of skeptical independent yards and aggregate volume, and recyclers such as Cyclic already court suppliers directly.
solution: Phase 1: run Rotor Rescue in 2-3 states with a loaner gauss meter and a price sheet by motor model, paying yards per unit and aggregating lots for recyclers. Each enrolled yard reveals throughput, mix and owner age, so the program flags retirement-age owners. Phase 2: cohort members get first look at flagged yards, a permit-transfer and environmental diligence pack, SBA-lender introductions, and a ready 'magnet program' they can run on day one in the acquired yard. First sellable product: cohort seats at $4-6K that include the Rotor Rescue playbook and pre-sourced sell-side LOIs.
why_now: AI-driven hiring freezes are producing capable managers with cash and time. Greenfield battery and plastics recycling is failing (Ascend Elements and Li-Cycle bankruptcies), while permitted, cash-flowing yards look safe. DOE announced $134M for critical-mineral demonstrations in June 2026, and DoD-backed magnet plants create domestic pull and funded recyclers that need feed.
revenue_model: Cohort tuition of $4-6K per seat. Buy-side success fee of $25-50K or 1.5-2% at close. 2-5% advisory equity in each acquisition. Sell-side listing fees from retiring owners. Spread on assayed magnet feed sold to recyclers, plus a small SaaS fee for the identification and price app. Diligence-pack licensing to lenders.
non_obvious_insight: A yard that you pay every month for rotors trusts you, and your purchase log is a quality-of-earnings proxy for its volume and mix. Retiring owners rarely list with brokers; they tell whoever already writes them checks. That makes Rotor Rescue a proprietary deal-sourcing channel disguised as a price-discovery service. In the other direction, an owned portfolio of yards turns the magnet-feed aggregation problem into contracted supply, which a national recycler would rather buy from than chase yard by yard.
first_30_days: Pull permit and owner-age lists for two states and buy 5 gauss meters. Visit 10 yards, measure 200 units and build the price sheet. Get an offtake LOI from one magnet recycler and pay 3 yards on the first 50 units. Run a webinar for laid-off managers ('buy a yard that already has a magnet program') to enroll about 10 for the first cohort. Ask the yards you visit which owners want an exit, sign two sell-side LOIs, and line up an environmental consultant and one SBA lender.
lineage: hybrid of I0626 + I0939 (Search-Fund Accelerator for Buying Scrap Yards + Rotor Rescue: Scrapyard Magnet Pick-and-Pay). Why stronger: The accelerator gets proprietary deal flow and a concrete margin-improvement thesis at day one, which is the hardest thing for a first-time searcher to show a lender or seller. Rotor Rescue gets trusted access to yards, guaranteed volume through acquired yards, and a second revenue line that does not depend on rare-earth prices. Each side removes the other's biggest customer-acquisition cost.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Search Fund Accelerator (SFA), Kingsway Search Xcelerator (KSX), Codie Sanchez / Contrarian Thinking ('boring business' acquisition education), University ETA programs and search fund ecosystem (Stanford GSB, Kellogg, WashU Olin, Yale, Cleveland ETA program). White space: I found no scrap, recycling or transfer-station-specific acquisition accelerator. Every searcher or ETA program I could verify is sector-agnostic, and none packages this asset class for a first-time buyer. That is limited evidence. The session's 200-call WebSearch budget was already spent. I fell back on Google News RSS, the Hacker News API, the Federal Register API and direct fetches, and could not reach Crunchbase, Product Hunt, Reddit, Searchfunder or BizBuySell.

What looks unserved:
1. A vertical diligence and financing pack for sub-$5M scrap and recycling yards. It would cover Phase I/II and fire-history checks, insurance, permit transferability and offtake contracts. Horizontal ETA programs leave that to each buyer. Fire and insurance risk is live: EMR's Camden yard was shut after 15 fires in six years (NJ PEN, 29 May 2026), Resource Recycling wrote 'Battery fire risk isn't going away. Insurance is responding' (24 Feb 2026), and a 9,000-car Idaho salvage yard burned (Yahoo, 19 Jun 2026).
2. A succession desk for owner-run yards. Nothing I found targets ReMA-type family operators with a packaged successor, and the big consolidators only want larger yards.
3. A permit-and-owner-age target list. Nothing I found offers one for scrap dealers.

The premise needs two corrections:
- The BIS rule is real. It is a temporary final rule, published 6 Aug 2026 and effective 27 Aug 2026. However, it covers only black mass and tungsten waste and scrap, not ordinary ferrous or nonferrous yards (Federal Register 2026-16078). The 'domestic scrap re-rating' story is much narrower than the pitch implies.
- The idea leans on 'laid-off managers with $100-300K'. That is a crowded buyer-education market, with Codie Sanchez, Kingsway and the universities all courting the same buyers. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Cyclic Materials, HyProMag USA (CoTec / Mkango JV), ERI (Electronics Recyclers International), Noveon Magnetics. White space: Evidence caveat: the session's WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted, so I ran zero successful web searches and relied on direct page fetches of about 20 company and source URLs. Several were 404, 503 or blocked. Coverage of forums, RFPs, Crunchbase, Product Hunt and open-source tools is therefore missing. Treat this as a partial check, not a clean bill of health.\n\nWhat remains unserved, judged from the company pages I could read:\n(1) A yard-facing price and identification product. No fetched page (Cyclic, HyProMag, ReElement, Ionic, Noveon) publishes a payout by motor make and model, a magnet-mass lookup, or a handheld gauss-meter workflow for yard staff. Cyclic's supplier page explicitly gives no pricing, logistics or ID tools ('contact us to get started').\n(2) The long tail of small and mid-size auto shredders, motor rebuilders, elevator and industrial motor shops, and e-bike hub-motor scrap. ERI is anchored on e-waste and the OEM/ITAD channel, and Cyclic's named categories are drive motors, HDDs, robotics, defense and wind. Elevator, servo and e-bike hub motors are not named.\n(3) Chain-of-custody and assay data for defense-traceable lots.\n\nWhere the idea is weak: the buyers are building their own procurement. Cyclic takes whole units without dismantling, so the 'mobile pull cell' adds little. Cyclic and HyProMag have stated supply pipelines and can capture the aggregator margin by paying yards directly once yards know what they hold. The spread-based aggregator model is exposed to that squeeze. The durable wedge is the data and identification layer.

title: Auto Add-On Refund Cascade: Payoff and Return Desk
one_liner: One refund engine for auto add-ons (GAP and service contracts) with two triggers, California's new 3-day return for dealers and the loan payoff for credit unions, sold through the lender who touches both.
customer: California credit unions and regional auto lenders (payoff and indirect-lending departments), who pay for payoff recovery and can introduce their dealer networks. California independent and buy-here-pay-here used-car dealers selling 30-200 cars a month, who pay per return. Later, MGAs and insurers buying return-risk data.
problem: Dealers with no back office must unwind a returned car (lender, add-on administrators, DMV, sales-tax reversal, commissions) inside a very short refund deadline, and fragmented dealers are expensive to reach. Credit unions leave unearned GAP and service-contract refunds unclaimed at payoff because consumer refund sites wait for borrowers to show up. Both jobs depend on knowing what roughly 60 administrators actually require and how fast they pay.
solution: A shared cancellation-cascade engine: administrator playbook and response-time data, a 50-state pro-rata rule set, and generated cancellation packets tracked to payment. Trigger A (dealers): forward the cancellation notice and the desk notifies the lender, submits administrator cancellations, prepares DMV and tax reversals, calculates refund and permitted deductions, and stores the compliance file, at $195-250 per return or a $99 per month standby plan. Trigger B (lenders): free retrospective audit of 500 past payoffs, then $3-6 per payoff or 20-30% of recovered refunds. Pitch the credit union as the channel: 'Your dealers' returns start hitting your payoff desk October 1. We give your dealer network a standby unwind plan, and your members automatic refunds.'
why_now: California's SB 766 takes effect Oct 1, 2026, two days from today, so the first returns arrive within days. No US state has run a mandatory used-car return at this scale. Roughly 3M repossessions a year, 84-month loans and about 30% of trade-ins underwater mean many loans die early with stacked add-ons, and buyers who suddenly cannot afford the payment are the likeliest to return. LLMs can now read messy contract images cheaply.
revenue_model: Per-return fee of $195-250 and $99 per month per-store standby retainer. Credit union payoff fee of $3-6 per payoff or 20-30% of recovered money. Attorney deficiency audits at $99 each. Phase 2: 10-20% of premium as MGA on a $60-120 per used unit return-risk cover. Phase 3: license the cascade workflow to dealer management systems and eContract vendors, and sell administrator refund-speed benchmarks.
non_obvious_insight: These are one business with two triggers. Every California return teaches the desk how each administrator behaves (what they demand, how fast they pay), which makes payoff-refund collections faster and more predictable, and every payoff audit produces the dollar totals that open lender doors. The credit union's indirect dealer network is the only cheap channel to hundreds of small dealers, and the lender is motivated because a dealer's botched unwind becomes the lender's compliance and funding headache. Return and payoff data together also price the return-risk insurance nobody can price today.
first_30_days: Write the cascade checklist for the 20 most common California indirect lenders and 15 administrators. Approach the California Independent Automobile Dealers Association and 10 high-volume independents with the $99 standby plan and a 24-hour turnaround promise. Pitch 3 California credit unions with indirect programs on a free 500-payoff retro audit plus a dealer-network standby offer. Handle the first 20 returns manually with a spreadsheet and e-sign, and log the time and dollar cost of every step.
lineage: hybrid of I0109 + I1151 (Payoff-Triggered Refund Recovery for Credit Unions + Unwind Desk for California's 3-Day Car Return). Why stronger: The lender relationship solves the return desk's distribution problem, and the return desk hands the payoff product a must-have, time-boxed reason to get a meeting. One administrator database serves both, so unit cost falls with volume and collection speed improves. The combined dataset is what makes the return-risk MGA product priceable, which neither parent can reach alone.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Origence (formerly CU Direct) - loan origination/indirect platform (CUDL), Assurant (F&I administrator and TPA), Unverified: consumer GAP/VSC refund-claim services (contingency), Unverified: in-house lender recovery and collections teams and BPO vendors. White space: Verification was limited. The WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted before I could run any queries, and only about 15 direct URL fetches were possible, many of which 404'd or were blocked. That leaves three points.

1. I found no direct competitor selling a payoff-triggered GAP/VSC refund plug-in to credit unions. Origence, the dominant CU indirect-lending platform, and Assurant, a major administrator, show no such product on their homepages.

2. Genuinely unserved and specific, if the market read holds:
   - A per-payoff, lender-integrated refund workflow for dealer-sold, financed add-ons at credit unions.
   - A 50-state pro-rata rules engine combined with an administrator-by-administrator cancellation-requirements database.
   - An attorney-ready audit of repossession deficiency notices that reconciles unearned add-on credits. Consumer-bankruptcy and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid are plausible buyers, because the lender's or dealer's incentive runs against the borrower.

3. Weaknesses in the idea as written, from reasoning rather than found evidence:
   - The claim that the lender never owned the product is shaky. Under many state retail installment sales acts, and under the FTC Holder Rule, the assignee or holder can carry refund and credit obligations. That helps demand, as a compliance and UDAAP driver, but it changes the pitch from 'find hidden money' to 'reduce liability'.
   - A 20-30% success fee taken from a member's own refund has poor fee optics for a credit union. It also conflicts with the idea's own member-experience rationale.
   - On payoff, the refund goes to the borrower, so the CU gets no direct economic benefit. The CU's incentive is goodwill and compliance, not revenue.
   - CU vendor due diligence and core/LOS integration will make the sales cycle slow.
   - The California SB 766 citation in the idea did not check out. The leginfo summary I fetched for the 2023-24 bill described an unrelated social-worker licensing bill. Do not rely on that cite until it is confirmed. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ComplyAuto (exclusively licensed by CNCDA), CDK Global (DMS), CNCDA (California New Car Dealers Association), DealerCenter (DMS for independent dealers). White space: Research limitation: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200), so no searches were run. That means no Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or forum searches, and no search for startups by name. Everything below comes from direct WebFetch of about 30 primary and vendor URLs, with model-generated page summaries. I found NO dedicated 'unwind-as-a-service' for CARS Act cancellations, but I cannot rule out a small startup. Re-run the startup and forum searches before committing.

The idea's premise is weaker than written. Statute text (SB 766, Civ. Code 1784.43, 1784.31(g), 1784.44, as returned by WebFetch and quoted verbatim by the summarizer):
1. The 48-hour duty is only to cancel the contract and refund the buyer. The dealer 'is not responsible for any delays outside the control of the dealer, including delays attributable to the processing of a refund by a bank, credit card company, or other financial institution.' Check payments get a 2-business-day delay. Lender and administrator lag therefore does not create violation exposure. The exposure is the dealer's cash float and its own process failures.
2. The statute lists no duty to cancel service contracts or GAP within 48 hours. The add-on cascade is a business and recovery problem, governed by existing law and contract terms. It is not a statutory deadline.
3. Permitted deductions are formulaic: a restocking fee of 1.5% of price (min $200, max $600), plus $1 per mile over 250 (capped at $150), plus trade-in liens. They are not damage-based. The claim that permitted deductions depend on condition documentation, which justifies the photo and video capture bundle, does not hold up. What does matter is the 400-mile eligibility gate and the trade-in refund rule. If the trade-in is already sold or in title transfer, the refund is the greater of the agreed value, the sale price, or fair market value.
4. Remedies are non-exclusive (1784.22). No explicit private right of action or civil penalty was found. Enforcement runs through DAs, city attorneys and the DMV, plus existing consumer laws.
5. Dealers already run unwinds. California had a 2-day contract cancellation option with a 2-day refund including sales tax (Veh. Code 11713.21), repealed effective Oct 1, 2026. Failed-financing spot-delivery unwinds are also routine (from my background knowledge, not verified here). Buy-here-pay-here lots hold their own paper, so they have no lender cascade at all. The $195 to $250 per-return price competes with a title clerk or F&I manager plus a DMS 'reverse deal' function.

What remains unserved:
(a) Independent, indirect-financed dealers with no back-office bench. Compliance vendors and associations found are aimed at franchised dealers or at pricing, ad and disclosure compliance.
(b) A per-return calculator and checklist: restocking fee, mileage, the trade-in 'greater of three' refund, lender payoff, F&I commission chargeback, and the administrator-by-administrator cancellation basis, with timers and a 2-year compliance file.
(c) Above all, the dealer's economic loss per return. Dealers lost the fee they could charge for the old cancellation option ($75 to $250 or 1%). Restocking is now capped at $200 to $600, against recon, carrying cost and resale loss. Nobody was found pricing or covering that loss.

title: Special-Ed Parent Tracker Feeding Host-School Programs
one_liner: A $20-a-month IEP chief of staff for Texas parents whose service-minute logs identify the families and districts where a clinician-led, voucher-funded host-school program is the real solution.
customer: Texas parents of children with IEPs, reached through special-ed parent groups and pediatric practices, some holding Texas Education Freedom Account (TEFA) funds of about $10K, up to about $30K for IEP students at accredited private schools. Partner: small accredited private schools with empty classrooms. Supply: speech-language pathologists, BCBAs and dyslexia therapists.
problem: The parent tracker has a low-ARPU, high-CAC consumer business at $20 per month. The host-school program has a high-value payer but no cheap way to find qualified families or to decide where to site a cohort. Parents with documented missed services and a stalled district are stuck, and the money that could fix it is locked behind accreditation and a two-year operating history that they do not have.
solution: Parents upload the IEP and get a legal clock, a service-minute log, records requests and meeting briefs (independent advocates on demand at $75 per 30 minutes). When the log shows sustained missed minutes, the parent sees a clearly labeled 'Plan B' in the app: apply their TEFA funds at a clinician-led program running inside a partner accredited school, where the school is school of record and the operating company supplies the clinical director, staff, curriculum, IEP-style compliance, testing and ESA billing. Firewall: advocate income is flat-fee and never tied to placement, and parents get the compensatory-services claim documented before they leave. First sellable products: the Texas parent subscription plus a January 2027 pilot cohort of 8-10 students at one host school.
why_now: TEFA's first year is underway (2026-27) with $1B in funding and 130,000+ applications in the first three weeks. Texas public schools lost about 76,000 students and are closing campuses. Federal special-ed enforcement was hollowed out (OSEP layoffs in Oct 2025, with the office reportedly moving to HHS in June 2026), so parents are actively looking for alternatives and an organized paper trail.
revenue_model: Parent subscriptions at $20 per month, advocate sessions at $75 with a revenue split to a vetted co-op, and per-member fees from parent centers and pediatric groups. Host-program management fee of about 20-25% of ESA revenue per student (about $6-7.5K per $30K student, $60-75K per 10-student program per year), a 15-20% host-school share, plus a $3-5K design fee per host.
non_obvious_insight: A parent's service-minute log is both a legal claim and a qualified lead: it documents exactly who is failing, in which district, for which disability. Aggregated (with consent), the logs form a district-level heat map that tells the operating company where to place the next host program, because demand is proven in the data. One placed student is worth about 25 years of a $20 subscription in a single year, which pays for the tracker's whole acquisition cost, while the tracker's advocate-first brand makes the placement offer credible rather than salesy.
first_30_days: Publish a free Texas IEP clock calculator and letter templates. With admins of 10 state-level special-ed groups, concierge 30 families and measure violations found. List about 150 small accredited private schools in DFW, Houston, San Antonio and Austin and send heads of school a one-page economics sheet. Recruit 10 clinicians. Sign 1-2 pilot hosts for a January 2027 cohort and collect pre-enrollment interest from the 30 concierge families and TEFA parent groups.
lineage: hybrid of I0289 + I1032 (IEP Chief of Staff for Special-Ed Parents + AltSchool Without Buildings: Disability Programs in Host Schools). Why stronger: The tracker's CAC is subsidized by a payer worth an order of magnitude more per family, and the host program gets pre-qualified, motivated, documented leads instead of buying ads. Shared data tells the business where to open programs. Together it is a full lifecycle (enforce, then exit if enforcement fails) that a competitor with only one half cannot offer.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: IEP Advocate.ai, ChatGPT and general LLMs (endorsed by CADRE's parent guide), Parent Training and Information Centers (PTIs/CPRCs), Wrightslaw. White space: Confidence is moderate-low. The WebSearch budget hit 200/200 before I could run the planned 6-12 searches, so I found competitors mostly by fetching guessed and known URLs. More direct competitors probably exist that I did not see, and this should be re-run once the search limit is raised.

The core pitch is NOT white space. Deadline extraction, procedural letter generation, meeting prep briefs and state-complaint drafting are already live at IEP Advocate.ai for $30/mo. Free ChatGPT covers much of the rest. A $20/mo 'AI IEP chief of staff' would be a cheaper copy.

Specific gaps I could not find served in the pages I reached:
1. A service-delivery ledger. This means logging minutes promised vs delivered per IEP service line and turning the shortfall into a compensatory-services claim packet. IEP Advocate.ai's fetched pages do not describe service-minute logging or comp-ed calculation.
2. Human-in-the-loop verification. CADRE and K-12 Dive document AI-drafted complaints with fabricated case law and wrong IDEA readings. A product that combines grounded output with vetted advocate or attorney review, at $75 per 30 minutes, is unserved. IEP Advocate.ai has no human tier.
3. B2B2C distribution through parent centers, disability law clinics, pediatric practices and credit unions at $3-6 per member per month. IEP Advocate.ai lists only individual pricing. The channel is unproven.
4. Evidence-grade record keeping. Time-stamped, tamper-evident logs that a hearing officer will accept, rather than chat history. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Fusion Academy (Nord Anglia), Brightmont Academy, Prenda (microschool platform), KaiPod Learning. White space: Research caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before any searches ran, so this verdict rests on about 30 direct page fetches, not the planned 6-12 searches. Google-style discovery of funded startups was not possible, and the negative finding below is unproven. Crunchbase (403), the Comptroller TEFA program pages (404), TEPSAC (503) and several news sites failed.

What the fetches found: no direct competitor was located that runs clinician-led disability programs inside host accredited private schools as the school-of-record structure and bills against TEFA. Adjacent players cover each piece separately.
- Learning-differences schools that build their own campuses: Fusion, Brightmont, Rawson Saunders, Fairhill.
- Microschool platforms: Prenda, KaiPod, Primer.
- Clinician marketplaces: Presence.
- Outside operators embedded in private schools: Catapult.

The unserved wedge is the three-way structure itself. It is a management company that supplies the clinical director, staff, IEP compliance, norm-referenced testing and ESA reconciliation inside a host school. It targets IEP families holding up to $30k accounts in metro Texas in the first TEFA year.

Three risks decide whether the white space is real, and none is resolved:
1. **Legality and accreditor acceptance.** Statute text says a private school must be accredited by a TEPSAC-recognized organization and have continuously operated a campus for at least two school years. It does not address programs within a school or microschools. If the Comptroller, TEA or the accreditor treats a hosted program as a separate campus, or as renting accreditation, the model fails. A 100% pass-through of the ESA to the host with a 20-25% management fee could also draw scrutiny.
2. **Incumbents and hosts.** Existing specialist schools already have eligibility and expertise and may simply expand. Host schools take on IEP compliance liability and reputational risk.
3. **Unit economics.** A 10-student cohort at 20-25% yields $60-75k a year, before clinician cost. Whether that covers a BCBA or dyslexia therapist plus a clinical director was not tested.

title: One Binder Scan: Lender Monitoring Plus Warranty Recovery
one_liner: One AI read of a data hall's closeout binders yields both a lender's ready-for-service probability and an owner's serial-level warranty ledger, with contingency warranty recovery as the reason the owner grants access.
customer: Private credit funds, banks and insurers lending against GPUs and neocloud contracts (pay a fixed monitoring fee). Colo developers, powered-shell landlords and neocloud owners with energized but idle halls (pay a share of recovered warranty value).
problem: Lenders need interior truth about the last 90 days before ready-for-service but borrowers resist giving data-room access to a monitor. Owners of energized-but-empty halls don't know their OEM warranty clocks are silently running out. Both parties need the same documents (gear serials, startup sheets, Cx reports, integrated test results, punch lists) and neither has staff to read them.
solution: An LLM pipeline ingests POs, bills of lading, startup sheets, Cx sign-offs and maintenance logs into one serial-level ledger. Lender view: a Readiness Ladder score with probability of ready-for-service by date, covenant and draw triggers, and OEM startup-tech calendar risk. Owner view: warranty expiry dates, voiding conditions, and a hit list of claims and start-date deferrals to file within 90-120 days. Sold as a $25K two-week lender second opinion, made economical by a contingency warranty scan (25-30% of recoveries) offered free to the owner. Structure the two views as separate teams with an information wall, and route recoveries through the lender-controlled operating account so the independence of the monitor is not compromised.
why_now: About half of 2026 US capacity is slipping and neocloud credit is a live worry, so lenders are capping exposure. Many halls are powered, commissioned and idle. Equipment was bought at peak, tariff-inflated prices, so each lapsed warranty is worth more. Satellites have commoditized the exterior, leaving the interior (binders and commissioning data) as the scarce truth. LLMs now read messy closeout binders cheaply.
revenue_model: Lender side: $25K two-week second opinions, $40-120K full pre-close diligence, $8-20K per month per facility monitoring. Owner side: 25-30% of recovered value or avoided cost on claims and deferrals, $150-400 per asset per year tracking, $15-40K closeout audits, and PO-stage clause packs that defer warranty start to beneficial occupancy.
non_obvious_insight: The warranty ledger and the readiness score are built from the same binder, so the second product costs almost nothing to produce. The biggest barrier to interior monitoring is borrower cooperation, and a free contingency service that recovers money is the best incentive to provide it. Expiring warranties and unavailable OEM startup techs are also leading indicators of delay, so each product improves the other's signal. The lender's covenant becomes the distribution channel to owners at the moment they have binders and idle halls. Ethyco offers warranty-phase support but not idle-hall contingency or lender integration.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 retired or between-jobs Cx leads and PMs on 1099 contracts. Find 3 owner-operators through Cx and PM networks whose halls energized 8-11 months ago and are not fully loaded, and offer a free 10-day binder scan on contingency. Build the extraction on real binders (gensets, UPS and chillers first) and deliver an 'expiring in 90 days' hit list. Publish a free 'RFS credibility checklist' and pitch 5-10 private credit desks a $25K two-week second opinion on one live deal, using the scan as proof of depth.
lineage: hybrid of I0365 + I0229 (Ground-Truth Diligence for GPU-Backed Lenders + Warranty Clock Recovery Audits for Idle Halls). Why stronger: Double revenue from one document-processing pipeline, with two payers whose interests line up. Owners get paid to be monitored, lenders get better collateral and cleaner data, and access friction disappears. A serial-number equipment register across financed halls becomes a data moat that single-purpose competitors (satellite monitors or Cx firms) cannot replicate.
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SynMax Vulcan (with Industrial Info Resources data partnership), Currence (formerly Sightline Climate), Epoch AI Frontier Data Centers Hub, SemiAnalysis (consulting, AI Datacenter Model, ClusterMAX). White space: The unserved wedge is narrow but real. (1) No product found in this session combines a binary, evidence-backed 'Readiness Ladder' for the last 90 days before RFS (utility energization letter, MV gear energization, Cx Level 4/5 and IST pass/fail counts, CDU flush and pressure tests, fiber acceptance, punch-list burn-down, OEM startup-tech availability) with a probabilistic RFS-by-date output and draw or covenant triggers. (2) Satellite and database vendors (SynMax, IIR, Currence, Epoch) cover the exterior and the announced schedule, and their materials do not claim commissioning or energization evidence. (3) GPU-deal technical advisors, as described by Peony, focus on fleet, telemetry and power documents rather than data hall commissioning. (4) Traditional IEs are slow, tied to a single lender or borrower, and priced for large project-finance deals. A fixed-fee, two-week, desk-plus-site 'second opinion' for a private credit desk, insurer or offtaker appears unserved. (5) The offtaker and backstop side (AI labs signing take-or-pay capacity, Google or Nvidia-style backstop providers) is structurally underserved because IEs work for lenders. Risks: incumbent IEs and Cx firms can add this as a service line, SemiAnalysis could bolt it on, and the business is people-bound (bench of ex-Cx leads) with limited software moat. Access to sites, contractors and Cx records depends on borrower cooperation, which means lender-imposed information covenants or offtaker leverage. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ethyco (data center commissioning, warranty-phase support), Anyset AI (agentic closeout / warranty tracking), Nomic (AEC document AI, closeout), Trane delayed start-up warranty (OEM rider). White space: Nobody I found combines all of these for data center MEP: (1) a serial-number-level clock ledger built for idle or deferred-start halls, (2) a pre-expiry loaded stress test using the idle capacity, (3) OEM claim filing and start-date deferral negotiation, and (4) success-fee or fixed-fee pricing sold to the owner or its lender. The pieces exist separately. Anyset and Nomic do doc extraction. Ethyco-style Cx firms do a 10-month warranty review. Wind and solar have end-of-warranty inspection and claims firms. OEMs sell delayed-start riders. Load-bank vendors have the hardware. Data center power and cooling MEP has no dedicated end-of-warranty claims specialist that I could find. Three structural weaknesses limit the wedge. (a) The clocks mostly start at OEM startup, and startup plus IST with load banks already loads equipment in Cx, so the 'idle for 12+ months' exposure is narrower than the pitch implies. It mainly hits gear started early or shipped more than 18 months before use. (b) 'Recovered value' is really avoided repair cost. It is hard to measure and easy for OEMs to dispute, and OEMs can deny on storage or light-load grounds (wet stacking is explicitly excluded, https://cliffordpower.com/wet-stacking-why-its-important-to-load-bank-your-diesel-generator/). A pure 25-30% contingency model will be hard to collect. (c) Documents are the commodity step, so the moat has to be inspection plus OEM leverage, not the LLM pipeline.
